title: Lane dispute on a spiral roundabout
type: Roundabout collision
story: Policyholder reported a collision on a two-lane spiral roundabout off the A4 in Reading at about 17:40 on a wet November evening. Her Kia Ceed and a Ford Transit Custom made contact as both left at the third exit. Each driver says the other cut across their lane. Nobody was hurt.
statement: I was in the left lane the whole way round because I was taking the third exit, and that's what the arrows tell you to do. As I went to come off, the van came from the right-hand lane and squeezed across in front of me. I braked but couldn't stop in time and my front right corner went into the side of his van. He got out shouting that I'd changed lanes, which I hadn't. My dashcam was recording, so I've sent you the clip.

accounts.who: Other driver, Gary Holt (Ford Transit Custom)
accounts.text: I was in the left-hand lane going round to the third exit. The Kia was on my right and drifted into me just as we came off, probably because she'd gone too far round in the inside lane. The spiral markings send the right-hand lane off at the third exit as well, so she should have stayed where she was. The damage to my van is on the passenger side, by the sliding door.

whatHappened: Most likely the van was in the right-hand lane and crossed into the left lane at the exit. The damage pattern (the Kia's front right corner against the van's nearside sliding door) fits the claimant's version, because it puts the Kia on the van's left. The full dashcam clip should settle it.
damage: Kia Ceed: front right bumper corner, headlamp and wing. Ford Transit Custom: scrape and dent along the nearside sliding door.
thirdParties: Gary Holt, driver of the Ford Transit Custom (company van insured on a fleet policy)
evidence: Front dashcam clip from the Kia, 1 minute 20 seconds, timestamped 17:38
Photos of both vehicles taken at the scene by the claimant
Recent street imagery of the roundabout showing the lane arrows on each approach
Van driver's name, phone number and his employer's fleet insurer
missing: The van's telematics or camera footage, if the fleet has them
An independent witness
Engineer inspection of both vehicles to confirm the impact angles
inconsistencies: Both drivers say they were in the left-hand lane
The van driver says the Kia was on his right, but the van's damage is on its nearside (left), which fits the Kia being on his left
Each driver reads the spiral lane markings differently
innocent: Drivers often misjudge which lane serves which exit on spiral roundabouts, so both may honestly believe they were right
Lane arrows are hard to see on a wet road at dusk
questions: Ask the claimant for the full, unedited dashcam file, including the minute before she entered the roundabout
Ask the fleet insurer whether the van has telematics or a camera, and for the data from 17:30 to 17:45
Ask Mr Holt where on the roundabout he first saw the Kia, and where it was relative to his van
steps: Review the dashcam clip frame by frame at the exit
Request the fleet's telematics and any van camera footage
Compare the impact points on both vehicles with each driver's version
Check the lane markings against the approach the claimant used
assessment: A genuine collision with a liability dispute. The damage pattern supports the claimant: a van moving across from her right would strike her front right corner with its nearside, which is what the photos show. The van driver's own description of his damage contradicts his account. If the dashcam shows the van crossing the lane line, liability should fall on the van. Nothing suggests dishonesty on either side.
action: Treat as a liability dispute. Secure the dashcam and the van's telematics, hold the third-party insurer liable, and pay the own-damage claim meanwhile so the outlay can be recovered later.
outcomes: Third-party insurer accepts liability after viewing the dashcam; outlay recovered and the claimant's no-claims discount restored
Footage inconclusive; liability split 50/50, as often happens in unresolved roundabout disputes
Van telematics shows the van held its lane; liability falls on the claimant

title: Fog concertina on the M25
type: Multi-vehicle shunt in fog
story: Policyholder was one of five vehicles in a concertina collision on the M25 anticlockwise between junctions 10 and 11 at 07:15 in dense fog. His Skoda Octavia was hit from behind and pushed into the car in front. Surrey Police attended and closed lane 1 for 40 minutes. He mentioned a sore neck but did not go to hospital.
statement: Visibility was maybe 50 metres. Traffic ahead suddenly stopped and I managed to stop, just, with a bit of room to spare. Then a lorry or a van hit me hard from behind and shoved me into the Honda in front. I'm sure I'd stopped before I was hit, because I remember breathing out. My back end is smashed and the front is damaged too. The police took everyone's details.

accounts.who: Driver in front, Helen Marsh (Honda Jazz)
accounts.text: I had stopped behind the queue when I felt two bumps from behind, very close together. The first one was light, more of a nudge. The second was much harder and pushed me forward. I didn't see what happened behind me.

accounts.who: Police incident log extract, Surrey Police
accounts.text: 07:16 report of multi-vehicle collision M25 anticlockwise J10 to J11, lane 1, dense fog. 07:31 officers on scene, five vehicles involved. Vehicle 3 (Skoda Octavia) shunted into vehicle 2 (Honda Jazz) by vehicle 4 (DAF LF box van), which was struck by vehicle 5. No serious injuries reported.

whatHappened: The Skoda probably nudged the Honda while braking hard, then was pushed into it again by the van. The rear damage is clearly the van's responsibility; part of the front damage may be the claimant's own.
damage: Rear bumper, boot lid, rear panel and both lamps; front bumper, bonnet edge and radiator support. Estimate £7,900, possibly uneconomic to repair.
thirdParties: Driver of the DAF LF box van (vehicle 4), commercially insured
Helen Marsh, driver of the Honda Jazz (vehicle 2)
Driver of vehicle 5, which struck the van
evidence: Surrey Police incident log listing the order of the vehicles
Photos of the Skoda at the recovery yard
Statement from the Honda driver describing two impacts
Repair estimate from the approved repairer
missing: Statements from the van driver and the driver of vehicle 5
Dashcam footage from vehicles 4 or 5
Crash data from the Skoda's airbag control module
Medical evidence if the neck pain continues
inconsistencies: The claimant is sure he had stopped before he was hit, but the Honda driver felt a light bump first and then a harder one
innocent: A light first bump could come from the Skoda creeping forward under hard braking, which a shaken driver may not notice
The two impacts could also both have come from the van hitting twice
questions: Ask the claimant whether his car moved forward at all after he stopped and before the hard impact
Ask the van's insurer for their driver's account and any dashcam footage
Ask Ms Marsh roughly how much time passed between the two bumps
steps: Obtain the van driver's version through the third-party insurer
Download the Skoda's airbag module data if the car becomes a total loss
Apportion the front damage once the sequence of impacts is clearer
Watch for a later injury claim and handle it on medical evidence
assessment: A genuine motorway pile-up. The rear damage is the van's responsibility. The Honda driver's two-bump description suggests the claimant may have lightly touched her car before being pushed, so the front damage may partly be his own. That is a liability question, not a question of honesty.
action: Accept the claim, treat the car as a likely total loss, and recover from the van's insurer. Negotiate a split on the front damage if the sequence evidence supports a first light impact.
outcomes: Van's insurer accepts full liability for both impacts
Rear damage recovered in full and front damage shared
Total loss settlement at market value, salvage retained

title: Uninsured van merges on the A34
type: Blind-spot merge by an uninsured driver
story: Policyholder reported that a white Vauxhall Vivaro moved from lane 1 into her Toyota Yaris in lane 2 on the A34 dual carriageway near Didcot at 13:20. The van driver stopped in a lay-by, gave a first name and a phone number, then drove off. A Motor Insurance Database check returned no policy for the van's registration.
statement: I was overtaking the van in the right-hand lane at about 65. It just started coming across, like he hadn't looked. He hit my passenger side and I nearly ended up in the central barrier. We pulled into a lay-by and he said his name was Daniel and gave me a number, then he said he had to go and drove off before I could take a picture of his licence. I got his number plate. The number he gave me doesn't work.

accounts.who: Telematics report, black box fitted to the Yaris
accounts.text: 13:19:48 speed 64 mph. 13:19:51 lateral jolt of 0.41 g to the right, speed 61 mph. 13:19:53 harsh braking event, speed falling to 38 mph. 13:21:10 vehicle stationary at a location matching the northbound lay-by.

whatHappened: An uninsured van driver changed lanes without looking, then gave false contact details; the telematics and the database checks bear out the policyholder's account.
damage: Nearside front door, rear door and wing mirror of the Toyota Yaris; nearside front tyre scuffed. Estimate £2,350.
thirdParties: Van driver who gave the name 'Daniel'
Registered keeper of the Vauxhall Vivaro, not yet identified
evidence: Van registration number noted by the claimant
askMID result showing no insurance on the van on the date
Telematics showing a sideways jolt and harsh braking at 13:19
Photos of the damage taken in the lay-by
missing: Registered keeper details from the DVLA
Dashcam footage from other traffic
A police report (not yet made)
innocent: The van driver may have believed he was insured, for example if his policy lapsed on a failed payment
questions: Ask the claimant to report the collision to the police, since the other driver did not give valid details
Ask the DVLA for the registered keeper of the van
Ask the claimant whether the van had any company name, ladder rack or other markings
steps: Report to the police for failing to give details and driving without insurance
Request the registered keeper from the DVLA
Notify the Motor Insurers' Bureau under the Uninsured Drivers Agreement
Apply the policy's uninsured driver promise to protect the no-claims discount
assessment: Genuine. The telematics jolt, the nearside damage and the immediate askMID result all fit the claimant's account. The difficulty here is recovery, not credibility.
action: Pay the claim, apply the uninsured driver promise so the claimant keeps her no-claims discount and pays no excess, and pursue the van driver through the police and the MIB.
outcomes: Driver traced; the MIB handles the uninsured claim and the outlay is recovered
Driver never identified; claim stays open on the policy with no recovery
Police prosecute the van driver for driving without insurance

title: Scraped in the supermarket car park
type: Car park hit-and-run
story: Policyholder came back to her Ford Fiesta after 25 minutes in a large supermarket in Leicester and found the rear bumper and quarter panel scraped. No note was left. She reported the claim 33 days later, after getting a quote from a local body shop.
statement: I came out with my shopping and the back corner was all scuffed and dented, with blue paint in it. I didn't think it was worth claiming at first, I was going to pay for it myself, but the garage wants £1,140. I asked the shop about their cameras but they said I was too late. I don't want to lose my no-claims.
whatHappened: Genuine car park damage by an unknown driver. The delay is ordinary: she hoped to pay for it herself.
damage: Rear bumper scuffed with blue paint transfer and a dent in the rear nearside quarter panel. Estimate £1,140.
thirdParties: Unknown driver of a blue vehicle
evidence: Photos taken by the claimant in the car park, with file dates matching the shopping trip
Supermarket receipt showing her in the store from 10:52 to 11:17
Email from the store saying CCTV is kept for 28 days
missing: CCTV footage (already overwritten)
Witnesses
Any report of the damage to the store on the day
indicators: Claim reported more than a month after the damage
innocent: People often try to pay for small damage themselves and only claim when the quote is higher than expected
Same-day photos and a timed receipt make the account credible
questions: Ask the claimant for the original photo files so the dates can be checked
Ask the claimant whether she told anyone at the store on the day
Ask whether the car has had any other damage since she bought it
steps: Check the photo metadata against the receipt time
Explain the excess and the effect on the no-claims discount before she decides
Offer a repair through an approved repairer
assessment: Low risk and genuine. The late report is explained, and the photos and receipt line up. With no traceable third party it would be a fault claim, so the main job is helping the customer decide whether claiming is worth it.
action: Explain the £250 excess and the effect on the discount, let the customer decide, and if she goes ahead pay it as an own-damage claim.
outcomes: Customer withdraws and pays privately to protect her discount
Claim paid less the excess and recorded as a fault claim with no recovery

title: Red deer at dusk on the A9
type: Animal collision
story: Policyholder reported hitting a red deer on the A9 north of Pitlochry at about 18:30 in October. The deer ran into the trees. He reported the claim nine days later, after a fishing holiday, and the Volvo XC60 had been driven about 300 miles since.
statement: It leapt out from the left. I braked but caught it full on with the front. By the time I'd stopped and walked back it had gone into the woods, so I didn't call anyone. The car was driveable so I carried on to the lodge and used it for the rest of the week. I know I should have called sooner.
whatHappened: A genuine deer strike. Drivers in Great Britain do not have to report a deer collision to the police, though it is advised, so not calling anyone is unremarkable.
damage: Front bumper cracked, grille broken, nearside headlamp smashed and bonnet dented, with brown hair caught in the grille. Estimate £3,600 including sensor recalibration.
evidence: Photos showing hair and blood traces in the grille
Lodge booking near Pitlochry for that week
Fuel receipt from Pitlochry timed 18:52 the same evening
missing: Any police or council report
Photos at the scene
Dashcam footage
indicators: Reported nine days after the event
Car driven about 300 miles after the damage
innocent: He was on holiday and the car was still driveable
The hair in the grille and the fuel receipt place him near the spot that evening
questions: Ask the claimant for the fuel receipt and any photos taken that evening
Ask whether any warning lights showed while he kept driving
Ask the repairer whether any damage was made worse by driving on, such as a leaking radiator
steps: Check the receipt and the booking against the route
Ask the repairer to separate collision damage from anything caused by continued use
Settle as an own-damage claim
assessment: Genuine and low risk. The delay and the continued use are explained by the holiday, and the physical traces support an animal strike. Damage made worse by driving on should be checked but is unlikely to be large.
action: Pay the claim under comprehensive cover once the repairer confirms nothing was made worse by continued use.
outcomes: Paid in full less the excess
Paid with a small deduction for damage worsened by driving on

title: Seventeen, three weeks, one bollard
type: New driver hits a bollard
story: Policyholder, 17, passed his test three weeks earlier and has a telematics (black box) policy. He reported clipping a steel bollard in a narrow residential street in Bristol at 22:40, damaging the front and the nearside wheel.
statement: I was going slowly because it's a really tight street with cars parked on both sides. A car came the other way with its full beams on and I moved over to let it past and didn't see the bollard. I was doing maybe 15. Nobody got hurt and I didn't hit anyone else's car.

accounts.who: Telematics report, black box fitted to the Corsa
accounts.text: 22:39:12 speed 31 mph, road speed limit 20 mph. 22:39:20 harsh braking from 29 mph to 12 mph. 22:39:21 impact event detected, 0.9 g. 22:41 vehicle stationary. No further driving recorded that night.

whatHappened: A genuine low-speed impact made worse by speed: the new driver was doing about 30 in a 20 zone and braked late when dazzled.
damage: Vauxhall Corsa: front bumper torn, nearside front wheel and tyre damaged, track rod bent. Estimate £1,480.
thirdParties: Bristol City Council, owner of the bollard (leaning but intact)
evidence: Photos of the car and the bollard
missing: The council's inspection of the bollard, in case it claims for it
inconsistencies: He says he was doing about 15 mph; the black box shows 31 mph eight seconds before the impact and 29 mph when he started braking
innocent: New drivers often underestimate their speed, and dazzle makes it worse
He may be remembering his speed at the moment of impact (about 12 mph) rather than before braking
questions: Ask the claimant what speed he was doing before he saw the oncoming car
Ask the council whether the bollard was damaged and whether it intends to claim
steps: Pay the own-damage claim
Check whether the council claims for the bollard
Log the speeding event under the telematics terms and offer the driver feedback
assessment: A genuine accident with negligence. The understated speed is a common new-driver error rather than dishonesty: he described the moment of impact. The black box makes the facts clear.
action: Settle as a fault claim, apply the telematics policy's speeding rules (a warning or a premium adjustment), and record the claim against the no-claims discount.
outcomes: Paid as a fault claim; no-claims discount reduced
Telematics provider issues a speeding warning

title: Opening the door on a cyclist
type: Car door struck a cyclist
story: Policyholder parked his Audi A3 on a busy street in Hackney, London and opened the driver's door into a passing cyclist at 08:10. She fell into the road, injuring her wrist and damaging her bike. A bus stopped behind her. Her solicitors have since sent a letter of claim.
statement: I checked my mirror before I opened the door, I always do. She came out of nowhere, she must have been going really fast and too close to the parked cars. I feel terrible she got hurt, I stayed with her until the ambulance came. My door is bent at the hinge now.

accounts.text: I was cycling to work at around 12 mph in the cycle lane, about a metre from the parked cars. The driver's door swung open right in front of me with no warning. I hit it and went over the handlebars into the road. I fractured my right wrist and my bike frame is cracked.

Forward-facing camera 08:09:58: cyclist travelling in the marked cycle lane. 08:10:01: driver's door of a parked grey Audi opens into the lane as the cyclist arrives. Cyclist falls to the right into the carriageway. Bus stops about 6 metres behind.

whatHappened: The driver opened his door without seeing the cyclist. The Highway Code says you must make sure you will not hit anyone when opening a door, and recommends opening it with the hand furthest from the door (the "Dutch reach") to make you look over your shoulder.
damage: Audi A3 driver's door bent at the hinge. Cyclist: fractured right wrist, cracked carbon bike frame valued at £1,900, torn clothing.
evidence: Cyclist's letter of claim with a hospital discharge note
missing: Medical report on the wrist injury
Bike replacement quote and proof of value
Statements from the bus driver or passengers
inconsistencies: The claimant says the cyclist came out of nowhere at speed; the bus camera shows her riding in the marked cycle lane when the door opened
innocent: A cyclist can sit in the door mirror blind spot, so checking the mirror alone may genuinely have missed her
questions: Ask the claimant whether he looked over his shoulder as well as in the mirror before opening the door
Ask the cyclist's solicitors for the medical report and proof of the bike's value
steps: Accept liability on the strength of the bus footage
Handle the injury claim under the standard pre-action process (cyclists fall outside the whiplash portal)
Pay for the bike on proof of value
Pay the door repair as own damage under the policyholder's cover
assessment: A genuine accident caused by the policyholder's negligence. The bus footage is clear and the Highway Code puts the duty on the person opening the door. His belief that the cyclist was going too fast is not supported by the footage.
action: Admit liability early to keep legal costs down, obtain medical evidence, and settle the injury and bike claims. Pay the policyholder's door damage under his comprehensive cover.
outcomes: Liability admitted; injury claim settled on the medical evidence
Bike and clothing paid on proof of value; the claim closes without court proceedings

title: Stone chip that spread overnight
type: Windscreen damage
story: Policyholder reported a stone chip thrown up by a lorry on the M6 near Stafford, which spread into a 30 cm crack two days later on a frosty morning. Her Ford Kuga has a lane-assist camera mounted on the windscreen.
statement: A lorry flicked up a stone and there was a little star-shaped chip, about the size of a 5p. I meant to book a repair, but on Thursday morning it had spread right across after I put the heater on full to defrost it. Now it's in my line of sight. The glass company says the camera needs calibrating as well.
whatHappened: A chip from the motorway spread into a crack when the glass was heated suddenly on a cold morning, which is a common way small chips fail.
damage: Windscreen cracked across the driver's side; the lane-assist camera needs recalibration after replacement. Quote £780 including calibration.
evidence: Photo of the original chip dated Monday
Photo of the crack dated Thursday
Glass specialist quote including camera calibration
missing: Nothing further is needed for a glass claim of this size
innocent: A small chip spreading into a long crack overnight is normal when the temperature drops sharply or the heater is turned up
questions: Ask the claimant whether she wants to use the insurer's glass partner, which avoids paying up front
steps: Book the replacement and camera calibration with the glass partner
Apply the windscreen excess
assessment: A straightforward genuine glass claim. The only notable cost is the camera calibration, which modern cars with driver-assistance systems need after a screen replacement.
action: Approve replacement with calibration through the glass partner. Windscreen claims usually do not affect the no-claims discount.
outcomes: Screen replaced and camera calibrated; windscreen excess applied

title: One pothole, two claims
type: Pothole damage
story: Policyholder hit a deep, water-filled pothole on an unlit B-road near Harrogate at night. Two nearside alloy wheels cracked and a tyre split. He mentioned he has also put in a claim with the council.
statement: The pothole was full of water so you couldn't see it. Bang, both wheels on the left side, and the tyre went. I had to get recovered. I've reported it to North Yorkshire Council because it's their road and they should pay, but they say it'll take months, so I'm claiming on my insurance as well to get the car sorted.
whatHappened: Genuine pothole damage. The council claim is legitimate, but the same loss can't be paid twice.
damage: Two nearside alloy wheels cracked, front tyre split, wheel alignment out. Estimate £960.
evidence: Photos of the pothole with a tape measure showing 11 cm depth
Copy of the claim submitted to the council
missing: The council's inspection records for that stretch of road
Whether the council has paid or offered anything
indicators: The same loss is being claimed from the council and the insurer at the same time
innocent: Many drivers do not realise claiming from both is a problem, and he disclosed the council claim himself
questions: Ask the claimant whether the council has paid or offered anything yet
Ask whether he will withdraw his council claim, or pass any council payment to the insurer, if the insurer pays
steps: Pay the claim and take over the recovery from the council
Tell the claimant in writing not to accept a council payment for the same loss
Request the council's inspection records for that road
assessment: Genuine. The only risk is double recovery, and the claimant was open about the council claim, which points to a misunderstanding rather than intent. The council may defend itself by showing it inspected the road reasonably often.
action: Pay the claim and pursue the council in the insurer's name, making sure the claimant does not also receive the council's money.
outcomes: Paid; the council later reimburses the insurer
The council shows a reasonable inspection regime and refuses; the loss stays with the insurer

title: The car wash took the mirror
type: Damage in an automatic car wash
story: Policyholder's BMW 1 Series lost its nearside mirror housing and glass in a roll-over car wash at a petrol station. The site manager refused to pay, pointing to a sign saying the operator is not responsible for mirrors and aerials.
statement: I folded the mirrors in like the sign says. Halfway through, the big side brush caught the passenger mirror and pulled it right off, I heard it crack. The attendant saw it happen. The manager just pointed at the sign. It's £420 for a new mirror with the indicator and the heating in it.

accounts.text: I was on shift. The left side brush got stuck for a second and pulled the lady's mirror off. I have seen this happen before with that brush when it is set too low. I think her mirrors were folded in when she went in.

whatHappened: The machine damaged the mirror, quite possibly because a brush was set too low. A sign does not automatically protect an operator whose faulty or badly set equipment causes damage.
damage: Nearside mirror housing, glass and indicator unit. Quote £420.
thirdParties: Car wash operator at the petrol station
evidence: Attendant's email describing the brush catching the mirror
Photo of the sign at the entrance
missing: The car wash maintenance and fault log
CCTV of the wash bay
innocent: The operator's refusal may be a routine response rather than a considered view of the facts
questions: Ask the operator for the maintenance and fault log for the brushes on that day
Ask the operator whether there is CCTV of the wash bay
steps: Tell the claimant that the sign may not protect the operator if the machine was faulty or badly set
Help her claim directly from the operator first, given the amount is close to her excess
If the operator still refuses, pay under the policy and recover
assessment: Genuine. The attendant's account suggests a machine fault, which weakens the operator's reliance on the sign.
action: Help the customer claim directly from the operator; if refused, pay under the policy less the excess and pursue the operator.
outcomes: Operator pays after seeing the attendant's email
Insurer pays less the excess and recovers from the operator

title: Parked in the flood, or driven into the ford?
type: Flood damage with a changing account
story: During a named storm in February, policyholder reported that his Ford Focus flooded while parked on his street in a village near Tadcaster, North Yorkshire. The engine has seized. The car has a telematics device fitted for an insurance discount.
statement: The river came up overnight and the whole street was under water. In the morning the car was sitting in about two feet of water. When it went down I tried to start it and it made a horrible noise. The garage says water has got into the engine.

accounts.who: Telematics trip report, black box in the Focus
accounts.text: Trip start 21:47 at the home postcode. 21:58 vehicle at the ford on Mill Lane, speed 2 to 4 mph for 40 seconds. 21:59 engine stop event. 22:31 ignition on, engine cranking, no start. No further movement recorded. Vehicle collected by a recovery truck at 09:12 the next day.
Collected the Focus from Mill Lane next to the ford, not from the home address. Water line inside the car at seat-cushion height.

whatHappened: He drove into the flooded ford at night, the engine drew in water and stalled, and he tried to restart it. Embarrassment probably led him to say the car was parked at home.
damage: Engine hydrolocked with bent connecting rods, water in the cabin to seat height, damp electrics. Likely total loss; market value about £6,800.
evidence: Photos of the water line inside the car
Environment Agency flood warnings for the area that evening
missing: A witness to where the car was parked overnight
An engineer's strip-down report on the engine
inconsistencies: The claimant says the car flooded while parked at home overnight; the black box shows it was driven into the ford at 21:58 and stopped there
He says he tried to start it in the morning; the black box shows a restart attempt at 22:31 the same night
The recovery note says the car was collected from the ford, not from his street
indicators: His account of where and how the damage happened is contradicted by system data
innocent: Drivers often feel foolish about driving into floodwater and play it down
He may believe the street flooding was the real cause if the ford overflowed onto his road
questions: Ask the claimant, without accusing him: the black box shows a trip at 21:47 ending at the ford on Mill Lane. Can you tell me about that journey?
Ask who was driving that evening
Check the policy wording: does it exclude or limit damage from deliberately driving into floodwater?
steps: Put the telematics and recovery evidence to the claimant in a recorded call
Check the policy wording on driving into floodwater
Obtain an engineer's report confirming water ingestion while the engine was running
Decide cover on the true circumstances
assessment: The flood loss is real, but the account of how it happened is contradicted by the black box and the recovery note. This looks more like an embarrassed customer than a planned fraud, but the misstatement matters if the policy treats driving into floodwater differently from flooding while parked.
action: Hold the claim and put the evidence to the customer. If he corrects his account and the policy covers it, settle. If he sticks to a version the data contradicts, refer it to the fraud team.
outcomes: Customer corrects his account; paid as a flood loss
Policy excludes deliberately driving into floodwater; claim declined with a clear explanation
Customer maintains the false account; referred for fraud investigation and possible cancellation

title: Council oak on a parked Mini
type: Storm branch falls on a parked car
story: A large branch from a street oak fell on the policyholder's parked Mini during a named storm with gusts of 70 mph in Cardiff. The roof and windscreen were crushed. The tree belongs to the council.
statement: We heard a crack at about 2 in the morning and the car alarm went off. The branch had come down right across the roof. The council's tree surgeons came the next day to cut it up. My neighbour says she reported that branch as dead last year.

accounts.text: I reported the oak outside number 14 to the council in April last year because a big branch over the road had no leaves on it. I got an automatic reply with a reference number, but nobody came out that I saw.

whatHappened: A storm brought down a branch. If the council had been told the branch was dead and did nothing, it may be liable in negligence.
damage: Roof crushed, windscreen shattered, A-pillar bent. Likely total loss; market value £8,200.
thirdParties: Cardiff Council, owner of the tree
evidence: Photos of the branch on the car
Met Office gust records for that night
Neighbour's email and the council reference number from her earlier report
missing: The council's tree inspection records
An arborist opinion on whether the branch was dead before the storm
innocent: Storm-damaged trees fall on parked cars every winter; the timing matches the storm and the council's own records
questions: Ask the council when the tree was last inspected and what happened to the April report
steps: Settle the total loss under comprehensive cover
Request the council's inspection and complaint records
Pursue recovery if the council ignored a report of a dead branch
assessment: Genuine storm damage. A storm alone is nobody's fault, but the neighbour's earlier report gives a real chance of recovery from the council if it ignored a known hazard.
action: Pay the total loss now and open a recovery against the council, supported by the neighbour's report.
outcomes: Total loss paid; the council accepts liability after its records show the report was ignored
The council shows it inspected the tree; the storm is treated as an act of nature and there is no recovery

title: Black ice on a side street, into a garden wall
type: Loss of control on ice with third-party property damage
story: Policyholder's Skoda Octavia slid on black ice at about 07:20 on a January morning while going downhill on a residential side street in Crookes, Sheffield, and hit the front garden wall and gatepost of number 41. No one was hurt. The homeowner has sent a builder's quote to rebuild the wall.
statement: I was doing maybe ten miles an hour in second gear because I know the hill gets icy. About halfway down the back end just went and the car slid sideways into the wall. I tried steering into it but nothing happened. The main road had been gritted but our street never is. I knocked on the door straight away and gave the owner my details. The wall was already leaning a bit before, to be honest, but I did knock the end of it down.

accounts.who: Email from the homeowner, Mrs Joan Pickering
accounts.text: Your policyholder was very apologetic and did the right thing. The end of the wall and the stone gatepost are down and the rest is cracked. My builder says the whole 12-metre length has to come down and be rebuilt because a new section won't tie into the old one. His quote is £7,400 plus VAT. I'd like this sorted before the gate falls on someone.

accounts.who: Sheffield City Council gritting schedule extract
accounts.text: Priority 1 routes treated 03:30 to 06:15 on the night in question, including the main road at the top of the hill. The side street is not on a gritting route. Road surface temperature at the nearest sensor: minus 2.1°C at 07:00.

whatHappened: Exactly what he describes: a slow slide on untreated ice into a wall that was already in poor condition. The open question is not liability but how much of the rebuild the insurer should pay for.
damage: Skoda: nearside rear quarter and rear door dented, rear wheel scuffed. Wall: about 3 metres of the end section and the gatepost knocked down; the remaining 9 metres cracked and leaning.
thirdParties: Mrs Joan Pickering, owner of the wall and gatepost at number 41
evidence: Claimant's photos of the car against the wall
Homeowner's builder quote for a full 12-metre rebuild
Council gritting schedule and road temperature
Street imagery from last summer showing the wall
missing: An independent surveyor or loss adjuster view of the wall
Photos of the wall before the accident, other than the street imagery
inconsistencies: The claimant says the wall was already leaning; the builder quote treats the whole length as accident damage
innocent: The builder may honestly believe a partial rebuild will look patched and fail
The homeowner may not have noticed how far the wall was leaning
questions: Ask the homeowner whether the wall had any cracks or lean before the accident, and whether she has older photos
Ask the builder to price repairing only the damaged 3 metres and the gatepost as a separate line
Ask the claimant exactly where the car first touched the wall
steps: Accept liability for the wall: sliding into it on ice is still a loss of control
Compare the street imagery with the photos to see how much of the lean is new
Ask a surveyor or desktop adjuster to split accident damage from age and wear
Settle the wall on the cost of the damaged section, or the full rebuild less a deduction for betterment
assessment: A genuine, low-value claim. The driver was careful and honest, even volunteering that the wall was leaning. Liability for the wall is his, but the insurer should pay only for damage the accident caused, not for replacing an old, failing wall with a new one. A claim against the council is unlikely to succeed: its duty under section 41(1A) of the Highways Act 1980 is limited to what is reasonably practicable, and this street is not on a gritting route.
action: Accept liability, repair the car under the comprehensive cover, and settle the wall after a surveyor separates accident damage from pre-existing deterioration.
outcomes: Wall settled on the damaged section plus the gatepost, about £2,600
Full rebuild paid with a betterment deduction agreed with the homeowner
Homeowner disputes the deduction and asks her own home insurer to pursue the balance

title: Electric car catches fire while charging on the drive
type: Fire during home charging
story: Policyholder's 2020 Hyundai Kona Electric caught fire on her driveway in Milton Keynes at about 03:10 while plugged into a wall charger. The fire service attended and the car is burnt out. The fire also scorched the front of the house and melted the garage door. Nobody was hurt.
statement: I plugged the car in at about ten when I got home from my shift. At around three the smoke alarm went off and the front of the house was orange. My husband got the children out and called 999. The charger was put in about a year ago by my brother-in-law, who is an electrician. It has always worked fine. I had a letter from Hyundai last year about a battery recall and the dealer did the update.

accounts.who: Buckinghamshire Fire and Rescue Service incident summary
accounts.text: Vehicle fire, electric car, on a private driveway. Crews arrived 03:22. Fire well developed at the front of the vehicle near the charging inlet. Cause recorded as accidental, electrical. Area of origin: charging cable connector and vehicle inlet. Wall unit casing heat-damaged. No fire investigation officer attended.

03:06:12 small flicker of light at the front left of the car near the charging cable. 03:06:40 smoke from the same area. 03:07:30 flames along the cable towards the wall unit. 03:08:51 front of the car on fire. No one visible near the car at any time.

whatHappened: An electrical fault at the charging connection started the fire. Whether the fault was in the car's inlet, the cable or the home installation is not yet known, and that decides who the insurers can recover from.
damage: Kona Electric burnt out, total loss; market value about £17,500. House: scorched render and fascia, melted uPVC garage door, a cracked window. The house damage falls under the home insurance.
thirdParties: The claimant's home insurer, for the damage to the house
The installer of the wall charger, a family member
Hyundai, if the car is at fault
evidence: Recall letter and dealer invoice for the battery update
Photos of the burnt car and the charger
missing: An installation certificate for the wall charger
A forensic fire investigation before the car is moved or crushed
The car's connected-services charging log for that night
innocent: There is nothing to explain away: an overnight charging fire in an empty car fits an electrical fault
questions: Ask the claimant for the installation certificate and whether the installer is registered with a competent person scheme
Ask whether anyone used an extension lead or adapter, or whether the cable had ever been damaged
Ask Hyundai whether this car's VIN was subject to any other recall, and whether the update was completed
steps: Preserve the car, the cable and the wall unit; do not release the wreck for salvage yet
Instruct a forensic fire investigator, sharing the cost with the home insurer
Settle the vehicle total loss under the fire section without waiting for the cause
Pursue a recovery against the installer or the manufacturer if the investigation identifies a fault
assessment: A genuine fire claim with no warning signs. The car is covered under the fire section whatever the cause. The real work is preserving the evidence so that both insurers can recover their costs from whoever is responsible, without delaying the customer's settlement.
action: Pay the total loss now, keep the wreck and the charger for a joint inspection, and decide on a recovery once the investigator reports.
outcomes: Fault found in the home installation; recovery pursued against the installer's liability insurer
Fault found in the car's inlet; recovery pursued against the manufacturer
Cause undetermined; each insurer bears its own loss

title: Petrol in a diesel, and a story about the pump
type: Misfuelling
story: Policyholder put about 40 litres of unleaded petrol into his diesel Volkswagen Passat at a supermarket forecourt in Newport and drove about two miles before it cut out on the A48. On the first call he said the pump was wrongly labelled. His policy includes misfuelling cover up to £750.
statement: First call: The diesel pump at number 4 had the green nozzle on it, so the forecourt has made a mistake and I want them to pay. Second call, two days later: Look, I've thought about it and I was on a hands-free call and just picked up the wrong nozzle. I'm sorry I said it was the pump. I just want the car sorted.

accounts.who: Forecourt manager email with CCTV stills
accounts.text: Pump 4 has two nozzles: green for unleaded and black for diesel, both clearly labelled. Our CCTV at 08:14 shows the customer lifting the green nozzle. Receipt: 39.6 litres unleaded, pump 4. No other complaints that day, and Trading Standards tested the pumps last month.

Called out 08:41 to the A48, Newport. Vehicle had been driven after fuelling and stalled. Tank drained and flushed, filters replaced, fuel lines purged. Engine started but runs rough; high-pressure fuel pump suspected. Charge £285. Recommend a diagnostic at a VW specialist.

whatHappened: An ordinary distracted misfuel. Driving on after filling up let petrol reach the high-pressure pump, which is why the bill may grow. The first account blaming the pump was an embarrassed attempt to shift the cost, dropped two days later.
damage: Contaminated fuel system. Drain and flush done for £285; possible high-pressure fuel pump and injector damage, estimated at £1,900 if confirmed.
thirdParties: None. The forecourt is not at fault
evidence: Recordings of both calls to the claims line
missing: A VW specialist's diagnostic report on the fuel pump
The policy wording on damage caused by driving after misfuelling
inconsistencies: The first call blames a mislabelled pump; the CCTV and receipt show he took the green unleaded nozzle, and he later admits it
innocent: People often blame the equipment in the first moment of embarrassment
He corrected the account himself before being shown the CCTV
questions: Ask the claimant how far he drove and whether any warning lights came on
Ask the specialist to confirm whether the fuel pump damage came from this misfuel
steps: Note the corrected account on file and do not pursue the forecourt
Pay the drain and flush under the misfuelling cover
Get a diagnostic before agreeing to replace the fuel pump
Apply the £750 limit and explain any shortfall in writing
assessment: Genuine, with a reporting error that the claimant corrected himself. The false first account would matter if he had kept to it, but he volunteered the truth before being confronted with the CCTV. The cover limit, not honesty, is what decides this claim.
action: Settle under the misfuelling extension up to the £750 limit. Record the first call accurately but do not treat it as fraud.
outcomes: Drain and flush paid; fuel pump damage confirmed and paid up to the limit, customer pays the rest
Diagnostic shows no lasting damage; claim closed at £285
Customer complains about the limit; complaint not upheld because the limit was clear in the policy

title: Keyless theft of a Range Rover with a lapsed tracker
type: Relay attack theft from a driveway
story: Policyholder's 2022 Range Rover Sport was stolen from his driveway in Solihull at about 02:40. Both keys are accounted for. The policy has an endorsement that theft cover requires a Thatcham-approved tracker to be fitted and subscribed. The tracker subscription lapsed 19 days before the theft. Market value about £71,000.
statement: We woke up and the car was gone. The doorbell camera shows two men, one holding something like a laptop bag near the front door and the other at the car. It took them under a minute. The keys were in a bowl on the hall table, maybe four metres from the door. I didn't know the tracker had lapsed. The renewal emails must have gone to my old work address. I've paid it now, for what it's worth.

accounts.who: Doorbell camera, front of the house
accounts.text: 02:39:58 two men in dark clothing walk onto the drive. 02:40:10 one stands by the front door holding a rectangular bag towards it. 02:40:22 the car's indicators flash once. 02:40:51 the car reverses off the drive with its lights off. No one touches the door or the house.

Subscription expired on the 3rd. Reminder emails sent on three dates to the email address on the account, a corporate domain. No location data is held after expiry. The unit is still fitted but not monitored.
Theft of a motor vehicle reported at 07:05. ANPR: the vehicle passed a camera on the M42 at 02:58 on false plates matching a similar vehicle. No further sightings. Not recovered.

whatHappened: A typical relay attack: the thieves picked up the key's signal through the front door and drove away. The theft is genuine. The question is cover, because an active tracker would probably have led police to the car.
damage: Vehicle stolen and not recovered. Value about £71,000; about £38,000 outstanding with a finance company.
thirdParties: Finance company with an interest in the vehicle
evidence: Both keys inspected by the insurer
Police crime report with the ANPR sighting
missing: Key data showing neither key was cloned
Proof of how the renewal reminders were addressed and whether a postal reminder was sent
innocent: Renewal reminders going to an old work email is common and unremarkable
Keeping keys in the hall is ordinary behaviour, not a breach unless the policy says so
questions: Ask the tracker company whether any reminder was sent other than by email
Ask the claimant whether the insurer reminded him of the tracker condition at renewal
Ask the finance company for the settlement figure
steps: Confirm the theft through the footage, the keys and the police report
Check whether the tracker condition was clearly drawn to his attention at inception and renewal
Consider section 11 of the Insurance Act 2015: could the lapse have increased the risk of this loss?
Decide on cover and, if paying, settle the finance company first
assessment: Genuine theft by a known method, with no sign of the owner's involvement. Cover turns on the tracker condition. Because an active tracker is meant to reduce exactly this risk, the insurer may be entitled to rely on the lapse, but only if the condition was made clear and the outcome is fair. A strict decline is likely to be challenged at the Financial Ombudsman Service.
action: Treat it as a cover question, not a fraud question. Review how the condition was communicated, make a reasoned decision and explain it in writing; consider a negotiated settlement if the communication was weak.
outcomes: Paid in full because the condition was not clearly highlighted at renewal
Declined under the tracker endorsement; an ombudsman complaint follows
Settled at an agreed percentage of the value

title: Catalytic converter cut from a Prius at the station
type: Theft of vehicle parts
story: Policyholder parked her 2016 Toyota Prius at Bedford station car park at 07:10 and found the catalytic converter missing when she returned at 18:35. She reported it online to Bedfordshire Police and has a crime reference. A CUE search shows a catalytic converter theft claim on the same car 14 months ago.
statement: When I started it, it sounded like a tractor, and a man in the next space said he'd seen the same thing last week. I looked underneath and there were cut pipes. It's the second time. After the first one I asked the garage about a cage for it, but they said there was a waiting list for the part. I commute every day, I can't be without a car.

accounts.text: Our cameras cover the entrance, the exit and the ticket machines. The row where the Prius was parked is not covered. The entrance camera shows the vehicle arriving at 07:09. We have had four similar reports this month.
Supply and fit catalytic converter and front pipe, new gaskets, oxygen sensor wiring repair, Toyota catalytic converter protection plate. Parts £2,140, labour £380. Parts available in 9 working days.

whatHappened: A routine catalytic converter theft from an unattended car. Hybrid converters contain more precious metal and are a common target, which is why it has happened to her twice.
damage: Catalytic converter and part of the exhaust removed; oxygen sensor wiring cut. Estimate £2,520 including a protection plate.
evidence: CUE record of the earlier theft
missing: Confirmation that the converter fitted after the first theft was a genuine part
innocent: A second theft from the same model is common and does not suggest involvement
The protection plate she asked about last year was genuinely in short supply
questions: Ask whether the converter replaced after the first theft was a genuine Toyota part
Ask whether she needs a courtesy car under the policy
steps: Confirm the crime reference
Authorise the dealer repair, including the protection plate
Arrange a courtesy car if the policy provides one
Note the new security device on the policy record
assessment: Genuine. The earlier claim is explained by the model being targeted, not by anything the claimant did. Paying for a protection plate now is cheaper than a third claim.
action: Settle the repair, including the protection plate, and arrange a courtesy car if covered.
outcomes: Repaired with a protection plate fitted; claim settled at about £2,520 less the excess
Renewal premium rises because of the two theft claims

title: Left running to defrost, gone in two minutes
type: Theft of a car left running to defrost
story: Policyholder left her Vauxhall Corsa running on her driveway in Leeds at about 07:45 to clear the frost and it was stolen. It was found two hours later, crashed into a lamp post about two miles away and abandoned. The policy excludes theft when the keys are left in or on the vehicle while it is unattended.
statement: I was right there, literally a minute. I nipped in to get my lunch out of the fridge and when I came out it was going round the corner. I ran after it screaming. The police found it later against a lamp post, all smashed at the front. Everyone leaves their car running on cold mornings, I don't see how that's my fault.

accounts.text: 07:44:30 Corsa engine running, windscreen fogged, no one in it. 07:44:41 claimant walks from the car into her house and closes the door. 07:50:58 a young man in a grey hoodie walks up the street, gets into the Corsa and drives off. 07:51:20 claimant comes out of the house and runs to the end of the drive.
Vehicle located at 09:52 on Roundhay Road against a street lamp, driver's door open, keys in the ignition. No suspect identified. The lamp column has been made safe by the council.

whatHappened: She left the car running and unattended for about six and a half minutes, and an opportunist took it. Her "one minute" was a guess that turned out to be wrong, not a calculated lie.
damage: Corsa: front bumper, bonnet and radiator damaged and airbags deployed; likely total loss, value about £8,900. Council lamp column knocked over.
thirdParties: Leeds City Council, owner of the lamp column
missing: The exact wording of the keys exclusion in her policy
An engineer's report on whether the car is a total loss
inconsistencies: She says she was gone about a minute; the doorbell footage shows six and a half minutes inside the house
innocent: Time feels short when you are rushing to work; her estimate need not be a lie
She reported straight away and gave the police the footage herself
questions: Ask her to watch the footage with the handler and confirm the timings
Check whether she bought any add-on that changes the keys exclusion
steps: Confirm that the exclusion is clearly worded and was prominent in the policy documents
Explain the decision with reference to the footage
Tell the council that the thief's use is not covered by her policy and that it can claim from the Motor Insurers' Bureau
assessment: A genuine theft, but the keys were left in an unattended car with the engine running, which is exactly what the exclusion is for. Her account of the timing is wrong but not dishonest. The fair outcome is a clear, kind decline, not a fraud referral.
action: Decline the theft and damage claim under the keys exclusion with a plain explanation, and redirect the council's claim to the MIB.
outcomes: Claim declined under the exclusion; customer accepts
Customer complains to the ombudsman; the decline is upheld because the exclusion was clear
Ombudsman finds the exclusion was not made clear at sale; insurer pays the claim

title: Looking at the phone, into the back of a Juke
type: Rear-end collision caused by phone use
story: Policyholder ran into the back of a Nissan Juke waiting at traffic lights on the A38 in Bristol at about 17:30. He admits he was looking at the map on his phone, which was in his hand. Police attended and issued a fixed penalty for using a hand-held phone. The Juke had a driver and one passenger, who both say they have neck pain.
statement: I'll be honest, I was checking the route on my phone because the mount had broken. I looked down for a second and when I looked up the lights had changed and the Juke had stopped. I hit it at maybe 15 miles an hour. I've told the police the same. I feel awful about it. They were both shaken but walking around fine at the scene.

accounts.text: We had been stopped at a red light for a few seconds when we were hit hard from behind. My daughter, who is 19, was in the front. We both felt our necks go. The next morning I could hardly turn my head and my daughter had a headache. We went to the GP two days later. The boot will not close properly.
Using a hand-held mobile phone while driving: 6 penalty points and a £200 fine. Driver admitted the offence at the scene. Both drivers exchanged details. No arrests.

whatHappened: Exactly as reported. He was distracted by his phone and ran into a stationary car. The two people in the Juke may well have the short-term neck injuries they describe.
damage: Policyholder's Peugeot 308: front bumper, bonnet and radiator. Juke: rear bumper, boot lid and rear panel. Two possible soft-tissue injury claims.
thirdParties: Mrs Rachel Odenigbo, driver of the Juke
evidence: Admission at the scene and in the statement
missing: Medical reports for both occupants through the Official Injury Claim process
An engineer's check of the Juke repair estimate
innocent: There is nothing to explain away; the policyholder caused the crash and says so
questions: Ask the third party whether she wants the insurer to arrange the Juke repair directly
Ask both occupants to register their injury claims through the Official Injury Claim portal
steps: Accept liability quickly to keep third-party costs down
Offer the third party a direct repair and a courtesy car
Value any whiplash claims on the fixed tariff once the medical reports arrive
Repair the policyholder's car under the comprehensive cover
assessment: A clear-cut liability claim. The phone use is a criminal offence but does not affect cover for the third party. The insurer should accept liability and handle the injury claims through the tariff system rather than with suspicion: a 15 mph rear impact can cause short-term neck strain.
action: Accept liability, take over the third party's repair, and settle the injuries on the tariff after medical reports.
outcomes: Third-party repair and two tariff injury payments settled within a few months
Renewal premium rises and the conviction must be declared

title: Delivering takeaways on a social-only policy
type: Collision while using the car for paid delivery work
story: Policyholder's Toyota Aygo was hit on the passenger side by a car pulling out of a side road in Rusholme, Manchester, at about 20:15 in the rain. His policy covers social, domestic and pleasure use only. Photos from the scene show an insulated food delivery bag on the back seat and a delivery app open on his phone mount.
statement: I was going to pick up some food for me and my brother. The other car came out without looking. The bag is just something I keep in the car. I did a bit of delivering last year but I stopped.

accounts.text: I was pulling out of Claremont Road and the Aygo came quicker than I thought in the rain. I clipped his passenger door. He was very upset and kept saying his order was going cold and he would lose his rating. There was a takeaway bag on his back seat.

accounts.who: Delivery platform reply to the insurer's data request
accounts.text: The account linked to this phone number was online and on an active delivery from 19:52. Order collected at 20:06 from a restaurant on Wilmslow Road; delivery marked as failed at 20:31 with the reason "courier had an accident". Account active since March with 412 completed deliveries.

whatHappened: He was in the middle of a food delivery, using the car for hire and reward on a policy that does not cover it. He played it down because he knew the policy did not cover delivery work.
damage: Aygo: passenger doors and sill, about £2,300. Other car: front corner, about £1,600.
thirdParties: Mr Leon Fairclough, the other driver, and his insurer
evidence: Scene photos showing the delivery bag and the app
Policy schedule showing the class of use
missing: Junction layout and any camera footage to settle liability between the drivers
inconsistencies: He says he stopped delivering last year; the platform shows an active order and 412 deliveries since March
He says he was collecting his own food; the platform shows a customer's order collected at 20:06
indicators: A false account of the purpose of the journey that would bring it within the class of use
innocent: Some drivers wrongly believe their normal policy covers occasional delivery work
The other driver probably caused the collision, so he may feel the purpose of the journey is irrelevant
questions: Ask him to explain the platform record of an active delivery at the time
Ask whether he has, or had, a separate delivery insurance policy
steps: Decide liability between the drivers on the junction evidence
Decline his own-damage claim because the use was not covered
Deal with any valid third-party claim as the insurer of the vehicle and recover that outlay from him
Review the policy for cancellation and record the false statement
assessment: The collision is genuine and probably not his fault, but the journey was business use that the policy does not cover, and he gave a false reason for it. That is a breach of cover rather than an invented accident. If the other driver is at fault, he can still recover his own losses from that driver's insurer.
action: Decline own-damage cover, handle any third-party claim with a right of recovery against him, and support his claim against the other driver for his uninsured losses.
outcomes: Other driver found at fault; that driver's insurer pays for the Aygo repair
Liability split 50/50; the insurer pays the third party and recovers the cost from the claimant
Policy cancelled and the false statement recorded

title: Sudden stop on a roundabout exit, four whiplash claims
type: Induced rear-end collision ("crash for cash")
story: Policyholder, 58, ran into the back of an older BMW 3 Series as both cars left the Perry Barr roundabout in Birmingham at about 14:20. She says the BMW stopped dead with no brake lights. Within a week, solicitors acting for the BMW's driver and three passengers sent injury claims, all through the same claims management company.
statement: We'd just come off the roundabout and were picking up speed when the BMW stopped dead in front of me. There was nothing in the road, no lights, no one crossing. I didn't see any brake lights. I hit it at maybe 20. All four of them got out holding their necks, but one was laughing on his phone. The driver said a cat ran out. I didn't see a cat.

accounts.who: BMW driver, Mr Imran Bashir, through his solicitors
accounts.text: I braked because a cat ran across the exit. Your insured was too close and could not stop. I and my three passengers all suffered neck and back injuries and have been unable to work. My car is being repaired at an approved garage and I need a replacement vehicle while it is off the road.

accounts.who: Bus operator CCTV, forward-facing camera, two vehicles behind
accounts.text: 14:19:52 BMW and Honda leave the roundabout in lane 1. 14:19:57 BMW slows sharply from about 25 mph to a stop in under two seconds. No brake lights are visible on the BMW at any point. No animal, pedestrian or obstruction is visible ahead. 14:19:59 Honda hits the BMW. 14:20:30 four people get out of the BMW.

accounts.who: Claims database check on the BMW and its occupants
accounts.text: BMW insured 11 days before the collision. The registered keeper changed 6 weeks before. The driver has two previous claims as a third party in rear-end collisions, in 2023 and 2025. One passenger appears as a passenger in one of those earlier claims. Same claims management company in all three.

whatHappened: Very probably a deliberately induced collision: the BMW braked hard on an open road with its brake lights disabled so that the following car would hit it, creating a liability claim for damage, hire and four injuries.
damage: Honda Jazz: front bumper, bonnet and radiator. BMW: rear bumper and boot, with older repair marks in the rear panel. Four soft-tissue injury claims plus hire and repair costs, likely over £25,000 in total.
thirdParties: Mr Imran Bashir, driver of the BMW
The claims management company and solicitors acting for all four
evidence: Bus CCTV with a clear view of the stop
Database results linking the driver and one passenger to earlier claims
Photos of both cars at the scene
missing: An engineer's inspection of the BMW's brake light circuit before it is repaired
The BMW driver's phone records around 14:20
Medical records for the four occupants
inconsistencies: The driver says he braked for a cat; the bus CCTV shows nothing in the road
The BMW stopped hard with no brake lights showing, which is consistent with deliberately disabled lights
Four people claim serious injury, yet the policyholder saw one of them laughing on his phone at the scene
indicators: Sudden braking on a clear road with no visible reason
No brake lights during an emergency stop
Recently insured vehicle with a recent change of keeper
Driver and a passenger linked to earlier rear-end claims through the same claims management company
Fully occupied car, with all occupants claiming injury
innocent: A small animal can be hard to see on a camera two vehicles back
Brake light bulbs fail in ordinary cars, and the driver may not have known
Several people in one car can genuinely be hurt in a 20 mph impact
questions: Ask the BMW driver exactly where the cat came from and where it went
Ask each passenger separately where they had been going, where they were sitting and how they know the driver
Ask the garage holding the BMW to keep the rear light cluster and wiring for inspection
steps: Secure the full bus CCTV and the BMW before any repair
Refer the claim to the counter-fraud team and share the network links with the Insurance Fraud Bureau
Have an engineer test the BMW's brake lights
Deny liability on the basis that the collision was deliberately induced, and plead fundamental dishonesty if the injury claims are issued
assessment: The usual rule that the driver behind is to blame does not survive this evidence. The stop had no reason, the brake lights did not work, and the occupants are linked to earlier claims of the same kind. Taken together this is strong evidence of an induced accident, although the insurer will need the engineer's report and the full footage to prove it in court.
action: Do not admit liability or pay hire charges. Investigate as organised third-party fraud and defend the injury claims; keep the policyholder informed and protect her no-claims discount if the defence succeeds.
outcomes: Claims withdrawn once the CCTV is disclosed
Court finds the collision was induced; the claims are dismissed and costs awarded against the claimants
Insufficient proof of fraud; liability accepted for the damage but the injury claims are reduced or defeated on the medical evidence

title: Flashed out of a junction, then blamed for pulling out
type: Junction collision with an alleged induced manoeuvre ("flash for cash")
story: Policyholder, 19, pulled out of a side road onto Dunstable Road in Luton at about 18:45 and was hit on the driver's side by a Ford Mondeo. He says the Mondeo flashed its lights to let him out. The Mondeo driver says he pulled out without looking, and an independent witness supports her. The witness's phone number appears in four earlier claims as a witness.
statement: The Mondeo was coming from the right and it slowed and flashed its lights, so I thought it was letting me out. I started to go and it sped up and hit me. The driver got out and was really calm, like it was nothing. A man walked up within about a minute and said he'd seen it all and gave her his number, not me.

accounts.text: I was driving along Dunstable Road at about 30 when a Fiesta came straight out of the side road without stopping. I had no chance. I definitely did not flash my lights. A gentleman who was walking past saw the whole thing and kindly gave me his details.
I was walking towards the shops and saw the small car pull out right in front of the Mondeo. The Mondeo had no time to stop. I didn't see any lights flash. I have no connection to either driver.

accounts.who: Insurer's internal claims search on the witness
accounts.text: Mobile number given by Mr Holt matches a witness in four previous third-party claims at other insurers since 2024, under the names D. Holt and Darren Holtby. Three of those claims involved a driver alleged to have pulled out of a junction. One claim used the same hire company as this one.

whatHappened: Unclear. It could be a genuine misunderstanding at a junction, which is common, or a set-up in which the Mondeo flashed him out and a planted witness backed up the story. The witness link is serious but not yet proof.
damage: Policyholder's Ford Fiesta: driver's doors and B-pillar, probably a total loss. Mondeo: front bumper and wing. The Mondeo driver has claimed hire and a back injury.
thirdParties: Mrs Shabana Iqbal, driver of the Mondeo
A credit hire company providing a replacement car
evidence: Claims search linking the witness number to four earlier claims
missing: Any camera footage from the shops or buses on Dunstable Road
The policyholder's phone records showing he was not using it
Links between the witness and the Mondeo driver, if any
inconsistencies: The witness says he has no connection to either driver; his number appears in four earlier claims, one using the same hire company
The witness gave his details only to the Mondeo driver, which fits a planted witness but also fits ordinary sympathy for the victim
indicators: A witness who repeatedly appears in similar claims under slightly different names
Classic junction "flash and go" allegation by a young driver
Calm behaviour from the other driver immediately after the collision
innocent: Drivers often flash to warn, not to give way, and the policyholder may have misread it
Some people do witness several accidents, especially if they work near a busy road
Two similar names may belong to two different people sharing a family phone
questions: Ask the witness, in a recorded interview, where he was going, whether he has given witness evidence before and how he knows the hire company
Ask the Mondeo driver whether she knows Mr Holt or anyone connected to the earlier claims
Ask the policyholder exactly where the Mondeo was when it flashed and how long he waited before pulling out
steps: Request footage from businesses and buses on Dunstable Road before it is deleted
Run a link analysis on the witness, the hire company and the Mondeo driver, and share it with the Insurance Fraud Bureau
Do not admit liability while the witness is being investigated
Value the hire and injury claims critically in case liability falls on the policyholder
assessment: A young driver pulling out of a junction would normally be found at fault, so the witness decides this case. His repeated appearances in similar claims make his evidence unsafe, but suspicion is not proof. The claim should be investigated, not paid and not yet treated as fraud.
action: Hold liability, investigate the witness and the hire company links, and look for independent footage. Decide liability only when the evidence supports it either way.
outcomes: Footage shows the Mondeo flashing and accelerating; claim defended as an induced collision
Witness refuses to give a signed statement; liability split 50/50
No further evidence; liability accepted against the policyholder as a junction emergence, with the hire claim reduced

title: Insurance bought from an Instagram "broker"
type: Ghost-broked policy exposed by a claim
story: Policyholder, 23, rear-ended a taxi at traffic lights in Catford, south-east London. When the claim was checked, the policy showed a date of birth making him 31, an address in Cumbria and five years' no-claims discount. His DVLA licence shows a London address and a licence held for 14 months. He says he bought the policy through an Instagram account for £640.
statement: I found them on Instagram, they do cheap insurance for young drivers. I sent my licence photo and my address on WhatsApp and paid £640 to the account they gave me. They sent me a certificate with your name on it. I never told anyone I was 31 or lived in Cumbria, I've never even been there. The crash was my fault, I'll admit that, I looked away for a second.

accounts.who: WhatsApp messages supplied by the claimant
accounts.text: "Send pic of licence front and back and postcode bro" ... claimant sends a London postcode and a licence photo ... "Sorted £640 to this acc, cert in 10 mins" ... "Don't call the insurer direct, any issues come to me, they mess you about." The account was deleted two days after the accident.

Policy bought online 9 weeks before the accident. Proposer date of birth 31 years earlier, Cumbria address, five years no-claims declared, occupation warehouse supervisor. Premium £1,190 paid by a debit card in a different name. Email address on the policy is not the claimant's.

whatHappened: A ghost broker bought a genuine policy using false details to get a cheap price, charged the claimant £640 and probably intended to cancel the policy for a refund. The claimant was the victim of the fraud, but he was careless in not checking the documents he received.
damage: Policyholder's Seat Leon: front bumper and bonnet, about £1,800. Taxi: rear damage, loss of earnings and a possible injury claim from the driver, estimated £6,500.
evidence: WhatsApp messages and bank transfer receipt
Admission of fault for the collision
missing: Identity of the person behind the Instagram account
Records of the card used to pay the premium
Whether the claimant was ever sent the full policy schedule
inconsistencies: The policy shows a date of birth, address and driving history that do not match his licence
The premium was paid by a card in a different name, from an email address that is not his
indicators: Policy bought through a social media seller rather than an authorised broker
Premium paid by a third party, with false proposer details
Seller told him not to contact the insurer and deleted the account after the accident
innocent: Young drivers facing very high premiums are the usual targets of ghost brokers and often do not realise the policy is false
He supplied his true details and kept the messages that prove it
questions: Ask the claimant whether he ever received or read the policy schedule and the certificate details
Ask him for the bank details of the account he paid
Ask whether friends bought insurance from the same account
steps: Treat the policy as obtained by misrepresentation and take legal advice on avoiding it
Handle the taxi claim as the Road Traffic Act insurer, then consider recovering the outlay
Report the ghost broker to Action Fraud and the Insurance Fraud Bureau with the account and bank details
Explain to the claimant that he has no valid insurance and must stop driving until he buys a real policy
assessment: The fraud was committed by the ghost broker, not, on the evidence, by the claimant, who seems to have been a careless victim. The policy cannot stand as written, but the injured taxi driver must still be compensated. The claimant loses his own-damage cover and probably faces a recovery claim and a charge for driving without insurance, which is why he needs clear, early advice.
action: Avoid the policy with legal advice, deal with the third party under the Road Traffic Act, report the broker, and record the claimant as a victim of ghost broking rather than as a fraudster.
outcomes: Policy avoided; third-party claim paid; partial recovery from the claimant by instalments
Ghost broker traced through the bank account and prosecuted
Claimant complains that he was a victim; ombudsman agrees the insurer acted fairly in avoiding the policy

title: Three passengers that the CCTV never saw
type: Low-speed car park collision with phantom passenger claims
story: Policyholder reversed out of a bay at a retail park in Wolverhampton at about 11:30 and touched the side of a passing Vauxhall Insignia at walking pace. She accepted fault at the scene. Five weeks later, solicitors sent injury claims for the Insignia's driver and three passengers.
statement: I was reversing out very slowly and didn't see him coming along behind. It was a bump, nothing more. I said sorry straight away and we swapped details. There was only him in the car, I'm sure of it. He was on his own and on his phone a lot of the time.

accounts.who: Letter of claim from solicitors for the Insignia occupants
accounts.text: Our clients, the driver and his three passengers, were travelling together to the retail park when your insured reversed into the nearside of their vehicle with considerable force. All four occupants suffered whiplash injuries and have attended physiotherapy. We enclose medical reports.

11:29:40 Insignia enters car park lane C, one occupant visible in the driver's seat, no passengers visible through the side or rear windows. 11:31:05 contact with the reversing Kia. 11:31:20 driver gets out alone. 11:38:10 Insignia leaves. No other person gets in or out at any time.

whatHappened: A minor reversing knock that was her fault. The three passengers almost certainly did not exist and were added later to multiply the injury claims.
damage: Insignia: scuffed rear passenger door and wheel arch, about £650. Kia: scratched rear bumper.
thirdParties: Three named passengers who appear only in the letter of claim
evidence: Policyholder's statement that the driver was alone
Medical reports supplied by the solicitors
missing: Statements from the passengers explaining where they sat and how they travelled
Any evidence linking the passengers to the driver
inconsistencies: The letter of claim describes four occupants; the CCTV shows only the driver, who gets out alone
The letter describes "considerable force"; the damage is a scuff from a walking-pace impact
indicators: Passengers added to the claim weeks after the accident
Injury claims out of proportion to a walking-pace impact
All claims submitted together through the same solicitors
innocent: The solicitors may have been misled by their clients and may not have seen the CCTV
The driver's own injury claim may be exaggerated rather than invented
questions: Ask the solicitors for each passenger's account of where they sat and where they got out
Ask the driver why no one else is seen getting out of the car on the CCTV
steps: Accept liability for the vehicle damage only
Disclose the CCTV to the solicitors and deny the passenger claims
Challenge the driver's injury claim on the low impact and the overall dishonesty
Refer the passenger names to the counter-fraud team for links to other claims
assessment: Liability for a small knock is not in doubt, but the passenger claims are contradicted by clear CCTV. Adding people who were not in the car is fraud, and it taints the driver's claim too. The insurer should pay for the scuffed door and defend the rest.
action: Pay the vehicle damage, deny the three passenger claims, defend the driver's injury claim, and consider a fundamental dishonesty argument if the case is issued.
outcomes: Passenger claims withdrawn after the CCTV is disclosed; driver accepts a small payment for the damage
Claims pursued to court; found fundamentally dishonest and dismissed

title: The same Mercedes, three crashes, three keepers
type: Collision linked to an organised claims network
story: Policyholder, a retired teacher, was involved in a low-speed collision on the A580 in Salford when a Mercedes C-Class moved into his lane at about 30 mph. The Mercedes driver blames him. An accident management company has notified claims for credit hire, storage, repairs and three injuries. Checks show the Mercedes has been in two earlier claims in 14 months under different registered keepers.
statement: I was in the right-hand lane and the Mercedes came alongside on my left, then drifted over into me. I had nowhere to go. The driver was very quick to take photos of my number plate and my face. Another car pulled up behind us straight away and the man in it said he was a witness, but he seemed to know the driver.

accounts.who: Accident management company letter of claim
accounts.text: Our client was driving in lane 1 when your insured changed lanes without warning and struck the offside of our client's vehicle. Our client has been provided with a like-for-like replacement vehicle at £289 per day. The vehicle is held in secure storage at £45 per day pending inspection. Three occupants have suffered injuries. Liability is denied by our client in full.

Mercedes: three claims in 14 months, each time with a new registered keeper, all three handled by the same accident management company and stored at the same yard. The "witness" in this claim was a passenger in the second claim. Two of the three occupants share an address with a driver from the first claim. Repairer and storage yard have a common director. Eleven other claims are linked to the same people, phones or addresses.
