whatHappened: The policyholder was very probably targeted by an organised group that stages or induces collisions with the same vehicles and the same people, then makes the most of each one through hire, storage, repairs and injury claims.
damage: Policyholder's Skoda Superb: nearside doors scraped. Mercedes: offside front wing and door, including old damage. Claims presented: hire about £9,800 so far, storage £1,900, repairs £4,200 and three injury claims.
thirdParties: Two passengers and a "witness" linked to earlier claims
Accident management company, storage yard and repairer with a shared director
evidence: Companies House records showing the shared director
missing: A forensic engineer's comparison of the damage on both cars
Dashcam or roadside camera footage from the A580
Telematics or phone location data for the Mercedes occupants
inconsistencies: The witness presents as independent but was a passenger in an earlier claim involving the same Mercedes
The Mercedes damage includes older damage that the letter of claim attributes to this collision
indicators: One vehicle involved in three claims in 14 months under three different keepers
Repeat people, addresses and phone numbers across 14 claims
Accident management company, repairer and storage yard linked through a shared director
An immediate "witness" connected to the claimants
Hire and storage charges building up while inspection is delayed
innocent: A popular used car can have several owners and more than one accident without anything sinister
The policyholder himself is clearly not part of the scheme
questions: Ask the policyholder whether the "witness" arrived before or after the collision, and whether he saw them talk before it
Ask the accident management company to make the Mercedes available for inspection within 48 hours
Ask each occupant to explain how they know each other and why they were travelling together
steps: Refer the claim and the network to the Insurance Fraud Bureau
Offer an immediate inspection of the Mercedes to stop hire and storage building up
Deny liability and reserve the position on fraud
Coordinate with other insurers holding linked claims, and consider civil action or a referral to the Insurance Fraud Enforcement Department
assessment: Strong evidence of organised fraud with the policyholder as an innocent target. No single fact proves it, but repeat vehicles, repeat people and linked businesses across 14 claims make coincidence implausible. The insurer should defend the claim and work with the industry bodies, while protecting the policyholder's no-claims discount.
action: Deny liability, stop the hire clock by offering inspection, refer to the IFB and support a coordinated investigation. Keep the policyholder informed and reassure him that he is not under suspicion.
outcomes: Claims abandoned after the IFB referral
Network members arrested by the Insurance Fraud Enforcement Department; linked claims dismissed
Civil judgment for fraud against the claimants and the accident management company

title: Two new policies, one empty road, rust in the dents
type: Alleged collision that may never have happened (paper accident)
story: Policyholder reported that at about 23:40 he pulled out of a unit on an industrial estate in Stoke-on-Trent and hit the side of a passing Audi A4. He admitted fault on the first call. His policy started 18 days earlier and the Audi's policy started 23 days earlier. There were no witnesses and no police. The Audi's owner has claimed repairs, hire and an injury through a credit hire firm.
statement: It was totally my fault, I pulled out and didn't see him. I want to make sure he gets sorted out because he's been really decent about it. I don't need my car fixed, it's only a bit of damage. Can you just pay him and close it?

accounts.who: Insurer's engineer inspection of both cars
accounts.text: Audi: offside doors pushed in, with rust and road dirt inside the dents and old paint overspray on the trim. Damage height 38 to 61 cm. Policyholder's Vauxhall Astra: front bumper scraped, impact zone 44 to 52 cm, no transfer of the Audi's dark grey paint. In my opinion the damage on the two vehicles does not correspond and the Audi damage is several months old.

The policyholder and the Audi owner are friends on two social media platforms and appear together in photos from a wedding last summer. Neither mentioned knowing the other. The Audi owner listed the car for sale online four months ago, describing "light damage to the offside doors, priced to sell".

whatHappened: Very probably a paper accident: two friends took out new policies and reported a collision to get old damage on the Audi repaired, plus hire and an injury payment, at the insurer's expense. The policyholder's eagerness to admit fault is part of the pattern.
damage: Audi: offside doors and sill, with old damage. Astra: light front scrape. Claims presented: repairs £3,900, credit hire £5,600 so far, and an injury claim.
thirdParties: Owner of the Audi A4, a friend of the policyholder
evidence: Open-source evidence that the drivers are friends
Old sale listing describing the Audi damage
missing: Phone location data for both drivers at 23:40
Industrial estate CCTV
The Audi's MOT history and photos from its last inspection
inconsistencies: The damage heights and paint transfer do not match between the two cars
The Audi damage contains rust and was described in a sale listing four months earlier
The drivers present as strangers but are friends
indicators: Both policies taken out within weeks of the accident
Late-night collision with no witnesses or police
Immediate, eager admission of fault and no interest in his own repair
Pre-existing damage presented as new
Undisclosed relationship between the drivers
innocent: Friends can genuinely collide, especially near a shared workplace
Old damage may be included by mistake if the owner did not realise it was visible
questions: Ask both drivers, separately, how they know each other and where they were coming from
Ask the Audi owner about the sale listing and the damage it described
Ask the policyholder why he did not mention knowing the other driver
steps: Withdraw any admission of liability on the engineer evidence
Put the sale listing and the friendship to both drivers in recorded interviews
Notify the credit hire firm that the claim is disputed and hire will not be paid
Review both policies for cancellation and refer to the counter-fraud team
assessment: The damage evidence and the hidden friendship point strongly to a collision that did not happen as described, if at all. It is still "potential" fraud until the drivers are interviewed, because an innocent explanation for the friendship exists, but there is none yet for the rust, the paint and the sale listing.
action: Deny the claim pending investigation, interview both drivers, and pursue cancellation and a fraud referral if the explanations fail.
outcomes: Claim withdrawn after interviews; both policies cancelled
Proceedings issued; claim dismissed as fundamentally dishonest
Drivers prosecuted for fraud by false representation

title: Forty days of storage for a driveable Focus
type: Inflated recovery and storage charges
story: Policyholder admitted rear-ending a Ford Focus in slow traffic in Coventry. The Focus was taken away by a recovery firm called by the other driver's accident management company. Six weeks later the insurer received a bill for recovery, 40 days' storage at £60 a day and an "engineer's inspection fee", totalling £3,130. The Focus is worth about £3,200.
statement: It was a gentle bump in a queue. Her car only had a mark on the bumper and she drove it into the side road. Then a recovery truck turned up within about ten minutes, which I thought was strange because no one had called one in front of me.

accounts.text: Recovery from Coventry ring road to secure compound: £480. Storage at £60 per day for 40 days: £2,400. Independent engineer inspection fee: £250. Total: £3,130. Vehicle deemed unroadworthy and unsafe to drive.

Day 3: emailed the accident management company offering an inspection within 48 hours or a pre-agreed repair. No reply. Day 12: offer repeated by email and phone. Reply on day 31 saying the vehicle "remains in storage pending your acceptance of liability". Companies House: the recovery firm and the accident management company share a director and a registered address.

whatHappened: A minor bump was turned into a profit opportunity: a recovery firm linked to the accident management company took away a driveable car and left it in storage while charges built up, ignoring offers to inspect it.
damage: Focus: rear bumper scuffed and slightly displaced. Policyholder's car: front number plate and grille.
thirdParties: Recovery and storage firm sharing a director with it
evidence: File notes of repeated inspection offers
Policyholder's account of a driveable car
missing: The other driver's own account of whether she asked for recovery
The "independent" engineer report
inconsistencies: The invoice says the car was unroadworthy; the policyholder says it was driven off the road after the bump, and the photos show light damage
Storage continued for weeks after inspection was offered
indicators: Recovery and storage firms linked to the accident management company
Charges approaching the value of the vehicle
Refusal to allow inspection while charges grew
innocent: The other driver may genuinely have been told the car was unsafe and had no say in the storage
Some modern bumpers hide damage to parking sensors and crash bars
questions: Ask the Focus owner directly whether she asked for recovery and who told her the car was unsafe
Ask for the engineer report and the engineer's qualifications
steps: Pay the Focus repair and a reasonable recovery charge only
Refuse storage after day 3, when inspection was first offered, citing the failure to mitigate
Offer the owner direct help to get her car back
Flag the companies' shared director to the counter-fraud team
assessment: Liability for the bump is clear, but the storage bill is not a loss the insurer should pay. The failure to allow inspection breaks the chain. Whether this is fraud or aggressive commercial practice depends on what the owner was told, so it is treated as potential fraud rather than confirmed.
action: Settle repair and reasonable recovery, reject unreasonable storage, and help the owner recover her car directly.
outcomes: Accident management company accepts repair, recovery and three days of storage
Small claims court awards repair and limited storage only
Pattern found across other claims; referred to the counter-fraud team

title: Mum is the main driver, on paper
type: Single-vehicle crash revealing a fronted policy
story: Policyholder's Volkswagen Golf GTI hit a crash barrier on the A580 at 02:10 on a Saturday. Her son Ryan, 19, a named driver, was driving with two friends. The policy lists the policyholder as the main driver. She has a company car through her work.
statement: It's my car and I drive it most of the time, Ryan just borrows it now and then. He was bringing his friends home from a party in Liverpool. He swerved for something in the road and hit the barrier. Thank God nobody was hurt.

accounts.text: A fox ran out and I swerved. I was doing about 50, it's a 50 there. I've had the car since I passed my test, Mum got it for me but she put it in her name because it was cheaper. I use it every day for uni and my job at the gym.

Ryan's social media posts the car with the caption "first car" and photos of it outside his student house in Liverpool across two terms. The last three service invoices are in Ryan's name, at a Liverpool garage. Policyholder's employer confirms she has a company car with fuel card for personal use.

whatHappened: A genuine single-vehicle crash by a young driver, which exposed fronting: the son was the real main driver, and the mother was named as main driver to cut the premium.
damage: Golf GTI: front end, offside wing and wheel; likely total loss, value about £11,500. Crash barrier damaged; the council, as highway authority, will claim for repairs.
thirdParties: The local council, as highway authority, for the crash barrier
evidence: Service invoices in the son's name
Employer's confirmation of the company car
missing: The policy proposal and what was asked about the main driver
Phone data or telematics confirming the speed
inconsistencies: The policyholder says she drives the car most of the time; her son says he has had it since he passed his test and uses it every day
The car spends term time at his student house, 40 miles from the policyholder
indicators: Young driver named only as an occasional driver on a powerful car
Main driver with a separate company car
Son's own admission that the car was put in his mother's name because it was cheaper
innocent: Some parents genuinely believe that owning and paying for the car makes them the main driver
The policyholder may not have understood the main driver question
questions: Ask the policyholder how many miles a week she drives the Golf and when she last drove it
Ask her what she understood by "main driver" when she bought the policy
steps: Obtain the proposal questions and the answers given
Decide whether the misrepresentation was deliberate or reckless, or careless, under CIDRA 2012
Pay the barrier claim as the Road Traffic Act insurer and consider recovery
If careless, settle proportionately, based on the premium the son as main driver would have paid
assessment: The crash is genuine but the policy was very probably fronted. The son's own words suggest the family knew the real arrangement and chose the cheaper option, which points to deliberate misrepresentation. If that is right, the insurer can avoid the policy and keep the premium; if the mother honestly misunderstood, CIDRA requires a proportionate settlement instead.
action: Investigate the proposal answers, interview the policyholder, and decide between avoidance and proportionate settlement on what she knew.
outcomes: Deliberate fronting found; policy avoided, own damage declined, barrier repair paid and recovered
Careless misrepresentation; claim paid proportionately to the premium difference

title: Stolen and burnt out, three months behind on the finance
type: Theft and fire with signs of owner involvement
story: Policyholder reported his BMW 420d stolen from outside his flat in Dennistoun, Glasgow, overnight. It was found burnt out in a park in Easterhouse the next afternoon. The car is on a PCP agreement that is three months in arrears. He has handed in two keys, one of them cut by a locksmith five weeks before the theft.
statement: I parked it outside at about eleven and it was gone at seven when I went to work. I've no idea how they took it, I had both keys in the flat. I lost the second original key a couple of months ago, so I got a new one made to be safe. Yes I'm behind on the finance, I lost hours at work, but I was going to sort it. I'd been trying to sell the car anyway.

accounts.text: Two keys examined. Key 1: original, last used to start the vehicle at 01:52 on the night of the theft. Key 2: locksmith-programmed five weeks earlier, never used to start the vehicle. The vehicle's records show no unknown keys and no sign of the key programming port being accessed in the last 60 days.

Report of stolen vehicle at 07:20. Vehicle found on fire at 14:05 the next day in parkland, Easterhouse. Fire service: fire started inside the cabin, accelerant suspected. No witnesses. Enquiry ongoing, no suspects.
BMW 420d M Sport, listed for sale three times in four months at £21,000, then £19,500, then £18,000. The finance settlement figure is about £22,800. No sale recorded.

whatHappened: Unclear, but the key data is hard to explain: the car was last started with the original key that the policyholder says was in his flat. Together with the arrears, negative equity and failed sale, that points towards an arranged theft. It is not yet proven.
damage: Vehicle burnt out, total loss. Market value about £18,000; finance settlement about £22,800.
thirdParties: Finance company, as owner under the PCP agreement
missing: Who else has had access to the flat and the keys
The policyholder's phone location overnight, if he agrees to provide it
Doorbell or street CCTV near the flat
inconsistencies: He says both keys were in the flat all night; the key data shows the original key started the car at 01:52
He says the second original key was lost; it has not been reported to the police or the finance company
indicators: Financial pressure: arrears, negative equity and a car he could not sell
Car started with a key the policyholder holds
Vehicle burnt out, destroying forensic evidence
Fire started inside the cabin with accelerant
innocent: Someone with access to the flat, such as a partner or friend, could have taken the key without his knowledge
Key data can occasionally be misread, so the report should be checked independently
Cars that are hard to sell are still stolen sometimes
questions: Ask who else lives in or visits the flat and could have used the key that night
Ask him to explain the 01:52 start with the original key, after showing him the data
Ask when and where he lost the second original key, and why he did not report it
steps: Hold the claim and keep the finance company informed
Get an independent review of the key data
Conduct a recorded interview and request CCTV from the street and nearby shops
Share the findings with Police Scotland and decide the claim on all the evidence
assessment: Suspicious, not proven. The key data, the money pressure and the burnt car together make an arranged theft the leading theory, but there are innocent explanations that must be ruled out, especially other people with access to the key. A decline without that work would be unsafe.
action: Investigate before deciding: independent key analysis, a recorded interview and CCTV enquiries. Decline and report only if the evidence holds.
outcomes: Policyholder withdraws the claim after the interview
Another person with access to the key is identified; claim paid
Evidence of involvement established; claim declined, policy voided and police informed

title: The same cracked bumper, claimed twice
type: Duplicate claim with an old insurer and a new one
story: Policyholder reported hitting a bollard while parking at a gym in Northampton "last Thursday" and sent photos of a cracked front bumper and broken fog light. His policy started three weeks ago. A CUE search shows a claim with his previous insurer, settled six weeks ago as a cash payment of £2,100, for front damage from "hitting a bollard".
statement: I clipped a bollard at the gym when I was parking, it's a tight car park. I know I had a claim before but that was a different accident, a completely different bollard, months ago. The car was fixed after that.

accounts.who: Previous insurer's response to a data request
accounts.text: Claim notified 9 weeks ago: front bumper cracked and nearside fog light broken after hitting a bollard at a gym car park. Settled 6 weeks ago as cash in lieu of repair, £2,100, at the customer's request. Five photos supplied; copies attached.

accounts.who: Photo comparison by the counter-fraud team
accounts.text: Three of the four photos sent with this claim are identical to photos sent to the previous insurer: same crack pattern, same reflection and a parked white van in the background. The embedded camera data shows they were taken 10 weeks ago, before the current policy started.

whatHappened: He was paid cash for the bumper by his old insurer, did not repair it, moved to a new insurer and claimed for the same damage again with the same photos and a new date.
damage: Cracked front bumper and broken fog light, repair estimate £2,050. The damage pre-dates the current policy.
evidence: Previous insurer's claim file and photos
Identical photos with camera data from 10 weeks ago
missing: Gym car park records, which could confirm he was not there on the date he gave, although the photo evidence is already conclusive
inconsistencies: He says the car was repaired after the first claim; the first claim was paid in cash and the same damage appears in this claim
He says this was a different accident; three photos are identical to the earlier claim and were taken before the policy started
indicators: Same damage claimed with two insurers
Recycled photos with camera data that pre-dates the policy
Claim shortly after a new policy started
Previous claim settled in cash without repair
innocent: None that fits identical photos taken before the policy existed
questions: Ask him to provide the repair invoice from after the first claim
Ask him when and where the photos were taken
steps: Put the photo evidence to him in writing and give him the chance to respond
Decline the claim and cancel the policy for fraud
Record the outcome on the Insurance Fraud Register and update CUE
Consider reporting to the police or a civil recovery of investigation costs
assessment: Confirmed fraud. Identical photos with camera data from before the policy began leave no room for an innocent explanation. Asking him for the repair invoice gives him a fair chance to answer before the decision.
action: Decline, cancel the policy from the date of the fraud, record it on the Insurance Fraud Register and consider a police referral.
outcomes: Claim declined and policy cancelled; customer does not challenge
Customer withdraws the claim when asked for the repair invoice
Prosecuted for fraud by false representation

title: A genuine bump, and an old scratch added to the bill
type: Genuine rear-end collision with unrelated damage added
story: Policyholder's Kia Sportage was hit from behind at traffic lights in Norwich by a driver who admitted fault. The repair estimate from his chosen garage covers the rear bumper, tailgate and a long scratch along the nearside rear door. Recovery will be sought from the other driver's insurer.
statement: He went into the back of me at the lights, no question about it. The whole back of the car took a hit and that long scratch on the back door must have been from the impact too, it wasn't there before. I keep the car spotless.

accounts.text: Rear bumper and tailgate damage consistent with a rear impact at about 10 mph. Nearside rear door: horizontal scratch 70 cm long at 55 cm height, through to bare metal with surface rust and car wax in the groove. It does not align with the impact zone and could not have been caused by a rear-end collision. In my opinion the scratch is several months old.
I took my eyes off the lights and rolled into the back of the Kia. It was my fault. I hit the middle of his bumper. Nothing else on his car was touched.

whatHappened: A real, minor rear-end collision. The policyholder added an older door scratch to get it fixed at the same time, probably telling himself it might be related.
damage: Accident damage: rear bumper and tailgate, £1,640. Unrelated: rusty scratch on the nearside rear door, £560.
thirdParties: Mr Brian Kettle, the other driver, and his insurer
evidence: Photos of the rear and the door
missing: Photos of the car from before the accident, such as a recent sale or service photo
inconsistencies: He says the door scratch was caused by the impact; the engineer finds rust and wax in it and it is outside the impact zone
indicators: Old damage added to a genuine claim
innocent: He may never have noticed the scratch before and assumed it was new
People often look over their car for the first time after an accident and link everything to it
questions: Ask him when he last cleaned or waxed the car and whether he noticed the door then
Show him the engineer photos of the rust and ask whether he wants to keep the door in the claim
steps: Authorise the rear bumper and tailgate repair
Remove the door from the claim, explaining why with the engineer photos
Recover the accident cost from the other driver's insurer
Note the exaggeration on file; no referral if he accepts the explanation
assessment: Genuine claim, exaggerated at the edge. The extra damage is small and the explanation may be honest, so the right response is to pay what the accident caused and explain clearly, not to decline the whole claim. If he insists, after seeing the evidence, that the scratch is accident damage, the position changes.
action: Pay the accident damage, exclude the door scratch with the engineer evidence, and recover from the third party.
outcomes: Accepts the explanation; rear repair paid and recovered
Insists on the door; complaint not upheld on the engineer evidence
Pays the garage privately for the door at the same time

title: Wrong day, wrong car park, honest mistake
type: Car park damage reported with the wrong date and place
story: Policyholder, 86, reported through his daughter that his Honda Jazz was dented by another car in a supermarket car park in Worthing on Tuesday morning. The supermarket says its CCTV does not show his car on Tuesday. He later found a note from the other driver, dated Wednesday, at a garden centre.
statement: Reported by his daughter, Mrs Lynne Carter: Dad says someone dented his door at the supermarket on Tuesday. He found a note under his wiper with a phone number but he's lost it. He's very upset, he's never claimed in 60 years of driving. Later the same week: We found the note in his coat. It says Wednesday and it was the garden centre, not the supermarket. He gets his days muddled now. I'm so sorry for the confusion.

accounts.text: We have reviewed our car park CCTV for Tuesday between 08:00 and 13:00. We could not find a silver Honda Jazz with that registration. Footage is kept for 30 days if you need us to check another date.

accounts.who: Handwritten note found by the daughter
accounts.text: "Wednesday 11.15. So sorry, I caught your door with mine in the wind. Please call me. Margaret" followed by a mobile number and a car registration. The note is on the back of a garden centre receipt dated Wednesday.

whatHappened: An elderly customer muddled the day and the place. The note, the receipt and the other driver's details show the damage happened on Wednesday at the garden centre, caused by another driver's door.
damage: Dent and paint chip on the driver's door of the Honda Jazz, about £420.
thirdParties: Margaret, the driver who left the note, and her insurer
evidence: Handwritten note with a phone number and registration
missing: The other driver's confirmation of what happened
Her insurer's details
inconsistencies: The first report says Tuesday at the supermarket; the note and receipt show Wednesday at the garden centre
innocent: Memory slips about days and places are common in very elderly people and are not dishonest
The daughter corrected the report as soon as the note was found
questions: Ask the other driver, kindly, to confirm what happened and give her insurer's details
Ask the daughter whether her father would like her to be added as a contact on the policy
steps: Record the corrected date and place, with a note that the first report was an honest error
Contact the other driver and claim against her insurer
Repair under the policy if the other insurer is slow, then recover the cost
Flag the customer as potentially vulnerable so future calls are handled with care
assessment: Genuine. The supermarket CCTV result looked like a red flag, but the note explains everything. This customer needs patience and support, not suspicion, and the insurer's duty to treat vulnerable customers fairly applies.
action: Correct the record, claim against the other driver's insurer, and add a support note to the policy with the customer's consent.
outcomes: Other insurer accepts liability; repair paid by them and the customer's no-claims discount is protected
Other driver cannot be traced; repaired under the policy with the excess

title: Sixty days in a hired 5 Series for a ten-day repair
type: Third-party credit hire dispute
story: Policyholder rear-ended a Skoda Superb in Leicester and accepted liability. The Skoda's driver took a BMW 5 Series from a credit hire company for 60 days at £320 a day, £19,200 in total. The Skoda was repaired in 10 working days once the parts arrived. The hire company is claiming the full amount from the insurer.
statement: It was my fault and I said so. I just think it's wrong that they can run up a bill like that on my insurance.

accounts.text: Our client was provided with a vehicle of similar type and quality. The repair was delayed by parts availability and awaiting authorisation from the at-fault insurer. Our client is a self-employed electrician and needs a vehicle for work every day. Our client could not afford to hire a vehicle on ordinary terms. Hire period 60 days at £320 per day.

Day 2: offered the third party a direct replacement car and repair through an approved garage. Declined by the hire company. Day 9: engineer authorised the repair. Day 35: garage reports parts delayed by the manufacturer. Day 49: repair complete. Day 60: hire vehicle returned. Third party has a 2019 Skoda Superb estate.

whatHappened: A genuine accident with a genuine need for a car, but the hire was longer and more expensive than the loss required. The dispute is about need, period and rate, not about whether the accident happened.
damage: Skoda Superb rear end repaired for £3,800. Hire claim £19,200.
thirdParties: Credit hire company acting for him
evidence: File notes of the early offer
missing: The third party's bank statements, to test the claim that he could not afford to pay for hire
Evidence of how he uses the car for work
Basic hire rate quotes for a comparable car
inconsistencies: The hire continued for 11 days after the repair was complete
innocent: Parts delays are real and are not the claimant's fault
A self-employed tradesman genuinely loses income without a vehicle
questions: Ask why the hire continued 11 days after the repair was complete
Ask the hire company for evidence that the claimant could not afford ordinary hire
Ask why a BMW 5 Series was chosen to replace a Skoda Superb estate used for work
steps: Accept a reasonable period: authorisation, repair and the proven parts delay
Challenge the 11 days after the repair and any delay caused by the hire company
Value the hire at basic hire rates unless the claimant proves he could not afford to pay
Negotiate, or defend the excess if the case is issued
assessment: Not fraud: a dispute over how much hire is recoverable. Under the case law the claimant can recover hire charges only for a reasonable period, at basic hire rates unless he proves impecuniosity. The insurer's early offer of a replacement car strengthens its position.
action: Offer the hire for the reasonable period at basic hire rates, rejecting the post-repair days, and defend the balance if necessary.
outcomes: Settled at about £8,000 after negotiation
Court allows the full period but at basic hire rates
Claimant proves impecuniosity; the credit hire rate is allowed for the reasonable period

title: Written off in the rain, with a remap nobody declared
type: Total loss revealing undeclared modifications
story: Policyholder, 22, lost control of his Ford Fiesta ST on a wet bend near Swansea and hit a hedge bank. The car has been declared a Category S write-off. The engineer found an engine remap, aftermarket alloy wheels and lowered suspension. None were declared when the policy was bought.
statement: It was really wet and the back stepped out on the bend. I wasn't speeding. I bought the car like that from a guy in Cardiff a year ago. I didn't know a remap counted as a modification, I thought that meant body kits. The wheels I just thought were nicer wheels.

accounts.text: Category S: structural damage to the nearside rear suspension mounting. ECU remapped, estimated output 240 bhp against 197 bhp standard. 18-inch aftermarket alloy wheels. Lowering springs fitted. Tyres legal, 4 mm front and 3 mm rear. Pre-accident value £13,900 as modified, £12,600 as standard.

accounts.who: Sale advert from a year ago, found online
accounts.text: "Fiesta ST-3, Stage 1 remap, approx 240bhp, lowered, 18in alloys, loads of receipts." Seller in Cardiff. Asking price £14,500.

whatHappened: A genuine loss-of-control crash on a wet bend. The modifications came with the car, the advert shows he knew about them, but he probably did not understand that he had to declare them.
damage: Category S total loss. Value as standard £12,600; as modified £13,900.
thirdParties: None. The hedge bank is on unadopted land and the landowner has not claimed
evidence: Old sale advert listing the modifications
Proposal record showing no modifications declared
missing: The exact modifications question asked when he bought the policy
The underwriter's answer: would the insurer have covered the car with these modifications, and at what price?
inconsistencies: He says he did not know about the modifications in a meaningful way; the advert he bought from lists them clearly
indicators: Undeclared performance modifications on a young driver's car
innocent: Many drivers do not realise a remap counts as a modification
He bought the car already modified and did not make the changes himself
questions: Ask him to describe how he answered the modifications question when he bought the policy
Ask whether he has kept the receipts that came with the car
steps: Get the proposal question and decide whether it was clear
Ask underwriting what they would have done with full information
Classify the misrepresentation under CIDRA 2012 as deliberate or reckless, careless, or neither
Settle on the standard value, proportionately reduced if careless, or refund the premium if the insurer would not have covered the car at all
assessment: The crash is genuine; the issue is an undeclared remap. On the evidence this looks careless rather than deliberate: he bought the car modified and misunderstood the question. CIDRA then requires a proportionate remedy based on what the insurer would have done if he had told it.
action: Do not decline outright. Apply the CIDRA remedy for careless misrepresentation once underwriting confirms the premium or acceptance position.
outcomes: Insurer would have charged 35% more; claim paid at 74% of the standard value
Insurer would not have covered the car; premium refunded and claim declined
Question found unclear; claim paid in full at the standard value

title: Burnt out, reported nine days late, and entirely genuine
type: Theft discovered while the owner was abroad
story: Policyholder reported her 2011 Honda Civic stolen nine days after it was found burnt out in Bolton. She says she was in Pakistan visiting family for three weeks and only found out when the police contacted her brother. A late report of a burnt-out car normally prompts suspicion.
statement: I left the car on my drive and gave my brother the spare key so he could move it if needed. He didn't need to, so he didn't go round. The police found the registered keeper was me and got through to him through a neighbour. I flew back early to sort it out. I have all my tickets. I don't owe anything on that car, it's 13 years old, it's worth nothing to anyone except me.

accounts.text: Vehicle found on fire on wasteland in Farnworth at 22:40. No registered keeper contact at the home address. Neighbour gave a phone number for the keeper's brother on day 6. Brother attended the station on day 7 with the spare key. Keeper reported the theft by phone from abroad on day 9.

E-tickets Manchester to Lahore and return, with boarding passes, covering the full period. Passport stamps consistent. Both keys examined: the original was with the policyholder in Pakistan; the spare was held by her brother. The car has an older immobiliser with known weaknesses, and similar models have been stolen locally.

whatHappened: The car was stolen while she was abroad and burnt out by thieves. The late report is fully explained by her absence.
damage: Car burnt out, total loss. Market value about £2,400.
evidence: Flight tickets, boarding passes and passport stamps
missing: Street CCTV from the night the car disappeared, which may not exist
innocent: The late report, the fire and the old car are all explained by documented travel
questions: Ask the brother whether he noticed the car missing at any point
Ask whether anyone else had access to the drive
steps: Verify the travel documents
Confirm both keys with the police log
Settle the market value less the excess
Record why the late notification was accepted
assessment: Genuine. Several features that often go with false theft claims are present, but each is explained by solid evidence. The insurer should settle promptly and not let its first impression delay a fair outcome.
action: Settle the total loss at market value and close.
outcomes: Paid at market value of about £2,400 less the excess

title: A crash in Ilford by a car that was in Leeds
type: Claim against a policyholder whose number plates were cloned
story: The insurer received a claim from a driver in Ilford, east London, saying the policyholder's black Audi A3 hit her car and drove off at 16:05 on a Friday. She noted the registration. The policyholder says he and his car were in Leeds all that day.
statement: I was at work in Leeds all day Friday and the car was in the staff car park from 08:20 until gone six. I've never even driven in Ilford. I did get a speeding letter from London last month for a road I've never been on, and I ignored it because I thought it was a scam.

accounts.text: A black Audi A3 came out of a side road and hit my front wing, then reversed and drove off. I wrote down the registration on my hand. The driver was a young man with a beard. The Audi had roof bars and a big dent in the back bumper.

accounts.who: Staff car park access log and ANPR enquiry
accounts.text: Employer's car park: vehicle entered 08:21, exited 18:07 on the Friday. Police ANPR: the same registration recorded on the A13 in east London at 15:48 and on the M1 near Leeds at 07:55 the same day, 200 miles apart. The policyholder's car has no roof bars and an undamaged rear bumper.

whatHappened: Another Audi was using cloned copies of his number plates. The third party is a genuine victim of a hit-and-run by the clone; she is wrong only about which car was involved.
damage: Third party's Toyota Yaris: front wing and bumper, about £1,450. Policyholder's car undamaged.
thirdParties: Ms Yasmin Rahman, the driver who was hit
The unknown driver of the cloned Audi
evidence: Photos showing no roof bars and no rear dent on the real car
missing: A police crime reference for the cloned plates
DVLA confirmation that the case has been logged
inconsistencies: The third party describes roof bars and a dented rear bumper; the policyholder's car has neither
ANPR places the registration in east London and Leeds within hours
indicators: Number plates cloned onto another car of the same make, model and colour
Speeding notice from a road the owner never used
innocent: The third party honestly recorded the plate she saw and is not at fault for the confusion
questions: Ask the policyholder for the speeding notice so the police can link the offences
Ask the third party whether she has dashcam footage or photos of the Audi
steps: Deny liability with the alibi evidence and explain it kindly to the third party
Tell the third party she can claim through the Motor Insurers' Bureau untraced drivers scheme
Help the policyholder report the cloning to the police and DVLA and consider a new registration
Note the cloning on the policy so future claims are checked quickly
assessment: The policyholder is the victim of plate cloning, and the third party is the victim of the clone's driver. Neither is dishonest. The evidence clearly clears the policyholder, and the third party should be pointed to the untraced driver route rather than left without help.
action: Deny liability, redirect the third party to the MIB, and support the policyholder in stopping the cloning.
outcomes: Third party accepts the evidence and claims from the MIB
Police find the cloned car and the driver is prosecuted
Policyholder gets a new registration from DVLA

title: Paid the other driver privately, then the solicitor’s letter came
type: Late notification after a private settlement fell through
story: Policyholder notified the claim on 14 October, more than five months after a low-speed rear-end collision on 2 May at traffic lights on Fabian Way, Swansea. At the scene he agreed with the other driver to pay for her repairs himself to protect his no-claims discount, and paid £650 by bank transfer. On 9 October he received a letter from her solicitors notifying whiplash claims for her and her passenger, and asking for more money for the repairs.
statement: It was a tap in the queue at the lights, my fault, I'll say that straight away. She seemed fine and we agreed I'd sort her bumper so I didn't lose my no-claims. I paid what her garage asked. I never thought I'd hear any more about it. Now a solicitor says both of them were injured and the bumper cost more. I didn't tell you before because I didn't think there was anything to tell.

accounts.text: We act for Ms Leanne Morgan and her passenger Mr Kieran Morgan following a collision on 2 May at Fabian Way, Swansea. Both suffered whiplash injuries. Claims have been submitted through the Official Injury Claim portal. Our client also claims the balance of her repairs, £1,140, and 12 days of car hire. Please confirm your insurer's details within 21 days.
Transfer of £650.00 on 6 May from G Pryce to L Morgan, reference "bumper Fabian Way". No further payments between the two accounts.

whatHappened: A genuine low-speed rear-end collision for which he was at fault. He settled the damage privately to protect his discount and did not tell his insurer until the solicitor's letter arrived.
damage: Policyholder's Corsa: minor scuff to the front bumper, not claimed. Third party's Fiesta: rear bumper, £650 already paid privately; a further £1,140 and hire now claimed.
thirdParties: Leanne Morgan, driver of the Fiesta
evidence: Policyholder's photos of the Fiesta's bumper taken at the scene
missing: Medical reports for either injury claimant
The garage's invoice for the original repair
Messages exchanged with Ms Morgan after the accident
inconsistencies: The policyholder says Ms Morgan seemed uninjured at the scene; the solicitors say both occupants were injured
indicators: Injury claims arriving five months after a low-speed impact with no injury mentioned at the scene
Repair costs rising after a private settlement
innocent: Soft-tissue symptoms often appear a day or two after a collision
Drivers commonly settle small bumps privately to protect a no-claims discount, without realising the policy requires every incident to be reported
questions: Ask the policyholder for his scene photos, his messages with Ms Morgan and her garage's original quote
Ask whether the passenger was in the car and whether anyone mentioned pain at the scene
steps: Register the claim and take over the third-party claims now: late notice breaches the claims condition, but it does not remove the cover third parties rely on
Check whether the delay has prejudiced the insurer, for example lost evidence or costs that could have been avoided
Respond to the injury claims within the portal time limits and ask for the medical evidence
Give credit for the £650 already paid when settling the property claim
assessment: Genuine, at fault, notified late. The late notice and the private deal breach the policy conditions but the prejudice looks limited. The injury claims need the normal scrutiny given the low speed and the five-month gap, not an assumption of fraud.
action: Take over the third-party claims, investigate the injuries in the normal way, and remind the policyholder that every incident must be reported.
outcomes: Property settled with credit for the £650; injury claims settled at the tariff after medical reports
Passenger claim withdrawn when no medical evidence is produced

title: A claims firm that says it acts for him, and a signature he says is not his
type: Claim notified by a claims management firm without the policyholder’s authority
story: Insurer received an email from Apex Accident Assist saying it acts for the policyholder after a collision on the A40 in Oxford. It attached a signed authority form and asked the insurer to pay storage of £45 a day and release the car to its partner garage for repair. When the claims team called the policyholder, he said he had never heard of the firm. A recovery truck had stopped at the scene and taken his car "for safety", and the driver had asked for his details for the paperwork.
statement: Another car clipped my side as it came out of a petrol station. We swapped details. A tow truck pulled up within five minutes, I thought my breakdown cover had sent it. The driver took my licence photo and had me sign something on his phone screen, he said it was the tow receipt. I never asked anyone to make a claim for me. I want my car back and I don't want to pay storage to anyone.

accounts.text: Client: O. Adeyemi. I authorise Apex Accident Assist to act on my behalf in all matters arising from the accident on the A40, to arrange recovery, storage and repairs, and to receive payment. Signed electronically at 16:52, the time stamped as 18 minutes after the collision.
No call received from this member on the date of the accident. No recovery dispatched.

whatHappened: A genuine minor collision. An unsolicited recovery operator took the car and passed the policyholder's details to a claims firm, which is trying to build storage and repair charges against the insurer without his real consent.
damage: Policyholder's Golf: nearside doors scraped and dented. Storage invoice from the claims firm's yard: 6 days at £45 so far and rising.
thirdParties: The driver who came out of the petrol station
evidence: Authority form with an electronic signature
Photos of the damage taken by the policyholder
missing: The recovery operator's identity and trading name
The other driver’s insurer
The device record behind the electronic signature
inconsistencies: The form says he authorised a claims firm; he says he signed a tow receipt
indicators: Recovery truck at the scene within minutes without being called
Authority signed on a phone 18 minutes after the crash
Daily storage running at a yard the policyholder did not choose
innocent: Some recovery operators are called by police or passers-by; he may genuinely have signed a form he did not read
questions: Ask the policyholder to confirm in writing that he did not instruct the firm and wants the insurer to deal with the claim
Ask the firm for the full signed record, its regulatory authorisation and the basis of its storage charges
steps: Treat the policyholder as the customer and get his instructions directly, not through the claims firm
Do not pay storage or release the car to the firm until its authority is proved; arrange collection of the car to an approved repairer with the policyholder’s consent
Record how his personal data reached the firm and consider whether a data protection complaint is needed
Share the pattern with the counter-fraud team if the firm or the recovery operator appears on other claims
assessment: The accident looks genuine; the claims firm's involvement does not. The signature was obtained at the roadside under a misleading description, so the authority is doubtful and the storage charges should not be accepted.
action: Deal with the policyholder directly, move the car, refuse the storage and refer the firm's conduct to the counter-fraud team.
outcomes: Car moved to an approved repairer; the firm withdraws its storage invoice
Firm linked to other roadside sign-ups and reported

title: Borrowed a friend’s Golf, and his own policy did not follow him
type: Driving-other-cars extension used on a car that was not insured
story: Policyholder was driving a friend's Volkswagen Golf in Reading to collect a takeaway when he clipped a parked delivery van while pulling into a space. He has comprehensive cover on his own car with a driving-other-cars extension and has claimed under it for the van's damage. A check of the Motor Insurance Database shows the friend's own policy on the Golf lapsed three weeks before the accident.
statement: My policy says I can drive other cars, third party only, so I didn't think twice. Jamie said the car was fine to use. I had no idea his insurance had run out, he never mentioned it. I left a note on the van and called the number on the side straight away. I just want the van fixed, it was completely my fault.

accounts.text: You may drive a private car that does not belong to you and is not hired to you, with the owner's permission, for third-party cover only, provided the car is insured by its owner under a separate policy and you hold a full licence.
Golf registration: no current insurance record. Previous policy ended 21 days before the accident date. No continuous insurance enforcement letter yet issued.

whatHappened: A genuine low-speed parking collision. He relied on an extension that only applies when the borrowed car is itself insured, and neither he nor the owner checked.
damage: Delivery van: nearside rear corner panel and light, estimate £1,450. Golf: front bumper scuffed.
thirdParties: Jamie Fenwick, owner of the Golf
evidence: Photo of the note he left on the van
missing: The Golf owner's lapse notice from his former insurer
Confirmation from the van owner of how they want to claim
innocent: Many drivers believe the extension covers any car they borrow with permission
questions: Ask the Golf owner when he knew his policy had ended
Ask the van owner whether they hold their own cover and have claimed under it
steps: Confirm the extension’s condition that the borrowed car must be insured, and that it is not met here
Decline cover under the extension in writing, explaining the condition plainly
Explain the route for the van owner: their own policy or the Motor Insurers’ Bureau for an uninsured vehicle, and check whether the insurer has any role under the MIB arrangements before closing
Tell the policyholder that driving without valid cover may lead to enforcement and that he should not drive the Golf again
assessment: Genuine accident, honest driver, no cover. The extension only works when the borrowed car is insured, so the van's damage is not covered under his policy.
action: Decline under the extension with a clear explanation and point the van owner to the right route.
outcomes: Declined; the van owner claims from their own insurer, which recovers from the drivers
Complaint to the Financial Ombudsman not upheld because the condition is clear

title: Cancelled for a missed payment, by a notice she says never arrived
type: Collision two days after a cancellation for non-payment
story: Policyholder pays her premium monthly by direct debit. The July instalment was returned unpaid. The insurer's system shows a seven-day notice of cancellation issued by email on 18 July and the policy cancelled on 26 July. On 28 July she was in a collision at a junction in Leicester and called to claim, and was told she had no cover. She says she received no notice and that the payment failed because her bank changed her account number.
statement: My bank moved me to a new account in July and told me direct debits would carry over. Nobody told me one had failed. I've had no email and no letter. I check my email every day. If you'd told me I'd have paid the same afternoon. I've been with you for four years and never missed anything. The other driver went into the back of me, it wasn't even my fault.

accounts.text: 18 July 09:14: notice of cancellation for non-payment sent by email to priya.chauhan@gmial.com. 18 July 09:15: delivery failure returned, address not found. No letter generated: customer's preference set to email only. 26 July: policy cancelled.
If an instalment is not paid we may cancel your policy by giving you seven days' notice in writing to the email or postal address we hold for you.

whatHappened: A collision in which she was probably not at fault, two days after a cancellation whose notice never reached her because of a mistyped email address on her record.
damage: Her Corolla: rear bumper, boot lid and rear panel, estimate £3,200. The other car: front end damage.
thirdParties: The driver who hit her at the junction
evidence: Communications log with the failed delivery
Bank's letter about the account change
missing: Who entered the email address and when
The other driver's insurer and account of the collision
inconsistencies: The insurer says notice was given; its own log shows the notice was never delivered
innocent: A bank account switch can stop a direct debit without the customer knowing
A mistyped email domain would explain why nothing arrived
questions: Ask the policyholder for the bank’s account change letter
Check when the email address on file was last confirmed by her
steps: Review whether the cancellation was valid: the notice bounced and no letter was sent, so she may never have been given notice as the terms require
If notice was not validly given, treat the policy as in force on 28 July, take the unpaid instalment, and handle the claim
Pursue the other driver’s insurer for her losses if she was not at fault
Fix the record and check for other customers affected by the same failure mode
assessment: Disputed cover, but the evidence favours the customer: notice was never delivered and the insurer knew it the same minute. Relying on that cancellation would be hard to defend and unfair.
action: Reinstate cover for the date of the accident, collect the missed instalment and handle the claim.
outcomes: Cover reinstated; claim handled and recovered from the other driver’s insurer
Root-cause fix: bounced cancellation notices now trigger a letter

title: A learner, her brother in the passenger seat, and two years too few
type: Learner driver supervised by someone who did not meet the legal requirements
story: Policyholder is 17 and holds a provisional licence and a learner driver policy. While practising reversing into a bay at a retail park in Norwich she struck a parked Kia, damaging both cars. Her supervisor was her brother, aged 22, who passed his test two years and four months before the accident. The policy requires the supervisor to meet the legal conditions for supervising a learner.
statement: My brother's been driving for ages and he's really careful, Mum couldn't come that day. I misjudged the turn and the back corner went into the Kia. We waited for the owner and gave our details. I didn't know there was a rule about how long he'd had his licence. Will I lose my cover?

accounts.who: DVLA licence check of the supervisor
accounts.text: Full licence category B issued 2 years and 4 months before the accident date. Age 22. No endorsements.
You are covered only while you are supervised by a person aged 21 or over who has held a full UK licence for that type of vehicle for at least three years.

whatHappened: A genuine low-speed reversing accident. Her supervisor was over 21 but had not held his licence for the three years the law and the policy require.
damage: Her Fiesta: rear bumper and light, £900. Parked Kia: front wing and bumper, £1,700.
evidence: DVLA check of the brother's licence
missing: Whether a qualified supervisor was available that day
innocent: Many families do not know the three-year rule
questions: Confirm who was supervising and that the licence details are his
steps: Decline her own repairs: the supervision condition was not met

Handle the Kia owner’s claim: the insurer’s duties to third parties under the Road Traffic Act are wider than its own cover, and the policy may give a right to recover the outlay from the policyholder
Explain plainly why the own damage is not covered and what qualifies as a supervisor in future
assessment: Genuine accident, careless but honest. The supervision condition is a clear legal requirement and it was not met, so her own damage is not covered; the third party should not suffer for it.
action: Decline own damage, pay the Kia owner and consider recovery, with a clear explanation to the family.
outcomes: Kia owner paid; recovery of £1,700 agreed in instalments
Recovery waived after a hardship review

title: A winter in Alicante, and the 90-day limit in the small print
type: Collision abroad after the period of full cover in Europe had run out
story: Policyholder took his car on the ferry to Santander on 2 January to spend the winter near Alicante. On 15 April, 104 days later, he collided with a Spanish driver's Seat on a roundabout and has claimed for both cars. His schedule gives comprehensive cover in the EU for up to 90 days in any one period of insurance, then the minimum cover required by law in the country visited. He flew home for a week in March but the car stayed in Spain.
statement: The broker told me I was fully covered in Europe. I came home in March for my grandson's christening, so I thought the 90 days started again when I went back. The Spanish lady was very nice, we filled in the blue and yellow form together. I pulled onto the roundabout and misjudged her speed. My car needs a new wing and headlamp.

accounts.text: Completed and signed by both drivers at the roundabout. Vehicle B (policyholder) entering the roundabout; vehicle A already on it. Both boxes ticked consistent with B failing to give way. Sketch agrees.
Portsmouth to Santander, 2 January, one car and one passenger. Return sailing booked for 30 April.

whatHappened: A genuine roundabout collision abroad, after the 90 days of comprehensive cover in the period of insurance had been used up.
damage: His Qashqai: front wing, headlamp and bumper, about £3,900. The Seat: rear door and quarter panel.
missing: The broker's notes of what he was told about cover abroad
innocent: A trip home without the car could easily be mistaken for the start of a new trip
questions: Ask the broker for its record of the advice given
Confirm the dates the car was in Spain
steps: Handle the Spanish driver’s claim: the minimum legal cover still applies after the 90 days
Decline his own repairs: the 90 days run per period of insurance, not per trip, and were used up
If the broker told him he was fully covered, explain how to complain to the broker
assessment: Genuine collision abroad. Third-party cover still applies at the legal minimum, but comprehensive cover had ended after 90 days in the period of insurance.
action: Pay the Spanish third party, decline own damage with a clear explanation of the wording, and point him to the broker about the advice.
outcomes: Third party paid; own damage declined
Broker pays part of his repairs after a complaint about the advice

title: Three nurses, one car, and £20 each for petrol
type: Car-share passengers injured; hire-and-reward exclusion queried
story: Policyholder drives two colleagues to the hospital in Bristol for their early shifts, and each gives her £20 a week towards fuel. In fog she pulled out of a side road into the path of a van; both passengers were injured. The claims handler noted the weekly payments and asked whether the policy's exclusion for carrying passengers for hire or reward applies.
statement: We all live on the same estate and work the same shifts, so I drive. The girls give me £20 a week each, it doesn't even cover the diesel, I worked it out once. I didn't see the van in the fog, I looked twice. Ngozi hurt her neck and Sam broke her wrist on the door. I feel terrible.

accounts.who: Fuel and mileage note from the policyholder
accounts.text: Round trip 31 miles, five days a week, about 155 miles a week. Diesel about £27 a week, plus servicing and tyres. Contributions £40 a week in total, agreed before the arrangement started.
She came out of the side road right in front of me. Visibility was poor, maybe fifty metres, and I had my lights on. I braked but I couldn't stop.

whatHappened: A genuine junction collision in fog for which she was at fault. The fuel money is a car-sharing contribution towards running costs, not a fare.
damage: Her Octavia: front end and nearside wing. Van: nearside side panels. Passengers: a neck sprain and a fractured wrist.
evidence: Photos of the junction and vehicles
Hospital discharge note for the wrist fracture
missing: Medical reports for both passengers
innocent: Regular payments between colleagues can look like fares until the running costs are worked out
questions: Confirm the contributions were agreed before the journeys began and do not exceed the running costs
steps: Apply section 150 of the Road Traffic Act 1988: car-sharing contributions that do not exceed running costs, in a car carrying no more than eight passengers and arranged before the journey, are not hire or reward
Confirm cover and handle the passengers’ injury claims and the van owner’s claim
Record the reasoning so the exclusion is not raised again on renewal
assessment: Genuine and covered. The payments are a car-sharing contribution below the running costs, which the law treats as outside the hire-and-reward exclusion.
action: Confirm cover, accept liability for the junction collision and handle both injury claims and the van.
outcomes: Cover confirmed; injury claims settled
Policyholder reassured and keeps the car share

title: The supplement after the strip-down, and the rust behind the wing
type: Hidden damage found on strip-down, mixed with older corrosion
story: Policyholder slid into a stone gatepost in the rain on a farm track near Brecon. The first estimate, agreed from photos, was £2,800 for the bumper, headlamp and wing. After strip-down the repairer asked for a supplement of £3,600 for the nearside chassis leg, inner wing and radiator support. Strip-down photos show a kinked chassis leg with fresh bare metal, and an inner wing with rust holes and old filler.
statement: I took the corner too fast and the front corner hit the gatepost, it was quite a bang. The garage rang and said there's more damage underneath. The car's eleven years old, I know it's not perfect, but it drove fine before. I just want it put back how it was.

accounts.text: On strip-down: nearside chassis leg kinked 40 mm, requires section repair. Inner wing damaged and corroded, recommend replacement. Radiator support cracked at the mounting. Additional £3,600 including jig time.
Advisory recorded 2 years before the accident: "Nearside front inner wing corroded." Same advisory 1 year before. No advisories for the chassis leg or radiator support.

whatHappened: A genuine impact that bent the chassis leg and cracked the radiator support. The corroded inner wing was already failing and its replacement is partly old wear, not crash damage.
damage: Kuga: bumper, headlamp, wing, chassis leg, radiator support, and an inner wing that is both damaged and corroded. Agreed £2,800 plus £3,600 requested.
missing: An engineer's inspection of the inner wing
Close-up photos of the chassis leg fracture surfaces
inconsistencies: The repairer lists the inner wing as crash damage; the MOT history shows it was corroded for two years
indicators: Supplement larger than the original estimate
Old corrosion presented as crash damage
innocent: Hidden damage behind a front corner impact is common and photos cannot show it
The repairer may simply have recommended the inner wing because it cannot be welded to sound metal
questions: Ask the repairer for close-ups of the inner wing and the chassis leg
Ask the engineer whether the inner wing could be repaired locally once the corrosion is cut out
steps: Send an engineer to inspect before authorising the supplement
Accept the chassis leg and radiator support as crash damage
Treat the corroded inner wing as betterment or wear: pay only for the crash-related part of the work
Recheck whether the total now makes the car uneconomical to repair
assessment: Mixed. The impact was genuine and the hidden damage is mostly real, but the corroded inner wing pre-dates the accident and should not be paid in full.
action: Inspect, approve the crash-related supplement and agree a contribution for the corroded inner wing.
outcomes: Supplement approved at £2,450 after the inner wing is split
Car declared uneconomical to repair when the total passes its value

title: A new exhaust and four tyres after one kerb
type: Betterment on parts that were worn before the accident
story: Policyholder lost grip on a frosty morning in Perth and slid sideways into a high kerb at low speed. The nearside wheels, two tyres and the exhaust were damaged. Her garage replaced the whole exhaust system, all four tyres and the nearside wheels. The insurer's assessor has deducted a betterment contribution from the invoice, and she has phoned to complain.
statement: It's a 2012 Jazz with 160,000 miles on it and it's my lifeline, I care for my mum. The garage said the exhaust was knackered anyway and they couldn't fit just the middle section, so they did the lot. They said you should never have two new tyres and two old ones. Why should I pay for any of it when the ice did this?

accounts.text: Full exhaust system £640, of which middle section damaged by impact. Two nearside alloy wheels £420. Four tyres £380: two nearside damaged, two offside at 2 mm tread. Labour £210.
Front and rear exhaust sections heavily corroded before the incident. Offside tyres not damaged. Betterment applied: £330 for the exhaust sections not damaged, offside tyres removed from the claim.

whatHappened: A genuine low-speed slide into a kerb. Part of the repair replaced worn parts that were not damaged, which put the car in a better state than before.
damage: Jazz: two nearside wheels and tyres, exhaust middle section. Worn but undamaged: exhaust front and rear sections, two offside tyres.
evidence: Photos of the exhaust and the tyres
missing: Whether the middle exhaust section was available on its own
innocent: Garages often replace worn neighbouring parts to give a sound repair
questions: Ask the garage whether a middle section alone was available and at what price
steps: Pay for the parts the accident damaged: the two wheels, two tyres and the exhaust section
Explain the betterment clearly: the undamaged worn sections and tyres were replaced by choice
If a middle section could not be bought alone, reduce or drop the exhaust contribution
Note her caring responsibilities and handle the complaint promptly
assessment: Genuine claim; a fair betterment question. The worn tyres should not be paid, but the exhaust contribution depends on whether a partial repair was really possible.
action: Pay the damaged parts, keep the tyre deduction, and recheck the exhaust contribution with the garage.
outcomes: Exhaust contribution dropped when no middle section was available; tyre deduction kept
Complaint closed with an explanation she accepts

title: Agreed at £24,000, offered £17,500
type: Total loss of a classic car on an agreed value policy
story: Policyholder's 1972 Triumph Stag was written off when a tractor pulled out of a field entrance into its side on a lane near Ludlow. The car is insured on an agreed value policy at £24,000, set at inception from an owners' club valuation with photographs. The insurer's total loss team has offered £17,500, based on recent auction results for similar cars.
statement: I've owned her for nineteen years. We agreed the value with you three years ago, you had the club's report and thirty photos. Nothing about the car changed since then except it got better, I had the hood replaced. Why am I being offered auction prices now? The tractor driver admitted it at the scene.

accounts.text: Agreed value: £24,000. Basis of settlement for a total loss: the agreed value shown in the schedule, less any excess. Valuation report and photographs held on file at inception.
I was coming out of the gate and the hedge blocks the view. I edged out and didn't see him. My fault, I've told my boss and our insurer.

whatHappened: A genuine collision caused by the tractor. The car is a total loss and the policy pays the agreed value, not a market value.
damage: Stag: chassis and offside body crushed, total loss. Tractor: minor scrape to the front weight.
thirdParties: Farm that owns the tractor and its insurer
evidence: Policy schedule with the agreed value
Club valuation and photos from inception
missing: The farm insurer's acknowledgement of liability
inconsistencies: The settlement offer uses auction values; the policy promises the agreed value
innocent: A total loss team may have applied the standard market value process by mistake
questions: Ask whether anything about the car has changed since the valuation that would affect the agreed value
steps: Settle at the agreed value less the excess, as the schedule says
Pursue the farm’s insurer for the outlay; liability is admitted
Offer the policyholder the chance to retain the salvage at an agreed deduction if he wants to rebuild
Find out why the agreed value basis was missed and fix the process
assessment: Genuine and straightforward on cover. The agreed value binds the insurer unless something material changed or was misstated, and nothing suggests that.
action: Pay £24,000 less the excess and recover from the tractor's insurer.
outcomes: Agreed value paid; full recovery from the farm insurer
Policyholder retains the salvage for a rebuild

title: Paid out for the stolen RAV4, then the police found it
type: Stolen car recovered after the total loss settlement
story: Policyholder's Toyota RAV4 was stolen from her driveway in Solihull without the keys. After 30 days the insurer paid a total loss settlement of £27,400 and she bought another car. Seven weeks later police found the RAV4 in a lock-up in Coventry on false plates with a damaged ignition, a missing rear seat and scratched paintwork. She has asked whether she can have it back.
statement: I loved that car, it had my dad's old sat nav mount and everything. I've bought another car now but if I can get the RAV4 back for a sensible price I'd sell the new one. Does it belong to me or to you now? The police said to ring my insurer.

accounts.text: Vehicle identified by its chassis number in a lock-up with three other stolen vehicles. False registration plates fitted. Ignition barrel damaged, rear seat missing, paint scratched on both sides. Released to the owner's insurer on request.

Total loss settlement £27,400 paid to the policyholder 30 days after the theft. Signed form of discharge transfers the vehicle to the insurer on payment. Vehicle recorded on the theft register; register update pending.

whatHappened: A genuine theft. The car was recovered after the settlement, so it belongs to the insurer under the discharge she signed.
damage: RAV4: ignition barrel, missing rear seat, scratches to both sides; repair estimate about £3,100. False plates removed.
thirdParties: Owners of the other vehicles in the lock-up
missing: A full inspection for hidden damage or tampering with the chassis number
innocent: The forced ignition and false plates fit a professional theft for resale, not owner involvement
questions: Ask whether she wants to buy the car back and at what price she would consider it
steps: Confirm the chassis number and inspect the car for hidden damage and tampering
Explain that the car now belongs to the insurer under the signed discharge
Offer a buy-back at a fair figure reflecting the damage, or sell it through salvage if she declines
Update the theft register and the police so the car is no longer shown as stolen
assessment: Genuine theft, correctly settled. The recovered car is the insurer's; a fair buy-back offer is good customer treatment.
action: Inspect, update the register and offer her a buy-back.
outcomes: Bought back at £19,800 and repaired at her chosen garage
Sold at auction after she decides to keep her new car

title: Eight miles an hour, whiplash, and a travel anxiety uplift
type: Low-speed whiplash claim with a psychological element and loss of earnings
story: Our policyholder rolled into the back of Ms Brennan's car in slow traffic on Kirkstall Road, Leeds, at about 8 mph by his own account. Her representatives have submitted a whiplash claim through the Official Injury Claim portal for neck pain lasting 9 to 12 months with travel anxiety, ask for an uplift for exceptional circumstances, and claim £2,000 of lost earnings as a self-employed hairdresser.
statement: It was a proper jolt, my head went forward and back. My neck was stiff the next morning and I couldn't do colour work for weeks, it's all arms up. I get nervous in traffic now and I tense up when anyone's behind me. I had to turn clients away. I'm self-employed so if I don't work, I don't get paid.

accounts.text: Seen 7 weeks after the accident. Neck pain, moderate at first, now mild. Prognosis for the whiplash injury: 6 months from the accident. Reports anxiety as a passenger and driver in heavy traffic, expected to resolve within 3 months. No pre-existing neck problems reported.
The traffic was crawling and I looked down at the satnav. I touched her bumper, it barely moved her car. She got out, said she was fine and we swapped details. I've told my insurer it was my fault.

whatHappened: A genuine low-speed rear-end collision with a real but short-lived neck injury. The duration claimed and the lost earnings are overstated.
damage: Her Mini: rear bumper scuff, repaired for £420. Our policyholder's Astra: no visible damage.
thirdParties: Kelly Brennan, driver of the Mini
evidence: Screenshot of her salon's Instagram showing her at work styling a client's colour, posted two days after the accident
missing: Appointment book or invoices showing turned-away clients
Tax returns for the last two years
GP records
inconsistencies: She says she could not do colour work for weeks; the salon posted her doing colour work two days later
Claim says 9 to 12 months; the medical expert says 6 months
indicators: Duration claimed longer than the medical prognosis
Lost earnings claimed without business records
innocent: A post can be scheduled in advance or show a colleague’s work
Some people work through pain and pay for it later
questions: Ask her representatives for the appointment book, invoices and tax returns
Ask who posted the Instagram photo and who is in it
steps: Value the injury on the tariff using the medical prognosis, in the column for whiplash with minor psychological injury if the evidence supports it
Resist the uplift: an increase for exceptional circumstances is capped and needs evidence that the injury was exceptionally severe or its effects exceptional
Require business records before paying any lost earnings
Put the Instagram post to her representatives rather than alleging dishonesty outright
assessment: Genuine accident and a genuine minor injury, exaggerated in duration and financial effect. Pay the tariff the evidence supports; the uplift and the earnings claim are not proved.
action: Offer the tariff amount for a 6-month injury with the minor psychological element, and ask for proof of the lost earnings.
outcomes: Settled at tariff for 6 months; earnings claim dropped
Claimant accepts after the Instagram post is raised

title: A Polish artic on the M20, and whose blind spot it was
type: Lane change collision with a foreign-registered lorry
story: Policyholder says a Polish-registered articulated lorry moved from lane 1 into lane 2 of the M20 near Maidstone and pushed his BMW into the central barrier. The lorry driver stopped and gave his details and his insurer's name. The lorry's insurer has appointed a UK claims handling agent, which says its driver checked his mirrors and the BMW was accelerating in his blind spot.
statement: I was overtaking in lane 2 in the rain, doing about 65, steady. The lorry's indicator came on and it moved over at the same time, there was no gap. I braked and went left of the barrier, the trailer wheels caught my passenger side. My dashcam only faces forwards, but you can see the trailer come across.

accounts.who: Lorry driver, through the claims handling agent
accounts.text: I indicated and checked my mirrors three times. Lane 2 was clear. The car came very fast from behind and was in my blind spot when I started to move. I stopped on the hard shoulder and gave my details.

Trailer's rear lights visible ahead and to the left. Trailer moves into lane 2 over about 2 seconds, starting 0.6 seconds after its indicator first shows. Speed shown on the overlay: 64 mph, steady before braking.

whatHappened: A lane change by the lorry with too little time between indicating and moving. The policyholder was not speeding, but whether he was in the blind spot is genuinely disputed.
damage: BMW 3 Series: nearside doors, wheel and front wing, offside scraped along the barrier; estimate £7,800. Lorry trailer: scuffed side guard.
thirdParties: Lorry's insurer and its UK claims handling agent
evidence: Photos of the barrier and the car
missing: The lorry's own camera footage and tachograph record
The lorry's lane-change or blind-spot sensor data
inconsistencies: The driver says the car came very fast; the dashcam shows a steady 64 mph
innocent: Blind spots on the nearside of right-hand-drive cars passing a left-hand-drive lorry are a well-known hazard on both sides
questions: Ask the claims handling agent for the lorry's camera footage and tachograph download before they are overwritten
Ask the policyholder how long he had been alongside the trailer
steps: Claim against the lorry's insurer through its UK claims handling agent; if it had none, the Motor Insurers' Bureau acts for foreign vehicles in the UK
Ask now, in writing, for the lorry’s camera footage, tachograph and sensor data to be preserved
Pay the policyholder’s repairs under his comprehensive cover and recover the outlay
Expect the barrier repair to be claimed by National Highways from whoever is found liable
assessment: Disputed, but the dashcam supports the policyholder: the lorry moved 0.6 seconds after indicating and he was at a steady legal speed. Liability likely falls mostly or wholly on the lorry.
action: Pay the repairs, preserve the lorry's data and pursue a full recovery through the claims handling agent.
outcomes: Lorry footage confirms a late check; full recovery agreed
Settled 80/20 after the lorry footage shows the BMW alongside for several seconds

title: A nine-year-old between parked cars, and parents who want it settled quickly
type: Child pedestrian injury where the settlement needs court approval
story: Policyholder was driving past a primary school in Bradford at 15:20 when a nine-year-old boy ran out between parked cars. The boy suffered a broken shin and a cut that will scar. The policyholder's telematics box recorded 24 mph in a 20 mph zone at the moment of braking. The boy's parents have phoned the insurer asking for £8,000 now to settle everything, without solicitors.
statement: He came out from between two vans, I had no chance to see him. I braked hard. I know I was a bit over twenty. I went to the hospital the next day to see how he was. His dad was decent about it. They just want it over with, and so do I.

accounts.text: Speed 24 mph at the start of hard braking, 9 mph at impact, stopped 1.1 seconds later. Posted limit 20 mph. Time 15:20, school day.
Nine-year-old male. Closed fracture of the left tibia, treated in a cast. 4 cm laceration to the left knee, sutured, likely to scar. Follow-up in fracture clinic.

whatHappened: A genuine accident in which the driver was over the limit outside a school at home time, and a child was injured. Any settlement must protect the child.
damage: Child: fractured tibia and a scar. Policyholder's Kia: dent to the bonnet.
