missing: A full medical report on the fracture and the scar
Witness accounts from other parents at the school gate
innocent: A child running out between parked vans may not have been avoidable even at 20 mph; the speed still weighs heavily on liability
questions: Ask the parents whether they have taken legal advice and explain why the court has to approve a child’s settlement
steps: Do not agree a settlement directly with the parents: an agreement for a child is only binding once the court approves it under Part 21 of the Civil Procedure Rules
Accept that primary liability is likely given the speed outside a school; a contributory negligence argument against a nine-year-old is weak
Get a full medical report, including on the scar, and offer an interim payment if the family has costs now
Diary the limitation position: time does not start to run until the child turns 18
assessment: Genuine and serious. Liability will probably rest with the driver. The parents' wish to settle quickly is understandable but cannot be met without court approval.
action: Accept liability in principle, fund medical evidence and any interim needs, and settle only through an approved settlement.
outcomes: Settlement of £14,500 approved by the court and invested for the child
Family instruct solicitors; approval hearing after the scar report

title: A Part 36 offer on the handler’s desk while she was on leave
type: Disputed cyclist injury claim with a time-limited settlement offer
story: A cyclist was injured when our policyholder's van turned left across her at a junction on Oxford Road, Manchester. The van driver says she rode up his inside as he turned. Her solicitors sent a Part 36 offer dated 3 March to settle for £38,000. The handler was on leave and the file was picked up on 20 March; nobody has responded.
statement: I was in the cycle lane going straight on. The van overtook me and then turned left right in front of me. I had nowhere to go. I broke my collarbone and two ribs and I was off work for three months. I've cycled that route for six years.

accounts.text: I was indicating left for a good while and checked my mirror before I turned. She must have come up the inside fast. I felt a bump and stopped straight away.
This offer is made under Part 36. Our client will accept £38,000 in settlement of her whole claim. The relevant period is 21 days from the date of this letter.

whatHappened: A left-turn collision with a cyclist going straight on in a cycle lane. Liability is disputed but the van driver's position is weak. A time-limited offer is about to expire.
damage: Cyclist: fractured collarbone and two ribs, three months off work. Bicycle written off. Van: no damage.
evidence: Photos of the junction showing the cycle lane
missing: Van camera footage
Nearby CCTV
A valuation of the claim from counsel or a senior handler
inconsistencies: The van driver says he indicated well before the turn; the cyclist says the van overtook her first
innocent: A cyclist close to the kerb in a cycle lane can be hidden from a van’s nearside mirror
questions: Ask the van operator for its camera footage
Ask how long the van was alongside the cyclist before turning
steps: Work out the deadline today: 21 days from 3 March is 24 March
Get the claim valued and liability reviewed before the deadline, including a realistic view of contributory negligence
Decide whether to accept, or make a well-judged Part 36 offer of the insurer’s own
Explain to the business why: if the claimant later beats her own offer at trial, the insurer faces enhanced interest, indemnity costs and an additional sum
Fix the diary process so offers are picked up when a handler is away
assessment: Disputed on paper, but liability is likely to fall mainly on the van. The urgent risk is procedural: an ignored Part 36 offer can cost far more than the claim.
action: Value the claim and respond to the offer before 24 March, with a counter-offer if £38,000 is too high.
outcomes: Settled at £33,500 after a counter-offer within the relevant period
Offer accepted after counsel advises it is within the likely range

title: Lent to a mate for the airport run, and only one name on the policy
type: Uninsured friend driving with permission; third parties paid and the outlay recovered
story: Policyholder's policy covers him as the only driver. He lent his car to a friend, who has no insurance of his own, to drive to Liverpool airport. In heavy rain the friend lost control on a bend, hit a bus shelter and a parked car. The council and the parked car's owner have both claimed against the policy, and the policyholder wants his own car repaired too.
statement: Ryan's a good driver, he's just never had his own car. It was one trip. I didn't think about the insurance, I thought it covered the car. I know it was stupid. Can you not just fix it and put my premium up?

accounts.text: The road was flooded on the bend and the back end went. I hit the shelter and slid into a parked Clio. Nobody was hurt. I don't have any insurance, Callum said it would be fine.
Persons entitled to drive: the policyholder only. Use: social, domestic and pleasure and commuting.

whatHappened: An uninsured friend drove with the policyholder's permission and crashed. The policy does not cover him, but the third parties must still be paid.
damage: Bus shelter: glass and frame, council estimate £3,600. Parked Clio: rear quarter and door, £2,900. Policyholder's Focus: front and side, £4,100.
missing: Police report, if one was made
innocent: Many people believe insurance follows the car rather than the driver
questions: Confirm the driver has no policy of his own that might give cover
steps: Decline the policyholder’s own repairs: the driver was not insured
Pay the council and the Clio owner: section 151 of the Road Traffic Act 1988 requires the insurer to meet third-party claims of this kind even though the driver was not covered
Recover the outlay from the person who permitted the use (the policyholder) or the driver, as section 151(8) allows, and agree a realistic repayment plan
Tell both men that driving without insurance is an offence
assessment: Genuine accident caused by an uninsured driver with permission. Third parties are protected by law; the policyholder's own damage is not covered and the insurer can recover what it pays.
action: Pay the third parties, decline own damage, and pursue recovery from the policyholder or the driver.
outcomes: £6,500 paid to third parties; recovery agreed at £150 a month
Recovery pursued against the driver after the policyholder shows hardship

title: The barrier came down on the roof, and the car park’s sign says not our problem
type: Car park barrier damage with an exclusion of liability in the operator’s terms
story: Policyholder was leaving a multi-storey car park in Nottingham when the exit barrier came down on her roof and windscreen. She had paid at the machine. The car park's CCTV shows her following the car in front closely through the raised barrier instead of waiting for it to reset. The operator says its displayed terms exclude all liability for damage to vehicles.
statement: I'd paid, the ticket was in my hand. The barrier went up for the car in front and stayed up, so I went. It came straight down on me. There's a sign saying don't follow other cars but I didn't see it until afterwards. Surely a barrier shouldn't come down on a car that's under it?

accounts.text: Our terms, displayed at the entrance, state that barriers may lower without warning, that drivers must not follow other vehicles, and that we accept no liability for damage to vehicles. We decline your claim.
Exit barrier 2: safety loop sensor fault reported two days before the incident; engineer visit booked for the following week. Barrier left in service.

whatHappened: She followed another car too closely, but the barrier's safety sensor was known to be faulty and the operator left it in service. Both share responsibility.
damage: Her Yaris: dented roof panel and cracked windscreen, estimate £1,850.
evidence: CCTV still showing the gap between the cars
missing: The operator's full terms and where they are displayed
innocent: Following through a raised barrier is a common mistake
questions: Ask the operator when the sensor was repaired
steps: Pay her repairs under her comprehensive cover, less her excess

Pursue the operator: a term excluding liability for negligence is subject to the fairness test in the Consumer Rights Act 2015, and leaving a barrier with a known sensor fault in service is strong evidence of negligence
Expect a deduction for her following too closely and settle the recovery on a shared basis
Seek her uninsured excess as part of the recovery
assessment: Genuine damage with shared fault. The exclusion sign is not the end of the matter: the known sensor fault makes a recovery worth pursuing, reduced for her tailgating.
action: Pay the claim and recover from the operator on a shared-liability basis.
outcomes: Operator pays 60% after the maintenance log is raised
Recovery abandoned after the operator shows the sensor was repaired the day before

title: A dashcam clip with the wrong font on its clock
type: Lane change claim supported by an edited dashcam video
story: Policyholder claims a delivery van drifted into his lane on the A13 in Essex and sideswiped his Audi, and has sent a 40-second dashcam clip that appears to show the van moving across. The van operator's insurer has sent its own forward and side camera footage, which shows the Audi changing lanes into the van. A digital forensics review of the policyholder's clip found signs of editing.
statement: The van came over on me, simple as that, it's all on my dashcam. I've sent you the clip. The van driver's lying to save his job. I want the other side to pay and I want my no-claims protected.

accounts.text: File re-encoded by consumer video editing software; original camera file names and GPS track absent. Frame rate drops from 30 to 24 for 3 seconds around the contact. Timestamp overlay uses a different typeface from this camera model's standard overlay. The clip cannot be relied on as an original recording.

Forward and nearside cameras, with GPS. Van steady in lane 1 at 52 mph. Audi enters lane 1 from lane 2 without indicating and makes contact with the van's offside front. Time and position match the reported accident.

whatHappened: The Audi cut into the van's lane. The policyholder's clip was edited to make the van appear to move across.
damage: Audi A4: nearside doors and wheel arch, estimate £4,300. Van: offside front wing and mirror.
missing: The dashcam's memory card and the original files
The make and model of the dashcam
inconsistencies: The policyholder's clip shows the van moving across; the van's own GPS-stamped cameras show the Audi moving across
indicators: Re-encoded file with no original metadata
Frame rate change around the moment of contact
Overlay typeface that does not match the camera model
innocent: Phones and apps sometimes re-encode video when files are shared, which strips metadata
questions: Ask the policyholder for the memory card and the original files from the camera
Ask how the clip was copied and sent
steps: Ask for the memory card before reaching any conclusion: an innocent re-encoding would not explain the frame rate change or the overlay typeface
Refer to the counter-fraud team with the forensics report and the van footage
Treat liability as resting on the policyholder on the current evidence and deal with the van operator’s claim
If editing is confirmed, decline the claim and consider the policy and reporting consequences of a fraudulent claim
assessment: Potential fraud with strong evidence. The independent van footage shows the policyholder at fault, and the clip he sent shows signs of deliberate editing.
action: Request the original files, refer to the counter-fraud team, and handle the van operator's claim against the policy.
outcomes: Memory card not produced; claim declined as fraudulent and policy cancelled
Policyholder withdraws his own claim and accepts fault

title: New bank details, from an email address one letter wrong
type: Attempt to divert a total loss settlement by impersonating the customer
story: A total loss settlement of £14,200 was due to the policyholder, aged 71, after her Honda was stolen and burnt out in Dundee. Two days before payment an email arrived from jean.fairbairn@outIook.com asking for the money to go to a new bank account "because my bank is moving my accounts", with a scanned letter. Her earlier emails came from jean.fairbairn@outlook.com. The handler had started to update the bank details.
statement: I haven't sent you any new bank details. My bank is the same bank I've had for forty years. I did get a phone call last week from someone saying they were from the insurance helping with my claim, and they knew all about the car. I told them when the money was coming. Have I done something wrong?

accounts.text: Earlier messages: sender jean.fairbairn@outlook.com, sent from a home broadband address in Dundee. New message: sender jean.fairbairn@outIook.com (capital I in place of the letter l), sent from a hosting provider abroad. Domain outIook.com registered nine days ago.
Name check on the new account: no match. Account holder name returned: J F Services Ltd.

whatHappened: A genuine claim. A fraudster who knew the claim details impersonated the customer to divert the settlement, probably after phoning her for information.
damage: Honda Jazz: stolen and burnt out, total loss settlement £14,200 due. No money lost yet.
evidence: Customer's account of the phone call
missing: How the caller knew the claim details
inconsistencies: The new email claims to be from the customer; she says she sent nothing
indicators: Look-alike email domain registered days ago
Request to change bank details just before payment
Payee name check fails
innocent: Genuine customers do change banks, which is why a change is verified with them rather than refused
questions: Ask the customer what she told the caller and whether she gave any security details
Check whether any other claim has had a similar request
steps: Stop the bank detail change and pay only to the account verified with the customer by phoning the number on file
Treat the customer as the victim: she has done nothing wrong and is now a target
Report the attempt to the fraud team and to Action Fraud, and check how the claim details leaked
Warn her about follow-up calls and offer to note a password for future contact
assessment: The claim is genuine and the customer is innocent. This is an outside attempt to divert her payment, stopped by the payee check.
action: Pay the settlement to her verified account, report the attempt and look for a data leak.
outcomes: Settlement paid safely; fraud reported
Investigation finds a compromised supplier mailbox and other customers are warned

title: Insured at 23:52, crashed at 22:14
type: Policy bought after an accident, with the time of the accident moved
story: Policyholder bought a policy online at 23:52 on 11 November for a 2016 Audi A3 that had had no insurance for two months. At 00:40 on 12 November he reported hitting a parked Ford Puma at 00:25 while turning into a street in Wolverhampton. The Puma's owner had called the police at 22:17 on 11 November, saying her doorbell camera had just recorded an Audi hitting her car, and gave the registration.
statement: It happened after midnight, about twenty past twelve. I clipped her car turning in and I went straight to my mate's to ring you. I'd sorted the insurance earlier that night. I don't know why she's saying a different time, maybe her camera clock is wrong.

accounts.text: Call received 22:17 on 11 November. Caller reports a dark Audi A3 has just struck her parked Puma and driven off; registration given from her doorbell camera, matching the policyholder's car.
Clip time-stamped 22:14:36 on 11 November. Audi hits the Puma's rear quarter while turning, pauses, then drives away. The camera's clock agrees with the network time on a later test.

whatHappened: He hit the parked car at 22:14 while uninsured, then bought a policy at 23:52 and reported the accident as happening after the policy started.
damage: Ford Puma: rear quarter panel and light, estimate £2,650. Audi: front corner scuffed.
missing: An account from the friend whose house he says he rang from
inconsistencies: He says the accident was at 00:25; the police log and camera show 22:14, before the policy was bought
indicators: Policy bought after two months without cover, less than an hour before the reported accident
Accident time moved to fall after the policy start
He left the scene
innocent: A camera clock can be wrong, but this one was tested and the police call was made at 22:17
questions: Put the police log and camera time to him in an interview under caution if the police take it on
steps: Decline the claim: the accident happened before the policy began, and the claim misstates the time
Treat the claim as fraudulent: the insurer can refuse it, end the policy from the time of the fraud and recover its costs
Tell the Puma owner the vehicle was not insured by this insurer at the time, so her claim falls to the Motor Insurers’ Bureau as an uninsured driver claim
Record the fraud on industry databases and share the evidence with the police
assessment: Confirmed fraud: independent, time-stamped evidence puts the accident 98 minutes before the policy was bought.
action: Decline, end the policy for fraud, direct the third party to the Motor Insurers' Bureau and report.
outcomes: Claim declined, policy cancelled; police charge him with driving without insurance and fraud
Third party paid by the Motor Insurers’ Bureau

title: A subject access request while the investigators are still working
type: Data access request during a fraud investigation of a theft claim
story: Policyholder claims his Range Rover Sport was stolen from a gym car park in Reading. The claim has been with the investigation unit for six weeks because one of the two keys has not been produced and the car's finance was in arrears. On 3 February he sent a subject access request asking for all his personal data, including investigators' notes, call recordings and "the real reason my claim is delayed".
statement: I've given you everything. The second key was lost years ago, I told you that. You've had investigators ringing my gym and my bank. I'm entitled to see what you're saying about me, it's the law. If I don't get it all within a month I'll go to the regulator.

accounts.text: Dated 3 February. Under the UK GDPR I request a copy of all personal data you hold about me, including notes, emails, call recordings, investigator reports and any data shared with third parties, and the reasons for the delay in my claim.
Enquiries ongoing with the finance company and a tracking provider. A witness statement from the gym is awaited. Disclosure of the investigation plan now would be likely to prejudice the enquiries.

whatHappened: A theft claim under genuine investigation. The data request is lawful and must be answered, but some investigation material can be withheld while disclosure would prejudice the enquiry.
damage: Range Rover Sport: reported stolen, value about £48,000; not recovered.
missing: The second key
The tracking provider’s report
indicators: One key missing
Finance in arrears before the theft
innocent: Keys are often lost over years of ownership
People in financial difficulty are also victims of theft
questions: Confirm his identity before releasing any data
steps: Log the request and diary the deadline: one month from receipt, 3 March
Disclose everything that is not exempt, including call recordings and correspondence
Withhold only the material whose disclosure would be likely to prejudice the prevention or detection of crime, using the crime exemption in the Data Protection Act 2018, and record why
Tell him that some information has been withheld under an exemption where that is allowed, and how to complain to the Information Commissioner
Keep the investigation moving: the data request does not pause it
assessment: Suspicious theft claim, legitimately under investigation, and a valid data access request that must be answered on time. The exemption allows narrow withholding, not a refusal.
action: Respond by 3 March with everything not exempt, withhold the investigation plan with a recorded reason, and continue the enquiries.
outcomes: Request answered on time with redactions; claim later paid after the tracker report
Claim declined after the second key is found in his car at a garage

title: His policy, her phone call, the week of the funeral
type: Claim reported by a bereaved spouse after the policyholder died in a collision
story: Policyholder died when a car crossed the central reservation of the A1 near Newark and struck his car head-on. The other driver survived and has been arrested. His wife, a named driver on the policy, called to report the claim the week of the funeral. She needs a car to take their three children to school and has asked what happens to the policy and the car.
statement: I'm sorry, I don't really know what I'm supposed to do. Everything is in David's name. The police have the car. People keep asking me for the death certificate and I've only got two copies. I need to get the kids to school next week. I can't keep telling the story.

accounts.text: Collision on the A1 southbound. Northbound vehicle crossed the central reservation. Other driver arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving. Vehicle held for examination; will be released to the family's insurer when the examination is complete.
Policyholder: David Mensah. Named driver: Abena Mensah. Comprehensive. Renewal in four months. Monthly payments by direct debit from his account.

whatHappened: A fatal head-on collision caused by the other driver. The family is grieving and the policy is in the name of the man who died.
damage: Policyholder's Skoda: total loss, held by the police. Fatal injury to the policyholder.
thirdParties: The other driver and their insurer
missing: Who is acting for the estate (executor or administrator)
innocent: Gaps in what she knows about the policy and the paperwork are expected from a bereaved relative
questions: Ask gently, once, who will be dealing with his estate and how she would like to be contacted
steps: Give her one named contact and record her needs so she does not have to repeat the story
Accept a copy of the death certificate once, by photo or email, and do not ask again
Arrange a replacement vehicle under the policy if available, or through the other driver’s insurer as she is not at fault
Explain plainly that the total loss settlement will be paid to the estate, and that the injury and dependency claim lies against the other driver’s insurer, where solicitors can help her
Do not cancel the policy or chase the direct debit abruptly; agree the next steps with her
assessment: Genuine, not at fault, and a customer in acute vulnerability. Good handling is about care, clarity and speed, not about investigating.
action: Give her a single contact, a car, and clear next steps for the estate and the claim against the other driver.
outcomes: Replacement car within two days; settlement paid to the estate
Family supported to instruct solicitors for the fatal accident claim

title: Pushed into the car ahead in an I-35 downpour
type: Chain-reaction collision in heavy rain
story: Policyholder's Honda CR-V was damaged front and rear in a four-vehicle chain reaction on northbound I-35 near Round Rock, Texas, at about 17:50 in heavy rain. Traffic ahead braked suddenly. She says she stopped in time and was then pushed into the car in front by a pickup that hit her from behind.
statement: The rain was coming down so hard the wipers couldn't keep up. Everyone ahead braked and I stopped, I'd left a gap. I was stopped for a second or two and then bang, the truck behind hit me and shoved me into the Corolla. My neck is a bit stiff but I'm OK. I have a dashcam on the front.

accounts.who: Texas Peace Officer's Crash Report (CR-3), narrative
accounts.text: Unit 1 (Corolla) slowed for congestion. Unit 2 (CR-V) stopped behind Unit 1. Unit 3 (Ram 1500) failed to control speed and struck Unit 2, which struck Unit 1. Unit 4 (Malibu) struck Unit 3. Contributing factors for Unit 3: failed to control speed, driver inattention. Wet roadway, heavy rain.

17:49:31 brake lights ahead. 17:49:34 CR-V stopped, about one car length behind the Corolla. 17:49:36 impact from behind; the CR-V moves forward and strikes the Corolla at 17:49:37. Speedometer overlay 0 mph from 17:49:34 until the rear impact.

whatHappened: As she says: she stopped safely and was pushed into the car ahead by the pickup behind her, which was going too fast for the conditions.
damage: CR-V: rear bumper, liftgate and rear frame rail; front bumper and grille from the push. Estimate $11,300. Minor neck strain.
thirdParties: Driver of the Ram 1500 (Unit 3) and his insurer
evidence: CR-3 crash report with contributing factors
Dashcam footage showing she was stopped
missing: The Ram driver's recorded statement
Medical records if her neck strain needs treatment
innocent: Being pushed into the car ahead explains the front damage, which might otherwise suggest she was following too closely
questions: Ask the Ram driver's insurer to confirm acceptance of liability for both the front and rear damage
Ask the policyholder whether she has seen a doctor about her neck
steps: Pay the repair under her collision coverage less the deductible, or direct her to the Ram driver's insurer
Subrogate against the Ram driver's insurer for the full repair and her deductible
Send the dashcam to the Corolla driver's insurer to show she did not hit the Corolla first
assessment: A genuine chain reaction. In Texas a claimant who is more than 50% responsible recovers nothing, so the dashcam matters: it shows she had stopped, which puts the whole of her loss, including the front damage from the push, on the Ram driver.
action: Pay under collision for speed, then subrogate the full amount, including her deductible, against the Ram driver's insurer.
outcomes: Ram driver's insurer accepts 100% liability; deductible refunded
Corolla driver claims against her; denied on the dashcam evidence

title: Left turn on yellow, or straight through on red?
type: Intersection collision with conflicting witnesses
story: Policyholder was turning left from Western Avenue onto Addison Street in Chicago at about 08:10 when an oncoming Nissan Altima going straight hit his passenger side. He says the Altima ran a red light. The Altima driver says the light was yellow. Two witnesses disagree with each other. The intersection has a red-light camera.
statement: I was waiting in the middle of the intersection to turn left. The light went yellow, then red, and I started my turn because the cars coming the other way had stopped, except this Altima that came flying through in the left lane. I couldn't have stopped him. He was going way too fast.

accounts.text: My light was yellow when I entered the intersection. I was doing the speed limit. The Camry turned right in front of me, he didn't yield. Left turns have to yield to oncoming traffic, everyone knows that.

accounts.who: Witness 1, Mr Luis Ortega (pedestrian waiting to cross)
accounts.text: The light for Western had just gone red. I was waiting for the walk sign and the Altima came through after the red. The Camry was already turning.

accounts.who: Witness 2, Ms Patricia Novak (driver behind the Altima)
accounts.text: We were both going through on yellow. The Camry just turned across her. I stopped because I was further back and it was going to change.

whatHappened: Probably the Altima entered just after the light turned red, as the camera evidence is likely to show, while the policyholder turned without checking that every oncoming lane had stopped. Both may share the blame.
damage: Policyholder's Toyota Camry: passenger doors and B-pillar, estimate $8,900. Altima: front end, about $6,200.
thirdParties: Ms Kendra Wallace, driver of the Altima, and her insurer
evidence: Photos of the cars and the final positions
Police crash report with no citation issued
missing: Red-light camera images and any violation notice for the Altima
Signal timing records from the city
Event data recorder speed from the Altima
inconsistencies: Witness 1 says the Altima entered after the light was red; Witness 2 says both cars went on yellow
The Altima driver says the Camry turned in front of her; the policyholder says he was already turning when she entered
innocent: Witnesses at intersections often see different phases depending on where they stand
Both drivers may honestly believe they had the right of way
questions: Ask the city for the red-light camera images and whether a violation was issued to the Altima
Ask Witness 2 which light she was watching: the main signal or the countdown timer
Ask the policyholder whether he could see the left lane before turning
steps: Request the red-light camera evidence before it is purged
Pay the policyholder under collision and pursue recovery once liability is clearer
Apply Illinois comparative fault: a party more than 50% at fault recovers nothing, others recover a reduced share
Consider inter-company arbitration if the camera evidence is unclear
assessment: A genuine dispute with honest disagreement. The left-turning driver usually bears more responsibility, but a vehicle entering on red shifts most of it back. The camera evidence will likely decide the split.
action: Secure the camera evidence, pay the policyholder's collision claim, and negotiate a comparative fault split.
outcomes: Camera shows the Altima entered 0.6 seconds into red; liability split 80/20 in favour of the policyholder
No camera violation; liability split 50/50 through arbitration
Altima on yellow; policyholder found mostly at fault for failing to yield

title: Hit by a driver who never stopped, in Tampa
type: Hit-and-run with injury in a no-fault state
story: Policyholder's Kia Forte was hit on the driver's side at a junction in Tampa, Florida, at about 21:30 by a car that ran a stop sign and drove off. He broke his left wrist. Tampa Police took a report. His policy includes Personal Injury Protection and uninsured motorist cover.
statement: The car came out of the side street without stopping and hit my door. It spun me around. It was a dark sedan, maybe a Chevy, with one headlight out. It just kept going. A guy from the gas station called 911 for me. I went to the ER that night and they put my wrist in a cast. I'm a line cook, I can't work with one hand.

accounts.who: Tampa Police Department crash report summary
accounts.text: Vehicle 1 (Kia) traveling east with right of way. Vehicle 2, unknown dark sedan, failed to stop at the stop sign and struck Vehicle 1, then fled north. Paint transfer collected from Vehicle 1. Witness at the gas station confirms the sedan did not stop. Driver 1 transported by private vehicle to the hospital.

Arrived 22:41. Distal radius fracture, left wrist, closed reduction and cast. Emergency medical condition: yes. Follow-up with orthopedics in one week. Unable to use the left hand for work for at least six weeks.

whatHappened: Exactly as described: an unidentified driver ran a stop sign, hit him and fled.
damage: Kia Forte: driver's doors and front wing, estimate $5,400. Fractured wrist, ER and orthopedic care, about six weeks of lost wages.
thirdParties: Unidentified driver of a dark sedan
evidence: Police report with an independent witness
ER records confirming an emergency medical condition
missing: Wage records from his employer
Orthopedic follow-up notes and the prognosis
innocent: The paint transfer and the independent witness explain why there is no other driver to interview
questions: Ask his employer for his average weekly wage
Ask whether he has health insurance that may also pay medical bills
steps: Pay medical bills and lost wages under PIP: 80% of medical and 60% of lost income up to the $10,000 limit
Pay the car repair under collision, or under uninsured motorist property damage if the policy includes it
Open an uninsured motorist bodily injury claim for losses beyond PIP
Follow up the paint transfer with police in case the driver is identified
assessment: Genuine. He sought treatment the same night, which satisfies Florida's 14-day rule, and the ER recorded an emergency medical condition, which gives access to the full PIP benefit. Uninsured motorist cover fills the gap for a driver who cannot be identified, subject to the usual injury threshold for non-economic damages.
action: Start PIP payments promptly, repair the car, and evaluate the uninsured motorist claim once the orthopedic prognosis is known.
outcomes: PIP pays medical and wages; uninsured motorist claim settles for pain and suffering
Driver identified through the paint; claim subrogated to that driver's insurer

title: Said he hit the deer, but he missed it
type: Animal avoidance reported as an animal strike
story: Policyholder reported hitting a deer at about 05:50 on a rural road in Centre County, Pennsylvania, damaging his Ford F-150. His comprehensive deductible is $250 and his collision deductible is $1,000. The appraiser found guardrail damage on the truck and no sign of an animal strike.
statement: First report: A deer ran out and I hit it, smashed up the front right side. After the appraisal: OK, I didn't actually hit it. It jumped out and I swerved and caught the guardrail. A deer caused it either way. I just figured it all counted as a deer claim.

accounts.text: Right front fender, door and bed side scraped in a long horizontal line at guardrail height, with galvanized metal transfer. No hair, blood or tissue anywhere on the vehicle. Front grille and bumper undamaged. Damage consistent with a sideswipe against a guardrail, not an animal impact. Estimate $6,350.
Damage to 40 feet of guardrail reported at the location by a maintenance crew on the same morning. PennDOT will seek repair costs from the responsible driver once identified.

whatHappened: A deer made him swerve and he hit the guardrail. Hitting an animal is usually a comprehensive loss, but swerving into a fixed object is a collision loss, with a higher deductible. He described it as a deer strike, probably partly because of that difference.
damage: F-150 right side scraped and dented, estimate $6,350. About 40 feet of state guardrail damaged.
evidence: Appraiser report with metal transfer and no animal evidence
missing: Photos of the scene showing the deer, if any were taken
inconsistencies: First report says he hit a deer; the truck shows only guardrail damage and he later admits he did not hit it
indicators: First account matched the cover with the lower deductible
innocent: Many drivers honestly think any accident caused by a deer is a "deer claim"
He corrected the account as soon as the appraisal was discussed
questions: Ask whether he reported the guardrail damage to the police or PennDOT
Ask whether he understood the difference between comprehensive and collision when he reported
steps: Reclassify the loss as collision and apply the $1,000 deductible
Notify PennDOT and handle its guardrail claim under the property damage liability coverage
Record the corrected account; no fraud referral given the prompt correction
assessment: A genuine accident misdescribed in a way that would have saved him $750. Because he corrected it at the first challenge and the misunderstanding is common, it is treated as a reporting error, not fraud. The coverage follows what actually happened.
action: Pay as a collision loss with the collision deductible and accept PennDOT's guardrail claim.
outcomes: Paid under collision less $1,000; guardrail repair paid to PennDOT
Policyholder disputes the deductible; complaint not upheld

title: A pedestrian in the crosswalk at dusk in Queens
type: Left-turn collision with a pedestrian
story: Policyholder turned left from Northern Boulevard onto 82nd Street in Jackson Heights, Queens, at about 17:20 in light rain and hit a 67-year-old man crossing in the crosswalk. He has a fractured hip. Her first account was that he stepped out against the signal. Two days later she said she never saw him.
statement: At the scene, to police: He just came out of nowhere, he wasn't on the walk sign. Two days later, to us: I've been going over it and I honestly don't know where he came from. The windshield was wet and the sun was low. I looked for cars, not people. I keep seeing it. I can't sleep.

accounts.who: Witness, Mr Hector Ruiz (food vendor at the corner)
accounts.text: The man was already halfway across when the SUV turned. The white walking man was on, I'm sure, because I was looking at it to cross myself. She didn't brake until she hit him. She was screaming afterwards, she was in a bad way.

Vehicle 1 turning left from Northern Boulevard struck the pedestrian in the marked crosswalk. Pedestrian signal: walk phase per witness. Driver stated pedestrian crossed against the signal; driver visibly distressed. Weather: rain, wet road, dusk. Pedestrian removed to Elmhurst Hospital.

whatHappened: She turned without seeing a pedestrian who was lawfully crossing on the walk signal, in poor light and rain. Her first account was a shocked reaction, not a considered lie.
damage: Pedestrian: fractured hip needing surgery, likely long rehabilitation. Policyholder's Toyota RAV4: minor hood dent.
thirdParties: The injured pedestrian, a 67-year-old retired man, and his family
missing: Traffic camera or business CCTV footage
The pedestrian's medical prognosis
Whether the pedestrian has his own auto insurance, which affects which policy pays no-fault benefits
inconsistencies: At the scene she said he crossed against the signal; two days later she said she never saw him; the witness says he had the walk signal
innocent: Drivers in shock often blame the person they hit before they have processed what happened
She corrected herself without being shown the witness evidence
questions: Ask the pedestrian's family whether he owns a car with its own auto policy
Ask the policyholder what speed she was turning at and whether her wipers were on
steps: Open a no-fault claim for the pedestrian's medical bills and lost earnings under the policy, if he has no auto policy of his own
Accept that liability is very likely; a fractured hip will probably meet New York's serious injury threshold
Reserve near the bodily injury limit and notify the policyholder if the claim may exceed her limits
Offer the policyholder information about support after a traumatic event
assessment: A serious, genuine claim in which the policyholder is very probably liable. Her changing account comes from shock and should not be treated as dishonesty. The priorities are prompt no-fault benefits for the injured man, realistic reserves, and protecting the policyholder from an excess judgment by trying to settle within limits.
action: Accept liability in principle, pay no-fault benefits promptly, and work toward a settlement within the policy limits.
outcomes: Settled within the $100,000 bodily injury limit after rehabilitation
Claim exceeds limits; settled with the policyholder's umbrella insurer contributing
Lawsuit filed; settled before trial

title: A nine-year-old, a bike and Dad's car door
type: Minor household damage to a parked car
story: Policyholder reported that his son, 9, rode his bike into the side of the family's Subaru Legacy in the garage in Columbus, Ohio. The handlebar dented and scratched the rear door. The repair estimate is $1,150 and his collision deductible is $500.
statement: He was riding in circles in the garage because it was raining, which he's not supposed to do, and he lost his balance and the handlebar went right into the door. He's fine, he was more scared of telling me. I'm not sure it's worth claiming but I wanted to ask.

accounts.text: Left rear door: one dent 4 inches long with a paint scratch. Paintless dent repair not possible because the paint is broken. Repair, refinish and blend into the adjacent panel: $1,150.

whatHappened: Exactly as described: a child's bicycle accident inside the garage.
damage: Dent and scratch on the rear door, $1,150.
missing: A note of any other recent claims, which affects the advice about the premium
innocent: A child riding indoors on a wet day is an ordinary household accident, and the small amount and the frank account fit it
questions: Ask whether he wants to proceed after hearing the effect of the deductible and a claim on his record
steps: Explain that the claim would pay $650 after the $500 deductible
Explain how a paid claim may affect his premium at renewal
Let him decide; if he proceeds, pay under collision
assessment: Genuine and low value. The right service here is a clear explanation of the deductible and the likely effect on premium, so that the customer can make an informed choice, rather than simply opening a claim.
action: Explain the options; pay $650 under collision if he chooses to claim.
outcomes: Customer withdraws and pays the body shop himself
Claim paid at $650 after the deductible

title: "Just driving home", with the rideshare app on
type: Collision while logged in to a rideshare app
story: Policyholder ran a stop sign in Atlanta at about 23:15 and hit the side of a Jeep Cherokee. He told the claims line he was driving home from a friend's house. Data from the rideshare company shows his driver app was online and waiting for ride requests at the time. His personal policy excludes the period when a driver is logged in to a transportation network app, and he has no rideshare endorsement.
statement: I was on my way home, that's all. I might have had the app open but I wasn't taking rides, I was done for the night. The stop sign is hidden behind a tree there, I didn't see it until I was in the intersection.

accounts.who: Rideshare company response to the insurer's request
accounts.text: Driver account online from 19:02 to 23:31. Last trip ended 22:48. Status at 23:14 to 23:16: available, no request accepted. The driver was in "Period 1". The company's contingent liability coverage applies in this period if the driver's personal policy does not respond. Contingent comprehensive and collision is provided only where the driver carries those coverages personally.

He came straight through the stop sign and hit my door. He jumped out and the first thing he said was "Please don't call the police, I'll lose my driving job." My hip is bruised and my car is crumpled on the driver side.

whatHappened: He was logged in and waiting for passengers when he ran the stop sign. He described the trip as a private journey because he believed, correctly, that his personal policy would not cover him while the app was on.
damage: Jeep: driver's doors and B-pillar, about $9,700, plus a bruised hip. Policyholder's Nissan Altima: front end, about $4,800.
thirdParties: Mrs Denise Holloway, the Jeep driver, and her insurer
The rideshare company and its insurer
evidence: Jeep driver's statement, including what he said at the scene
Photos of the stop sign and the tree
missing: Street view or city records about the obscured stop sign
inconsistencies: He says he was done for the night and driving home; the app shows he was online and available
indicators: False description of the journey that would bring the loss within the personal policy
innocent: Drivers often leave the app on at the end of a shift without meaning to work
The obscured stop sign may share the blame with the city
questions: Ask him to explain why the app was online and available at 23:15
Ask whether he has ever bought a rideshare endorsement
steps: Deny coverage under the personal policy for the logged-in period, explaining the exclusion
Tender the Jeep driver's claim to the rideshare company's contingent liability insurer
Explain to him that his own car damage is not covered by the rideshare insurer because he has no personal collision coverage that applies
Consider a claim against the city if the sign obstruction is confirmed
assessment: A genuine accident caused by his negligence, during a period his personal policy does not cover. His account of the journey was false but the collision itself is real, and the injured driver must still be paid by the right insurer.
action: Deny under the rideshare exclusion, redirect the third-party claim to the rideshare insurer, and record the misstatement.
outcomes: Rideshare insurer pays the Jeep driver's claim; the policyholder pays his own repair
Policy non-renewed for misrepresentation
City accepts partial liability for the hidden sign

title: Rental car, a light pole and an 18-day loss-of-use bill
type: Rental car damage on a personal auto policy
story: Policyholder, from New Jersey, hit a light pole in a hotel car park in Orlando, Florida, while on vacation in a rented Hyundai Elantra. She declined the rental company's damage waiver because her personal auto policy covers rental cars. The rental company has billed $4,820 for repairs, 18 days' loss of use at $45 a day, $1,200 diminished value and a $150 administration fee.
statement: It was pouring, I was looking for a parking space and I didn't see the pole until I hit it. It was low speed, the airbags didn't go off. I declined their insurance because my agent told me my own policy would cover a rental. I don't understand these extra charges.

accounts.text: Repair cost per invoice: $4,820. Loss of use: 18 days at $45: $810. Diminished value: $1,200. Administrative fee: $150. Total due: $6,980. Payment is due within 30 days to avoid referral to collections.

whatHappened: A genuine low-speed parking collision in heavy rain. The repair is real; the extra charges need checking against what the rental company can actually show.
damage: Elantra front bumper, grille and headlamp, $4,820. Claimed extras $2,160.
evidence: Rental agreement showing the waiver was declined
missing: Fleet utilization records showing whether the company actually lost rentals while the car was repaired
A diminished value appraisal
Photos of the car at the start of the rental
innocent: Rental companies routinely add loss of use and fees; it is not dishonest, but it must be justified
questions: Ask the rental company for fleet utilization logs for the 18 days
Ask for the basis of the diminished value figure and the repair timeline
steps: Confirm that her policy extends collision coverage to rental cars and whether it covers loss of use
Pay the repair under her collision coverage less the deductible
Pay loss of use only if supported by fleet utilization records, and challenge the diminished value without an appraisal
Check whether the credit card she used for the rental provides secondary cover for the deductible or fees
assessment: A genuine claim where the dispute is about the add-on charges, not the accident. Loss of use and diminished value are recoverable only if proven, and many policies cover them only up to a limit or not at all.
action: Pay the repair, request evidence for the extras, and help her use any credit card benefit for the deductible.
outcomes: Repair and a reduced loss of use paid; diminished value dropped
Credit card benefit reimburses her deductible

title: Lane-splitting rider clipped by a car changing lanes
type: Motorcycle lane-splitting collision
story: Policyholder was riding his Yamaha MT-07 between lanes in slow traffic on the I-405 in Los Angeles at about 18:10 when a Honda Accord moved into his path without signaling. He fell and broke his collarbone. The Accord driver's insurer says the rider is to blame for lane splitting.
statement: Traffic was crawling, maybe 15. I was splitting between lanes one and two at around 25, which is normal here and legal. The Accord just drifted left, no signal, no mirror check. I hit his door with my right handlebar and went down. My helmet cam got all of it.

accounts.who: Helmet camera footage, with GPS speed
accounts.text: 18:09:40 traffic in lanes 1 and 2 at 12 to 16 mph. Rider between the lanes at 23 to 26 mph. 18:09:52 Accord in lane 2 moves left into the gap with no turn signal visible. 18:09:53 contact between the motorcycle's right handlebar and the Accord's left rear door. Rider falls.
Our insured was changing lanes when your rider passed between vehicles at an unsafe speed. Lane splitting is inherently dangerous and the rider assumed the risk. We deny liability for this loss.

whatHappened: The Accord changed lanes without signalling or checking, into a rider who was lane splitting legally and at a moderate speed difference.
damage: Fractured right collarbone; bike's right handlebar, lever, mirror and fairing damaged, $2,900. Accord: scratched rear door.
thirdParties: Driver of the Honda Accord and his insurer
evidence: Helmet camera footage with GPS speed
missing: Accord's own dashcam, if any
Final medical prognosis for the collarbone
inconsistencies: The other insurer says the rider passed at an unsafe speed; the footage shows about 10 mph faster than traffic moving at 15
innocent: The Accord driver probably honestly did not see the motorcycle
Many people, including some adjusters, still believe lane splitting is illegal
questions: Ask the Accord driver's insurer to review the footage and reconsider liability
Ask the rider about his time off work and treatment plan
steps: Pay the bike repair under his collision coverage and his medical bills under medical payments coverage
Send the footage to the other insurer and demand subrogation
Help him pursue his bodily injury claim against the Accord driver's liability coverage
If the other insurer insists on fault, argue California pure comparative negligence: any share of fault only reduces his recovery
assessment: Genuine. Lane splitting is legal in California, and riding about 10 mph faster than slow traffic is within long-standing safety guidance. The footage shows an unsafe lane change by the car. Any argument about the rider's share of fault reduces his recovery rather than defeating it.
action: Pay first-party benefits, subrogate against the Accord driver's insurer, and support the injury claim.
outcomes: Other insurer accepts 100% liability after viewing the footage
Arbitration finds the rider 10% at fault; recovery reduced accordingly

title: Denver hail on a car still carrying last storm's dents
type: Hail claim including earlier unrepaired hail damage
story: Policyholder's Subaru Outback was damaged in a hailstorm in Denver in May. A body shop estimate of $7,200 covers the roof, hood and trunk. A claims database search shows a hail claim on the same car two years ago, paid in cash at $3,900 with no repair invoice.
statement: The storm was crazy, golf balls. The car was in the open lot at work. The whole roof and hood are covered. I did have a hail claim before, but that was on the old car. Or, actually, it might have been this one, I'm not sure. I took the money because I was going to sell the car.

accounts.text: Roof: 142 dents, of which 61 show oxidation at the edges and wax residue inside, consistent with older damage. Hood: 74 dents, of which 29 older. Trunk lid: 22 dents, all fresh. Storm verified: hail up to 1.75 inches reported at the location on the date. New damage only: paintless dent repair estimate $4,100.
Hail claim two years ago, same vehicle identification number. Roof and hood. Settled as cash in lieu of repair, $3,900. No repair invoice or reinspection on file.

whatHappened: New hail damaged the car, but the estimate includes old dents from the previous storm that were paid in cash and never repaired.
damage: New damage $4,100 by paintless dent repair. Old unrepaired damage, previously paid: roughly $3,100 of the current estimate.
evidence: Dent mapping with oxidation and wax evidence
missing: Photos of the car between the two storms, if she has any
inconsistencies: She first says the prior hail claim was on another car; the record shows the same VIN
indicators: Previously paid, unrepaired damage included in a new claim
innocent: Hail dents from two storms look alike to an owner
She took cash intending to sell, which is allowed, and may not have realised the old dents would be excluded
questions: Ask her whether any repair was done after the first claim
Show her the dent map and ask whether she agrees with the split
steps: Pay only the new damage, $4,100 by paintless dent repair, less the deductible
Explain the prior-damage deduction with the dent map
Note the prior damage on the vehicle record so it is not paid a third time
assessment: A genuine hail claim with an exaggerated scope, probably from confusion rather than a plan. Paying the new damage and explaining the deduction is fair; a fraud referral would be appropriate only if she insisted the old dents were new after seeing the evidence.
action: Settle the verified new damage and document the prior damage.
outcomes: Accepts the split; paid $4,100 less the deductible
Disputes the split; independent appraisal under the policy confirms it

title: Storm surge in the garage, and an owner who wants to keep the car
type: Saltwater flood total loss
story: Policyholder's 2019 Toyota Camry was submerged to the dashboard by hurricane storm surge in his garage in Fort Myers, Florida. The appraiser has declared it a total loss. He wants to keep the car and dry it out, saying it "runs fine now".
statement: The water came up four feet in the garage in about an hour. When it went down I let it dry for a week, hooked up a new battery and it started. It's a Toyota, it'll be fine. I just want you to pay for the cleanup and I'll keep it. My cousin can sell it if I don't want it.

accounts.text: Saltwater line at dashboard height. Corrosion visible on the seat motors, wiring connectors under the carpet and the airbag control module. Electrical faults will develop over months. Actual cash value $19,400. Repair estimate exceeds the total loss threshold. If retained by the owner, the title must be branded as salvage with a flood designation.

whatHappened: A genuine storm surge loss. The car runs for now, but saltwater corrosion means it will deteriorate and may have unsafe airbags. Selling it without disclosure would be "title washing", a known post-hurricane problem.
damage: Saltwater flooding to dashboard height; total loss, actual cash value $19,400.
evidence: Storm surge records for the address
missing: Loan payoff figure, if any
innocent: Wanting to keep a car that seems to run is understandable; he is not trying to hide the flood
questions: Ask whether there is a loan on the car
Ask whether he understands that a retained car will carry a flood brand on its title
steps: Pay the actual cash value less the deductible under comprehensive
If he keeps the car, deduct the salvage value and have the title branded as flood salvage
Report the total loss to the National Motor Vehicle Title Information System
Explain the safety risk from corroded airbag and brake electronics and the legal duty to disclose the flood history if it is sold
assessment: Genuine. The work is in handling the total loss correctly: paying fairly, branding the title and making sure the car does not reach an unsuspecting buyer with its flood history hidden.
action: Settle as a total loss; allow owner retention only with a salvage deduction and a flood-branded title.
outcomes: Paid $19,400 less the deductible; car goes to a salvage auction with a flood brand
Owner retains the car; paid less salvage value, title branded

title: Tornado debris on a financed pickup
type: Tornado damage leading to a total loss with a loan
story: A tornado in Moore, Oklahoma, threw a neighbour's shed roof onto policyholder's 2023 Chevrolet Silverado, crushing the cab roof and smashing the windows. The truck is a total loss. He owes more on his loan than the truck is worth and bought GAP coverage from the dealer.
statement: We were in the storm shelter when it went over. When we came out the shed roof from two houses down was sitting on my truck. The house has damage too, but that's a different claim. I need something to drive to work, I'm a roofer and it's going to be the busiest month of my life.

accounts.who: Lender payoff letter and GAP contract summary
accounts.text: Loan payoff as of the loss date: $52,180. GAP waiver purchased at the dealership covers the difference between the insurance settlement (actual cash value less the deductible) and the loan balance, excluding late fees and the deductible over $1,000.

Cab roof crushed, all glass broken, debris penetration of the bed. Structural damage. Actual cash value $46,900. Total loss. The vehicle is in a debris field; release to the salvage yard requires a tow with a winch.

whatHappened: Exactly as described: tornado debris destroyed the truck.
damage: Silverado total loss, actual cash value $46,900; loan payoff $52,180.
thirdParties: Lender with a lien on the truck
missing: Confirmation of rental reimbursement coverage on the policy
innocent: Debris damage can look like deliberate damage, but the storm track and the neighbour's shed roof explain it
questions: Ask whether he has rental reimbursement coverage and how many days it allows
Ask the lender how it wants the payment made
steps: Pay actual cash value less the comprehensive deductible directly to the lender
Send the settlement breakdown to the GAP provider so it can cover the shortfall
Start rental reimbursement immediately if the policy includes it
Arrange removal to a salvage yard once the debris field is safe
assessment: A straightforward catastrophe claim. The value to the customer lies in speed: paying the lender quickly so GAP can close the balance, and getting him a rental for work during a busy rebuild period.
action: Settle the total loss promptly, coordinate with the lender and the GAP provider, and start the rental.
outcomes: Settled within 10 days; GAP clears the remaining loan balance
No rental coverage; customer arranges his own transport

title: Left behind in an evacuation, with no paperwork left
type: Wildfire total loss with lost documentation
story: Policyholder's 2016 Toyota 4Runner was destroyed in her driveway when a wildfire burned through her neighbourhood in Butte County, California. The family evacuated in their other car. She says the 4Runner had a lift kit, upgraded wheels and a roof rack worth about $6,000, but all the receipts burned with the house.
statement: We had about twenty minutes to get out. We took the kids, the dog and the Honda. The 4Runner is just a shell now. My husband put on the lift kit and the wheels about two years ago, he did it himself. All the receipts were in the filing cabinet. I have photos on my phone from camping trips though.

accounts.text: Structure at the address destroyed. Two vehicles destroyed on the property: one on the driveway and one in the garage area. Fire progression through the neighbourhood confirmed on the evening of the evacuation order.

Twelve photos from the last 18 months showing the 4Runner at campsites: visible lift, aftermarket black wheels with off-road tires, a full-length roof rack with a cargo box. Photo dates and locations recorded on the phone.

whatHappened: The fire burned through the street after the family left in their other car; the fire agency inspection confirms both the timing and the destruction.
damage: Total loss. Base actual cash value about $27,500; claimed aftermarket equipment about $6,000.
evidence: Dated phone photos showing the equipment
missing: Receipts for the aftermarket parts
Bank or card statements showing the parts purchases
innocent: Lost paperwork is expected when a house burns down
questions: Ask whether the parts were bought by card or online, so that statements or order history can replace the receipts
Ask whether the custom equipment was listed on the policy
steps: Pay the base actual cash value quickly
Accept dated photos and bank records as proof of the equipment instead of receipts
Check the policy limit for custom equipment
Waive non-essential documents in line with the regulator's guidance after a declared disaster
assessment: Genuine. The insurer should be flexible about proof in a disaster: dated photos and purchase records are good evidence of the upgrades. The only real limit is any cap on custom equipment in the policy.
action: Pay the base value now and the equipment once card statements or order histories support the photos, up to the policy limit.
outcomes: Base value paid within a week; equipment paid on photos and order history
Equipment capped at the $1,500 custom equipment limit; customer told clearly why

title: An aluminum ladder on the interstate at 70 mph
type: Road debris damage
story: Policyholder ran over an extension ladder lying in lane 2 of I-75 near Macon, Georgia, at about 70 mph. It damaged the front bumper, the radiator and the underbody. She saw it fall from a pickup two cars ahead but could not read the plate. She called 911 from the shoulder.
statement: A white pickup with ladders on a rack, two cars ahead, and one just slid off the back. The car in front of me swerved and there it was. I couldn't swerve, there was a truck on my right. It went under the car with an awful noise and the temperature light came on, so I pulled over.

accounts.text: Road debris reported 14:22: aluminum extension ladder in lane 2, removed by a highway emergency response operator at 14:40. Driver of a damaged sedan on the shoulder states the ladder fell from a white pickup. No plate obtained. Two other callers reported the ladder.
Front bumper cover and absorber, radiator, condenser, lower engine splash shield, front right control arm. Aluminum scoring on the underbody consistent with dragging a metal object. Estimate $5,860.

whatHappened: A ladder slid off an unidentified pickup and she had nowhere to steer; the scoring on the underbody and the other 911 callers confirm it.
damage: Front end and underbody, estimate $5,860.
thirdParties: Unidentified driver of a white pickup
evidence: State Patrol note and the other callers
Body shop estimate with aluminum scoring
missing: Plate of the pickup, unless a highway camera or another caller captured it
innocent: Underbody damage with no other car involved can look like an unreported crash, but three 911 callers reported the ladder
questions: Ask the State Patrol whether the other callers gave a plate or a business name on the pickup
steps: Pay under collision coverage less the deductible
Ask the State Patrol for the other callers' details
Subrogate against the pickup owner if identified, for the repair and her deductible
assessment: Genuine. Hitting road debris is a collision loss. If the pickup owner is traced, the unsecured load makes the owner liable and the insurer can recover.
action: Pay under collision and pursue the pickup owner if identified.
outcomes: Paid less the deductible; pickup never identified
Pickup owner traced through another caller; subrogation recovers the cost and her deductible

title: Into the back of a state snowplow on black ice
type: Rear-end collision with a government vehicle in winter
story: Policyholder slid into the back of a Minnesota Department of Transportation snowplow on Highway 10 near Elk River at about 06:40. The plow was spreading sand with its lights flashing. The plow driver says his back was jarred. The state will claim for damage to the plow's spreader.
statement: I saw the lights from a long way back and slowed down, but when I braked properly the car just kept going. It was glare ice under a little snow. I was doing maybe 35, which felt slow. I should have left more room, I know.

accounts.text: Unit 2 (Ford Fusion) struck the rear of Unit 1 (MnDOT plow truck) operating with warning lights and spreading material. Road: ice and snow. Unit 2 driver cited for speed too fast for conditions. Plow driver reports back pain, declined transport.

Damage to the rear sand spreader, conveyor guard and rear lighting of the plow truck. Estimated repair $14,300. Vehicle out of service during an active winter event; a replacement plow was diverted from another route.

whatHappened: He was following too closely and too fast for ice, and slid into a plow that was clearly visible.
damage: Ford Fusion: front end crushed, likely total loss, value about $9,800. Plow: spreader and lights, $14,300. Plow driver: possible back strain.
thirdParties: The plow driver, through workers' compensation
missing: The plow's camera footage, if fitted
The plow driver's medical records if he pursues a claim
innocent: Black ice under fresh snow is hard to see, even for careful drivers
questions: Ask MnDOT for an itemized repair invoice
Ask whether the plow driver has filed for workers' compensation
steps: Accept liability for the plow damage under property damage liability
Pay his own car under collision less the deductible
Expect a subrogation claim from the state's workers' compensation program if the plow driver is treated
assessment: Genuine negligence: he drove too fast for the conditions, as he admits. Liability for the plow damage is clear, and any workers' compensation benefits paid to the plow driver are likely to come back as a subrogation claim.
action: Accept liability, pay the state's itemized repair claim and handle any workers' compensation subrogation.
outcomes: Plow repair and the policyholder's total loss paid
Small workers' compensation subrogation claim paid later

title: A road bracket through an EV battery shield
type: Battery pack damage from road debris
story: Policyholder's 2022 electric crossover struck a steel bracket on a freeway in Phoenix, Arizona. The underbody shield was punctured and the car showed a battery fault warning. The dealer says the manufacturer requires a full battery pack replacement at $18,600 on a car worth $31,000.
statement: There was a loud bang under the car and then a message telling me to pull over safely because of a battery fault. I stopped and smelled something hot, so I got out and called for a tow. The car is at the dealer. They say they can't repair the pack, only replace it.

accounts.text: Battery enclosure deformation 4 inches by 2 inches with coolant seepage. Manufacturer repair policy: no module-level repair for enclosure damage. Full high-voltage battery replacement $18,600 including labor, plus shield $640 and coolant service. Vehicle quarantined outdoors per thermal event protocol.

EV towed on a flatbed per manufacturer guidance. Driver advised that the car smelled of hot coolant at the scene. Vehicle placed in an isolated area at the dealer, at least 50 feet from other vehicles.

whatHappened: Road debris dented the battery enclosure, and the manufacturer's repair policy, not the repairer's preference, is what requires a whole new pack.
damage: Battery enclosure and shield; repair about $19,500 on a car with actual cash value $31,000.
evidence: Freeway debris reports for the time
missing: An independent EV repairer's view of whether a certified pack repair is possible
Salvage value of a damaged EV in this market
innocent: A dealer insisting on a whole new battery can look like inflation, but it reflects the manufacturer's repair policy for enclosure damage
questions: Ask an independent certified EV repairer for a second opinion
Ask the salvage partner for a bid given the battery damage
steps: Compare repair cost plus storage risk against actual cash value minus salvage
Keep the car isolated while in storage because damaged packs can ignite days later
Decide repair or total loss quickly to limit storage cost and risk
assessment: Genuine, but expensive and technically tricky. Battery damage often pushes EVs toward total loss even when the rest of the car is perfect, and a damaged pack is a fire risk in storage. A fast, documented decision protects the customer and the salvage yard.
action: Get a second opinion, decide within days, and keep the car isolated until it is repaired or released to salvage.
outcomes: Pack replaced at $19,500; car returned
Declared a total loss because salvage value is low; paid $31,000 less the deductible

title: Cracked radiator, then 22 miles with the warning light on
type: Collision damage made worse by driving on
story: Policyholder hit a raised concrete parking divider leaving a shopping center in Phoenix in 112°F heat, cracking the radiator. She drove 22 miles home with the temperature warning on and the engine seized. She is claiming the radiator and a $6,800 replacement engine under collision.
statement: I bumped the divider, it didn't seem like much. Later a light came on but I didn't know what it meant and I just wanted to get home before my kids got off the bus. It started smelling hot near the end. I had no idea it would kill the engine. The accident caused all of this.

accounts.text: Radiator cracked at the lower tank from impact; coolant loss. Engine overheated and seized, with scored cylinder walls and a warped cylinder head. Engine computer shows 19 minutes of operation above the critical temperature with the warning active. Radiator and condenser $1,150; engine replacement $6,800.

whatHappened: The collision cracked the radiator. Driving 22 miles with the warning on caused the engine damage. Whether the engine is part of the collision loss is the question.
damage: Radiator and condenser $1,150; seized engine $6,800.
evidence: Shop findings with the engine computer data
Photos of the divider and the front of the car
missing: The exact policy wording on mechanical breakdown and on protecting the vehicle from further damage
The car's manual description of the warning light
inconsistencies: She says she did not know what the light meant; the dashboard displayed a temperature message for 19 minutes
innocent: Many drivers do not know how fast an engine fails once coolant is lost
Stopping in 112°F heat with children waiting is a real dilemma
questions: Ask what message the dashboard showed and whether she stopped at any point
Ask whether she had roadside assistance
steps: Pay the radiator and condenser under collision less the deductible
Review the policy terms on mechanical damage and failure to protect the vehicle
Consider whether the engine damage was a foreseeable direct result of the collision, as some courts and regulators do
Explain the decision in writing; offer an appraisal if she disputes it
assessment: Honest dispute, not fraud. The radiator is clearly covered. The engine is arguable: insurers often exclude damage from driving on, but some decision-makers treat it as a direct consequence of the collision, especially when the warning was unclear. A reasoned decision, or a compromise, is better than a flat denial.
action: Pay the radiator now; decide the engine on the policy wording, consider a partial settlement, and explain clearly.
outcomes: Radiator paid; engine denied under the policy terms
Compromise: insurer pays half of the engine as a collision consequence
State insurance department complaint; insurer pays the engine

title: Third catalytic converter in a year, and the last one was not legal
type: Repeat parts theft with a non-compliant previous repair
story: Policyholder's 2008 Honda Element had its catalytic converter cut off overnight on the street outside his apartment in Van Nuys, Los Angeles. It is the third theft in eleven months. After the second theft he fitted a cheap converter bought online himself. A California-compliant replacement costs $2,450.
statement: Third time. I heard the saw at 3am and by the time I got downstairs they were gone. Last time the insurance paid but the shop wanted so much I bought one online for $180 and my cousin put it in. It passed the smog fine. I don't have a garage. What am I supposed to do?

accounts.text: Theft from vehicle: catalytic converter removed with a power saw between 02:45 and 03:10. Victim heard cutting noise. No suspect description. Third report from the same victim address in 11 months.

Previous converter was an aftermarket unit with no California Air Resources Board executive order number, not legal for sale or installation in California. Replacement must be CARB-compliant: $2,450 including O2 sensors and labor. Recommend a converter shield, $390.

whatHappened: A genuine repeat theft from a model that thieves target. The previous self-installed converter was not legal in California, which affects what the insurer can pay for now.
damage: Converter and exhaust section cut out; CARB-compliant replacement $2,450, optional shield $390.
evidence: Police reports for all three thefts
Repair shop note on the previous non-compliant part
missing: Payment records for the second claim to see what was paid and for what part
innocent: Repeat thefts are common for this model on the street
He did not know the online converter was not legal in California
questions: Ask whether he can park off the street or in a lit area
Ask whether he would accept a shield as part of the repair
steps: Pay a CARB-compliant replacement less the comprehensive deductible
Recommend, or contribute to, a converter shield to prevent a fourth claim
Explain that repeated claims may affect renewal, within California rules
assessment: Genuine. The insurer must pay for a legal replacement, not the cheap illegal part he bought last time, even though it costs more. Preventing a fourth theft is in everyone's interest.
action: Pay the CARB-compliant repair and offer a shield.
outcomes: Paid with a shield fitted; no further thefts reported
Customer chooses to sell the car

title: Taken with a USB cable, found with a broken column
type: Theft of a vulnerable model without an immobilizer
story: Policyholder's 2017 Kia Optima was stolen from outside her house in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and found by police three days later, abandoned with the steering column broken open and the rear bumper damaged. While joyriding, the thieves also sideswiped a parked Chevy Malibu, whose owner left a note asking her to pay.
statement: They broke the back window and the column, that's how they do it with these cars. I know there was a software update, I got a letter, I just never got round to booking it. I need the car for work. And I'm not paying for some other car that a thief hit.

accounts.text: Stolen vehicle recovered on a residential street. Rear quarter glass broken, steering column cover removed, ignition cylinder broken, USB cable left in the vehicle. Damage to the right side consistent with a collision. Vehicle towed to the city tow lot. Owner notified.
Your car hit mine on Saturday night on 35th Street, my neighbor saw it and the plate. Mirror and both doors on the driver side. Please call me about paying for it.

whatHappened: A well-known theft method on a model without an immobilizer, followed by joyriding damage. She was not driving and did not give permission.
damage: Kia: column, ignition, rear glass, rear bumper and right side, estimate $4,300. Tow lot fees accruing at $25 a day. Malibu: driver's side mirror and doors.
thirdParties: Owner of the parked Chevy Malibu
evidence: Photos of the column and glass
The note from the Malibu owner
missing: The Malibu owner's insurance details
innocent: Not installing the free anti-theft update is careless, but it is not a policy breach
questions: Ask the Malibu owner whether she has collision or uninsured motorist property damage coverage
steps: Pay the theft damage under comprehensive less the deductible
Pay the tow lot fees and move the car to a repair shop quickly to stop daily charges
Explain to the Malibu owner that the thief was not a permitted driver, so the policyholder's liability coverage does not apply, and direct her to her own insurer
Recommend the anti-theft software update and a steering wheel lock
assessment: Genuine theft with straightforward cover. The only friction is the third-party note: a thief's driving is not the owner's liability, which needs explaining kindly to both sides.
action: Settle under comprehensive, release the car from the tow lot fast, and redirect the Malibu owner.
outcomes: Repaired and returned within two weeks
Malibu owner claims under her own collision coverage

title: A truck worth less than the loan, gone from the lot at 1am
type: Reported theft with signs of owner give-up
story: Policyholder reported his 2021 Ram 1500 stolen from his apartment complex car park in Houston, Texas. He owes $52,400 on the loan; the truck is worth about $38,000. The truck's connected services show it was driven from the complex at 01:06 to a rural property 40 miles away, where the signal stopped at 01:58.
statement: I parked it at like 9 and in the morning it was gone. Both keys are in my apartment. I've been struggling with the payment since I got laid off, but I'd never do something like that. I don't know anyone out that way.

accounts.text: Vehicle started with a valid key fob at 01:06. Drove 40.2 miles to a rural address near Cleveland, Texas, arriving 01:58. Telematics unit disconnected at 02:03. No alarm or forced entry events recorded.

accounts.who: Property records and social media check
accounts.text: The rural address is owned by a man who shares the policyholder's surname and is listed as his uncle on a public family memorial page. Policyholder posted a photo from the same property four months ago with the caption "Family land weekend".

whatHappened: Possibly an arranged "theft" to escape a loan he could not pay: the truck was started with a valid key and driven to a relative's property. It is not yet proven, and the interview may produce an explanation.
damage: Truck not recovered; actual cash value about $38,000. Loan balance $52,400.
thirdParties: Lender with a lien on the truck
missing: A search of the rural property by police
Records of who has had access to his keys
Phone location data, if he agrees to provide it
inconsistencies: He says both keys were in his apartment; the truck was started with a valid key
He says he knows no one out that way; the truck went to his uncle's land, where he has visited
indicators: Negative equity and loan arrears after a job loss
Started with a valid key, no forced entry
Driven to property owned by a relative
Telematics disconnected after arrival
innocent: A relative or friend with access to a key might have taken it without his knowledge
Key fobs can sometimes be cloned by organised thieves
questions: Ask, under oath if necessary, who has had access to the keys in the last six months
Ask whether he knows the rural address and when he was last there
Ask whether anyone else in the family has a key or has borrowed the truck
steps: Refer to the special investigations unit and the National Insurance Crime Bureau
Request an examination under oath as the policy allows
Share the location with police and ask for a property check
Hold payment, keep the lender informed, and decide on the evidence
assessment: Strong indicators of an owner give-up, which is a common fraud when vehicles are in negative equity. The data trail to a relative's land is hard to explain innocently, but the examination under oath must be done properly before any denial.
action: Investigate through the SIU, request an examination under oath and involve police; deny only if the evidence holds.
outcomes: Truck found on the property; claim denied and referred for prosecution
Relative admits taking it without permission; claim handled as theft
Policyholder withdraws the claim

title: Asleep at the wheel after a double shift
type: Fatigue collision with several parked cars
story: Policyholder, a nurse, fell asleep driving home in Cleveland, Ohio, at about 07:50 after a 16-hour double shift. Her Nissan Rogue drifted right and hit three parked cars and a front-yard fence. Nobody was hurt. Her policy has a $25,000 property damage liability limit.
