statement: I remember the light at the corner and then a bang. I must have nodded off. I'd worked two shifts back to back because we were short-staffed. I'm so ashamed. I knocked on every door to apologize. I've been told I'll get a ticket.

accounts.text: Unit 1 left the roadway to the right, struck parked Units 2, 3 and 4 in sequence, and came to rest against a wooden fence. Driver admitted falling asleep. Cited for failure to control. No impairment observed. Units 2 to 4 unoccupied.

Unit 2, Honda Civic: rear end, $5,900. Unit 3, Ford Escape: side and rear, $8,700. Unit 4, Toyota Tacoma: rear bumper, $2,100. Fence: 24 feet, $3,200. Total so far $19,900. Rental requests from two owners, about $1,500.

whatHappened: As she says: she fell asleep from exhaustion and drifted off the road.
damage: Three parked vehicles and a fence, about $21,400 including rental. Her Rogue: front and right side, about $7,800.
thirdParties: Owners of the Civic, the Escape and the Tacoma
evidence: Estimates and rental requests from each claimant
missing: Final repair invoices and rental durations
Supplements, which could push the total past the limit
innocent: Falling asleep after a long shift is negligent but not dishonest; she reported every detail herself
questions: Ask each claimant for the final repair invoice
Ask whether she has an umbrella policy
steps: Accept liability for all property damage claims
Track the total against the $25,000 limit and settle claims fairly in order
Pay her own vehicle under collision less the deductible
Warn her in writing if total claims may exceed her limit, so she can involve an umbrella insurer or her own lawyer
assessment: Genuine negligence with full cooperation. The practical risk is the property damage limit: with four claimants and rentals, supplements could exceed $25,000, so the claims need to be managed carefully and the policyholder kept informed.
action: Accept liability, settle claims within the limit, and keep the policyholder informed of any excess exposure.
outcomes: All property damage settled at $23,800, within the limit
Supplements exceed the limit; policyholder pays $1,200 personally or through an umbrella policy

title: The excluded son and the borrowed SUV
type: Crash by a driver excluded from the policy
story: Policyholder's son, 20, crashed her Jeep Grand Cherokee into a neighbour's fence and a utility box at about 01:30 in a suburb of Detroit. He was excluded from her policy by a named driver exclusion signed after his drunk driving conviction last year. She says he took the keys without permission. At the last renewal she told the insurer he had moved out.
statement: He doesn't have permission to drive it, ever, that's the whole point. He was staying over that weekend and took the keys from my purse while I was asleep. He moved out in the spring, he only comes back some weekends. I'm not responsible for him stealing my car.

accounts.text: I took Mom's keys because my friend needed a ride home. I've driven it a few times when she was at work, she knows. I live here, I just stay at my girlfriend's a lot. I wasn't drinking.

Driver lost control on a curve and struck a fence and an electrical utility box. Preliminary breath test negative. Driver's license address matches the policyholder's address. Driver cited for careless driving.

whatHappened: The excluded son was driving. Whether he took the car without permission or was a regular household driver, the exclusion applies; the bigger question is whether the renewal statement that he had moved out was untrue.
damage: Jeep: front end and airbags, about $14,500. Fence $2,800 and utility box about $9,000.
thirdParties: Utility company that owns the box
evidence: Police report with his license address
Renewal record stating he had moved out
missing: Proof of where the son actually lived, such as mail, a lease or work records
Michigan's rules on excluded drivers and minimum liability for third parties
inconsistencies: She says he moved out in the spring; his license address and his own statement say he lives there
She says he never drove the car; he says he has driven it several times while she was at work
indicators: Possible misstatement of household composition at renewal
innocent: Adult children often live between two homes, and a parent may honestly think of him as having moved out
A young man may claim more permission than he really had to protect himself
questions: Ask for evidence of the son's address since the spring
Ask the policyholder whether she knew he had driven the car before
steps: Deny collision coverage for the Jeep because an excluded driver was driving
Check state law on whether minimum liability must still be paid to third parties despite the exclusion
Investigate the renewal statement about his residence and consider rescission only if it was knowingly false
Explain the decision clearly in writing
assessment: A real coverage dispute rather than a staged event. The exclusion is likely to defeat the claim for her own car whatever the permission position, while third-party claims depend on state law. The renewal statement could be a material misrepresentation, but it needs evidence before it is treated as such.
action: Apply the exclusion to the Jeep, handle third-party liability as state law requires, and investigate the residency statement before deciding on the policy.
outcomes: Own damage denied; third-party claims paid to the state minimum and recovered from the policyholder
Misrepresentation proven; policy rescinded from renewal
Policyholder sues over the denial; settled

title: Drunk into a utility pole, and still covered
type: Single-vehicle crash while intoxicated
story: Policyholder crashed his Chevrolet Malibu into a utility pole in Charlotte, North Carolina, at 02:15. He was arrested for driving while impaired with a breath alcohol reading of 0.14. Power went out to 300 homes. The utility company is claiming $18,600 for the pole and the emergency crew.
statement: I was at a friend's birthday and I thought I was fine to drive. I wasn't. I went off the road on the curve. I'm lucky I didn't kill anyone. Whatever happens with the insurance, I deserve it.

accounts.text: Single vehicle left the roadway and struck a utility pole, snapping it at the base. Driver had slurred speech and the odour of alcohol. Breath test 0.14. Arrested for driving while impaired. No other vehicles or persons involved.
Replacement of a 45-foot distribution pole, transformer re-hang, conductor repair and an overnight emergency crew of six. Labor $11,900, materials $6,700. Total $18,600.

whatHappened: As he says: he drove after drinking and crashed.
damage: Malibu: front end, likely total loss, value about $12,000. Utility pole and equipment: $18,600.
missing: An itemized breakdown of the utility labor rates and crew hours
innocent: Paying a drunk driver's claim can look wrong, but standard US policies respond so that third parties are protected
questions: Ask the utility company for crew time sheets and the age of the pole
steps: Pay the utility claim under property damage liability after checking the itemization and any depreciation of the old pole
Pay his own car under collision if the policy has no applicable exclusion for impaired driving
File the SR-22 if the state requires it, and review the policy at renewal
assessment: Serious misconduct, but most standard US auto policies still respond to drunk driving accidents, because the law wants injured third parties and property owners paid. The consequences fall on the driver through the criminal process and through his premium and future insurability.
action: Pay the third-party claim after checking it, pay collision if no exclusion applies, and review the policy at renewal.
outcomes: Utility claim settled at $16,900 after a depreciation adjustment
Policy non-renewed; driver must buy high-risk insurance with an SR-22

title: Swoop, squat and four patients at the same clinic
type: Staged collision with organised medical fraud
story: Policyholder, 61, rear-ended a Toyota Sienna on the Palmetto Expressway in Miami after a dark sedan swerved in front of the Sienna and the Sienna braked hard. The sedan drove off. All four Sienna occupants began treatment at the same clinic the next morning and have claimed Personal Injury Protection under their own policies and bodily injury against the policyholder.
statement: A black car cut in front of the van really close and the van slammed on its brakes. There was no reason for the black car to do that, it just swooped in and then sped away. Within five minutes a tow truck and a man handing out business cards for a clinic were there. I thought that was very odd.

accounts.text: Our clients were lawfully travelling when they were violently struck from behind by your insured. All four suffered neck and back injuries and are receiving treatment at a medical center three times a week. Please confirm your insured's bodily injury limits.

The clinic is owned by a person with no medical license and was registered 8 months ago. It appears in 41 other claims this year, 38 of them involving rear-end collisions with a sudden stop. Two of the Sienna occupants were passengers in other claims treated at the same clinic. The Sienna was insured 19 days before the collision. The same attorney represents 33 of the linked claims.

whatHappened: Very probably a staged "swoop and squat": a swoop car cut in, the squat car (the Sienna) braked hard to cause a rear-end impact, and recruited occupants were funnelled to a clinic that bills PIP and builds up injury claims.
damage: Policyholder's Corolla: front bumper and hood. Sienna: rear bumper. PIP claims for four occupants at about $10,000 each, plus bodily injury demands.
evidence: Policyholder's account of the swoop car and the instant runner
Photos showing minor rear bumper damage
missing: Traffic camera footage from the expressway
Examinations under oath of each occupant
The clinic's licensing records and treatment notes
inconsistencies: The attorney describes a violent impact; the damage is minor bumper contact
The occupants describe lawful travel; the policyholder saw a car swerve in and a clinic runner arrive within minutes
indicators: Classic swoop and squat pattern with a car that fled
Clinic runner at the scene within minutes
Clinic owned by an unlicensed person and linked to dozens of similar claims
Occupants who appear in other claims at the same clinic
Recently insured vehicle
innocent: A driver can genuinely cut in and brake-check by accident
Injured people sometimes choose the nearest clinic or follow advice from strangers at the scene
questions: Ask each occupant, under oath, how they know each other, where they were going and how they chose the clinic
Ask the policyholder to describe the man with the business cards
steps: Refer the matter to the National Insurance Crime Bureau and the Florida Division of Investigative and Forensic Services
Coordinate with the occupants' own PIP insurers, which receive the clinic bills
Deny the bodily injury claims pending investigation and examinations under oath
Preserve traffic camera footage and the vehicle data from both cars
assessment: Strong evidence of an organised staged-accident ring targeting an innocent driver. The pattern, the runner and the clinic links make coincidence implausible. The policyholder should be told she is not under suspicion.
action: Treat as organised fraud: refer to state and national fraud bodies, require examinations under oath, and defend the injury claims.
outcomes: Claims abandoned after examinations under oath are requested
Clinic owner and recruiters charged after a multi-insurer investigation
Injury claims dismissed; policyholder's record cleared

title: Five riders on the camera, twelve injury claims
type: Bus sideswipe with jump-in passengers
story: Policyholder sideswiped a city transit bus while changing lanes in Philadelphia at about 16:30. He accepts fault. Twelve people have since made injury claims as bus passengers. The bus's interior cameras show five passengers on board at the moment of impact.
statement: I misjudged the gap and scraped the side of the bus with my mirror and door. It was a scrape, not a crash. The bus stopped and I saw people getting on through the front door after it stopped, which seemed strange.

accounts.text: Interior cameras 1 to 6 at 16:31:02, the moment of contact: five passengers on board, all seated, no visible movement from the impact. 16:32:40 to 16:36:10: seven people board through the front doors while the bus is stopped awaiting a supervisor. Several of them sit down and later report injuries to the supervisor.

Twelve bodily injury claims naming the policyholder, all describing neck and back pain from "a violent collision". Nine are represented by the same two law firms. Seven of the twelve names match the people seen boarding after the collision.

whatHappened: A minor sideswipe that was his fault. Seven people boarded the stopped bus afterwards to pose as injured passengers, a scheme known as "jump-ins". The five real passengers may or may not have minor injuries.
damage: Bus: scraped side panel. Policyholder's car: mirror and door. Twelve injury claims.
thirdParties: Five passengers on board at the time
missing: Medical records for the five genuine passengers
Identity checks matching the seven claimants to the footage
inconsistencies: Twelve claimants describe a violent collision; the cameras show five seated passengers who did not move on impact
Seven claimants boarded after the collision
indicators: Jump-in passengers boarding a stopped bus after a collision
Clustered representation by the same law firms
Claimed injuries out of proportion to a scrape
innocent: Some of the five real passengers may have been jolted and genuinely sore
questions: Ask each claimant to state when and where they boarded the bus, before showing them the footage
steps: Accept liability for the bus damage and evaluate the five real passengers' claims on their merits
Deny the seven jump-in claims with the camera evidence
Refer the jump-ins and the law firms to the state fraud unit
Work with the transit authority, which has the same interest in defeating the false claims
assessment: The camera evidence separates the genuine passengers from the impostors. The insurer should be fair to the five people who were on the bus and firm with the seven who were not.
action: Accept liability for the real loss, deny the jump-in claims and refer them for prosecution.
outcomes: Jump-in claims withdrawn after footage disclosed
Two of the five genuine passengers paid modest settlements
Several jump-ins charged with insurance fraud

title: A five mile an hour tap and $14,000 of chiropractic
type: Low-impact collision with a built-up injury claim
story: Policyholder rolled into the back of a Hyundai Elantra in a drive-through queue in Las Vegas, Nevada. There was no visible damage to either car beyond a scuffed bumper cover. Four months later, the Elantra driver's attorney demanded $85,000, including $14,200 of chiropractic treatment, an MRI and a recommendation for spinal injections.
statement: My foot slipped off the brake in the drive-through. I barely touched her. We both got out, there wasn't even a mark you could see, just a scuff. She said she was fine and we didn't call the police. She was laughing about it.

accounts.text: Our client suffered cervical and lumbar sprain and strain and a disc bulge at C5-C6. She has completed 46 chiropractic sessions over 16 weeks, MRI imaging and a pain management consultation recommending injections. Treatment is provided under a letter of protection. Specials to date $17,900. Demand $85,000.

accounts.who: Event data recorder download from the policyholder's car
accounts.text: Pre-crash: vehicle speed 3 mph, no braking for 1.2 seconds before contact. Delta-V (change in speed) of the struck vehicle estimated at under 2 mph. No airbag deployment event.

whatHappened: A genuine minor bump. Whether she was hurt is uncertain; the treatment pattern, under a letter of protection and arranged through an attorney, suggests the claim has been built up far beyond any injury the impact could plausibly cause.
damage: Scuffed bumper cover on the Elantra, $380. Injury demand $85,000 with $17,900 of medical specials.
missing: Her prior medical history and any earlier claims
An independent medical examination
Biomechanical analysis of the impact
inconsistencies: She said she was fine at the scene; four months later she reports serious spinal injury
indicators: Treatment volume far out of proportion to a 3 mph impact
Treatment under a letter of protection, arranged through the attorney
Escalating recommendations near the time of demand
innocent: Some people do develop symptoms after a minor impact, especially with existing degeneration
A disc bulge seen on MRI is common in adults without any accident
questions: Ask for her medical records for the five years before the collision
Ask how she was referred to the chiropractor
steps: Run a claims history check on the claimant and the providers
Obtain prior records and an independent medical examination
Value the claim on the evidence of a very low-speed impact
Make a fair offer for a short course of treatment, and defend the rest
assessment: Potential fraud through build-up rather than a staged crash. The collision happened and his liability is clear. The value is the issue: a 2 mph change in speed rarely causes lasting injury, and the treatment pattern points to a claim engineered for settlement. Some modest injury remains possible.
action: Accept liability for the bump, investigate medical history and providers, and offer a settlement based on a reasonable treatment period.
outcomes: Settled at $6,500
Tried before a jury; verdict for $3,000 of medical costs only
Provider network later investigated in a wider fraud inquiry

title: New parts on the invoice, used parts on the car
type: Repair shop billing for parts and work not supplied
story: Policyholder's Honda Accord was repaired at a direct repair program shop in St. Louis, Missouri, after a side-impact collision. The shop added $3,940 in supplements to the original estimate. A routine reinspection after the repair found parts that did not match the invoice, and one supplement photo shows a different car.
statement: I just picked my car up and it looks fine to me. The shop said they found more damage once they took it apart. I don't know anything about parts, I trusted them because the insurance recommended them.

accounts.text: Front bumper cover: aftermarket, invoiced as OEM, difference $412. Left headlamp: used OEM unit with old date code and scuffs, invoiced as new, difference $686. Left fender: invoiced as replaced, actually repaired and refinished. Blend labor billed on the hood, which shows no refinish. Supplement photo 7 shows a Honda Accord with a different license plate and a VIN tag ending 4471.

The aftermarket bumper was a parts-supplier mix-up and we will credit it. The headlamp came in a box marked new. Photo 7 was uploaded in error from another job. Our technicians replaced the fender and we stand by our invoice.

whatHappened: The shop appears to have billed for new OEM parts and work that were not supplied, and padded the supplement with a photo from another car. Some items could be errors; together they look like a pattern.
damage: Original estimate $5,120; supplements $3,940; reinspection identifies about $2,300 billed for parts or labor not supplied.
thirdParties: The repair shop in the direct repair program
evidence: Reinspection report with part numbers and date codes
Supplement photos including one from a different vehicle
missing: Parts supplier invoices for the job
An audit of the shop's other recent claims
inconsistencies: Invoice says OEM bumper and new headlamp; the car has an aftermarket bumper and a used headlamp
Invoice says the fender was replaced; it was repaired
A supplement photo shows a different car
indicators: Several billing discrepancies on one job, all in the shop's favour
Photo from another vehicle used to support a supplement
innocent: Parts suppliers do send wrong parts, and busy shops mix up photos
The policyholder knows nothing about the parts and has no involvement
questions: Ask the shop for its parts purchase invoices and fender order records
Ask the shop why photo 7 shows a different plate
steps: Recover the overbilling from the shop and make sure the policyholder's car is brought up to the invoiced standard or credited
Audit the shop's last 50 claims for the same pattern
Suspend the shop from the direct repair program pending the audit
Refer to the special investigations unit and the state insurance fraud unit if the pattern is confirmed
assessment: Potential repairer fraud. One discrepancy could be an error; four discrepancies in the shop's favour plus a borrowed photo suggest deliberate inflation. The policyholder is innocent and must be protected: her car should end up with the parts she is entitled to.
action: Recover the overpayment, put the car right, audit the shop and refer if the audit confirms a pattern.
outcomes: Shop credits $2,300 and replaces the headlamp; removed from the program after the audit
Audit finds the same pattern on 14 jobs; referred to the state fraud unit

title: Thirty days of rental from a cousin's agency
type: Rental reimbursement claim with a questionable receipt
story: Policyholder's Toyota Camry was hit in a parking lot in Newark, New Jersey, and repaired in six days. He then claimed $1,950 in rental reimbursement, 30 days at $65, with a handwritten receipt from a small rental business. The business is registered to a man with the same surname at the same street as his mother.
statement: The repair took longer than they said, and I needed a car for work. My cousin has a little rental business so I got one from him, it's cheaper than the big companies. I paid him cash. The receipt is what he gave me.

accounts.text: Vehicle dropped off on the 3rd, repairs completed and vehicle collected by the owner on the 9th. Customer signature on collection.

Access badge assigned to the employee, linked to plate of the 2018 Toyota Camry: entries on 21 of the 30 days in the rental period, including on the 10th to the 30th. No other vehicle is registered to the badge.

whatHappened: He used a rental, if at all, for at most six days. The receipt for 30 days from a relative's business appears to inflate the claim, while his own car was back in use and parking at work.
damage: Original claim: parking lot damage repaired for $2,700. Rental claim $1,950 for 30 days; supportable period six days.
thirdParties: His cousin, owner of the rental business
evidence: Repair invoice with the collection date
Handwritten receipt with no vehicle details
missing: Rental agreement with the vehicle's plate or VIN
Proof of the cash payment
The rental business's insurance and registration
inconsistencies: Rental claimed for 30 days; his own car was collected after six days
His own car entered the work garage on 21 days of the rental period
indicators: Related-party rental with a handwritten cash receipt
Rental period far longer than the repair
Own vehicle in use during the claimed rental
innocent: A family member may have helped him for a few days and written a receipt carelessly
He may have used the rental car for a relative while driving his own
questions: Ask for the rental agreement showing the vehicle and the dates
Ask why his Camry was at work during the rental period
steps: Pay rental for the six repair days at a reasonable rate, if supported by an agreement
Decline the remaining 24 days with the evidence
Refer to the special investigations unit if he insists on the full period
assessment: Potential fraud through inflated expenses. The repair claim is genuine; the rental claim is mostly unsupported and contradicted by the parking records. He should be given the chance to explain before a fraud finding.
action: Pay what is supported, decline the rest, and refer if he persists.
outcomes: Accepts six days of rental; claim closed
Insists on 30 days; referred to the New Jersey Office of the Insurance Fraud Prosecutor

title: A policy in her name, a face that is not hers
type: Policy and claim made with a stolen identity
claimant: Person using the name Angela Price
story: A policy bought online five weeks ago in the name of Angela Price covers a 2015 Dodge Charger. A collision claim was made for intersection damage in Dallas, with a request to pay $7,800 into a newly opened online bank account. The driver license photo sent with the claim does not match the photo held by the state licensing agency.
statement: Claim form: I was going through the light on green and another car hit me and drove off. I need the money as soon as possible to fix the car, I can't get to work. Please pay to the account below. I am not available by phone, email only.

accounts.text: License number, name and date of birth valid. The state's license photo shows a woman aged about 60. The image submitted with the claim shows a woman aged about 25 with different features; image metadata shows it was edited in a photo app. Premium paid by a prepaid card. Policy email created the day before purchase.

accounts.who: Contact with the real Angela Price
accounts.text: I have never owned a Dodge Charger and I didn't buy any insurance from you. I had a letter from my bank last year about a data breach. I'm 61 and I live in El Paso. Please tell me what I need to do.

whatHappened: Someone used Angela Price's stolen identity to buy a policy and claim for damage to a car, probably with old or staged damage, and to route the payout to an account they control.
damage: Claimed front-end damage $7,800, never inspected in person.
thirdParties: Angela Price, the identity theft victim
Unknown person who made the claim
evidence: License photo mismatch and edited image
Statement from the real Angela Price
Newly created email and bank account
missing: Location and ownership of the Charger
Identity of the bank account holder
inconsistencies: Claim photo ID does not match the licensing agency photo
The named policyholder says she never bought the policy or owned the car
indicators: Stolen identity used for the policy
Edited ID image
Prepaid card and new email
Payout requested to a new account, contact by email only
innocent: None that fits a denial from the real person and an edited ID
questions: Ask the bank, through proper legal channels, who opened the receiving account
Ask the claimant to attend an in-person inspection with original ID
steps: Stop payment and void the policy as obtained by fraud
Help the real Angela Price: confirm in writing that she has no liability and suggest she reports the identity theft
Report to the Texas Department of Insurance fraud unit and law enforcement
Flag the vehicle and account details across industry databases
assessment: Confirmed fraud. The real person whose identity was used has confirmed she had nothing to do with it, and the submitted ID was edited. The priority is to stop payment and protect the victim.
action: Deny, void, report, and support the identity theft victim.
outcomes: Payment stopped and policy voided; case referred to the state fraud unit
Account holder identified as part of a wider identity fraud ring

title: A stolen car that never existed
type: Theft claim on a "paper car" with a recycled VIN
story: Policyholder reported his 2020 Jeep Wrangler stolen from outside a restaurant in Memphis, Tennessee, two months after insuring it. He supplied a title, a bill of sale for $36,000 and photos. A title history check shows the VIN belongs to a Wrangler that was declared a total loss in a flood in another state and sold for parts.
statement: I bought it private, cash, from a guy in Mississippi. The title was clean when I registered it. I parked outside the restaurant for an hour and it was gone. I have both keys, they're right here.

accounts.text: VIN reported as a total loss by an insurer 26 months ago after flood damage in Louisiana. Salvage title issued and the vehicle sold at auction to a parts dismantler, who reported it as dismantled. A clean title for the same VIN was later issued in Tennessee on a bill of sale and an out-of-state title.

The six photos supplied match images from an online dealer listing for a different Wrangler, with the plate digitally altered. The two keys supplied are generic aftermarket remotes not programmed to any vehicle. The Mississippi title supplied has a document number that does not exist in that state's records.

whatHappened: No such car existed in his hands. The VIN of a dismantled flood vehicle was used to create a clean title, a policy was bought on that paper car, and a theft was reported to collect the payout.
damage: Claimed theft of a $36,000 vehicle that did not exist.
evidence: Title history showing the VIN was dismantled
Photos copied from a dealer listing
missing: Who prepared the forged title, and whether the same method was used on other VINs
inconsistencies: The VIN belongs to a vehicle reported as dismantled
The photos are of a different Wrangler
The keys are not programmed to any vehicle
indicators: Clean title issued for a salvage VIN
Cash private sale with no traceable seller
Stock photos and dummy keys
Theft reported soon after the policy started
innocent: A buyer could be deceived by a forged title, but that would not explain copied photos and dummy keys
questions: Ask him to provide any messages or call records with the seller
Ask for the bank records of the $36,000 cash withdrawal
steps: Deny the claim and rescind the policy
Report to the National Insurance Crime Bureau and the Tennessee Department of Commerce and Insurance
Notify the titling authority so the VIN is flagged
assessment: Confirmed fraud. Each element could have an explanation alone, but together, a dismantled VIN, borrowed photos, dummy keys and a non-existent title document, they show a fabricated vehicle.
action: Deny, rescind and refer.
outcomes: Claim denied; referred for prosecution
Investigation links the forged title to a ring producing paper cars

title: Both reversing, and Maryland says neither recovers
type: Parking lot collision under contributory negligence
story: Policyholder and another driver backed out of facing spaces at a shopping center in Towson, Maryland, and their rear bumpers met. The other driver's insurer denied her claim, saying she was partly at fault and that under Maryland's contributory negligence rule she cannot recover anything.
statement: I was already out of my space and stopped, waiting for him to finish so I could go. He reversed into me. His insurer says because I was moving at some point, I'm partly to blame and get nothing. That can't be right.

accounts.text: We were both backing out at the same time. I checked my mirrors and didn't see her because of the van next to me. She was moving when we hit, I'm sure of it.

16:12:05 the policyholder's Mazda begins reversing. 16:12:09 Mazda stops partly in the aisle. 16:12:11 the other driver's Buick begins reversing. 16:12:13 contact between the bumpers. The Mazda appears stationary at contact, though the image is low resolution.

whatHappened: Most likely she had stopped and he reversed into her. In most states this would be mostly his fault; in Maryland any proven fault on her part, however small, bars recovery from him.
damage: Mazda rear bumper $1,640; Buick rear bumper $1,200.
thirdParties: Mr Gordon Ellis and his insurer
missing: A clearer copy of the camera footage or another angle
inconsistencies: He says she was moving at contact; the footage suggests she had stopped two seconds earlier
innocent: In a reversing collision each driver honestly thinks the other was moving
questions: Ask the shopping center for the original-resolution file and other camera angles
steps: Pay her repair under collision less the deductible
Send the footage to the other insurer and argue she was stationary, so she has no contributory negligence
Subrogate if accepted, or use inter-company arbitration
assessment: Honest dispute in an unforgiving state. The contributory negligence rule makes the footage decisive: if she was stopped, she bears no fault and recovers in full; if she was still rolling, she recovers nothing from the other driver.
action: Pay under collision now and pursue subrogation using the footage.
outcomes: Other insurer accepts liability after the footage; deductible refunded
Arbitration finds both moving; no recovery, customer keeps the collision payment

title: "Hit while parked", said before she saw the video
type: Parking lot collision reported as damage to a parked car
story: Policyholder reported that her parked Toyota Highlander was hit by another car at a warehouse store car park in Sacramento, California. The other driver says she reversed out into him. The store's camera shows her reversing at the moment of contact. In a recorded statement she then said she had "just started to back out".
statement: First report: I was parked and loading the trunk when he hit me. Recorded statement, after hearing about the video: OK, I'd finished loading and I'd started backing out, only a foot or so. I thought because I was barely moving it counts as parked. I wasn't trying to lie.

accounts.text: I was driving slowly down the aisle and the Highlander backed out without looking and hit my passenger door. I honked but it was too late.
Highlander reverse lights on at 11:02:14, vehicle moves back about 3 feet into the aisle. Sedan travelling in the aisle at walking pace. Contact at 11:02:17. Highlander stops after contact.

whatHappened: She reversed into a car moving slowly along the aisle. Her first report that she was parked was a convenient description rather than the truth, which she corrected when the video was mentioned.
damage: Highlander rear bumper $1,100. Sedan passenger doors $3,400.
thirdParties: Mr Raymond Ochoa, the other driver
evidence: Both statements, including her corrected account
missing: The other driver's speed, which looks low on the video
inconsistencies: First report says she was parked; the camera and her later statement show she was reversing
indicators: An account that shifted liability onto the other driver
innocent: Many people think a car barely moving counts as parked
She corrected herself in the recorded statement
questions: Ask whether she looked over her shoulder or relied on the reversing camera
steps: Accept liability for the other driver's damage under property damage liability
Pay her bumper under collision less the deductible
Note the corrected account on file
assessment: A reporting error rather than fraud: the first account was self-serving but corrected quickly. Liability falls mainly on the reversing driver.
action: Accept liability, pay both damages, and record the correction.
outcomes: Liability accepted; other driver's repair paid
Claim recorded as at fault, affecting her premium

title: Two months old, repaired, and worth less
type: Third-party diminished value dispute
story: The insurer's policyholder ran a stop sign in Alpharetta, Georgia, and hit the side of a two-month-old electric sedan owned by the claimant. Liability is accepted and the car has been repaired for $11,800. The claimant now claims $8,400 for diminished value, supported by an independent appraisal. The insurer's own calculation gives $2,150.
statement: My car was brand new. Now it has an accident on its history report and every dealer I've asked offers me thousands less than they would for one without. The repair was good, but that's not the point. I'm not trying to profit, I just want to be made whole.

accounts.text: Pre-loss value $48,500. Post-repair value, based on three dealer trade-in offers that cite the accident history and structural repair to the B-pillar: $40,100. Diminished value $8,400.
Base loss of value capped at 10% of the pre-loss value, adjusted by damage multiplier (0.50, moderate structural) and mileage multiplier (1.0, under 1,000 miles). Result: $2,150 after rounding.

whatHappened: A genuine loss in market value after a well-repaired accident. Both sides have a method; the numbers are far apart.
damage: Repair paid $11,800. Diminished value claimed $8,400; insurer's figure $2,150.
thirdParties: The insurer's policyholder, who caused the collision
missing: A third valuation from a neutral appraiser
Market data for comparable cars with similar repairs
innocent: A large gap between two valuations is normal in diminished value claims and does not suggest bad faith on either side
questions: Ask the claimant for the dealers' written offers
Ask her whether she intends to sell the car now or keep it
steps: Explain that the formula is one method and not binding on her
Review the dealer evidence, especially the structural repair, which buyers price heavily
Negotiate toward a figure supported by market evidence
Consider a neutral appraisal if the gap remains
assessment: Legitimate dispute. Georgia recognises diminished value, and a formula that caps the loss at 10% and halves it again can understate it for a nearly new car with structural repairs. The claimant's evidence is credible, and an inflexible approach risks a lawsuit and a bad-faith allegation.
action: Negotiate on the market evidence rather than the formula alone, aiming for a reasoned settlement.
outcomes: Settled at $6,000
Neutral appraisal sets $7,100; paid
Claimant files suit in magistrate court and is awarded $7,800

title: An empty trailer, a wind warning and too many hours on the clock
type: Commercial truck blown over in high wind
claimant: High Plains Freight LLC (driver Carl Jessup)
story: An insured carrier's tractor pulling an empty 53-foot trailer was blown onto its side on I-80 near Arlington, Wyoming, at about 03:40. The trailer slid into the left lane and hit a pickup, whose driver has a broken wrist. A road advisory at the time warned that the section was closed to light, high-profile vehicles. The truck's electronic logging device shows the driver had been driving for 12 hours 35 minutes.
statement: Driver, Carl Jessup: The gusts came out of nowhere. I'd been checking the road reports and I didn't see the closure for light trucks, I thought it was just a wind warning. I was trying to get through to Laramie before stopping. I know my hours were close.

accounts.text: On duty from 13:20 the previous day. Driving time 12 hours 35 minutes since the last 10-hour break, exceeding the 11-hour driving limit by 1 hour 35 minutes. No log edits. Speed at the time of the event 61 mph.

accounts.who: Wyoming Department of Transportation road condition record
accounts.text: I-80 Laramie to Rawlins: "Closed to light, high-profile vehicles" from 01:15. Wind gusts recorded at 62 mph at the Arlington sensor at 03:30. Advisory displayed on overhead message signs at two locations before Arlington.

whatHappened: The driver drove an empty, wind-vulnerable rig past posted closures for light, high-profile vehicles, while over his legal driving hours, and the wind blew it over into another vehicle.
damage: Tractor and trailer total loss, about $142,000. Pickup: driver's side crushed; driver with a broken wrist. Road clean-up and guardrail costs.
evidence: WYDOT closure records and message sign locations
missing: Dispatch records showing whether the carrier pushed the driver to keep going
The pickup driver's medical records
inconsistencies: The driver says he saw only a wind warning; closure messages were displayed on two overhead signs before the crash site
innocent: Drivers do sometimes misread advisories when tired
The carrier may not have known the driver was over his hours
questions: Ask dispatch whether they contacted the driver about the closure or his hours
Ask the carrier whether it has a policy for parking during wind closures
steps: Accept liability for the pickup driver and the state's costs; violations of the hours rules and road closures make the case hard to defend
Settle the injury claim early, before litigation adds punitive damage risk
Pay the physical damage claim if the policy covers it, and review the carrier's safety practices
Prepare for regulatory scrutiny of the hours violation
assessment: Genuine accident caused by serious negligence. Driving over the federal hours limit and through a closure for light trucks expose the carrier to significant liability and possible punitive damages. Early, fair settlement with the injured driver is in everyone's interest.
action: Accept liability, settle the injury claim quickly and fairly, and work with the carrier on hours compliance.
outcomes: Injury claim settled for $180,000
Carrier faces a federal compliance review and changes its dispatch rules

title: Three weeks in hospital, and a no-fault form filed on day 45
type: No-fault benefits application filed after the 30-day notice period
story: Policyholder's car was T-boned at an intersection in the Bronx on 4 March. He was taken to hospital with a fractured pelvis and stayed 22 days, then went to a rehabilitation unit. His application for no-fault (personal injury protection) benefits reached the insurer on 18 April, 45 days after the accident. The adjuster's draft letter denies the application as late under the 30-day written notice rule.
statement: I woke up in the hospital and they told me I'd be there a while. I was on morphine for the first week, I didn't know what day it was. My daughter called the insurance from the hospital in the second week, she said they told her someone would send forms. The forms came to my house, and I wasn't home to see them. I filled them in as soon as I got out of rehab.

accounts.text: Admitted 4 March via the emergency department. Pelvic fracture, surgical fixation on 5 March. Discharged 26 March to an inpatient rehabilitation unit; discharged home on 12 April.
15 March: call from a woman saying she is the insured's daughter, reporting an accident and asking about medical bills. Claim forms mailed to the address on the policy on 16 March.

whatHappened: A genuine accident with a serious injury. He could not give written notice within 30 days because he was in hospital and rehabilitation, and his daughter did give oral notice within 15 days.
damage: Fractured pelvis requiring surgery; 39 days as an inpatient. Car: side damage, claimed separately under collision.
thirdParties: The driver who ran the red light and their insurer
evidence: Insurer phone log of the daughter’s call
missing: Written proof of justification for the late application, if not already supplied
innocent: A hospitalized claimant on strong pain medication cannot reasonably complete forms mailed to his empty home
questions: Ask him to provide a short written explanation for the late filing with the hospital dates
steps: Do not deny for lateness alone: the New York no-fault rules allow late written notice where the claimant gives clear and reasonable justification
Treat the hospital and rehabilitation stays, and the daughter’s call on 15 March, as justification and accept the application
Process the medical and lost-wage benefits within the regulatory time limits
Pursue the other driver’s insurer for property damage and consider subrogation for no-fault benefits paid where the law allows
assessment: Genuine and covered. The 30-day rule was missed for a reason the regulations recognise, and the insurer had oral notice within two weeks. A denial would be wrong and likely overturned.
action: Accept the late application with the justification on file and pay benefits.
outcomes: Application accepted; benefits paid
Draft denial withdrawn after a supervisor review

title: A pickup over the center line, a ditch, and no contact
type: Single-vehicle crash blamed on an unidentified "miss-and-run" driver
story: Policyholder says a pickup truck crossed the center line on a two-lane state road near Zanesville, Ohio, at night, and she swerved into a ditch. There was no contact and the pickup did not stop. She broke her wrist and the car's front end and suspension are damaged. She has claimed under collision for the car and under uninsured motorist coverage for her injury. Ohio law requires independent evidence, beyond her own account, that an unidentified driver caused an injury.
statement: Its headlights were in my lane, right in front of me, I just yanked the wheel. I ended up nose down in the ditch. I called 911 straight away, I was shaking. It was a big pickup, dark color, it kept going. I didn't hit anything except the ditch.

accounts.text: Call from the policyholder at 22:41 reporting a crash into a ditch after a truck came into her lane. A separate call at 22:31 from a commercial driver reports a dark pickup weaving across the center line about 4 miles east, heading west toward the crash location.

Single vehicle off the right side of the road into a ditch. Swerve marks begin in the westbound lane. No debris from another vehicle. Driver states a vehicle crossed the center line. No other vehicle located.

whatHappened: Probably a genuine evasive swerve caused by an unidentified driver; the earlier 911 call about a weaving pickup may provide the independent corroboration her injury claim needs.
damage: Her Malibu: front bumper, radiator, front suspension, estimate $6,200. Fractured right wrist.
thirdParties: The commercial driver who made the earlier 911 call
evidence: Deputy's crash report with swerve marks
Hospital record of the wrist fracture
missing: A statement from the commercial driver who called at 22:31
Any camera at the gas station a mile east
indicators: No contact and no independent witness at the crash itself
innocent: Miss-and-run crashes are real and often leave only swerve marks
The earlier 911 call fits the time and direction
questions: Ask the sheriff’s office for the commercial driver’s contact details
Ask her whether she was tired or on her phone
steps: Pay the car under collision, subject to the deductible: collision does not depend on another driver
For the uninsured motorist injury claim, look for independent corroborative evidence: her own account is not enough under Ohio law, but the earlier 911 call and swerve marks may be
Interview the commercial driver who called at 22:31
Decide the UM claim on the corroboration found, and explain the requirement to her plainly
assessment: Insufficient evidence for now, not suspicion. Collision cover applies to the car. The injury claim turns on independent corroboration, and a promising lead exists in the earlier 911 call.
action: Pay collision, trace the earlier caller and decide the uninsured motorist claim on the corroboration.
outcomes: Commercial driver confirms the weaving pickup; UM claim paid
Caller cannot be traced; UM claim declined with an explanation of the corroboration rule

title: He chose $250,000 of PIP, and the bills will pass a million
type: Catastrophic injury on a Michigan policy with a limited PIP medical choice
story: Policyholder's pickup was hit at an intersection in Grand Rapids by a driver who slid through a red light on ice. He suffered a spinal cord injury. At renewal in 2023 he signed a form choosing a $250,000 limit for personal injury protection medical benefits instead of unlimited cover. His rehabilitation team estimates lifetime medical and care costs well above $1 million. His wife has asked to be paid for caring for him at home.
statement: I picked the cheaper option because the agent said most people never get near the limit. I'm 46. I can't walk now. My wife has given up work to look after me. What happens when the $250,000 runs out? The other driver went through a red light, the police gave him a ticket.

accounts.text: Personal injury protection medical expenses coverage level selected: $250,000 per person per accident. Signed by the named insured. Includes the required notice explaining the coverage choices.
Vehicle 2 failed to stop for a red signal on an icy road and struck vehicle 1 on the driver's side. Vehicle 2 driver cited. Vehicle 2 insured with another carrier; liability limits on file.

whatHappened: A genuine catastrophic injury caused by the other driver. His chosen PIP limit will be exhausted, and costs above it can be pursued from the at-fault driver.
damage: Spinal cord injury with long-term care needs. Pickup: driver's side crushed, total loss.
missing: The at-fault driver's bodily injury liability limits
Whether the policyholder has health insurance or Medicare that pays after PIP
innocent: Many policyholders chose lower PIP limits after the 2019 reforms on the strength of brief sales advice
questions: Ask for the at-fault driver's liability limits
Ask whether he has health insurance that will pay once PIP is exhausted
steps: Pay PIP medical benefits up to the $250,000 chosen, applying the Michigan fee schedules
Assess family-provided attendant care within the statutory weekly hour limit for family members
Explain plainly that allowable expenses above his PIP limit can be claimed from the at-fault driver, and refer him for legal advice
Handle the pickup under collision and note the mini-tort claim of up to $3,000 against the at-fault driver for vehicle damage he cannot otherwise recover
Review the sales file: if the choice was not properly explained, treat it as a complaint and escalate
assessment: Genuine, catastrophic and covered to the limit he chose. The large exposure above $250,000 sits with the at-fault driver, not this policy.
action: Pay PIP to the limit, support the excess claim against the at-fault driver, and check how the PIP choice was sold.
outcomes: PIP paid to the limit; excess medical claim settled with the at-fault driver’s insurer for its limits
Sales complaint upheld and goodwill paid

title: Limited tort, eight physical therapy sessions, and a demand for pain and suffering
type: Bodily injury claim from a claimant who chose the limited tort option
story: Our policyholder rear-ended Ms Walsh's car at a light in Pittsburgh in the rain. Her attorney demands $60,000 for pain and suffering, saying she suffered a serious impairment of body function. Her own auto policy shows she chose the limited tort option. Her medical records show neck and back strain treated with eight physical therapy sessions, and she was back at her desk job two weeks after the crash.
statement: My neck and back were in agony for weeks. I still can't do my spin classes. Driving makes me anxious. I don't care what box I ticked on my insurance, I'm the one who got hurt and he hit me.

accounts.text: Tort option: limited tort. Signed selection form on file. First-party medical benefits: $5,000.
Cervical and lumbar strain. Eight sessions over five weeks. Full range of motion restored. Discharged with a home exercise program. Returned to full-time work after two weeks.

whatHappened: A genuine rear-end collision causing a soft-tissue injury that resolved in weeks. Under the limited tort option she cannot recover pain and suffering unless the injury is serious or an exception applies.
damage: Her Civic: rear bumper and trunk lid, $3,100, being paid. Injury: neck and back strain, resolved.
evidence: Her declarations page showing limited tort
Police report confirming our policyholder rear-ended her
missing: Any medical opinion that the injury is serious or permanent
inconsistencies: The demand describes a serious impairment; the treatment records show a full recovery in five weeks
indicators: Pain and suffering demand by a limited tort claimant with a resolved soft-tissue injury
innocent: Claimants often do not remember choosing limited tort when they bought the policy
questions: Ask the attorney which exception or which serious injury they rely on
Check whether any limited tort exception applies to our policyholder, such as a drunk-driving conviction
steps: Accept liability for the collision and pay her property damage
Decline the pain and suffering demand unless she shows a serious injury: limited tort bars non-economic damages otherwise
Consider economic losses above her own first-party benefits, which limited tort does not bar
Confirm no limited tort exception applies before closing the point
assessment: Genuine collision, real but minor injury, overstated demand. The limited tort election is decisive for pain and suffering unless a serious injury is shown.
action: Pay the property damage and documented economic loss, decline non-economic damages, and invite medical evidence of a serious injury.
outcomes: Demand withdrawn; small economic-loss settlement
Suit filed and dismissed on summary judgment under limited tort

title: The roommate took the keys from the bowl
type: Crash by a roommate who may or may not have had permission
story: Policyholder's roommate took her car keys from a bowl by the door while she was asleep in their Atlanta apartment and drove to a party. On the way back he hit a parked car and a fence. She says he never had permission to drive her car. Texts between them show she let him borrow it twice in the previous month. The owners of the parked car and the fence have both claimed against her policy.
statement: He asked me twice before and both times I said yes, but I was there and I knew where he was going. This time I was asleep and he just took it. I'd never have said yes at 1 in the morning when he'd been drinking. I don't want to get him in trouble but I'm not paying for this.

accounts.who: Text messages between the policyholder and the roommate
accounts.text: Three weeks before: "can I borrow ur car for the store" "yes keys in the bowl". Ten days before: "need ur car for work tmrw?" "fine bring it back by 6". Night of the crash: no messages before 01:12, when he wrote "im so sorry i hit a car".
She always said I could use it if I needed it, keys are in the bowl. I didn't wake her up because it was late. I'd had a couple of beers, I wasn't drunk. I feel terrible.

whatHappened: The roommate took the car without asking that night. Whether that was within an implied permission built up by earlier borrowing is the real question.
damage: Parked Altima: rear quarter and bumper, $3,900. Fence: two panels, $1,100. Policyholder's car: front end, $4,300.
missing: Whether the roommate has his own auto policy
Whether alcohol testing was done
inconsistencies: She says he had no permission; he says she said he could use it whenever he needed
innocent: Earlier permission with the keys left in a shared bowl can genuinely leave both sides with different understandings
questions: Ask whether she ever said he could use the car without asking each time
Ask whether the roommate has his own insurance
steps: Investigate permission: express permission, any pattern of implied permission, and whether this use went beyond it
If permission is found, the policy’s liability cover extends to him as a permissive user; if not, the third parties’ claims fall to his own cover or to them
Check his own auto policy, which may respond either way
Handle her own car under collision if cover applies and explain the decision
assessment: Genuinely disputed. The prior borrowing and the shared key bowl support implied permission, but taking the car at night without asking, after drinking, may fall outside it.
action: Take statements, check his own insurance, and make a reasoned permissive-use decision.
outcomes: Implied permission found; third parties paid under her policy
Use found to exceed any permission; third parties referred to his own insurer

title: A Tacoma valued with comparables 300 miles away
type: Total loss valuation dispute leading to the appraisal clause
story: Policyholder's 2019 Toyota Tacoma was declared a total loss after a rear-end collision in Phoenix. The insurer's valuation report put its actual cash value at $31,200, using comparables from dealers up to 300 miles away and a "rough" interior condition rating. He sent four local dealer listings for similar trucks priced between $35,900 and $37,400 and a photo of the interior, and has invoked the policy's appraisal clause in writing.
statement: The interior was spotless, I've got photos from the week before. Their comparables are from Tucson and Flagstaff, not Phoenix, and two of them were base models. Trucks like mine sell here in days. I don't want a fight, I just want what it's worth.

accounts.text: Base value $33,050 from five comparable vehicles within 300 miles. Condition adjustment: interior rough, minus $1,850. Final actual cash value $31,200. Two comparables are SR trims without the off-road package.

If we and you do not agree on the amount of loss, either may demand an appraisal. Each party selects an appraiser; the two appraisers select an umpire. A decision agreed by any two is binding on the amount of loss.

whatHappened: A genuine total loss where the valuation understated the truck's value through distant, lower-spec comparables and an unsupported condition deduction.
damage: Tacoma TRD Off-Road: rear frame and bed damage, total loss.
thirdParties: The at-fault driver who rear-ended him and their insurer
missing: The inspector’s notes or photos supporting the rough interior rating
inconsistencies: The report rates the interior rough; his recent photos show it clean
innocent: Valuation tools often widen the search radius when local stock is thin
questions: Ask the inspector for the photos behind the condition rating
steps: Re-run the valuation with local comparables of the same trim and remove the condition deduction unless it is supported
If agreement is still not reached, appoint the insurer’s appraiser within the policy time limit and cooperate with the umpire process
Pay the undisputed amount now rather than holding everything back
Recover the payout from the at-fault driver’s insurer
assessment: Genuine claim with a fair valuation complaint. The appraisal clause is his right; correcting the report may settle it without one.
action: Revalue with like-for-like local comparables, pay the undisputed sum, and take part in the appraisal if needed.
outcomes: Revalued at $35,800 and accepted; appraisal withdrawn
Appraisal panel sets $36,200

title: Aftermarket headlamps in front of the radar
type: Repair estimate using non-OEM parts on a nearly new car with driver assistance systems
story: Policyholder's one-year-old Honda CR-V hit a concrete parking barrier in the rain in Chicago. The insurer's estimate uses aftermarket parts for the bumper cover, the headlamps and the grille emblem. The repairer says the manufacturer's repair procedures call for original parts where they affect the radar and camera systems, and that an aftermarket grille emblem may stop the radar working. She wants original parts throughout.
statement: It's a year old with 10,000 miles. The adaptive cruise and the emergency braking are why I bought it. The body shop says cheap parts could make the radar unreliable. I don't want to find out on the highway. Surely you have to put it back the way Honda built it?

accounts.text: Manufacturer position statement: radar-transparent grille emblem must be genuine; non-genuine emblems may cause radar misreads. Headlamps with adaptive lighting require calibration with genuine units. Bumper cover: certified aftermarket acceptable if sensor brackets are genuine. Calibration of radar and camera required after repair.
Aftermarket bumper cover, headlamps (pair) and grille emblem. Calibration not included. Total $3,950.

whatHappened: A genuine low-speed impact. The estimate used aftermarket parts on safety-related components where the manufacturer requires genuine parts, and left out calibration.
damage: CR-V: bumper cover, grille emblem, both headlamps, radar bracket. No structural damage.
evidence: Repairer's note citing the manufacturer position statement
missing: The parts disclosure the estimate should have given her
innocent: Estimating systems default to aftermarket parts unless the assessor overrides them
questions: Ask the repairer for the manufacturer position statement document
steps: Specify genuine parts for the radar-transparent emblem, the sensor bracket and the adaptive headlamps, as the manufacturer requires
Add radar and camera calibration to the estimate
Allow a certified aftermarket bumper cover only if the repairer confirms it does not affect the sensors, and disclose any non-original parts to her in writing as Illinois requires
Fix the estimating rule for ADAS-related parts on newer vehicles
assessment: Genuine claim and a reasonable objection. Safety systems are the deciding factor: parts in the radar and camera path should be genuine, with calibration.
action: Revise the estimate to genuine safety-related parts plus calibration, and disclose any remaining aftermarket parts.
outcomes: Revised estimate $5,480 with calibration; repair completed
Customer complaint closed with the revised estimate

title: A total loss offer with no sales tax, and a lift kit with no receipts
type: California total loss settlement missing tax and fees, with unproven upgrades
story: Policyholder's 2020 Ford F-150 was a total loss after a head-on collision on a rural road near Fresno. The insurer offered $34,000 less her $500 deductible. The offer does not include sales tax or the license and transfer fees for a comparable vehicle. She has also claimed $8,000 for aftermarket upgrades: a lift kit, wheels and a light bar. She has no receipts, and the photos on file show the wheels and light bar but a standard ride height.
statement: My husband did the upgrades himself, he paid cash at swap meets so there are no receipts. The wheels alone were $2,500. Everyone else I know got their sales tax back on a total loss. Why didn't I?

accounts.text: Actual cash value $34,000, less deductible $500. Total $33,500. Tax and fees: not included.
Custom parts or equipment are covered up to $1,500 unless scheduled on the policy for a higher amount. No custom equipment scheduled.

whatHappened: A genuine total loss. The insurer's offer left out tax and fees that California requires, and the claim for upgrades is partly unsupported: the truck was never lifted.
damage: F-150: front end and frame, total loss. Aftermarket wheels and light bar fitted; no lift kit visible in photos.
thirdParties: The other driver and their insurer
evidence: Photos of the truck before and after the crash
missing: Any proof of the cost of the wheels and light bar
A photo showing a lift kit
inconsistencies: She claims a lift kit; the photos show a standard ride height
indicators: Undocumented upgrades claimed at a round figure
innocent: Cash purchases at swap meets genuinely leave no receipts
She may be repeating what her husband told her
questions: Ask for any photos, bank records or listings for the wheels and the light bar
Ask whether the lift kit was fitted or only bought
steps: Add sales tax and the license, registration and transfer fees for a comparable vehicle, as California’s fair claims regulations require for a total loss settlement
Pay the wheels and light bar within the $1,500 custom equipment limit, on reasonable evidence of value
Decline the lift kit unless there is evidence it was fitted
Explain the revised figure in writing
assessment: Genuine total loss with two separate problems: the insurer underpaid by leaving out tax and fees, and the claimant overstated the upgrades.
action: Reissue the offer with tax and fees, pay custom equipment up to the limit, and decline the unproven lift kit.
outcomes: Revised settlement paid with tax and fees plus $1,500 for equipment
Department of Insurance complaint closed after the revised offer

title: Totaled by the numbers, but he wants to keep his Civic
type: Owner-retained total loss in Texas
story: Policyholder's 2015 Honda Civic was rear-ended in heavy rain on the I-10 in Houston. The repair estimate of $9,800 exceeds the car's actual cash value of $9,200, so it is a total loss. He wants to keep the car and repair it himself at his cousin's shop. The salvage bid is $1,700. He has claimed under his own collision cover rather than wait for the other driver's insurer.
statement: The car runs fine, it's just the back end. My cousin can fix it for half what the body shop wants. I've had it since high school. I'd rather keep it and take less money. What do I have to do?

accounts.text: Repair estimate $9,800. Actual cash value $9,200. Salvage bid $1,700. Repair exceeds value: total loss. Owner requests to retain the vehicle.
Vehicle 2 failed to control speed in heavy rain and struck vehicle 1 from behind. Vehicle 2 driver cited. Vehicle 2 insured.

whatHappened: A genuine not-at-fault total loss where the owner wants to keep the car.
damage: Civic: rear bumper, trunk, rear panel and both rear quarter panels. Drivable.
thirdParties: The driver who rear-ended him and their insurer
missing: Confirmation there is no lienholder on the title
innocent: Older cars often become total losses on cost even when they still drive
questions: Confirm whether there is a loan on the car
steps: Agree the owner-retained settlement: actual cash value less the salvage value and the deductible
Follow Texas rules for owner-retained total losses: report it so the title is branded salvage, and explain that the car needs a rebuilt title and inspection before it can be registered again
Recover the payment and his deductible from the at-fault driver’s insurer
Explain the effect of a branded title on the car’s future value
assessment: Genuine and straightforward. He can keep the car with the salvage value deducted, provided the title is handled correctly.
action: Pay the owner-retained settlement, complete the salvage title steps, and pursue subrogation.
outcomes: Paid $7,000 after salvage and deductible; deductible later reimbursed through subrogation
Owner changes his mind and releases the car for salvage

title: A new knee for a knee that was already due for one
type: Bodily injury claim from a Medicare beneficiary with a pre-existing condition
story: Our policyholder rear-ended Mr Jensen, aged 72, at a light in Tucson. He claims the crash injured his right knee and caused the need for a knee replacement, which Medicare paid for. His records show osteoarthritis in that knee and a surgeon's note recommending replacement eight months before the crash. Medicare has paid $18,400 for treatment since the accident. His attorney demands the policy limit of $100,000.
statement: My knee hit the dashboard hard. Before the accident I was managing, I played golf twice a week. Afterwards I couldn't walk without a cane. The surgeon said it had to be done. I'm not trying to get anything I don't deserve.

accounts.who: Orthopedic note, eight months before the crash
accounts.text: Severe osteoarthritis of the right knee, bone on bone medially. Discussed total knee replacement; patient wishes to delay. Continue injections and a cane as needed.
Conditional payments related to the accident date: $18,400, including the knee replacement. Final demand to be issued once the settlement is reported.

whatHappened: A genuine collision that probably aggravated a knee that already needed replacing. The claim treats the whole surgery as caused by the crash.
damage: Knee contusion with aggravation of existing osteoarthritis; knee replacement. Car: rear bumper and trunk.
missing: An independent orthopedic opinion on how far the crash advanced the surgery
Golf club or activity records before and after the crash
inconsistencies: He says he was managing well before the crash; his surgeon recommended a replacement eight months earlier
indicators: Claiming a planned surgery as wholly caused by the accident
innocent: A collision can genuinely bring forward an operation that someone was putting off
questions: Ask the attorney for all records for the knee in the five years before the crash
steps: Value the claim as an aggravation: the crash may have brought the surgery forward, but it did not cause the arthritis
Get an independent orthopedic opinion on the acceleration
Because he is a Medicare beneficiary, report the settlement under Section 111 and resolve Medicare’s conditional payment claim before or at settlement, so Medicare is reimbursed
Make sure the settlement terms deal with Medicare’s interest
assessment: Genuine accident, real aggravation, overstated causation. The Medicare obligations are mandatory whatever the amount agreed.
action: Value as an aggravation with an independent opinion, and build Medicare reporting and reimbursement into the settlement.
outcomes: Settled at $42,000 with Medicare reimbursed from the settlement
Mediation agrees $55,000 after the independent opinion

title: A food truck off the road for six weeks, and the profits it says it lost
type: Third-party property claim with lost profits for a commercial vehicle
story: Our policyholder backed out of a space in Austin and hit a parked food truck, damaging its side and serving window. Liability is accepted. The truck's owner claims $6,800 for repairs and $24,000 for six weeks of lost profits while it was off the road. The body shop's records show the repair took 9 working days, after the owner waited three weeks before authorizing it.
statement: That truck is my whole business. We do lunch at the tech campuses and a brewery every weekend. I had to cancel two festival bookings. I waited to authorize the repair because your adjuster hadn't confirmed you'd pay, and I couldn't afford to front $6,800.

accounts.text: Vehicle dropped off 2 days after the collision. Estimate sent to the owner the same day. Authorization received 23 days later. Repair completed in 9 working days.
Liability accepted on day 4. Owner asked whether we would pay the shop directly. Callback promised; next contact recorded on day 22.

whatHappened: A genuine claim for a working vehicle. Some of the time off the road was caused by the insurer's own slow response, so the delay cannot all be blamed on the owner.
damage: Food truck: nearside panels and serving window, $6,800. Lost trading for about six weeks.
thirdParties: Rosalind Pierce, owner of the food truck
missing: Tax returns or sales records for the same weeks in earlier years
The cancelled festival booking contracts
indicators: Lost profits claimed at a round figure without records
innocent: Small businesses often cannot fund repairs before the insurer confirms payment
questions: Ask for sales records and tax returns to calculate net lost profit
Ask for the festival booking confirmations and cancellations
steps: Pay the repair cost
Assess loss of use as net lost profit, not gross sales, supported by records
Include the period caused by the insurer’s own delay in confirming payment; the owner’s duty to mitigate does not cover delay the insurer caused
Pay the documented amount promptly and explain the calculation
assessment: Genuine and recoverable in principle. The amount needs records, and the insurer's own 18-day silence weakens any mitigation argument.
action: Pay the repairs, request sales records, and pay net lost profit for the whole period the insurer's delay caused.
outcomes: Net lost profit of $14,900 paid on the sales records
Owner files a complaint about the callback delay; upheld

title: A policy-limits demand with 30 days to run, and 22 already gone
type: Time-limited demand for the policy limits on a serious injury claim
story: Our policyholder ran a red light in Atlanta and struck Ms Carter's car; she suffered a fractured femur. His bodily injury limit is $50,000 per person. Her medical bills already exceed $92,000. Her attorney sent a time-limited demand to settle for the $50,000 limit, open for 30 days, with conditions on payment timing and a sworn statement of any other insurance. Twenty-two days have passed. The adjuster has asked for medical records that were already enclosed.
statement: He told me he looked away for a second. I was in surgery twice and I still can't walk properly. My lawyer says the other side has thirty days and they're wasting them.

accounts.text: Offer to settle all claims against your insured for the $50,000 bodily injury limit. Acceptance must be in writing within 30 days of receipt. Payment within 10 days of acceptance. Provide a sworn statement of all other insurance available to your insured. Medical records and bills totalling $92,416 enclosed.
Vehicle 1 entered the intersection against a steady red signal and struck vehicle 2. Vehicle 1 driver cited for failing to obey a traffic control device. Two independent witnesses.

whatHappened: Clear liability and damages far above the limit. The insurer is close to letting a reasonable demand within limits expire.
damage: Fractured femur, two surgeries, medical bills $92,416 so far. Her car: total loss.
evidence: Police report with citation and witnesses
missing: Confirmation of any other insurance covering the policyholder, such as an umbrella policy
innocent: The adjuster may not have realised that the demand carries a strict deadline and conditions
questions: Ask the policyholder at once whether he has an umbrella or any other policy that might apply
steps: Escalate today to a senior handler and coverage or defense counsel
Calculate the exact deadline from the date of receipt and diarize it

Accept the demand in writing within the time limit if, as it appears, liability is clear and damages exceed the limit, and meet every condition exactly, including the sworn statement and payment timing
Tell the policyholder in writing about the demand and his personal exposure above the limit
Do not ask again for records already provided; record the reasons for the decision
assessment: Genuine, clear liability, damages well above limits. Letting this demand lapse would expose the insurer to a bad faith claim for the full excess judgment.
action: Accept the policy-limits demand within the deadline and comply with all its conditions.
outcomes: Demand accepted on day 27; settled for the limit
Missed deadline leads to a $410,000 verdict and a bad faith claim

title: Turning left in Orlando, hit by a driver doing 58 and texting
type: Injury lawsuit where the claimant may be more than half at fault
story: Our policyholder turned left at a green light in Orlando and was struck by Ms Nguyen's oncoming car. She has sued him for her injuries, saying he failed to yield. The accident happened in 2025. Her car's event data recorder shows 58 mph five seconds before impact in a 40 mph zone. Her phone records, obtained in discovery, show a text sent 4 seconds before the crash.
statement: I had a green light. He turned right in front of me, there was nothing I could do. Yes, I was going a bit fast, everyone does on that road. I wasn't texting, I might have sent a voice message.

accounts.text: Speed 58 mph at 5.0 seconds before the event, 57 mph at 1.0 second, brake applied 0.6 seconds before the event. Posted limit 40 mph.
I waited for a gap. Her car was far enough away when I started to turn, it just arrived much faster than I expected. I never saw her brake.

whatHappened: A left-turn collision where the turning driver had a duty to yield, but the oncoming driver was 18 mph over the limit and probably using her phone. Fault may well be more than half hers.
damage: Claimant: fractured wrist and facial injuries. Both cars: total losses.
evidence: Phone records showing a text 4 seconds before impact
missing: An accident reconstruction of whether the turn was safe at the legal speed
Witness accounts
inconsistencies: She says she was not texting; her phone records show a text sent 4 seconds before impact
innocent: Voice-to-text can register as a sent text
questions: Commission a reconstruction: would she have stopped or passed safely at 40 mph?
steps: Apply Florida’s modified comparative negligence rule for accidents after 24 March 2023: a claimant more than 50% at fault recovers nothing
Build the fault case with the event data, the phone records and a reconstruction
Value the case on a realistic apportionment and consider a proposal for settlement if exposure remains
Check the claim was filed within Florida’s two-year limitation period for negligence
assessment: Disputed liability with strong evidence against the claimant. If she is found more than 50% at fault, the 2023 rule bars her claim entirely.
action: Defend on comparative fault with reconstruction evidence, and settle only at a figure that reflects the risk.
outcomes: Jury finds her 60% at fault; no recovery
Settled at a modest figure before trial

title: A flashing red, two drivers who both stopped first, and a 70/30 award
type: Inter-company arbitration of a disputed intersection collision
story: Policyholder collided with another car at a Denver intersection where the signals were flashing red in all directions after a snowstorm. Each driver says they stopped first. Her collision claim was paid at $7,400 less her $1,000 deductible. The insurer filed for inter-company arbitration seeking 100% from the other insurer, which answered 50/50. The arbitrator awarded 70/30 in her favour. She has asked when she gets her deductible back.
statement: I stopped, looked both ways and went. He came from the right without stopping, I'm sure of it. I've paid my deductible and I've been told I might get it back. When?

accounts.text: Flashing red signals operate as an all-way stop. Witness evidence favours the applicant's insured as first to arrive; respondent's insured likely failed to stop fully. Liability: respondent 70%, applicant 30%.
The blue car stopped and pulled out. The silver car slowed down but I don't think it stopped, it kind of rolled through.

whatHappened: A genuine intersection collision with shared fault. The arbitration award recovers 70% of the payment, and the policyholder is owed a share of it for her deductible.
damage: Her Subaru: front-left corner, $8,400 total including the deductible. Other car: right front.
thirdParties: The other driver and their insurer
missing: Traffic signal maintenance log confirming the flashing mode
inconsistencies: Each driver says they stopped first
innocent: After a storm, drivers often misjudge who arrived first at an all-way stop
questions: Confirm what the policy and Colorado law say about sharing recoveries with the insured
steps: Collect 70% of the $8,400 loss from the other insurer under the award
Reimburse her deductible from the recovery as the policy and Colorado law require, at least in proportion to the recovery
Tell her the outcome and the amount refunded, and explain the 30% that stays with her
Close the file only once the recovery is received
assessment: Genuinely disputed liability, resolved fairly by arbitration. The remaining task is to pass on her share of the recovery promptly.
action: Collect the 70% and refund her deductible share without delay.
outcomes: $5,880 recovered; $700 of her deductible refunded
Full deductible refunded under the made-whole rule

title: The tread came off the rear tire on the I-40
type: Rollover after a tire tread separation, with a possible product claim
story: Policyholder's SUV rolled over on the I-40 near Amarillo when the tread came off the left rear tire at highway speed. She and her son had minor injuries. The tires were two years old with 28,000 miles, bought and fitted at a national tire chain with service records showing rotations and pressure checks. The SUV, with the tire still on it, is at a tow yard and the salvage team plans to sell it next week. The total loss is $38,000.
statement: There was a bang and the back end swung round, then we rolled. The tires were nearly new, I keep the receipts for everything, they rotated them in the spring. I thought tires just didn't do that anymore.

accounts.text: Four tires fitted 23 months before the crash. Rotations and pressure checks at 7,400, 15,100 and 22,800 miles; all pressures within specification; no damage noted.
