Left rear tire tread separated; tread found on the shoulder 200 feet before the rollover. No signs of speeding. Weather hot and dry.

whatHappened: A rollover caused by a tread separation on a properly maintained, nearly new tire, pointing to a possible manufacturing defect.
damage: SUV total loss, $38,000. Minor injuries to the driver and her son.
evidence: The tire and the separated tread at the tow yard
missing: A tire expert's examination
The tire identification number and any recall check
innocent: Tread separations can also follow an unseen puncture or road hazard, which an expert can identify
questions: Ask whether she hit anything on the road before the bang
steps: Stop the salvage sale and preserve the vehicle, the tire, the wheel and the separated tread with a documented chain of custody
Check the tire identification number against recalls
Instruct a tire expert, and notify the manufacturer and retailer so they can attend a joint inspection, avoiding any spoliation argument
Pay her total loss and injury benefits now; pursue subrogation for the total loss and benefits paid if a defect is found
assessment: Genuine loss with a credible product claim. The recovery will depend entirely on preserving the tire before the salvage sale.
action: Pay the claim, hold the vehicle and tire, and pursue the manufacturer after an expert inspection.
outcomes: Expert finds a manufacturing defect; full subrogation recovery
Expert finds an old puncture repair; no recovery

title: A rental payment to a vendor nobody had heard of
type: Customer reimbursement diverted to a fictitious vendor created by an adjuster
story: Policyholder complained that she never received the $1,260 rental reimbursement promised after her car was rear-ended in Denver. The payment system shows it was paid to "Mile High Auto Rentals". That vendor was set up four months ago by the adjuster who handled her claim. The same vendor account has received 23 payments on 19 claims, all handled by that adjuster, and its address is a mailbox store.
statement: I paid for the rental myself with my credit card and sent you the receipt from the real rental company. The adjuster said the check was in the mail. That was eight weeks ago. Now nobody calls me back.

accounts.text: Vendor: Mile High Auto Rentals. Created by user ID of the handling adjuster. Tax ID not verified. Address: a mailbox store. Bank account added the same day. 23 payments totalling $31,870 on 19 claims, all assigned to the same adjuster.
Rental paid by the policyholder's card: 14 days, $1,260. Rental company is a national chain, not Mile High Auto Rentals.

whatHappened: The customer's claim is genuine. Her reimbursement was diverted to a fictitious vendor controlled by the adjuster, who appears to have done the same on other claims.
damage: Customer unpaid $1,260. Possible insider loss of $31,870 across 19 claims.
evidence: Payment history for the vendor account
missing: Bank records for the vendor account
Whether other customers on the 19 claims were paid
inconsistencies: Payment recorded to a rental company she never used
indicators: Vendor created by the same person who approves its payments
Unverified tax ID and a mailbox address
Payments concentrated on one adjuster’s claims
innocent: Data entry errors can misdirect a single payment, but not 23 payments to an unverified vendor
questions: Check every one of the 19 claims for customers who were not paid
steps: Pay the customer her $1,260 now and apologize: she is not part of the problem
Refer to the special investigations unit and internal audit, preserve the system records, and restrict the adjuster’s access pending investigation
Contact every customer on the affected claims and pay anyone who was not paid
Fix the control gap: no user should be able to create a vendor and approve payments to it
Report as required to the state fraud bureau and law enforcement
assessment: The claim is genuine; the fraud is internal. The priority is to make the customer whole, then contain and investigate the insider scheme.
action: Pay the customer, escalate to investigations and audit, and close the control gap.
outcomes: Adjuster dismissed and charged; all affected customers paid
Vendor controls changed to require independent approval

title: Stolen from the mall on the 12th, on a ship since the 25th of last month
type: Theft claim for a car already exported
story: Policyholder reported his 2022 Lexus RX stolen from a mall parking lot in Newark, New Jersey, on 12 September. He produced both keys. A routine export check of the VIN shows the vehicle was declared for export and loaded into a container at Port Newark on 25 August, eighteen days before the reported theft. The vehicle is financed and he made his 1 September loan payment.
statement: I parked by the food court and went in for an hour. When I came out it was gone. I've got both keys right here. I don't know anything about any export, maybe someone cloned my VIN. I need the money to pay off the loan.

accounts.text: VIN matches a used vehicle export declaration filed 22 August. Container loaded at Port Newark on 25 August. Exporter: a freight forwarder in Elizabeth, NJ. Title copy submitted with the declaration in the policyholder's name.
No camera coverage of the stated parking row. Entrance camera footage for 12 September reviewed for the plate: no match found entering the lot.

whatHappened: The car was exported with a copy of his title before he reported it stolen. The theft report is false.
damage: Claimed total loss $52,000. No damage; vehicle overseas.
missing: The freight forwarder’s booking records and who paid them
inconsistencies: Reported stolen on 12 September; exported on 25 August
Entrance cameras show no sign of the car entering the lot
indicators: Export with his title copy before the reported theft
Both keys produced
Financed vehicle
innocent: VIN cloning exists, but a declaration with his own title copy makes it very unlikely
questions: Ask the freight forwarder who booked and paid for the export
Ask the policyholder to explain how a copy of his title was used
steps: Refer to the special investigations unit and to the National Insurance Crime Bureau
Get the freight forwarder’s records through the proper legal process
Take an examination under oath under the policy if the facts are disputed
Deny the claim on the evidence and report to the state fraud bureau as required
assessment: Confirmed fraud: the car was exported with his title copy 18 days before he reported it stolen.
action: Deny, refer to the special investigations unit and NICB, and report to the state.
outcomes: Claim withdrawn after the forwarder names him as the customer; prosecuted
Denied after the examination under oath

title: Fifty-two days and no decision, in California
type: Claim handling outside California’s regulatory time limits
story: Policyholder reported a collision claim on 2 June after her car was sideswiped in a San Jose parking structure. She sent photos, the repair estimate and the other driver's details on 10 June. The adjuster went on leave. Nobody acknowledged the claim until 21 June, and on 1 August, 52 days after her proof of claim, there is still no decision and no letter explaining what is needed. She has filed a complaint with the Department of Insurance.
statement: I sent everything you asked for in the first week. I've called nine times and left messages. Nobody told me anything was missing. I'm paying for a rental out of my own pocket. I've complained to the state because I didn't know what else to do.

accounts.text: 2 June: first notice. 10 June: proof of claim received (estimate, photos, other party details). 21 June: acknowledgment sent. No further written communication. Nine inbound calls logged, no return calls. Adjuster on leave from 8 June; file not reassigned.
Consumer complaint received regarding delay in claim handling. Please provide a full response and copies of all correspondence.

whatHappened: A straightforward claim left unattended when the adjuster went on leave, breaching California's time limits for acknowledging, deciding and communicating.
damage: Her Corolla: driver's side doors, estimate $2,950. Rental costs paid by her.
thirdParties: The other driver and their insurer
missing: Any reason the file was not reassigned during the leave
innocent: An unplanned leave without a handover can leave a file invisible to the rest of the team
questions: Check whether other files of the same adjuster were left unassigned
steps: Decide the claim now and pay within the time allowed after acceptance
Recognise the breaches: acknowledgment is due within 15 calendar days of notice, and acceptance or denial within 40 days of proof of claim, with written notice every 30 days if more time is needed
Respond fully and promptly to the Department of Insurance with the file history
Reimburse her reasonable rental costs caused by the delay and apologize
Reassign the adjuster’s other files and fix the leave cover process
assessment: Genuine claim, clear regulatory breaches by the insurer. The fix is to pay, answer the regulator candidly and stop it recurring.
action: Pay the claim and rental costs, respond to the Department of Insurance, and review the leave cover process.
outcomes: Claim paid in 3 days; complaint closed with a finding against the insurer
Audit finds 14 other files of the same adjuster overdue

title: The claim file that went to the other Michael Brown
type: Claim documents with personal data emailed to the wrong claimant
story: An adjuster in Boston emailed the injury claim file of policyholder Michael J. Brown to a different claimant, Michael R. Brown, because the email address auto-completed. The attachment included his driver's license image, medical records and a medical bill showing his Social Security number. The recipient replied an hour later: "I think this isn't mine." The adjuster has not told anyone.
statement: I was rear-ended in March and I've been through enough. Now you're telling me a stranger has my medical records and my Social Security number? What are you going to do about it?

accounts.text: Sent 14:06 to michael.r.brown@ (another claimant's address) instead of michael.j.brown@. Attachment: claim file PDF, 41 pages, not encrypted. Reply received 15:02: "I think this isn't mine, I haven't opened most of it."
Driver's license image; hospital and physical therapy records; a medical bill showing the full Social Security number; claim notes.

whatHappened: A genuine claim, and a privacy incident caused by an auto-completed email address. Sensitive personal information went to an unintended recipient.
damage: Exposure of driver's license, medical records and Social Security number. No financial loss known yet.
thirdParties: Michael R. Brown, the unintended recipient
missing: Written confirmation from the recipient that the email and attachment are deleted
innocent: Auto-complete errors are a common cause of misdirected email
questions: Ask the recipient to confirm in writing that he has deleted the email and any copies
steps: Report the incident to the privacy or compliance team today, as company policy requires
Contain it: ask the recipient to delete the email and confirm in writing
Assess notification duties under the state breach notification and insurance data security laws: a Social Security number and medical records are sensitive data
Notify the policyholder, offer credit monitoring, and notify regulators if the law requires
Fix the cause: send sensitive files only through a secure portal, and turn off auto-complete for external addresses
assessment: The injury claim is genuine; the incident is the insurer's. Sensitive data was exposed, so containment, assessment and likely notification are needed promptly.
action: Escalate to the privacy team, contain the disclosure, notify the policyholder with support, and assess regulatory notification.
outcomes: Recipient confirms deletion; policyholder notified with credit monitoring; regulator notified
Secure portal made mandatory for medical records

title: A recorded statement in English, and a customer who speaks Spanish
type: Fault decided from a statement taken without an interpreter
story: Policyholder, whose first language is Spanish, gave a recorded statement in English two days after a collision at a stop sign in San Antonio. In it she answers "yes" to the question "So you didn't stop at the sign?" The adjuster assigned her 100% fault. Her daughter has called to say her mother did not understand the questions and did stop. A neighbour's doorbell camera has since been found.
statement: (Through her daughter, translated) I stopped at the sign. I always stop there, my grandchildren's school is on that street. The man on the phone talked very fast. I said yes because I thought he was asking if I was okay. Nobody asked me if I wanted Spanish.

accounts.text: Adjuster: "So you didn't stop at the sign?" Insured: "Yes." Adjuster: "Okay, and the other car had the right of way?" Insured: "Yes, yes, okay." No interpreter offered. Duration 6 minutes.
Her car slows to a near stop at the line, then pulls forward. The other car enters the frame at speed from the right, without slowing, about 1.5 seconds before impact.

whatHappened: She did essentially stop. Her "yes" answers came from a language misunderstanding, and the fault decision rested on them.
damage: Her Altima: front-right corner, $3,600. Other car: driver's side.
thirdParties: The other driver and their insurer
missing: The other driver's speed
A statement from her taken with a qualified interpreter
inconsistencies: The transcript records her agreeing she did not stop; the camera shows she slowed to a near stop
innocent: People answering in a second language often say yes to show they are listening
questions: Retake her statement in Spanish with a qualified interpreter
Ask the other driver about his speed
steps: Do not rely on the English statement: it was taken without checking her language needs
Retake the statement with a qualified interpreter, and record her language preference on the file
Re-decide fault on the camera footage and the new statement; the other driver’s speed may make fault shared or his
Apologize, explain the review, and correct any fault record or premium effect
assessment: Disputed, but the fault decision is unsafe: it rests on a statement she did not understand, and the independent camera contradicts it.
action: Retake the statement with an interpreter, reopen the fault decision on the camera evidence, and correct the record.
outcomes: Fault changed to 50/50 after review; record corrected
Other driver found mainly at fault for speeding; recovery made

title: Rear-ended at Botanical Garden junction, with extras
type: Genuine collision with an inaccurate account and older damage added
story: Policyholder reported that his Hyundai Creta was hit from behind by a Maruti Swift at Botanical Garden junction, Hyderabad, at about 9:15 PM on 14 October 2026, while he was stopped at a red signal in heavy rain. The garage estimate of ₹1,86,500 includes the rear and the front-left headlamp and bumper.
statement: On 14 October, around 9:15 PM, I was driving home from my office in Gachibowli towards Kondapur in my Hyundai Creta. It was raining heavily and the road was wet. I had stopped at the red signal at Botanical Garden junction when a white Maruti Swift hit my car from behind. I was alone in the car. The other driver admitted he was looking at his phone. This car has never been in an accident before.
whatHappened: The Swift did hit the Creta from behind at low speed, just after the signal turned green, when the Creta stopped suddenly. A woman passenger got out and walked away. It had not rained; the road was wet from a water tanker. The garage received the car at 20:40, before the time he gave for the accident, and the front-left damage is older.
damage: Accident damage: rear bumper, boot lid and rear left tail lamp, ₹1,48,500. Older damage added to the claim: front-left headlamp and front bumper, ₹38,000.
thirdParties: Arvind Rao, driver of the Maruti Swift, and his insurer
Unidentified woman passenger in the Creta
evidence: Tea-stall owner as an independent witness
Garage job card SSM-2318 with intake time and damage notes
missing: Traffic police camera footage from the junction
Tow receipt with the call time
Photos from the policy renewal inspection showing the front of the car
The identity of the passenger
inconsistencies: He says heavy rain; the other driver and the witness say it had not rained
He says he was alone; both the other driver and the witness saw a woman get out of the passenger side
He says the accident was at about 9:15 PM; the garage logged the car in at 20:40
He says the car was never in an accident; the garage found dust and rust on the front-left damage
He says he was stopped at a red signal; the witness says the light had just turned green
indicators: Older damage included in the estimate
Timeline that cannot be right as given
Several misstatements that favour the claimant
innocent: A wet road from the water tanker could be mistaken for rain at night
He may have a personal reason for not mentioning the passenger that has nothing to do with the claim
Times given after an accident are often guesses
questions: Ask the claimant who the passenger was and why she left before anyone arrived
Ask when and how the front-left headlamp was damaged
Ask for the tow operator's receipt showing when he called
steps: Arrange a spot survey and compare with the renewal inspection photos
Request junction camera footage from the traffic police
Take a recorded statement that puts each inconsistency to the claimant
Settle the rear damage under own damage, excluding the front, if the collision is confirmed
assessment: Mixed. The rear-end collision is real and supported by everyone, but the claim has been inflated with older front damage, and his account is wrong on the weather, the passenger, the signal and the time. These points need explanations before settlement; the older front damage should not be paid.
action: Investigate the inconsistencies, pay only the accident damage if confirmed, and warn him in writing that misstatements can lead to repudiation.
outcomes: Claimant withdraws the front damage; rear repair settled at ₹1,48,500 less depreciation and the compulsory deductible
Claimant maintains his account; claim repudiated for misrepresentation and referred to the fraud control unit

title: A delivery rider, off duty, in a Bengaluru pothole
type: Two-wheeler skid in monsoon rain with rider injury
story: Policyholder's Honda Activa skidded in a water-filled pothole on Hosur Road, Bengaluru, at about 11:20 PM during heavy rain. He fractured his right collarbone. He works as a food delivery rider, and his scooter has a private two-wheeler policy with the compulsory personal accident cover for the owner-driver.
statement: Sir, I had finished my shift and switched off the app, I was going home to Bommanahalli. The road was full of water and I could not see the pothole. The front wheel went in and I fell. Some people helped me and took me to the hospital. Please don't cancel my policy because I do delivery, I was going home only.

accounts.who: Delivery platform data, shared by the claimant with consent
accounts.text: Rider logged out at 22:58. Last delivery completed at 22:41 in Koramangala. No active order between 22:58 and 23:40.
Arrived 23:55. Fracture of the right clavicle, fall from a two-wheeler on a wet road. No smell of alcohol. Arm sling and orthopaedic review. Advised rest from work for six weeks.

whatHappened: As he says: he was riding home after logging out and fell in a hidden, water-filled pothole.
damage: Scooter: front fork, handlebar, body panels and headlamp, estimate ₹14,800. Fractured collarbone; six weeks off work.
thirdParties: Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike, responsible for the road
evidence: Platform log showing he was off duty
Photos of the pothole and the scooter
missing: A police record of the accident, such as a daily diary entry
Final medical bills
innocent: The platform data confirms he was off duty, which removes the only doubt about how he was using the scooter
questions: Ask whether he wants to make a complaint to the municipal corporation about the pothole
Ask whether he has a separate health or accident policy through the platform
steps: Settle the scooter repair under own damage
Assess the personal accident claim: a fracture is not permanent disablement, so check the policy for temporary benefits or medical expenses
Confirm in writing that the trip was personal and does not affect his policy
assessment: Genuine. His worry about delivery work is understandable, but the platform data shows he was off duty. The own damage claim is straightforward; the personal accident cover may pay only for permanent disablement or death, so his medical costs may fall to other cover.
action: Pay the scooter repair, explain clearly what the personal accident cover does and does not pay, and reassure him about the policy.
outcomes: Scooter repaired; personal accident claim not payable as the injury is temporary
Medical costs paid by the platform's rider health cover

title: Car against motorcycle at an unsignalled Pune junction
type: Junction collision with an injured rider and a tribunal claim
story: Policyholder's Maruti Baleno collided with a motorcycle at an unsignalled junction in Kothrud, Pune, at about 7:40 PM. The rider, 24, fractured his tibia. Police registered an FIR against the policyholder for rash driving. The rider has filed a claim petition before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal against her and the insurer.
statement: I was going straight on the main road at about 30. The bike came from the side lane on my left at high speed without slowing and hit my front left side. He had no helmet. People gathered and started shouting at me because I was in a car. The police wrote the FIR against me without asking for my side properly.

accounts.text: Complainant (rider's brother) states that the car driven in a rash and negligent manner hit the motorcycle at the Kothrud junction, causing grievous injury. Case registered against the car driver for rash driving and causing grievous hurt. Spot panchnama: car's front left bumper damaged, motorcycle's front wheel bent. Rider not wearing a helmet.

19:38:12 car on the main road at moderate speed. 19:38:13 motorcycle enters from the side lane without slowing, two people visible on it. 19:38:14 collision. The car brakes at the moment of impact. Image quality is poor at that distance.

whatHappened: Both contributed: the motorcycle came out of a side lane without slowing, carrying a pillion, and the car driver probably did not slow for the junction. The tribunal is likely to apportion negligence.
damage: Rider: fractured tibia with surgery, about four months off work. Car: front-left bumper and wing, ₹42,000. Motorcycle front wheel and fork.
thirdParties: The injured rider and his family
evidence: Rider's medical records filed with the petition
missing: The rider's driving licence
A statement from the pillion passenger
Engineer opinion on the speeds
inconsistencies: The FIR says the car hit the motorcycle through rash driving; the CCTV shows the motorcycle entering the main road without slowing
innocent: FIRs are often written from the complainant's side in the heat of the moment
Neither driver may have seen the other in time
questions: Ask the rider's advocate for his driving licence
Ask the policyholder what speed she was doing and whether she slowed for the junction
steps: Appoint an advocate to defend the tribunal petition and file the CCTV
Verify the rider's licence: if he had none, it does not defeat his claim but may affect apportionment
Argue contributory negligence: no helmet, a pillion rider and entering the main road without slowing
Settle the car damage under own damage separately
assessment: A genuine accident with disputed fault. The insurer must pay the rider whatever the tribunal awards, as third-party injury cover is unlimited, but the CCTV and the missing helmet support a reduction for contributory negligence. Settling at Lok Adalat on a fair split may be better than a long trial.
action: Defend the tribunal claim on apportionment using the CCTV and consider a Lok Adalat settlement; pay the car damage.
outcomes: Tribunal finds 60:40 negligence; award reduced accordingly
Settled at Lok Adalat for ₹4.8 lakh
Full liability on the car driver; insurer pays the full award

title: Sideswiped by an auto with a lapsed policy in Chennai
type: Collision with an uninsured auto-rickshaw
story: Policyholder's Hyundai i20 was sideswiped by an auto-rickshaw on Anna Salai, Chennai, at about 10:30 AM. The auto's insurance lapsed four months ago according to the Vahan record. The auto driver offered ₹2,000 cash to settle; the policyholder refused and is claiming under her own-damage cover.
statement: The auto cut in from the left to pick up a passenger and his rear scraped all along my door. The driver was apologising and offering two thousand rupees. The damage is much more than that. I took photos of his number plate and his licence.

accounts.text: Auto-rickshaw registration valid. Owner: a different person from the driver. Insurance valid until four months before the accident; no renewal recorded. Fitness certificate valid. Permit valid for Chennai city.
Left front and rear doors dented and scratched, left rear quarter panel scratched. Denting and painting of three panels, ₹24,600. No parts replacement needed.

whatHappened: As she says: the auto cut in and scraped the car.
damage: Three panels dented and scratched, ₹24,600.
thirdParties: Auto-rickshaw driver and the owner, both uninsured
evidence: Photos of the auto, its plate and the driver's licence
Vahan record showing the lapsed policy
missing: The auto owner's address, if the policyholder wants to pursue him for the deductible
innocent: Refusing the auto driver's cash offer and claiming instead is sensible, not opportunistic: the damage is worth far more
questions: Ask whether she wants to pursue the auto owner for her deductible and lost No Claim Bonus
steps: Settle under own damage at the network garage on a cashless basis
Explain the effect on her No Claim Bonus
Advise that the auto owner, who had no valid insurance, is personally liable and that driving uninsured is an offence
assessment: Genuine. Her own-damage cover responds; recovering from an uninsured auto owner is possible in principle but rarely worth it for this amount.
action: Settle cashless and explain the No Claim Bonus impact.
outcomes: Repaired cashless; No Claim Bonus reset at renewal
Policyholder recovers ₹5,000 from the auto owner informally

title: A cow on NH44 at midnight
type: Animal collision on a national highway
story: Policyholder's Kia Seltos hit a cow that walked onto NH44 near Kamareddy, Telangana, at about 11:45 PM. Both front airbags deployed. The cow died. Villagers gathered and the policyholder paid ₹15,000 to a man who said he owned the cow. He is claiming the car repair under his own-damage cover with a zero-depreciation add-on, and the ₹15,000.
statement: I was doing about 80 on the highway, high beam was on, and the cow just came from the divider gap. No time to brake fully. The airbags opened. After two minutes twenty people came and said I must pay for the cow or they won't let me go. I paid fifteen thousand by UPI because I was alone with my mother at night.

accounts.who: Police daily diary entry, Kamareddy rural station
accounts.text: Information received at 00:30 about a car hitting a cow on NH44. Car driver and his mother unhurt. Cow died on the spot. Matter settled between the parties at the spot. No case registered.

Front bumper, grille, radiator, condenser, bonnet and both headlamps damaged. Driver and passenger airbags deployed. Animal hair and blood traces on the bumper. Damage consistent with an animal impact. Estimate ₹2,46,000.

whatHappened: A cow walked out of a divider gap into his path at night; the hair and blood on the bumper confirm the impact. The payment to the villagers was made under pressure at the scene.
damage: Front end and airbags, ₹2,46,000. ₹15,000 paid to a person claiming to own the cow.
thirdParties: The person who claimed to own the cow
missing: The name of the person paid ₹15,000, which matters for the explanation but not for the car claim
innocent: Payments to settle a crowd at night are common and understandable
questions: Ask whether he has the UPI receipt and the name of the person paid
steps: Settle the repair under own damage with the zero-depreciation add-on, less the compulsory deductible
Explain that the ₹15,000 cash payment is not covered: the policy pays for damage to the car, and the policy does not cover payments made voluntarily to others
Note that the airbags need replacement at an authorised workshop
assessment: Genuine. The car repair is covered in full under zero depreciation. The payment to the villagers, though understandable, is outside the policy because it was a voluntary settlement, not a legal liability decided under the policy.
action: Pay the repair; decline the ₹15,000 with a sympathetic explanation.
outcomes: Repair of ₹2,46,000 settled less the deductible; cow payment declined
Customer complains to the insurance ombudsman about the payment; complaint not upheld

title: Wrong side to skip the U-turn, and a shop camera
type: Wrong-side driving collision with a motorcyclist
story: Policyholder's Honda City collided head-on with a motorcycle on a service road in Sector 29, Gurugram, at about 9:10 AM. The rider has a fractured wrist. The policyholder says the rider was on the wrong side. A shop's CCTV shows the car driving against traffic to avoid a long U-turn.
statement: First statement: The bike came on the wrong side at speed and hit my car. After the CCTV was shown: Fine, I was on the wrong side for maybe 100 metres, everyone does it there because the U-turn is two kilometres away. But he was also going fast.

accounts.who: Shop CCTV, sweet shop facing the service road
accounts.text: 09:09:20 Honda City enters the service road against the direction of traffic. 09:09:41 motorcycle travelling in the correct direction at moderate speed. 09:09:43 head-on collision. Rider falls. Car driver gets out and argues with bystanders.
I was going to my office on my side of the road. The car came straight at me on the wrong side. I tried to move left but could not. My wrist is broken and I am a computer operator, I cannot type.

whatHappened: The policyholder drove against traffic to avoid a U-turn and hit a rider who was on the correct side. His first account blamed the rider.
damage: Rider: fractured wrist, about eight weeks off work. Motorcycle: front end. Car: front bumper and headlamp, ₹38,000.
thirdParties: Mr Sunil Yadav, the injured rider
missing: Police FIR, if registered
Rider's salary records
inconsistencies: He first said the rider was on the wrong side; the CCTV shows the car on the wrong side, and he later admits it
indicators: A false first account that shifted blame to the rider
innocent: Drivers in a confrontation often say whatever defends them first
questions: Ask the rider whether he intends to file a tribunal petition or would consider a settlement
steps: Accept liability for the rider's injury and motorcycle damage
Settle the third-party claim fairly, possibly before a tribunal petition is filed
Pay the car damage under own damage
Record the false first statement on file
assessment: Genuine negligence: wrong-side driving caused the collision. The first account was false but corrected. Third-party liability is clear and should be settled quickly and fairly.
action: Accept liability, settle the rider's claim, and pay the car repair.
outcomes: Rider settles for ₹1.6 lakh including loss of earnings
Rider files a tribunal petition; award of ₹2.1 lakh paid by the insurer

title: A state transport bus through a red light in Kolkata
type: Collision with a government-owned bus
story: Policyholder's Tata Nexon was hit on the right side at the Park Circus crossing in Kolkata at about 6:15 PM by a state transport bus that ran a red light. Kolkata Traffic Police issued an e-challan to the bus for jumping the signal. The policyholder wants his car repaired quickly and asks whether the bus company should pay.
statement: My signal was green and I had started moving. The bus came from the right at speed and the driver didn't even slow down. The conductor said they were late. Thank God my daughter was sitting on the left side.

accounts.text: Violation: jumping red light, Park Circus crossing, 18:14:52. Vehicle: state transport undertaking bus. Camera image shows the bus entering the junction 3 seconds after red.

whatHappened: The bus entered the junction three seconds after its light turned red, as the camera shows, and hit the car on its right side.
damage: Nexon: right doors, pillar and wheel, ₹1,12,000. No injuries.
thirdParties: The state transport undertaking that owns the bus
evidence: Traffic police e-challan with camera image
missing: The bus's insurance or self-insurance arrangements
innocent: Claiming on his own policy rather than against the bus owner is a practical choice, not a sign of anything wrong
questions: Ask the transport undertaking whether it holds third-party insurance or handles claims itself
steps: Settle the repair under the own-damage cover so the customer is not kept waiting
Explain that he could instead claim from the bus owner, but that it is likely to be slower
Consider a recovery claim against the transport undertaking using the e-challan
assessment: Genuine and clear. The fastest route for the customer is his own-damage cover; a claim against a government transport undertaking is possible but usually slow, so it is a recovery question for the insurer, not a reason to delay the customer.
action: Pay under own damage and consider recovery from the transport undertaking.
outcomes: Repaired within two weeks under own damage
Recovery from the undertaking succeeds after several months

title: A scrape in Andheri traffic, a claim for a new bumper and headlamp
type: Minor scrape with an inflated repair request
story: Policyholder's Maruti Ciaz was scraped by a taxi in slow traffic in Andheri, Mumbai. Her zero-depreciation policy covers parts in full. The garage estimate asks for a new front bumper and a new left headlamp, ₹48,000. The surveyor found a light scrape on the bumper corner and an old, yellowed crack in the headlamp.
statement: The taxi pushed into my front left corner in the jam and drove off. The bumper is scratched and the headlamp is cracked. I have zero dep, so I want new parts, not patch work. I pay so much premium every year.

accounts.text: Front bumper: scrape 12 cm at the left corner, no crack, no broken clips; repairable by refinishing. Left headlamp: hairline crack with dust and moisture inside and yellowing at the crack edges, consistent with damage several months old; no fresh impact marks. Assessed loss: bumper refinish ₹4,200. Headlamp not related to this accident.

whatHappened: A taxi lightly scraped the bumper. She hoped to use the zero-depreciation cover to replace the bumper and an old cracked headlamp as well.
damage: Bumper scrape, repairable for ₹4,200. Old headlamp crack, not accident damage.
evidence: Photos of the bumper and headlamp
missing: Photos of the car from before the accident
inconsistencies: She says the headlamp was cracked in this accident; the surveyor finds old dust, moisture and yellowing inside the crack
indicators: Old damage presented as part of a new claim
Request to replace a repairable part
innocent: Many customers believe zero depreciation means any damaged part will be replaced
She may not have noticed the headlamp crack before
questions: Ask whether she had noticed the headlamp crack before
Explain the difference between zero depreciation and replacement of repairable parts
steps: Approve the bumper refinish only
Exclude the headlamp with the surveyor's findings
Advise that a ₹4,200 claim will cost her the No Claim Bonus, so she may prefer to pay herself
assessment: A genuine minor accident with an inflated request, probably from a misunderstanding of zero-depreciation cover. Zero depreciation removes depreciation on parts that need replacing; it does not turn repairable parts into replacements or cover old damage.
action: Approve the bumper repair, exclude the headlamp, and explain the No Claim Bonus trade-off.
outcomes: Customer withdraws the claim and pays the garage herself to keep her No Claim Bonus
Bumper repair approved; headlamp excluded

title: A tempo in an Old City lane, and the No Claim Bonus question
type: Low-speed collision in a narrow lane, cashless repair
story: Policyholder's Hyundai Venue was hit by a small goods tempo reversing out of a narrow lane near Charminar, Hyderabad. The tempo driver left before details could be taken. Damage to the rear door and quarter panel is estimated at ₹22,000 at a network garage. The policyholder has a 45% No Claim Bonus from four claim-free years.
statement: The tempo was reversing out of the lane with no one guiding, and his back hit my rear door. Before I could get out he went off into the market. I don't have his number. Should I claim or not? Last time I asked, nobody explained the bonus.

accounts.text: Rear right door and quarter panel: denting, painting and door moulding. Parts ₹3,800, labour and paint ₹18,200. Total ₹22,000. Cashless facility available.

whatHappened: A goods tempo reversed out of the lane without a guide, hit the rear door and drove off into the market before details could be taken.
damage: Rear door and quarter panel, ₹22,000.
missing: The tempo's registration, which would allow a claim against its owner
innocent: Not getting the tempo's number is normal when a vehicle drives off into a crowded market
questions: Ask for his current own-damage premium so the No Claim Bonus loss can be estimated
steps: Explain that a claim will reset the 45% No Claim Bonus at renewal and roughly what that costs
Compare that with the claim amount less the compulsory deductible
Process cashless if he chooses to claim
assessment: Genuine and small. The best service is a clear comparison: on an own-damage premium of about ₹18,000, losing a 45% bonus can cost more over the next few years than the claim is worth.
action: Explain the trade-off clearly and process cashless if he still wants to claim.
outcomes: Customer pays the garage directly and keeps the bonus
Customer claims; repaired cashless; bonus reset at renewal

title: A learner rider, alone, and a pedestrian with a broken hip
type: Pedestrian injury by a rider on a learner licence
story: Policyholder's Suzuki Access scooter, ridden by his son, 19, hit a 71-year-old woman crossing a road in Maninagar, Ahmedabad, at about 8:00 AM. She fractured her hip and needed surgery. The son holds only a learner licence and was riding alone, without a licensed person and without "L" plates. The woman's family has filed a claim before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal.
statement: My son was going to his coaching class. He has a learner licence and his test date was in two weeks. The lady came between two parked cars and he could not stop. We visited her in hospital and offered to help. We did not know the insurance would make an issue of the licence.

accounts.text: Scooter rider holding a learner licence, riding alone. Pedestrian crossing the road between parked vehicles struck by the scooter and fell. Case registered for rash riding causing grievous hurt. Scooter's front mudguard broken. No "L" plates displayed.

accounts.who: Hospital discharge summary for the pedestrian
accounts.text: Fracture neck of femur, right side. Hemiarthroplasty performed. Hospital stay 11 days. Bill ₹3,85,000. Needs physiotherapy and assistance for three months.

whatHappened: A young learner riding alone in breach of the learner licence conditions hit an elderly pedestrian stepping out from between parked cars. Both share some blame, but the rider most.
damage: Pedestrian: hip fracture with surgery, ₹3.85 lakh hospital bill, future care and pain and suffering. Scooter: minor damage.
thirdParties: The injured pedestrian and her family
missing: CCTV from shops at the location
The pedestrian's income or dependency details for the tribunal
innocent: Learners often ride alone to practise before a test, not realising the legal condition matters to insurance
questions: Ask the family what support the pedestrian now needs at home
Ask whether the son had ever ridden with a licensed person beside him
steps: Defend the tribunal petition on quantum and on the pedestrian stepping out between parked cars
Pay the award as the third-party insurer; the injured woman must be compensated

Take advice on recovery from the owner: courts have generally treated a learner licence as a licence, so a breach of its conditions supports recovery only if it is fundamental and contributed to the accident
Consider an early settlement through Lok Adalat, given the victim's age
assessment: A genuine accident caused mainly by a learner riding alone. The insurer must pay the pedestrian. Whether it can then recover from the father is uncertain, because Indian courts have treated a learner licence as a valid licence for this purpose; the breach of conditions is a weaker ground than having no licence at all.
action: Settle the pedestrian's claim fairly and quickly; pursue recovery from the owner only if legal advice supports it.
outcomes: Settled at Lok Adalat for ₹7.2 lakh; no recovery pursued
Tribunal awards ₹8.5 lakh and allows pay and recover; insurer recovers from the owner

title: Basement flood, then he tried to start it
type: Flood damage with engine hydrostatic lock
story: Policyholder's Skoda Slavia was parked in his building's basement in Kandivali, Mumbai, when heavy monsoon rain flooded it to about 2.5 feet. After the water drained he tried to start the car several times. The engine is now seized. His policy is a standard comprehensive policy without an engine protection add-on.
statement: Next morning the water was gone and the car looked OK from outside. I sat in it and cranked it three or four times to see if it would start, because I had to go to office. It made a knocking sound and stopped. Then the workshop told me the engine has water inside. Nobody told me not to start it.

accounts.text: Water found in the air intake and in two cylinders. Connecting rods bent: hydrostatic lock caused by cranking with water in the cylinders. Interior carpets, seats and electrical modules damaged by flood water. Estimate: interior and electrical ₹1,35,000; engine overhaul ₹2,90,000.

Water mark on the basement wall at 2.5 feet, matching the mark inside the car. Flood damage to the interior and electrics is admissible. Engine damage resulted from the attempt to start the vehicle after water ingress, which is consequential damage under the policy and not covered without an engine protection add-on.

whatHappened: The flood damaged the interior and electrics. The engine was ruined when he cranked it with water inside, which the standard policy treats as consequential damage.
damage: Flood damage ₹1,35,000 (covered). Engine hydrostatic lock ₹2,90,000 (consequential).
evidence: Surveyor note with matching water marks
missing: The date the engine protection add-on was last offered to him
innocent: Most people try to start their car after water drains; the advice not to is not widely known
questions: Ask whether he was offered the engine protection add-on at renewal
Ask whether the building society has any insurance for the basement
steps: Settle the flood damage to the interior and electrics under own damage
Decline the engine damage as consequential, with a clear written explanation
Check the sales record to see whether the engine protection add-on was offered and explained
assessment: Genuine flood loss with an expensive mistake afterwards. The policy wording on consequential damage is common across Indian motor policies, and the add-on exists for exactly this. If the add-on was never explained at sale, the customer may have a mis-selling complaint.
action: Pay the flood damage and decline the engine, explaining the add-on and his right to complain to the Insurance Ombudsman.
outcomes: Flood damage paid; engine declined; customer pays for the engine himself
Ombudsman complaint about the add-on not being explained; partial ex gratia settlement

title: Chennai floods, a total loss and a low IDV
type: Flood constructive total loss with an insured value dispute
story: Policyholder's Honda Amaze was submerged to roof level for two days in Velachery during floods in Chennai. The repair estimate exceeds 75% of the Insured Declared Value, so the surveyor has assessed it as a constructive total loss. The IDV on the policy is ₹4,80,000; the policyholder says the car was worth ₹6,50,000 on the market.
statement: The whole street was a river. When the water went down the car was full of mud up to the roof. Now you are telling me I get only 4.8 lakh, but I could have sold it for 6.5 lakh last month. I didn't choose the IDV, the agent did it to reduce my premium.

accounts.text: Vehicle submerged to roof level, mud deposits throughout the cabin and engine bay. Estimated repair ₹4,10,000, which is 85% of the IDV of ₹4,80,000. Assessed as a constructive total loss. Options: settle at IDV less salvage value (₹55,000) with the salvage retained by the owner, or at full IDV with the salvage transferred to the insurer, less the compulsory deductible in either case.
At renewal the IDV was reduced from ₹6,10,000 to ₹4,80,000, with a premium saving of ₹2,350. Renewal done through an agent. Proposal shows the customer's consent by OTP to the quotation.

whatHappened: A genuine flood total loss. The settlement is limited by the lower IDV chosen at renewal, which the customer says was the agent's decision.
damage: Constructive total loss. IDV ₹4,80,000; market value claimed ₹6,50,000.
evidence: Renewal record with the reduced IDV and OTP consent
missing: The agent's explanation of how the IDV was chosen
Whether the customer was shown the IDV on the quotation
innocent: Customers often accept a quotation without noticing the IDV, and some agents reduce it to make the premium look lower
questions: Ask the agent how the IDV reduction was explained to the customer
Ask whether he wants to keep the salvage
steps: Settle at the IDV, with the salvage option he prefers, less the compulsory deductible
Explain that the IDV is the contractual limit, whatever the market value
Review the agent's conduct if the reduction was not explained
assessment: Genuine. The insurer is bound to pay up to the IDV, which the customer agreed to, even if an agent chose it. If the agent reduced it without explanation, that is a mis-selling complaint against the agent, not a reason to pay above the contract.
action: Settle at the IDV and investigate the agent's sales process.
outcomes: Settled at ₹4,80,000 with salvage transferred
Ombudsman complaint about mis-selling; agent disciplined

title: A cyclone tree, moved before the surveyor came
type: Storm damage where the scene was disturbed
story: A tree fell on policyholder's Maruti Ertiga parked outside his house in Visakhapatnam during a cyclone. By the time the surveyor arrived two days later, the municipal crew had cut and removed the tree and neighbours had pushed the car aside to clear the road. The policy wording asks the insured not to move the vehicle before inspection.
statement: The cyclone came at night. In the morning the big neem tree was lying on the car. The road was blocked, so the municipality people cut it and my neighbours helped push the car. I could not wait two days with the road blocked. I took many photos and videos before they moved anything.

accounts.who: Photos and video from the policyholder and a neighbour
accounts.text: Eighteen photos and two videos timestamped the morning after the cyclone, showing the tree trunk across the Ertiga's roof and bonnet, broken windscreen, and the street with other fallen trees. Metadata location matches the policyholder's address.

Vehicle moved from the original position. Roof crushed, windscreen and rear glass broken, bonnet dented. Bark fragments and leaves embedded in the roof panel. Damage consistent with a tree fall. Cyclone recorded by IMD on the date. Estimate ₹1,72,000.

whatHappened: The cyclone brought down the neem tree onto the car. The car was moved only to clear the road, after it had been photographed in place.
damage: Roof, glass and bonnet, ₹1,72,000.
missing: The municipal crew's record of removing the tree, which would add to the photos
innocent: Moving the car to clear a blocked road after a cyclone is reasonable
questions: Ask whether any other cars on the street were damaged, in case of a wider claim pattern
steps: Accept the photos and the surveyor's findings in place of an undisturbed scene
Settle under own damage
assessment: Genuine. The condition not to move the vehicle exists to protect evidence; here the evidence was well preserved and the reason for moving it was compelling. Rejecting the claim on that ground would be unfair.
action: Settle the claim.
outcomes: Settled at ₹1,72,000 less the compulsory deductible

title: A tyre burst on the Samruddhi expressway
type: Tyre burst with wheel and suspension damage
story: Policyholder's Mahindra XUV700 suffered a front-left tyre burst on the Samruddhi Mahamarg near Nagpur at about 2:30 PM in 44°C heat, after hitting a broken expansion joint. He kept control and stopped on the shoulder. The alloy wheel cracked and the lower control arm bent. He is claiming the tyre, wheel and suspension.
statement: There was a big bang and the steering pulled left. I was doing about 100, the limit is 120. I managed to stop. There was a broken joint in the concrete just before. The tyre was only 8 months old. I want everything covered, the tyre also.

accounts.text: Front-left tyre: sidewall rupture consistent with an impact. Alloy wheel cracked at the rim. Lower control arm bent. Tyre tread 6.5 mm, manufactured 9 months ago. Damage consistent with hitting a raised edge at speed. Estimate: tyre ₹16,500, alloy ₹28,000, control arm and alignment ₹14,200.

whatHappened: A sharp-edged broken expansion joint burst the tyre at speed and cracked the alloy, and the impact bent the control arm.
damage: Tyre ₹16,500, alloy wheel ₹28,000, suspension ₹14,200.
thirdParties: The expressway operator, for the broken expansion joint
evidence: Photos of the tyre, wheel and road
missing: Photos of the broken expansion joint
innocent: A tyre burst on a hot concrete expressway after a sharp impact is common and needs no other explanation
questions: Ask whether he has a tyre protection add-on
Ask whether he photographed the expansion joint
steps: Pay the alloy wheel and suspension under own damage
Pay the tyre at 50% of the replacement cost, because the vehicle was damaged at the same time, as the standard wording provides
Pay the tyre in full if a tyre protection add-on applies
assessment: Genuine. Under standard Indian motor wording, tyre damage alone is excluded, but when the vehicle is damaged at the same time the tyre is paid at 50%. The customer should be told this clearly, as it often causes disputes.
action: Pay the wheel and suspension in full and the tyre at 50%, unless an add-on covers it fully.
outcomes: Settled: wheel and suspension in full, tyre at 50%
Tyre protection add-on applies; tyre paid in full

title: Debris from a construction site onto a parked car
type: Falling object damage with a recoverable third party
story: Concrete blocks and a steel rod fell from an under-construction building in Whitefield, Bengaluru, onto policyholder's Tata Altroz parked on the street below. The builder's site supervisor admitted the debris came from the site, where the safety netting had been removed that morning.
statement: I heard a crash from my office window and saw people around my car. The windscreen was smashed and the roof dented. The supervisor said sorry and said the company would pay, but now they are not answering my calls. I just want my car repaired.

accounts.who: Apartment security CCTV across the street
accounts.text: 14:02:10 blocks and a rod fall from the fifth floor of the construction site onto the parked Altroz. No safety netting visible on that side of the building. Two workers look down from the slab.
Madam, sorry, the netting was removed for shifting the material. Company will take care of the damage. Please send estimate.

whatHappened: Blocks and a rod fell from the fifth floor of a site with its safety netting removed, as the CCTV across the street shows.
damage: Windscreen, roof and bonnet, ₹86,000.
missing: The builder's liability insurer details
innocent: The builder going quiet after admitting fault is common and does not cast doubt on the claim
questions: Ask the builder for its contractor's all risks or third-party liability insurance details
steps: Settle under own damage so the customer is not waiting for the builder
Recover from the builder or its liability insurer using the CCTV and the supervisor's message
assessment: Genuine, with a clear right of recovery. Paying first and recovering later serves the customer better than leaving her to chase the builder.
action: Pay the claim and pursue recovery from the builder.
outcomes: Paid; recovered in full from the builder's liability insurer

title: Rats in the wiring loom
type: Rodent damage to wiring
story: Policyholder's Kia Sonet would not start after being parked for two weeks in an open parking area in Dwarka, Delhi, while she was travelling. The workshop found rodents had chewed through the engine wiring harness and the washer pipes. She asks whether her comprehensive policy covers it.
statement: When I came back the car wouldn't start and there were droppings in the engine. The workshop says they need to change the whole harness, almost fifty thousand. My neighbour says rat damage isn't covered, but nobody told me anything when I bought the policy.

accounts.text: Rodent bite marks on the engine wiring harness, ABS sensor cable and washer hoses. Rodent nesting material near the battery. Harness replacement required. Estimate ₹48,500.

whatHappened: Rodents nested in the engine bay while the car stood unused for two weeks and chewed through the wiring harness and hoses.
damage: Wiring harness and hoses, ₹48,500.
evidence: Workshop report with photos of bite marks
missing: The exact policy wording on rodent or animal damage and on electrical breakdown
Whether she holds any rodent protection add-on
innocent: Rodent nests are common in cars left unused in open parking, so the damage fits the two weeks she was away
questions: Ask for her policy schedule to check add-ons
steps: Check the wording: some insurers cover rodent damage as accidental external damage, others exclude it unless an add-on is bought
Pay if the wording covers it; if not, explain the exclusion and the available add-on
assessment: Genuine. Whether it is paid depends entirely on this insurer's wording, which varies across the market. The decision must be based on the actual words and explained clearly.
action: Decide on the wording and explain the outcome.
outcomes: Covered as accidental external damage; paid less the deductible
Excluded under the wording; customer offered the add-on at renewal

title: A CNG kit fire, and a kit no one endorsed
type: Fire from an undeclared retrofitted fuel kit
story: Policyholder's petrol Maruti Dzire caught fire while parked in the sun in Jaipur in May. The fire service found it started at a CNG cylinder pipe joint in the boot. The CNG kit was fitted by a local workshop a year ago. It is not endorsed on the registration certificate or on the policy.
statement: CNG is so much cheaper, everyone in my area has fitted it. The workshop said they would do the RC paperwork, then they kept delaying. I didn't know I had to tell the insurance company. The car was parked, nobody was inside, I was in the shop.

accounts.text: Vehicle fire, parked car. Origin in the boot area at the CNG cylinder outlet pipe. Joint fitting loose with signs of gas leakage. Ambient temperature 45°C. Fire spread to the cabin. Vehicle fully burnt.

RC shows fuel type: petrol. No alternative fuel endorsement. Policy issued for a petrol vehicle; no CNG kit declared, no additional premium for the kit. The workshop that fitted the kit is not an approved retrofitter.

whatHappened: A non-approved CNG kit leaked in the heat and caught fire. The kit was never endorsed on the RC or declared to the insurer, so the insurer was covering a different risk from the one on the road.
damage: Car burnt out, total loss; IDV ₹5,40,000.
thirdParties: The workshop that fitted the kit
evidence: Fire service report identifying the CNG joint
missing: The workshop's licence or approval status in writing
indicators: An undeclared material change to the vehicle that caused the loss
innocent: He relied on the workshop to handle the paperwork
Unendorsed CNG kits are common, and many owners do not know they must be declared
questions: Ask for the kit invoice and any messages with the workshop about the RC endorsement
steps: Repudiate on the basis of the undeclared kit that caused the fire, citing the policy condition on material changes
Explain his rights: an Ombudsman complaint, or a consumer court where non-standard settlements are sometimes ordered
Suggest he pursue the workshop for the faulty and unapproved installation
assessment: Genuine fire, but the cause was an unendorsed modification that changed the risk. Repudiation is defensible because the undeclared kit directly caused the loss. A consumer forum might still order a partial, non-standard settlement, so the decision should be well documented.
action: Repudiate with a clear explanation and documentation; consider a non-standard settlement only if the regulator's guidance or a forum requires it.
outcomes: Repudiated; customer pursues the workshop
Consumer forum orders a 50% non-standard settlement

title: An e-scooter fire in a Pune basement, and the neighbours' bikes
type: Electric scooter fire spreading to other vehicles
story: Policyholder's electric scooter caught fire while charging at a socket in his housing society's basement in Wakad, Pune, at about 1:00 AM. The fire destroyed the scooter and damaged three neighbours' motorcycles and the basement wiring. The society has asked him to pay for everything.
statement: I plugged it in at 11 like every night, with the company charger. At one the security guard called me. My scooter was burning and the smoke was everywhere. Three bikes next to it are damaged. The society secretary says I must pay for all of it. The company has a recall for some batteries, I don't know if mine is included.

accounts.text: Fire in the basement parking area. Origin: battery compartment of an electric scooter on charge. Fire spread to three adjacent motorcycles. Basement wiring and a distribution board damaged. No injuries. Cause recorded as electrical, thermal event in the battery.

Voluntary recall of battery packs from a specified production batch for inspection of cell modules. Customers to book a free inspection. The policyholder's scooter chassis number falls within the recalled batch. No inspection booked.

whatHappened: The scooter's battery, from a recalled batch, had a thermal event while charging and the fire spread to neighbouring vehicles.
damage: Scooter destroyed, IDV ₹98,000. Three motorcycles damaged, about ₹1,60,000 in total. Basement wiring about ₹70,000.
thirdParties: Three neighbours whose motorcycles were damaged
The housing society, for the wiring
evidence: Recall notice covering his chassis number
missing: The neighbours' own insurance details
A forensic battery examination
innocent: Not booking a recall inspection is careless but common, and it does not make the fire intentional
questions: Ask the neighbours whether their own policies cover fire
Ask the manufacturer to preserve the battery for examination
steps: Settle the scooter under the fire cover in own damage
Consider whether the third-party property damage cover responds to the neighbours' bikes: courts have read the use of a vehicle broadly, including when parked
Preserve the battery and notify the manufacturer of a recovery claim
Coordinate with the neighbours' insurers to avoid double payment
assessment: Genuine. The scooter is covered. The bigger questions are whether the policy's third-party property cover responds to damage to the neighbours' vehicles, and recovering from the manufacturer given the recall. Courts have often read "use" of a vehicle broadly, so the third-party cover may well apply.
action: Pay the scooter, take a position on the third-party property claims with legal advice, and pursue the manufacturer.
outcomes: Scooter paid; neighbours' bikes paid under the third-party property cover; recovered from the manufacturer
Neighbours claim under their own policies; their insurers pursue the manufacturer

title: "The steering locked": owner against manufacturer
type: Collision blamed on a steering defect
story: Policyholder's two-year-old Hyundai Verna hit the road divider on Shaheed Path, Lucknow, at about 60 km/h. He says the steering suddenly became heavy and locked. The car's electric power steering module stored a fault code. The dealer, on behalf of the manufacturer, says the fault code was caused by the impact, not the other way round.
statement: I was driving straight, then suddenly the steering became very hard, like a truck without power steering, and the car went towards the divider. I could not turn it back. I have read about this problem online. I want my car repaired, and I want the company to admit the defect.

accounts.text: Electric power steering control unit: fault code for "motor circuit malfunction" stored with an event time 0.3 seconds after the airbag deployment event. Steering column and rack bent from the impact. No prior steering complaints in the service history. In our opinion the fault resulted from the collision.

accounts.who: Independent automobile engineer, engaged by the policyholder
accounts.text: The control unit timestamps are generated by separate modules and are not synchronised to fractions of a second, so the order of events cannot be concluded from them. The steering motor connector shows corrosion that pre-dates the accident. A pre-impact assistance failure cannot be excluded.

whatHappened: Unknown. Either a steering assistance failure caused the crash, or the crash caused the fault code. The two experts disagree, and the evidence does not yet settle it.
damage: Front end, steering column and rack, airbags; estimate ₹3,60,000.
thirdParties: The vehicle manufacturer, through its dealer
missing: Data from the airbag control module, read by a neutral expert
Complaint records for the same model's steering
inconsistencies: The dealer and the independent engineer disagree on whether the fault came before or after the impact
innocent: Both experts may be honest: module timestamps are genuinely hard to interpret
questions: Ask the manufacturer for any service bulletins on the steering unit for this model
Ask the policyholder to preserve the steering unit for a joint inspection
steps: Settle the own-damage claim now: an accident is covered whatever its cause
Preserve the steering column and control unit
Consider a recovery claim against the manufacturer if a neutral expert supports a defect
Inform the policyholder that he can pursue the manufacturer separately in a consumer forum
assessment: The dispute is about the cause, not about cover. The insurer should pay the own-damage claim promptly and leave the defect question to a possible recovery and to the customer's own consumer complaint.
action: Pay the claim, preserve the parts, and decide on a recovery after a neutral inspection.
outcomes: Paid; neutral inspection inconclusive; no recovery
Defect established; manufacturer reimburses the insurer and compensates the customer

title: Bike stolen at the metro station, insurer told nine days later
type: Two-wheeler theft with late intimation to the insurer
story: Policyholder's Hero Splendor was stolen from the metro station parking at Dwarka Sector 21, Delhi. He filed an e-FIR the same night and informed the insurer nine days later. The policy asks for immediate notice of theft. The police have not yet traced the bike.
statement: I parked at 8 in the morning and when I came back at 7 it was gone. The parking attendant said he didn't see anything. I filed the e-FIR on my phone that same night. I didn't know I had to inform the insurance company also, my friend told me after one week.

accounts.text: Motor vehicle theft e-FIR registered at 21:40 on the day of the theft. Vehicle: Hero Splendor, parked at metro parking, Dwarka Sector 21, from 08:05 to 19:10. Parking token number recorded. Investigation assigned.
Token issued at 08:04 for a two-wheeler with the policyholder's registration. No exit record against the token. Cameras cover only the entry and exit gates; no recording of the vehicle leaving.

whatHappened: A genuine theft. The delay in telling the insurer came from not knowing it was required; the police were told within hours.
damage: Motorcycle not recovered. IDV ₹52,000.
evidence: Parking token record with no exit
missing: The police's untraced (final) report, accepted by the court
RC transfer papers in favour of the insurer
innocent: Many owners do not know they must notify the insurer separately from the police
questions: Ask him to submit both keys
Ask whether the bike had any finance
steps: Do not reject for late intimation: the police were told promptly and the theft is genuine, which is the regulator's long-standing guidance
Collect the keys, the RC and the signed transfer forms
Wait for the untraced report, then settle at the IDV
assessment: Genuine. Rejecting a genuine theft claim only because the insurer was told late, when the police were told at once, goes against IRDAI guidance and would not survive a complaint.
action: Process the claim and settle at the IDV once the untraced report arrives.
outcomes: Settled at ₹52,000 less the deductible after the untraced report
Bike recovered by police before settlement; claim closed

title: The hired driver who never brought the van back
type: Vehicle taken by a person it was handed to
story: Policyholder runs a small catering business in Ghaziabad. He hired a new driver through a contact and gave him the keys to his Maruti Eeco to deliver an order. The driver and the van never came back. The police registered an FIR for criminal breach of trust and cheating. The insurer is considering whether this is "theft" under the policy.
statement: He came recommended by my cook's cousin. I checked his licence photo on WhatsApp. He made two deliveries fine, then on the third day he took the van with the food for a wedding and switched off his phone. The address he gave doesn't exist. To me it's theft. My business is stuck without the van.

accounts.text: Complainant states that a driver engaged three days earlier took the vehicle for delivery and did not return. Driver's phone switched off. Address given by the driver found to be false. Case registered under the provisions for criminal breach of trust and cheating. Vehicle not traced.

The company will indemnify the insured against loss of or damage to the vehicle by burglary, housebreaking or theft. (No definition of theft in the policy; no specific exclusion for loss by a person to whom the vehicle is entrusted.)

whatHappened: The driver deliberately disappeared with the van. Whether that is "theft" for the policy, or a breach of trust after the owner handed over the vehicle, is the question.
damage: Eeco not recovered. IDV ₹3,90,000. Catering goods lost, not covered by the motor policy.
missing: Verification of the driver's licence on Sarathi
Police progress on tracing the vehicle
innocent: Small business owners often hire drivers informally through contacts
questions: Ask whether the licence on WhatsApp is genuine, by checking it on Sarathi
Ask whether the driver had permission to take the van home
steps: Take legal advice on the theft definition: insurers often argue that entrustment followed by dishonest retention is breach of trust, not theft
Note that the policy does not exclude loss by an entrusted person, and that ambiguous wording is read in favour of the insured
Decide, and explain the reasons in writing
assessment: Genuine loss and a real coverage dispute. There is some support for refusing claims where the vehicle was voluntarily handed over, but this wording has no such exclusion, and the driver obtained the van by deception. Paying, or settling on a fair basis, is likely to be the better and more defensible outcome.
action: Treat it as a coverage question with legal advice; lean towards paying given the wording.
outcomes: Paid at the IDV after the untraced report
Repudiated as breach of trust; customer wins in the consumer forum
Settled at 75% of the IDV

title: Reported stolen, actually repossessed
type: Theft claim for a vehicle taken by the lender's agents
story: Policyholder reported his Mahindra Scorpio-N stolen from outside his house in Noida overnight and filed an FIR. Police enquiries found that the lender's recovery agency had taken the vehicle for an EMI default of five months and informed the local police station that night.
statement: First statement: Someone stole my car at night, I heard nothing. Later: I knew I was behind on EMIs, but nobody told me they would come and take it. I thought it was thieves. They should have given notice, it's harassment.

accounts.text: Intimation received at 01:20 from a recovery agency acting for the lender, stating that the vehicle had been repossessed under the loan agreement and moved to the agency's yard in Greater Noida. Theft FIR filed by the owner at 08:30 the same morning. FIR closed as "not theft" after verification.

Three demand notices sent by registered post and email over four months, the last stating that the vehicle would be repossessed if dues were not cleared within 7 days. Postal tracking shows delivery to the policyholder's address.

whatHappened: The vehicle was repossessed by the lender, not stolen. He may genuinely have thought it was theft at first, but he had received repossession warnings and kept the claim going after he knew.
damage: No loss covered by the policy: the vehicle is in the lender's yard.
thirdParties: The lender and its recovery agency
evidence: Police record of the repossession intimation
Lender demand notices with delivery tracking
missing: Whether the policyholder was told the outcome of the police verification before he contacted the insurer again
inconsistencies: He reported a theft; the police record shows a lawful repossession reported the same night
He says nobody warned him; the lender sent three notices, one specifically about repossession
indicators: Theft claim for a vehicle under a loan in serious default
innocent: A repossession at night without warning can genuinely look like a theft
Notices sent by post are not always read
questions: Ask whether he was aware of the final repossession notice
Ask whether he has spoken to the lender since the FIR was closed
steps: Close the claim: repossession by the lender is not theft
Explain the decision with the police record
Note the file; refer to the fraud unit only if he continues to pursue a theft claim after being told
assessment: Not a covered loss. The first report may have been an honest mistake, but continuing to claim theft after learning of the repossession would be dishonest. The case needs a clear explanation, not an accusation.
action: Close the claim with an explanation and refer only if he persists.
outcomes: Claim withdrawn after explanation
Policyholder files a complaint against the lender about the repossession process

title: Recovered in Hyderabad, without its wheels and seats
type: Stolen car recovered stripped of parts
story: Policyholder's Maruti Swift was stolen from outside her apartment in Kukatpally, Hyderabad, and recovered by police five days later on an open plot in Medchal, without its wheels, front seats, battery and music system. Her policy has no zero-depreciation add-on.
statement: The police called to say they found it. It was sitting on stones, no wheels, no seats, even the battery was gone. The music system I had fitted after buying, I have the bill. They also broke the steering lock.

accounts.text: Vehicle recovered on an open plot in Medchal. Four wheels with tyres, two front seats, battery and aftermarket music system missing. Steering lock broken, ignition damaged. Vehicle handed over to the owner after formalities.

Parts to be replaced: four wheels and tyres, two front seats, battery, ignition switch and steering lock. Music system: aftermarket, purchase invoice for ₹18,000 provided; not declared as an electrical accessory on the policy. Assessed with depreciation as per policy: ₹71,400.

whatHappened: Thieves stole the car, stripped the parts that sell easily and abandoned it on an open plot, where police found it five days later.
damage: Wheels, tyres, seats, battery, ignition and steering lock; assessed ₹71,400 after depreciation. Undeclared music system ₹18,000.
missing: Proof that the music system was declared at any earlier renewal
innocent: Thieves often strip a car and abandon it within days; the missing seats and wheels fit that pattern
questions: Ask whether she declared the music system as an accessory at any renewal
steps: Pay the missing and damaged parts with policy depreciation applied
Explain that the undeclared aftermarket music system is not covered unless declared as an electrical accessory
assessment: Genuine. The two common friction points are depreciation, which reduces the payout without a zero-depreciation add-on, and the undeclared accessory. Both should be explained plainly.
action: Settle the parts with depreciation and explain the accessory exclusion.
outcomes: Paid ₹71,400 less the deductible; music system excluded

title: Into a tree at 2 AM, and a note saying "smell of alcohol"
type: Single-vehicle crash with possible drunk driving
story: Policyholder's Volkswagen Virtus hit a tree beside the Outer Ring Road in Bengaluru at about 2:10 AM. He was taken to hospital with minor injuries. The medico-legal case record notes "smell of alcohol". No blood alcohol test was done and the police did not register a drink-driving case. The policy excludes loss while driving under the influence of alcohol.
statement: I was coming from a friend's birthday dinner. I had one beer at around ten, that's all. A dog ran across and I swerved and lost control. I was not drunk. The doctor wrote that because I told him about the beer.

accounts.text: Brought at 02:45 by bystanders. Alert and oriented, speech normal, gait steady. Smell of alcohol present. History of alcohol consumption given by the patient. Blood alcohol not tested. Minor lacerations, discharged after treatment.

accounts.who: Bar bill and restaurant CCTV, provided by the policyholder
accounts.text: Bill for a table of six from 21:30 to 01:40 including 14 beers and 3 mocktails. CCTV at the exit shows the policyholder walking steadily to his car at 01:52.

whatHappened: He crashed after a night out where he had been drinking, possibly more than one beer. Whether he was "under the influence" in the legal sense cannot be proven without a test.
damage: Front end, radiator and airbags, ₹2,95,000. Tree damage minimal; no third party.
missing: A blood alcohol test
Any police breath test
Witnesses to the crash and the dog
inconsistencies: He says he had one beer; the bill shows 14 beers shared among six people over four hours
innocent: A smell of alcohol shows drinking, not intoxication
The doctor recorded normal speech and a steady gait
questions: Ask who drank what at the table
Ask whether anyone else saw the dog
steps: Weigh the evidence: the exclusion needs proof that he was under the influence, not merely that he had been drinking
Do not repudiate on the "smell of alcohol" note alone; courts have required stronger proof of intoxication
Decide on the balance of evidence and record the reasons
assessment: A careful case. He probably drank more than he admits, but the insurer must prove the exclusion applies. With normal clinical signs and no test, the evidence of intoxication is weak, and a repudiation would be at real risk in a consumer forum.
action: Unless stronger evidence of intoxication emerges, settle the own-damage claim and note the concerns on file.
outcomes: Paid in full after review
Repudiated; consumer forum orders payment for lack of proof of intoxication

title: A private car working as an app cab
type: Passenger injury in a private car used for hire
story: Policyholder's private Toyota Etios, registered for personal use, was being driven as a cab through a ride-hailing app when it rear-ended a truck on the Delhi-Gurugram Expressway. A paying passenger broke his arm and has filed a claim before the tribunal. The car has no commercial permit and a private car policy.
statement: I lost my job and started driving for an app with my own car. I know it should be a yellow plate but the permit costs too much. The truck braked suddenly. My passenger was in the back without a seatbelt and hit the front seat.

accounts.text: Trip accepted at 18:02, passenger picked up 18:11 at Sikanderpur, fare ₹420 to Dwarka. Trip ended abruptly at 18:34 with "incident reported". Vehicle registered on the app as a commercial vehicle with a photo of a yellow plate that does not match this car.

Petitioner, a passenger in the vehicle, suffered a fracture of the right humerus. Claims compensation for medical expenses, loss of income and pain and suffering from the driver-owner and his insurer.

whatHappened: He was using a private car as a commercial cab without a permit, and registered on the app with false vehicle details. He rear-ended a truck and his passenger was injured.
damage: Passenger: fractured arm, about three months' recovery. Car: front end, ₹1,30,000. Truck: rear underrun bar.
missing: Police FIR details
Truck driver's account of the braking
inconsistencies: The app listed a yellow-plate commercial vehicle; the car is privately registered with a private policy
indicators: Use of a private vehicle for hire and reward in breach of the policy and the permit rules
False vehicle details given to the app
innocent: Financial pressure after job loss is a common reason for this
The truck may have braked without reason
questions: Ask the app operator for its own passenger insurance details
Ask the truck driver why he braked
steps: Repudiate the own-damage claim for use outside the limitations of use
Defend the passenger's claim on quantum but expect to pay it; then seek to recover from the owner for the breach of policy and permit conditions
Notify the app operator of the false vehicle registration
assessment: A genuine accident during illegal commercial use. The injured passenger must be compensated, and Indian courts usually require the insurer to pay first and recover from the owner in such breaches. The owner's own car damage is not covered.
action: Decline own damage, pay the passenger's award, and pursue pay and recover against the owner.
outcomes: Tribunal orders the insurer to pay ₹3.4 lakh and recover from the owner
App operator's passenger accident cover contributes to the medical costs

title: Fourteen hours at the wheel, into the back of a car at 4 AM
