assessment: Potential fraud with strong evidence: the car is being driven openly, and a witness describes a private sale.
action: Investigate the sale, help the police trace the car, and repudiate if confirmed.
outcomes: Car traced to the buyer; claim withdrawn
Claim repudiated and FIR closed as false

title: Surveyor on day 3, report on day 28, no decision on day 48
type: Own-damage claim handled outside the regulator’s timelines
story: Policyholder intimated an own-damage claim on 1 July after her car was rear-ended in heavy rain in Pune. A surveyor was appointed on 4 July and inspected the car on 6 July. The survey report was submitted on 29 July. On 18 August there is still no decision. She raised a grievance with the insurer on 1 August and has had no reply, and has now registered a complaint on the Bima Bharosa portal.
statement: My car has been sitting at the garage for seven weeks. Every time I call, I'm told the file is under process. I have sent every document they asked for. I'm paying for cabs every day. Isn't there a rule about how long this can take?

accounts.text: 1 July: claim intimated. 4 July: surveyor appointed. 6 July: survey. 29 July: final survey report received. 1 August: grievance received, no response logged. 18 August: no decision. All documents received by 8 July.
Complaint registered against the insurer for delay in claim settlement. Insurer to resolve and update the portal.

whatHappened: A straightforward genuine claim delayed at every stage, in breach of the regulator's timelines.
damage: Her Baleno: rear bumper, boot lid and tail lamps; surveyor's assessment ₹72,000.
missing: Any reason recorded for the delays
innocent: Monsoon claim volumes can overwhelm surveyors, but that does not suspend the timelines
questions: Check whether other monsoon claims are similarly delayed
steps: Decide and settle the claim now on the survey report
Record the breaches: the surveyor should be appointed within 24 hours, the report submitted within 15 days of the survey, and the claim decided within 7 days of the report
Pay interest for the delay as the regulations require, and respond to the grievance and the Bima Bharosa complaint with what was done
Find out why the grievance went unanswered and fix the queue
assessment: Genuine claim and clear regulatory breaches by the insurer. Settle, compensate the delay and answer the complaint.
action: Settle now with interest, respond on Bima Bharosa, and fix the delays.
outcomes: Settled with interest within 3 days; complaint closed
Review finds 300 monsoon claims past the 7-day decision limit

title: ₹72,000 cut from a zero-depreciation claim with no explanation
type: Partial settlement with unexplained deductions, heading for the ombudsman
story: Policyholder's SUV was hit on its side at a junction in Kochi. His policy has a zero-depreciation add-on. The repair bill was ₹2,10,000 and the insurer paid ₹1,38,000. The settlement letter lists three deductions without detail: "depreciation ₹42,000", "not related to accident ₹18,000" and "labour cut ₹12,000". He wrote to the grievance cell 40 days ago and has had no reply. He is preparing a complaint to the Insurance Ombudsman.
statement: I paid extra every year for zero dep precisely so this wouldn't happen. Nobody has told me what "not related to accident" means. The surveyor saw the car with me. I've written to them, nobody answers. I'll go to the ombudsman if I have to.

accounts.text: Repair invoice ₹2,10,000. Less: depreciation ₹42,000; not related to accident ₹18,000; labour cut ₹12,000. Amount paid ₹1,38,000. Policy add-ons: zero depreciation.
Grievance received 40 days ago asking for a breakdown of the deductions. Status: open, unassigned.

whatHappened: A genuine claim underpaid. The depreciation deduction ignores his zero-depreciation add-on, and the other deductions were never explained.
damage: Mahindra XUV700: front door, rear door, B-pillar trim and side mirror; repair ₹2,10,000.
missing: The surveyor's working for the ₹18,000 and the labour cut
inconsistencies: Depreciation deducted on a policy with a zero-depreciation add-on
innocent: A settlement system may apply depreciation by default if the add-on is not read from the policy
questions: Ask the surveyor which parts were treated as not related to the accident and why
steps: Refund the ₹42,000 depreciation: the zero-depreciation add-on covers it
Review the other deductions against the survey report and give a written, item-by-item explanation; refund any not supported
Answer his grievance in writing now
Explain his right to approach the Insurance Ombudsman within a year of the insurer’s reply (or one month without a reply) for claims up to ₹50 lakh, and expect the deductions to be scrutinised there
assessment: Genuine and underpaid, with unexplained deductions and an ignored grievance. A clear ombudsman risk the insurer should fix itself.
action: Refund the depreciation, justify or refund the other deductions, and answer the grievance in writing.
outcomes: ₹54,000 refunded with an item-wise explanation; ombudsman complaint not filed
Ombudsman awards the full difference

title: A thumbprint on "full and final" at the garage counter
type: Discharge voucher signed by a vulnerable customer under pressure
story: Policyholder, aged 64, from a village near Gaya, Bihar, owns a car driven by her son for the family business. After it hit a tree, the surveyor assessed the loss at ₹1,10,000 and the garage bill came to ₹1,08,000. At the garage, the surveyor gave her a discharge voucher for ₹62,000 marked "full and final" and told her she would not get the car back unless she signed. She cannot read English and put her thumbprint on it. She now wants the balance.
statement: (Through her son) The sahib said sign here or the car stays here. I don't read English. I thought it was the paper to take the car home. When the money came it was only sixty-two thousand. The garage took the rest from my son.

accounts.text: Assessed loss ₹1,10,000 net of depreciation and excess. Recommended for settlement.
"I accept ₹62,000 in full and final settlement of all claims under the policy." Thumb impression of the insured. Witness: the surveyor. Printed in English only.

whatHappened: A genuine claim underpaid by ₹48,000 through a voucher obtained from an elderly customer who could not read it, under pressure.
damage: Maruti Ertiga: front bumper, radiator, bonnet and headlamps. Garage bill ₹1,08,000; surveyor assessment ₹1,10,000.
missing: Why the voucher amount differs from the surveyor’s own assessment
inconsistencies: The surveyor assessed ₹1,10,000 but witnessed a voucher for ₹62,000
innocent: A clerical error could explain the figure, but not the pressure to sign or the English-only form for a customer who cannot read it
questions: Ask the surveyor to explain the ₹62,000 figure and the circumstances of the signing
steps: Do not rely on the voucher: a discharge signed under pressure by a customer who could not read it does not prevent her claiming the balance, and forums treat such vouchers sceptically
Pay the balance of the assessed loss with interest for the delay
Investigate the surveyor’s conduct and report it if confirmed
Communicate with her in Hindi, through her son if she wishes, and check whether other customers were treated the same way
assessment: Genuine claim and a vulnerable customer who was pressured into an unfair discharge. The insurer should correct it before a consumer forum does.
action: Pay the ₹48,000 balance with interest and investigate the surveyor.
outcomes: Balance paid; surveyor removed from the panel
Review finds three more vouchers obtained the same way

title: A moose on the Trans-Canada at dusk
type: Large animal collision and total loss
story: Policyholder's Hyundai Elantra hit a moose on the Trans-Canada Highway near Gander, Newfoundland and Labrador, at about 20:30 in September. The moose went over the hood and into the windshield. She had cuts from glass and a sprained wrist. The car is a write-off.
statement: It was just after sunset. It stepped out from the trees on the right and there was no time. It came up over the hood and the roof caved in on the passenger side. I'm lucky I was alone. A trucker stopped and called 911. The RCMP came and dealt with the moose.

accounts.text: Single vehicle collision with a moose on the Trans-Canada Highway, westbound, 20:31. Animal deceased at the scene and removed by the wildlife division. Driver treated by paramedics for lacerations and a wrist sprain. Vehicle heavily damaged to the hood, windshield and roof. No contributing driver factors noted.
Hood, windshield, roof and A-pillars crushed. Moose hair embedded in the windshield frame. Repair exceeds the value of the vehicle. Actual cash value $16,200 based on comparable local listings.

whatHappened: A moose stepped out of the trees at dusk and came over the hood; the RCMP report and the hair in the windshield frame confirm it.
damage: Car written off, actual cash value $16,200. Cuts and a sprained wrist.
evidence: Appraiser valuation with moose hair in the frame
missing: Confirmation of any loan on the car before the settlement is paid
innocent: Moose collisions at dusk are frequent on this highway, and the hair in the frame confirms the impact
questions: Ask whether she has accident benefits on her policy for the wrist injury and any time off work
steps: Settle the total loss under comprehensive less the deductible: an animal strike is a comprehensive loss, not collision
Check her accident benefits coverage for medical costs and lost income
Arrange removal of the wreck to salvage
assessment: Genuine and straightforward. Moose collisions are common on this highway and the evidence is complete.
action: Pay the total loss promptly and handle any accident benefits.
outcomes: Paid $16,200 less the comprehensive deductible
Accident benefits pay her physiotherapy

title: Black ice pile-up on the 401
type: Multi-vehicle collision under Ontario fault rules
story: Policyholder's Toyota Corolla was the second car in a five-vehicle chain reaction on Highway 401 near Kingston, Ontario, on black ice at about 07:15. He stopped behind a car that had spun, then a minivan hit him from behind and pushed him into it. He wants to know whether he is at fault and who pays for his car.
statement: The car ahead spun out in front of me. I braked and stopped maybe a metre from it, the ABS was going crazy. Then the van behind slid into me and pushed me into the spun car. Three more cars piled in after that. I don't want this on my record, I did nothing wrong.

accounts.who: Ontario Provincial Police collision report summary
accounts.text: Five-vehicle collision, eastbound, icy surface. Vehicle 1 lost control and rotated across lanes 1 and 2. Vehicle 2 (Corolla) stopped behind Vehicle 1. Vehicle 3 (Dodge Grand Caravan) struck Vehicle 2, pushing it into Vehicle 1. Vehicles 4 and 5 struck Vehicle 3 and each other. No charges laid; road conditions a major factor.

whatHappened: He stopped in time behind the spun car and was then pushed into it by the minivan, the sequence the police report records.
damage: Corolla: front and rear damage, estimate $9,400. No injuries.
thirdParties: Drivers of the other four vehicles and their insurers
missing: Statements from the other drivers
The Corolla's dashcam footage, if fitted
innocent: Front damage on a car that was hit from behind is explained by the push into the car ahead
questions: Ask whether he has a dashcam
Ask the other insurers for their drivers' accounts
steps: Handle his vehicle damage with his own insurer under direct compensation property damage, if he kept that coverage when it became optional in Ontario in 2024
Apply the Fault Determination Rules for chain reactions: a car stopped in its lane and pushed into the car ahead is generally not at fault for that impact
Waive his deductible to the extent he is not at fault, and keep the claim off his record as at-fault
assessment: Genuine. In Ontario his own insurer pays his car damage under direct compensation, if he still carries it, and the Fault Determination Rules, not the police report, decide fault for insurance purposes. On the sequence described, he should be assessed as not at fault.
action: Pay under direct compensation with no deductible and record the claim as not at fault.
outcomes: Paid $9,400 with no deductible; recorded as not at fault
Other insurer disputes the sequence; resolved by inter-company arbitration

title: The tow truck that arrived first, and the clinic that called next
type: Tow steering with inflated towing, storage and treatment referrals
story: Policyholder's Honda Civic was rear-ended on Highway 427 in Toronto. Within minutes a tow truck that nobody called arrived and took the car to a body shop 40 km away. The tow bill is $1,640 and storage is $85 a day. The next day a rehabilitation clinic phoned her offering free treatment and a "settlement advocate".
statement: I was shaken and it was snowing. The tow driver said he'd take care of everything and I just needed to sign. He said the police wanted the road cleared. Now the shop won't release the car until my insurance pays their bill, and some clinic keeps calling me about my injuries, but I'm not even hurt.

accounts.text: Tow from Highway 427 to the body shop: hook-up $350, mileage 40 km $480, winching $250, "accident scene clean-up" $310, administration $250. Total $1,640. Storage $85 per day from the day of the tow. Authorization form signed at the scene.

The tow operator, body shop and rehabilitation clinic share a phone number on their websites. The same tow operator has towed 37 vehicles to this body shop this year, all from highway collisions, at an average invoice of $1,580. The provincial towing rules limit unauthorised steering and require rate disclosure before the tow.

whatHappened: A genuine minor collision. A tow chaser steered her car to a linked body shop, overcharged for the tow and storage, and passed her details to a linked clinic to create an injury claim.
damage: Civic: rear bumper and trunk, about $4,200. Tow and storage charges $1,640 plus $85 a day.
missing: Whether the operator disclosed rates before the tow, as required
The police officer's confirmation that no tow was requested
inconsistencies: The tow driver said the police wanted the road cleared; the police did not request a tow
indicators: Unrequested tow arriving within minutes
Car taken 40 km to a linked body shop
Inflated tow charges and daily storage
Unsolicited call from a linked clinic offering treatment
innocent: Some tow operators genuinely help clear dangerous highway scenes
questions: Ask her whether the tow driver showed her a rate sheet before towing
Ask the officer at the scene whether a tow was requested
steps: Move the car to the insurer's preferred shop and pay a reasonable tow and storage charge only
Report the operator under the provincial towing rules
Tell her she has no obligation to the clinic and should not sign anything with it
Refer the linked businesses to the special investigations unit
assessment: The customer is the victim of a known pattern in the Greater Toronto Area. The insurer should protect her, pay only reasonable costs and use the provincial towing rules against the operator.
action: Recover the car, pay reasonable charges, report the operator and warn the customer about the clinic.
outcomes: Car released after reasonable charges paid; operator reported
Linked network investigated by the provincial regulator

title: An attempted theft in a Montréal driveway
type: Attempted theft of a high-theft model
story: Thieves broke a rear window of policyholder's Toyota Highlander in his driveway in Laval, near Montréal, at about 03:00 and tried to program a new key through the diagnostic port. A steering wheel lock and an alarm stopped them. They fled. The car was not taken.
statement: The alarm woke us up and I saw two guys run to a car on the street. The back window was smashed and there were wires hanging under the dashboard. Thank God for the steering lock, the insurance told me to get one when I bought the policy. The police came and took photos.

accounts.text: Attempted theft of a motor vehicle. Rear quarter glass broken, dashboard panel removed near the diagnostic port, steering wheel lock still in place. Similar attempts on Toyota and Lexus models reported in the area this month.
Rear quarter glass, lower dashboard panel, diagnostic port wiring repair, security relearn of keys. Estimate $2,850.

whatHappened: Thieves tried to program a key through the diagnostic port; the steering lock and the alarm stopped them before they could drive away.
damage: Glass, dashboard panel and wiring, $2,850.
missing: A record of the anti-theft devices on the car, for the policy file
innocent: Thieves giving up on a car they cannot start is exactly what a steering lock is meant to achieve
questions: Ask whether he would like advice on a tracking device, which some insurers require for this model
steps: Settle under comprehensive less the deductible
Note the steering lock on the file as a protection in place
assessment: Genuine. The protections the insurer recommended worked, which is worth telling the customer.
action: Pay the repair.
outcomes: Paid $2,850 less the deductible

title: The damage was too high, until we saw the lifted truck
type: Damage height mismatch with an innocent explanation
story: Policyholder's Volkswagen Jetta was rear-ended at a red light in Calgary. The appraiser flagged that the damage on the Jetta's trunk lid sits 20 cm above the height of a normal pickup bumper. The other driver's pickup has been repaired already.
statement: A big black pickup with huge tires hit me at the light. It came right over my bumper and into the trunk. The driver was really apologetic. I have photos of his truck at the scene.

accounts.text: Jetta damage centred on the trunk lid and rear window, 78 to 96 cm from the ground; rear bumper only lightly marked. A standard pickup bumper sits at about 55 to 70 cm. Damage height inconsistent with a standard pickup. Recommend verification of the other vehicle.

accounts.who: Policyholder's scene photos of the pickup
accounts.text: Photos show a Ram 2500 with a 6-inch suspension lift, oversized off-road tires and an aftermarket steel front bumper. The bumper face has fresh paint transfer matching the Jetta's silver colour. Plate and driver's licence photographed.

whatHappened: A pickup with a six-inch lift rear-ended the car, so its raised bumper struck the trunk lid instead of the car's bumper.
damage: Trunk lid, rear window and rear panel, $6,700.
thirdParties: Driver of the lifted Ram 2500 and his insurer
evidence: Scene photos showing the lift kit and paint transfer
missing: The other insurer's confirmation of liability
inconsistencies: The damage height first looked inconsistent with a pickup; the photos show the pickup was lifted
innocent: Lifted trucks are common in Alberta and routinely override car bumpers
questions: Ask the other insurer whether it knew about the lift kit, which may affect their own customer's cover
steps: Clear the flag on the file with the photo evidence
Pay the repair and recover from the other insurer
assessment: Genuine. The height mismatch was a reasonable flag, and the photos explain it fully. This is how a red flag should be handled: checked, explained and cleared, not used to delay a genuine customer.
action: Clear the flag and settle.
outcomes: Paid and recovered in full from the other insurer

title: A Montréal lane change and the box she ticked
type: Fault decided from a joint accident report that contradicts her statement
story: Policyholder's Mazda 3 and a Kia Soul touched on Boulevard Décarie in Montréal in snow. Both drivers filled in a joint accident report at the scene. On it she ticked "was changing lanes". She now tells the insurer she never changed lanes. She also asks the insurer to pay for her physiotherapy.
statement: The other driver came into my lane. At the scene we were both stressed and cold, he helped me fill in the form and showed me where to tick. I think I ticked the wrong box. And my neck hurts, so I need the insurance to pay my physio.

accounts.text: Vehicle A (Mazda): box ticked "was changing lanes". Vehicle B (Kia): box ticked "was changing lanes". Sketch shows both vehicles moving towards the centre lane. Both drivers signed. No injuries recorded on the form.

whatHappened: Probably both cars drifted into the centre lane at the same time in snow. The report, signed by both, records that each was changing lanes, which under the inter-insurer fault grid usually means shared fault.
damage: Mazda: rear passenger door and quarter panel, $3,900. Neck strain reported a week later.
thirdParties: Driver of the Kia Soul and his insurer
evidence: Joint accident report signed by both drivers
missing: Any dashcam footage
Medical records for the neck strain
inconsistencies: She says she never changed lanes; the report she signed says she did, and the sketch shows both cars moving
innocent: The form is often filled in hurriedly at the roadside, and the other driver may have guided her pen
In snow, lane markings are often invisible
questions: Ask whether she has dashcam footage or a witness
Ask when the neck pain started and whether she has seen a doctor
steps: Apply the direct compensation agreement: her own insurer pays her car damage according to the fault grid
Explain that the signed report is strong evidence and that both cars changing lanes normally means 50% each
Direct her injury claim to the SAAQ, which covers bodily injury in Quebec regardless of fault
assessment: A genuine accident with a reporting problem. Her account conflicts with the report she signed, which will usually be followed unless she has other evidence. Her physiotherapy is not a matter for the private insurer; in Quebec bodily injury is compensated by the public insurer.
action: Settle her car on the fault grid and refer her injury to the SAAQ.
outcomes: Paid at 50% responsibility; deductible applied proportionately
Dashcam found; fault reassessed in her favour
SAAQ accepts the injury claim

title: Left in the driveway during a wildfire evacuation
type: Heat and ash damage to a car left behind in an evacuation
story: Policyholder evacuated from a town in northern Alberta during a wildfire, leaving his second vehicle, a Ford Escape, in the driveway. The house survived, but the neighbour's garage burned. The Escape has melted tail lights, blistered paint and ash in the engine bay and cabin vents. He also asks the insurer to pay his hotel bills during the evacuation.
statement: We had an hour's notice and only one driver, so the Escape stayed. When we got back after nine days the house was OK but the neighbour's garage was gone, and the Escape looked like it had been in an oven. The cabin smells of smoke. We spent $2,300 on hotels.

accounts.text: Radiant heat damage to the passenger side: melted tail lights and mirror housing, blistered paint on three panels, warped trim. Ash and soot in the engine air filter and cabin HVAC system. Smoke odour in the interior. Repair estimate $8,900 including HVAC cleaning and odour treatment. Vehicle repairable.

whatHappened: Radiant heat from the neighbour's burning garage blistered one side of the car and ash entered the engine bay and vents.
damage: Heat, ash and smoke damage, $8,900. Evacuation hotel costs $2,300.
missing: Hotel receipts, for his home insurance claim
innocent: Heat damage without the car itself burning is typical of radiant heat from a fire a few metres away
questions: Ask whether he has made a claim under his home insurance for additional living expenses
steps: Pay the vehicle repair under comprehensive (fire) less the deductible
Explain that evacuation hotel costs belong to his home insurance, not the auto policy
assessment: Genuine. The vehicle damage is a comprehensive loss. The hotel costs are real but belong under the home policy's additional living expenses, so the right help is to point him there.
action: Pay the repair and redirect the hotel costs to his home insurer.
outcomes: Repaired; home insurer pays the evacuation costs

title: All-season tires in December, in Quebec
type: Single-vehicle crash without the required winter tires
story: Policyholder's Honda Accord slid into a ditch on Route 117 near Mont-Tremblant, Quebec, on 10 December in snow. The car was on all-season tires. Quebec law requires winter tires on passenger vehicles from 1 December to 15 March. The police issued a fine.
statement: I had an appointment to change the tires on the 15th, the garages were all booked. The road was fine and then there was a patch of snow on the curve and the car just kept going. Nobody was hurt. Will the insurance still pay?

accounts.text: Single vehicle left the roadway on a curve and entered the ditch. Snow-covered surface. Vehicle equipped with all-season tires; statement of offence issued for failing to fit winter tires during the mandatory period. No injuries. Vehicle towed.
Appointment for winter tire installation booked on 18 November for 15 December, first available date.

whatHappened: He slid off the road on snow on tires that were not legal for the season, five days before his booked tire change.
damage: Front bumper, radiator, suspension and wheel, $7,300.
missing: Any policy condition on winter tires, which standard policies usually do not have
innocent: Garages are genuinely overbooked in late November and he had booked in advance
questions: Check the policy for any condition on winter tires
steps: Pay under collision less the deductible unless the policy has a specific winter tire condition
Record the claim as at fault
assessment: Genuine negligence. Driving without winter tires breaks the law and contributed to the crash, but it does not by itself remove collision coverage under a standard policy. The fine and the at-fault record are the consequences.
action: Pay under collision and record the claim as at fault.
outcomes: Paid less the deductible; premium rises at renewal

title: Details swapped on a Brampton street, and no report to the collision centre
type: Collision not reported to police or a collision reporting centre
story: Policyholder and another driver collided at a residential intersection in Brampton, Ontario, on an icy evening. They exchanged names and phone numbers and drove away. Neither reported the collision to the police or a collision reporting centre, although the combined damage is clearly over $2,000. Three weeks later he made a claim. The other driver now says the policyholder slid into her and that she will claim against him.
statement: We were both shaken and it was getting dark, so we took photos of each other's licences and left. I didn't know we had to go to the reporting centre. She was the one who slid through the stop sign, I was already in the intersection. Now she's changing her story.

accounts.text: Six photos time-stamped at the scene: both cars at the intersection, the other car's front bumper against the policyholder's rear passenger door, the other driver's licence, and the stop sign on her side of the intersection.
He came through the intersection too fast for the ice and slid into the front of my car. I had stopped at my sign. I will be making a claim.

whatHappened: A genuine collision that should have been reported within 24 hours. The photos are the strongest evidence of where each car was.
damage: His Civic: rear passenger door and quarter panel, $4,100. Her car: front bumper and headlamp, about $2,300.
thirdParties: The other driver and her insurer
evidence: Other driver's statement through her insurer
missing: A collision report
Any doorbell or dashcam footage from nearby houses
inconsistencies: Each driver says the other slid into them
innocent: Many drivers do not know that a collision with over $2,000 of damage must be reported
questions: Ask both drivers to report the collision now at a collision reporting centre
Ask neighbours on the intersection for doorbell footage
steps: Ask him to report the collision now; late reporting is a legal issue, not a bar to his claim
Use the photo of the impact point: her bumper against his rear door is consistent with her car striking his side, which supports his account
Apply Ontario’s Fault Determination Rules to the positions and the stop sign, and handle his damage under the coverages on his policy
Respond to her claim through her insurer using the same evidence
assessment: Genuine collision, not reported as required. The photos support his account; the reporting failure weakens the evidence but does not defeat the claim.
action: Have the collision reported now, decide fault on the photos and the rules, and handle both claims.
outcomes: Fault assigned to the other driver under the rules; claim paid
Doorbell footage confirms she rolled through the stop sign

title: A two-year-old leased SUV, valued as if it were used
type: Total loss settlement ignoring an endorsement that removes depreciation
story: Policyholder's leased SUV was written off in a three-car collision on Highway 7 in Vaughan, 20 months after she leased it new. Her policy includes the Ontario endorsement that removes the depreciation deduction for a vehicle leased new, for a set period after delivery. The adjuster offered the actual cash value of $41,000. The vehicle's original price was $52,400, and the leasing company is the loss payee.
statement: I paid extra for the no-depreciation endorsement because I knew a new car loses value fast. The broker said if it was written off in the first two years I'd get the full price. Now I'm offered $41,000 and the leasing company says I still owe them more than that.

accounts.text: Endorsement: removing depreciation deduction, leased vehicle. Vehicle leased new 20 months before the loss. Lessor shown as loss payee.
Actual cash value from comparable listings: $41,000, less deductible. Endorsement not referred to.

whatHappened: A genuine total loss within the endorsement period. The offer applied ordinary actual cash value and ignored the endorsement she paid for.
damage: SUV total loss.
thirdParties: The leasing company (lessor and loss payee)
missing: The lessor's payout statement
inconsistencies: The policy carries the endorsement; the offer ignores it
innocent: The total loss system may not pick up endorsements automatically
questions: Ask the leasing company for its payout figure
steps: Settle under the endorsement terms instead of actual cash value, since the loss is within the endorsement period
Pay the lessor as loss payee first, then any balance to her
Explain the calculation in writing and apologize for the first offer
Check other recent total losses for the same omission
assessment: Genuine and covered on better terms than offered. The endorsement she paid for applies.
action: Re-settle under the removing depreciation endorsement and pay the lessor and her accordingly.
outcomes: Re-settled at the original price; lessor paid and balance to her
Review finds four other files with the same error

title: Hit by a red-light runner in Kelowna, and told she cannot sue him
type: Injury claim under British Columbia’s no-fault Enhanced Care model
story: Policyholder was injured in Kelowna, British Columbia, when another driver ran a red light and hit her car. She has a fractured collarbone and cannot work as a dental hygienist for at least ten weeks. A friend in Alberta told her to hire a lawyer and sue the other driver for pain and suffering. She has asked her insurer why the claim is being handled through accident benefits only.
statement: He ran the red light, there's a witness and the police ticketed him. Why should I just get benefits? My friend in Calgary got a big settlement for less than this. I want him to pay for what he did to me.

accounts.text: Vehicle 2 entered the intersection against a red light and struck vehicle 1. Driver of vehicle 2 issued a violation ticket. Independent witness statement attached.

Accident occurred after May 2021: Enhanced Care benefits apply. Medical and rehabilitation benefits, income replacement at 90% of net income up to the statutory maximum, and a permanent impairment benefit if applicable.

whatHappened: A genuine not-at-fault injury in British Columbia, where the Enhanced Care model replaced most lawsuits for injuries with care-based benefits.
damage: Fractured collarbone, ten weeks off work. Car: front-left damage.
missing: Her pay records for the income replacement calculation
innocent: Rules differ sharply between provinces, and advice from Alberta does not apply in BC
questions: Ask for her pay records and her physiotherapy plan
steps: Explain that in BC, for accidents since May 2021, the right to sue an at-fault driver for injuries has been removed in most cases and replaced by care-based benefits
Pay her benefits promptly: treatment, income replacement and any impairment benefit
Tell her how to request a review if she disagrees with a benefit decision
Record the other driver as at fault for her vehicle damage and premium purposes
assessment: Genuine and covered under Enhanced Care benefits. Her wish to sue is understandable but generally not available in BC.
action: Explain the model clearly, pay all benefits she is entitled to, and set out the review route.
outcomes: Benefits paid; she returns to work after 11 weeks
Review request on income replacement partly upheld

title: Changing lanes on the Queensway, rated 100% at fault
type: Customer dispute about a fault determination, escalated through the complaint process
story: Policyholder was changing lanes on the Queensway in Ottawa when a car in the next lane hit his rear quarter. Under Ontario's Fault Determination Rules for a lane change, he has been rated 100% at fault, which will affect his premium. He says the other driver sped up to close the gap. He complained to the insurer, was unhappy with the reply, and asked how to take it further.
statement: I signalled for five seconds, there was a big gap. He saw me and floored it to stop me getting in. The dashcam shows him speeding up. How can a rule say I'm 100% at fault when he did it on purpose?

accounts.text: Indicator on for about five seconds before the lane change. The following car's headlights grow quickly in the frame in the last two seconds, consistent with it accelerating. Contact at the rear quarter as the lane change completes.

Fault has been determined under Ontario Regulation 668, the Fault Determination Rules. A vehicle changing lanes that collides with a vehicle in the other lane is 100% at fault. We cannot change this determination.

whatHappened: A lane-change collision where the other driver probably accelerated to block him. The Fault Determination Rules still put the lane-changing driver at fault for rating and direct compensation purposes.
damage: His Camry: rear quarter and bumper, $3,300. Other car: front corner.
thirdParties: The other driver and their insurer
missing: Any witness who saw the other car accelerate
inconsistencies: He says the other driver accelerated deliberately; the rules take no account of that
innocent: Customers reasonably expect fault to reflect what actually happened
questions: Ask whether he wants to report the other driver’s conduct to the police
steps: Explain clearly and without jargon that the Fault Determination Rules apply as written for rating and his own damage, whatever the other driver’s conduct
Note that the rules do not decide fault in a lawsuit, and that dangerous driving can be reported to the police
Escalate his complaint to the insurer’s internal ombudsman if he remains unhappy, and then explain his right to go to the General Insurance OmbudService and the regulator
Keep the dashcam on file in case it becomes relevant to any injury claim
assessment: Genuinely disputed in fairness, but the rule is applied correctly. Good handling means a clear explanation and an open path for his complaint.
action: Maintain the rule-based determination, explain it plainly, and guide him through the escalation route.
outcomes: Complaint closed after the internal ombudsman explains the rules
General Insurance OmbudService finds the rules were applied correctly

title: Bought on Marketplace, insured for four months, stolen all along
type: Collision claim reveals the insured vehicle is a re-VINned stolen car
story: Policyholder bought a two-year-old Toyota Highlander through an online marketplace in Laval, Quebec, for $38,000 in cash, and insured it. Four months later he rear-ended a car on an icy road and claimed for both. The appraiser noticed the public VIN plate had been re-riveted. A check of the hidden secondary VIN shows the vehicle was stolen in Mississauga, Ontario, five months before he bought it. The VIN on his paperwork belongs to a Highlander that was written off in Alberta.
statement: The seller met me at a mall, showed me the registration and a clean history report for the VIN. I paid cash because he said the bank transfer would take days. I had no idea. I've lost $38,000 and now you're telling me the car isn't even mine.

accounts.text: Public VIN plate shows non-factory rivets. Secondary VIN read from a concealed location does not match. Secondary VIN reported stolen in Ontario five months before the purchase. Public VIN belongs to a vehicle recorded as a total loss in Alberta.
Handwritten bill of sale, $38,000 cash. Copy of a registration in the seller's name bearing the cloned VIN. Vehicle history report for the cloned VIN, showing no accidents.

whatHappened: He is the victim of a re-VINning scheme: he bought a stolen vehicle disguised with the identity of a written-off car.
damage: Highlander: front end, $7,800. Other car: rear bumper and trunk, $4,200.
thirdParties: The original owner and their insurer
missing: The seller’s real identity
The original owner’s insurer and whether it paid a theft claim
inconsistencies: The paperwork VIN belongs to a written-off vehicle; the hidden VIN belongs to a stolen one
indicators: Re-riveted VIN plate
Cash sale in a mall car park
History report run on the cloned VIN
innocent: Clean history reports on a cloned VIN fool many buyers
questions: Ask for any messages with the seller and the listing
Identify the original owner’s insurer
steps: Treat the policyholder as a fraud victim and help him report to the police
Notify the police and the original owner’s insurer; the vehicle belongs to the original owner or to the insurer that paid its theft claim
Get advice on the third party’s claim: he was insured as the driver of that vehicle, and the person he hit should not be left without a remedy
Decline the own-damage claim, since he has no ownership interest in the stolen vehicle, and refund the premium for the vehicle cover
assessment: The policyholder is genuine and a victim; the vehicle is stolen. Ownership, not his honesty, decides the own-damage claim.
action: Report the stolen vehicle, deal fairly with the third party, decline own damage and refund the premium.
outcomes: Vehicle returned to the original owner’s insurer; third party paid; premium refunded
Police link the seller to a ring that re-VINned 40 vehicles

title: A kangaroo at dusk near Dubbo
type: Animal strike on a country road
story: Policyholder's Toyota Prado hit an eastern grey kangaroo on the Mitchell Highway near Dubbo, New South Wales, at about 18:40. The bull bar took most of the impact, but the radiator, a headlight and the bonnet are damaged. She called a wildlife rescue group, which collected a joey from the kangaroo's pouch.
statement: There was a mob of roos on the side and one bolted straight across. I braked but didn't swerve, like you're told. The bull bar did its job, but steam was coming from under the bonnet. The wildlife people came out for the little one, which was the saddest part.

accounts.text: Callout 18:52, Mitchell Highway, adult female eastern grey kangaroo deceased after vehicle strike. Pouch young retrieved alive and taken into care. Caller was the driver of a Toyota Prado.
Bull bar bent at the right upright, radiator and condenser punctured, right headlight broken, bonnet creased. Fur on the bull bar. Quote $6,850 including bull bar straightening.

whatHappened: A kangaroo bolted across the highway at dusk and she braked without swerving, which kept the damage to the front of the car.
damage: Bull bar, radiator, condenser, headlight and bonnet, $6,850.
evidence: Repairer quote with fur on the bull bar
missing: Confirmation that the bull bar is listed on the policy
innocent: A kangaroo strike at dusk on a country highway is common and well documented by the wildlife rescue record
questions: Ask whether the bull bar is listed on the policy as an accessory
steps: Pay under comprehensive less the excess
Include the bull bar if it is listed or covered as standard
assessment: Genuine. Braking without swerving is the safer response and limited the damage.
action: Pay the repair.
outcomes: Paid $6,850 less the excess

title: Hail in western Sydney, while Mum said it was at home
type: Hail claim with the wrong location given
story: Policyholder reported that her Mazda CX-3 was damaged by hail while parked at her home in Coogee, Sydney. Bureau of Meteorology radar shows no hail in Coogee that afternoon but a severe hail cell over Penrith. She then said her son, 22, who is not listed on the policy, had borrowed the car for the week.
statement: First call: The hail came down and the car was in the driveway. Later: I'm sorry, I panicked. Nick had the car at his place in Penrith all week while his was being fixed. I thought you'd refuse because he's young and not on the policy. The car was parked when the hail hit.

accounts.text: Severe thunderstorm with hail up to 4 cm recorded over Penrith and St Marys between 15:20 and 15:50. No hail recorded in the eastern suburbs. Light rain only in Coogee.
Approximately 180 hail dents on the roof, bonnet and boot. Damage consistent with large hail. No impact or driving-related damage. Repair by paintless dent removal $5,400.

whatHappened: The hail damage is real and happened at her son's home in Penrith while the car was parked. She gave the wrong location because she feared his age and not being listed would void the claim.
damage: Hail damage, $5,400 by paintless dent removal.
missing: Photos from the son's home, if any
inconsistencies: She first said the car was in her Coogee driveway; there was no hail in Coogee, and she later said it was in Penrith
indicators: Initial false location
innocent: She feared a rule that did not apply: an age excess normally applies only when a young driver is driving at the time of the loss
questions: Ask how often her son drives the car, as it may need adding to the policy
steps: Pay the hail damage less the standard excess: the misstatement made no difference to the cover
Record the corrected account and remind her of the duty to answer honestly
Offer to add the son as a listed driver if he uses the car regularly
assessment: Genuine loss with a misstatement that did not matter to the cover: the car was parked, so no driver-related excess applies. Under the insurer's duty of utmost good faith, the fair outcome is to pay and explain, not to treat a panicked correction as fraud.
action: Pay the claim and update the policy if the son is a regular driver.
outcomes: Paid $5,400 less the excess; son added to the policy

title: Burnt at the holiday house in East Gippsland
type: Bushfire total loss on an agreed value policy
story: Policyholder's Subaru Forester, kept at his holiday house near Mallacoota in East Gippsland, Victoria, was destroyed in a bushfire while he was at home in Melbourne. Roads were closed for a week and he could not reach the property. His policy is on an agreed value of $24,000; the market value is about $19,500.
statement: We leave the old Forester at the shack for when we drive up. When the fires came through, we watched the maps from Melbourne. A neighbour sent a photo of the shack and the car, both gone. We couldn't get there for eight days because of the road closures.

accounts.text: Property at the address within the fire perimeter on the date. House destroyed. One vehicle destroyed on the property. Road closures in place for 8 days.

whatHappened: The bushfire burned through the property while he was in Melbourne and the roads were closed, destroying the house and the car together.
damage: Total loss. Agreed value $24,000.
evidence: Policy schedule showing the agreed value
missing: Confirmation of any finance on the car
innocent: The eight-day delay in reaching the car is explained by the road closures
questions: Ask whether there is any finance on the car
steps: Settle at the agreed value of $24,000 less the excess
Arrange removal of the wreck when the area reopens
assessment: Genuine. On an agreed value policy the settlement is the agreed amount, not the lower market value, which is the point of agreed value cover.
action: Pay the agreed value promptly.
outcomes: Paid $24,000 less the excess

title: Past the "road closed" sign into a flooded causeway
type: Vehicle swept off a flooded crossing
story: Policyholder drove his Mitsubishi Pajero Sport past a "road closed" sign onto a flooded causeway near Gympie, Queensland. The water pushed the car off the crossing into the creek. The State Emergency Service rescued him from the roof. The car is a total loss. Police issued an infringement for driving past the closure.
statement: I've driven that causeway a hundred times. The water didn't look deep, maybe 30 centimetres. Halfway across, it was much faster than I thought and the back end lifted. I climbed out the window onto the roof. I know, "if it's flooded, forget it". I was stupid.

accounts.text: Swift water rescue, 17:45. One adult male on the roof of a vehicle in the creek downstream of the causeway. Rescued by boat, no injuries. Road closed signs in place on both approaches since 13:00.

Flood is a covered event. Exclusion: we will not pay for loss or damage if you deliberately drive into floodwater, or drive past a road closure or barrier, where a reasonable person would have known it was unsafe.

whatHappened: He deliberately drove past a road closure into fast floodwater, against clear warnings.
damage: Pajero Sport total loss, market value about $34,000.
missing: Proof that the exclusion was in the product disclosure statement he received
innocent: Locals often underestimate familiar crossings
questions: Confirm the exclusion appears in the product disclosure statement he received
steps: Apply the exclusion and decline with a clear explanation
Tell him about his right to internal dispute resolution and the Australian Financial Complaints Authority
assessment: Genuine negligence that the policy specifically excludes. Flood itself is covered, but driving past a closure into floodwater is not. A clear, respectful decline is appropriate.
action: Decline under the exclusion and explain the complaint options.
outcomes: Declined; customer accepts
Complaint to AFCA; decline upheld given the signage and his admission

title: A "dog on the road", and a burnout video online
type: Deliberate burnout damage claimed as an accident
story: Policyholder claimed that his Holden Commodore SS hit a power pole in an industrial area of Western Sydney after he swerved to avoid a dog at about 23:00. A video posted on social media that night shows the same car doing burnouts at the location and sliding into the pole.
statement: A dog ran out and I swerved and lost the back end on the wet road. I hit the pole. I wasn't doing anything stupid.

accounts.text: Caption: "RIP the SS". The video shows the Commodore, same plate and wheels, doing donuts and burnouts in front of a crowd at an industrial estate, then sliding sideways into a power pole. Smoke from the tyres. No dog visible. Dry road surface.
Left side impact with a pole. Rear tyres worn to the cords with fresh heat marks. Clutch and differential overheated. Damage consistent with a sideways slide during a burnout.

whatHappened: He was doing burnouts at a street meet and slid into the pole. The dog story was invented to make it an insured accident.
damage: Left side, suspension, clutch and differential; total loss, value about $28,000. Power pole damaged.
thirdParties: The electricity network operator, owner of the pole
evidence: Assessor report on the tyres and drivetrain
missing: His response to the video, which should be obtained before the decision
inconsistencies: He says he swerved for a dog on a wet road; the video shows burnouts on a dry road and no dog
indicators: Account contradicted by video
Deliberate dangerous driving presented as an accident
innocent: None that fits the video
questions: Give him the chance to respond to the video before the decision
steps: Decline the claim for fraud and the deliberate and reckless conduct
Consider cancelling the policy
Deal with the network operator's pole claim under the third-party section as the law requires, and recover from him
assessment: Confirmed fraud. The video contradicts the account completely, and burnouts are deliberate reckless conduct excluded by the policy anyway.
action: Decline, cancel and recover any third-party outlay.
outcomes: Claim declined and policy cancelled
Police charge him with hoon driving offences

title: A toolbox slides off the ute onto the bonnet
type: Loading accident to a work vehicle
story: Policyholder, an electrician in Brisbane, was loading a steel toolbox onto the roof rack of his Ford Ranger when it slipped and fell onto the bonnet and windscreen. The ute is insured for business use.
statement: I was lifting it up onto the rack by myself, which I shouldn't do, it's about 40 kilos. The ratchet strap slipped off the corner and it came down on the bonnet and cracked the windscreen. Nobody else around, just me swearing at myself. A couple of my meters inside the box got smashed too. I need the ute back fast, I've got jobs booked all week.

accounts.text: Bonnet dented and creased, windscreen cracked from the top edge, cowl panel broken. Windscreen replacement includes forward camera recalibration for lane keeping and emergency braking. Quote $3,950. Two days in the workshop.

Use: business use, ute. Cover: comprehensive. Standard excess $800; windscreen-only excess option not taken. Tools of trade: not covered under this policy; available under a separate business insurance policy. Hire car after an at-fault incident: not included.

whatHappened: A 40 kg toolbox slipped off the roof rack while he was loading it alone and landed on the bonnet and windscreen.
damage: Bonnet, windscreen and cowl, $3,950 including camera recalibration.
missing: Photos of the toolbox and strap, which would support the account but are not essential
innocent: Damage in a driveway rather than on the road is still accidental damage, and nothing in the account is unusual
questions: Ask whether he has separate business insurance that covers his tools
Ask whether he can do without the ute for two days or needs a repairer with a loan vehicle
steps: Pay under comprehensive (accidental damage) less the $800 excess
Arrange camera recalibration with the windscreen, as the safety systems depend on it
Explain that the broken meters fall under tools of trade cover, not the motor policy
Suggest a repairer that can fit the job in quickly or offer a loan vehicle
assessment: Genuine accidental damage, covered under comprehensive whether it happens on the road or in the driveway. The only things to explain are the excess and the fact that his tools need a separate business policy.
action: Pay the repair less the excess and point him to his business insurer for the tools.
outcomes: Paid $3,950 less the $800 excess; tools claimed under his business policy
He decides to pay for the windscreen himself and claim only the bonnet

title: Caravan sway on the Hume in a crosswind
type: Rollover while towing an overloaded caravan
story: Policyholder's Ford Everest and the caravan it was towing rolled on the Hume Highway near Gundagai, New South Wales, in strong crosswinds. A weighbridge check by the caravan insurer's assessor suggests the caravan was about 350 kg over its rated maximum and the towbar's limit. The car and the caravan are insured with different insurers.
statement: The wind was really gusty and a truck passed us, then the van started swaying and I couldn't pull it back. We ended up on our side in the grass. We'd packed for three months on the road, water tanks full, so it was heavy, but I thought it was within limits.

accounts.text: Caravan aggregate trailer mass rated at 2,800 kg. Weighed after recovery, with contents and water: about 3,150 kg. Towbar and vehicle towing capacity 3,100 kg. Ball weight estimated low, which increases sway risk. Weather station recorded gusts of 75 km/h at the time.

We will not pay for loss or damage when your car is being used in an unsafe or unroadworthy condition that caused or contributed to the loss, including towing a load beyond the manufacturer's specifications.

whatHappened: An overloaded caravan with low ball weight began to sway in gusty wind after a truck passed, and the combination rolled.
damage: Everest: total loss, about $52,000. Caravan: total loss, insured separately.
missing: Independent confirmation of the weighbridge method after the rollover
Whether contents shifted or water entered during the rollover, adding weight
inconsistencies: He thought the load was within limits; the assessor found it over both the caravan rating and the towing capacity
innocent: Many caravanners underestimate the weight of water and supplies
Strong gusts and a passing truck can cause sway even in a well-loaded rig
questions: Ask whether he had the rig weighed before the trip
Ask how much water was in the tanks
steps: Verify the weight independently, allowing for anything gained during the rollover
Assess whether the overload caused or contributed to the loss, as the exclusion requires
Coordinate with the caravan insurer on a shared position
assessment: Genuine accident with possible negligence. The exclusion applies only if the overload contributed, which is likely given low ball weight and excess mass, but the wind was also severe. The weight evidence must be robust before relying on it.
action: Verify the weights, then decide on causation; consider a partial settlement if the evidence is mixed.
outcomes: Exclusion applied after independent weighing; claim declined
Causation unclear; insurers settle 50% of each claim

title: Water in the diesel from a country servo
type: Fuel system damage from contaminated fuel
story: Policyholder's Isuzu D-Max broke down 80 km after he filled up at a service station in the Wheatbelt, Western Australia. The fuel was contaminated with water. Five other vehicles that filled up at the same servo that morning broke down too. The fuel injectors and high-pressure pump are damaged.
statement: It started stuttering and then just died on the highway. The mechanic drained the tank and it was half water. The servo owner told me their underground tank had flooded in the storm on the weekend. He said to claim on my insurance.

accounts.text: Fuel sample: about 40% water with sediment. Injectors and high-pressure fuel pump corroded and scored. Repair: fuel system flush, four injectors, high-pressure pump, filters. Quote $7,600. Damage consistent with water-contaminated diesel.
Sorry about this. Our tank had water get in after the storm and we didn't test it before opening. We've stopped selling diesel. Six customers affected. Our insurer has been told.

whatHappened: Storm water got into the service station's underground tank and the contaminated diesel damaged the fuel systems of every vehicle filled that morning.
damage: Fuel system repairs, $7,600.
thirdParties: The service station and its liability insurer
missing: The service station's liability insurer details
innocent: Six vehicles failing after filling at the same servo shows the fuel, not the vehicles, was the problem
questions: Ask for the fuel receipt
Ask the servo for its liability insurer
steps: Check whether the policy covers contaminated fuel or excludes mechanical failure
If covered, pay and recover from the service station under its liability and the consumer guarantees in the Australian Consumer Law
If not covered, help him claim directly against the service station
assessment: Genuine, with a clearly liable third party. Whether the insurer pays first depends on its wording, but either way the service station, which admitted the problem, should ultimately bear the cost.
action: Pay and recover if covered; otherwise support a direct claim against the servo.
outcomes: Paid and recovered from the servo's liability insurer
Servo's insurer pays all six motorists directly

title: The other driver gave a name, a number, and a car he no longer owned
type: Claim under an uninsured motorist extension with an unverified at-fault driver
story: Policyholder has a third party property policy with an uninsured motorist extension, which pays up to $5,000 for her car's damage if an identified, uninsured driver is at fault. Her car was rear-ended at lights in Brisbane in heavy rain. The other driver gave a name and mobile number, which no longer answers. The plate she photographed is registered to a woman who says she sold the car two months ago and the buyer never transferred the registration.
statement: He was really apologetic, he said he had no insurance and would pay me himself. I took a photo of his plate and his car. Now his number's dead. The repair quote is $6,800. I only have third party cover because I can't afford comprehensive.

accounts.text: I sold that car on an online marketplace two months ago for cash. I filled in my half of the transfer form and gave the buyer the rest. He obviously never lodged it. I have a screenshot of our messages and his first name.

Uninsured motorist extension: we pay up to $5,000 for damage to your car if the other driver was at fault, did not have insurance, and you can give us their name and address or the vehicle's registration details.

whatHappened: A genuine rear-end collision by an uninsured driver. The extension may apply, but the at-fault driver's identity is not yet established.
damage: Her Mazda 3: rear bumper, boot and tail lamps, quote $6,800.
thirdParties: The registered operator who sold the car
evidence: Photo of the other car and its plate
Registered operator's statement and sale messages
missing: The buyer’s full name and address
A police report
innocent: Unlodged registration transfers after private sales are common
questions: Ask the registered operator for the buyer’s messages and payment details
Ask the policyholder to report the collision to the police
steps: Check the wording: the extension can be met with the vehicle’s registration details and evidence the driver was at fault and uninsured
Help identify the buyer through the sale messages and a police report
If the conditions are met, pay up to the $5,000 limit; explain that the rest can only be pursued against the driver
Keep her informed while the identification is attempted
assessment: Insufficient evidence for now, with a genuine policyholder. The registration and photo may be enough under the wording; identifying the buyer would settle it.
action: Pursue the buyer's identity, assess the extension on the registration evidence, and pay up to the limit if met.
outcomes: Buyer identified through the sale messages; $5,000 paid and recovery pursued
Paid on the registration evidence alone under the wording

title: Lodged in February, still undecided in June
type: Claim handled outside the General Insurance Code of Practice timeframes
story: Policyholder lodged a comprehensive claim on 3 February after his parked car was hit in a shopping centre car park in Adelaide. An assessor was appointed but he was not told for three weeks. He received no updates for nine weeks. He complained on 1 June and has had no response. On 20 June, more than four months after lodgement, there is no decision and no exceptional circumstances are recorded.
statement: It's a straightforward scrape, the centre's CCTV shows the other car. I've rung every fortnight and I'm told it's with the assessor. I complained in writing three weeks ago and heard nothing. I've been driving around with a door held shut with tape.

accounts.text: 3 Feb: claim lodged. 10 Feb: assessor appointed; customer told 3 Mar. Assessor report received 28 Mar. No customer update between 3 Mar and 5 May. 1 Jun: written complaint received, not acknowledged. 20 Jun: no decision. Exceptional circumstances: none recorded.
Footage supplied 14 Feb showing a white ute reversing into the policyholder's car and leaving. Plate partly legible.

whatHappened: A straightforward claim left without a decision, updates or a complaint response, in breach of the Code's timeframes.
damage: His Corolla: driver's door and rear door dented; door does not close; quote $3,400.
missing: The reason no decision was made after the assessor’s report
innocent: Assessor backlogs after storms delay many claims, but the Code still applies
questions: Check whether the ute driver can be identified from the partial plate for recovery
steps: Decide the claim now: all the information has been on file since late March
Record the Code breaches: late notice of the assessor, no updates at least every 20 business days, no decision within 10 business days of having the information or within 4 months
Respond to the complaint in writing within the Code’s complaint timeframe, and tell him he can take it to AFCA if unhappy
Consider compensation for the delay and fix the update process
assessment: Genuine and overdue. The insurer has breached several Code timeframes and should decide, apologize and explain the AFCA route.
action: Approve the claim now, respond to the complaint with the AFCA option, and address the delay.
outcomes: Claim approved the same week; complaint closed with a goodwill payment
AFCA complaint finds the delays unreasonable

title: Her ex-partner smashed the car, and he is still on the policy
type: Deliberate damage by a co-insured ex-partner in a family violence situation
story: Policyholder holds a comprehensive policy on which her former partner is still listed as a named driver and joint policyholder. After they separated, he smashed the windscreen and lights and scratched the panels of the car outside her home in Geelong. Police attended and a family violence intervention order is now in place. She has claimed for the damage. The claims team has flagged the policy's exclusion for damage caused intentionally by "you or anyone acting with your consent".
statement: I just need the car fixed so I can get the kids to school. I didn't know he was still on the policy, we set it up together years ago. Please don't contact him about this. He doesn't know where I'm staying some nights.

accounts.text: Attended a family violence incident. Respondent damaged the protected person's vehicle with a steering lock: windscreen, headlights and both doors damaged. Intervention order applied for and granted. Respondent charged with criminal damage.

Joint policyholders: Sarah Mitchell and Jason Mitchell. Premiums paid from her account for the last two years. Exclusion: loss or damage caused intentionally by you or a person acting with your express or implied consent.

whatHappened: The damage was deliberate family violence by her former partner. She did not cause or consent to it.
damage: Kia Cerato: windscreen, headlights, scratched doors and panels; quote $5,900.
thirdParties: Jason Mitchell, the former partner and respondent
missing: Her preferred safe contact method
innocent: Joint policies set up during a relationship are often never updated after separation
questions: Ask her how and when it is safe to contact her
steps: Apply the insurer’s family violence policy under the Code: do not apply the intentional damage exclusion against a victim who did not cause or consent to the damage
Pay her claim without contacting the former partner or disclosing her details or location to him
Remove him from the policy at her request and update her contact details securely
Offer support referrals, flexible payment of any excess, and a single contact who knows her situation
assessment: Genuine, and a customer experiencing family violence. The exclusion should not be used against the victim; safety and discretion come first.
action: Pay the claim, keep her details from the perpetrator, and remove him from the policy.
outcomes: Claim paid in a week; former partner removed from the policy
Insurer pursues recovery from him through the courts without involving her

title: A cash offer at the insurer’s rates, and a quote that includes old hail
type: Cash settlement dispute where the customer’s quote includes unrelated damage
story: Policyholder reversed into a concrete pole in a Perth car park, damaging his rear bumper and tailgate. He asked for a cash settlement. The insurer offered $4,200, based on its preferred repairer's rates. His own repairer quoted $7,900. That quote includes paintless dent repair across the roof and bonnet, and the assessor's photos show hail dents that match a storm two years ago, which he never claimed.
statement: My repairer is who I trust, and he says $4,200 won't cover it. Your repairers get discounts I can't get. I don't see why I should be out of pocket. The hail dents were always there, I just thought they'd do them while it was in.

accounts.text: Collision damage: rear bumper, tailgate, reversing sensor. Customer's quote includes $2,600 of roof and bonnet dent repair for hail damage not related to this incident. Insurer's offer uses preferred repairer labour rates about 20% below the customer's repairer.
Hailstorm over the policyholder's suburb two years before this claim. No hail claim lodged on this policy.

whatHappened: A genuine collision. The customer's quote adds unrelated hail damage, while the insurer's offer uses discounted rates he cannot get.
damage: Rear bumper, tailgate and reversing sensor. Separate old hail dents on the roof and bonnet.
missing: A breakdown of the insurer’s offer that the customer can check
inconsistencies: His quote presents hail repairs as part of this claim
indicators: Unrelated damage added to the repair quote
innocent: Customers often ask repairers to fix everything at once without thinking about what the claim covers
questions: Ask his repairer to requote for the collision damage only
steps: Remove the hail repairs from the quote: they are unrelated and were never claimed
Make a fair cash settlement for the collision damage that reflects what it would reasonably cost him, not only the insurer’s discounted rates, and explain how it was worked out
Give him the itemised breakdown and the option of a repair through the insurer instead of cash
Tell him he can lodge a separate hail claim if within the policy terms, or arrange that repair himself
assessment: Mixed. The hail damage should come out, but a cash offer at internal discount rates is not fair either.
action: Exclude the hail items, recalculate a fair cash figure, and explain it with an itemised breakdown.
outcomes: Cash settled at $5,050 after a collision-only requote
Customer chooses an insurer-arranged repair instead

title: "Free hail repair, no excess", from a pop-up in the car park
type: Hail claims lodged by a repair business that inflates and adds old damage
story: After a hailstorm in Melbourne's north, a repair business set up in a shopping centre car park offering "free hail repair, no excess". It lodged a claim on the policyholder's behalf under a signed authority, with an estimate of $11,400. The assessor found light hail dents on the roof, but the estimate also includes old door dings and a cracked bumper. Forty claims from the same business show near-identical estimates, and six of the cars are registered to addresses outside the hail zone.
statement: They said my insurance would cover it all and I wouldn't pay a cent. I signed their form on an iPad. I didn't know they'd put in the bumper, that crack's been there since my son reversed into the letterbox.

accounts.text: Light hail damage to the roof and bonnet consistent with the storm, fairly priced at about $3,200. Estimate also claims door dings with old paint wear and a cracked bumper with dirt in the crack. Dent repair rates in the estimate about double the local market.

Forty claims from the same business in two weeks. Estimate wording and line items near-identical. Six vehicles registered to suburbs outside the storm footprint. Excess "waived" by the business on every claim.

whatHappened: The policyholder has genuine light hail damage. The repair business inflated the estimate with old damage and inflated rates, and is doing so across many claims.
damage: Light hail dents to the roof and bonnet. Old door dings and a cracked bumper not caused by hail.
missing: Where the six out-of-area cars actually were during the storm
inconsistencies: The estimate attributes old door dings and a cracked bumper to hail
indicators: Excess waived as a sales offer
Near-identical estimates across forty claims
Cars outside the storm footprint
Rates double the market
innocent: Customers sign authorities quickly when promised a free repair
questions: Ask the policyholder whether she understood what the form allowed the business to do
Ask the six out-of-area owners where their cars were parked
steps: Pay the genuine hail damage at a fair rate, directly or through a repairer she chooses, and tell her what was excluded and why
Explain her excess remains payable under her policy; a waiver offered by the business does not change it
Refer the business’s claims as a group to the fraud team and review all forty
Report the conduct to the regulator if the investigation supports it
assessment: Potential fraud by the repairer, not the customer. Pay her genuine hail damage and investigate the business across all its claims.
action: Pay the fair hail cost, decline the old damage, and investigate the business's forty claims together.
outcomes: Business’s claims reduced across the portfolio; two referred to police
Customer chooses her own repairer for the hail work

title: A sandstorm pile-up on the Dubai to Al Ain road
type: Multi-vehicle collision in a sandstorm
story: Policyholder's Nissan Patrol was one of eleven vehicles in a chain collision on the Dubai to Al Ain road during a sandstorm at about 16:20, when visibility dropped below 50 metres. He stopped behind a slowing pickup and was hit from behind by a Toyota Land Cruiser, which pushed him into the pickup. The police report names the Land Cruiser driver as at fault for both impacts.
statement: The sand came like a wall. I put my hazards on and slowed down, then stopped when I saw brake lights. A few seconds later the Land Cruiser hit me hard from behind and I went into the pickup. Nobody in my car was hurt, alhamdulillah. The police came quickly and gave everyone a report.

accounts.text: Chain collision involving 11 vehicles in low visibility due to dust. Vehicle 4 (Nissan Patrol) stopped behind Vehicle 3. Vehicle 5 (Toyota Land Cruiser) failed to keep a safe distance and struck Vehicle 4, pushing it into Vehicle 3. Responsibility: driver of Vehicle 5 for the damage to Vehicles 3 and 4. Driver of Vehicle 4 not at fault.

whatHappened: He stopped safely in the dust and was pushed into the pickup ahead by a Land Cruiser that had not kept a safe distance, as the police found.
damage: Patrol: rear bumper, tailgate and rear chassis member; front bumper and grille. Estimate AED 38,500.
thirdParties: Driver of the Land Cruiser and his insurer
missing: The Land Cruiser insurer's acceptance of the claim
innocent: Pile-ups in sudden sandstorms are common, and the police report confirms the order of the impacts
questions: Ask whether he prefers to claim from the at-fault insurer or under his own comprehensive cover
steps: Claim against the Land Cruiser insurer using the police report, or pay under his comprehensive cover and recover
Confirm that the claim will not count against his no-claims record, as he is not at fault
assessment: Genuine. The police report settles fault, which makes recovery from the at-fault insurer straightforward.
action: Pay or direct the claim to the at-fault insurer, and protect his no-claims record.
outcomes: Repaired at the agency; cost recovered from the Land Cruiser's insurer

title: Flooded in April, broken since January
type: Flood claim on a car already off the road with engine failure
story: Policyholder claimed for flood damage to his Lexus IS, including a replacement engine, after record rainfall flooded a garage in Al Quoz, Dubai, in April. The garage's job card shows the car was brought in on 14 January with a seized engine and was waiting for parts when the flood hit.
statement: My car was at the garage when the floods came, the water inside was up to the seats. Everything is damaged now, the electrics, the interior, the engine. The garage says it's not their fault, it was the rain. I want the insurance to pay for all of it.

accounts.text: Received 14 January, towed in. Complaint: engine seized, no start. Diagnosis: engine bearing failure due to oil starvation. Customer approved engine replacement, parts on order from overseas. Vehicle stored in the rear workshop bay pending parts.

Flood water mark 55 cm inside the cabin. Interior, seats, carpets and several electrical modules damaged by water. Engine already dismantled at the time of the flood, with parts removed. Flood-related damage estimated at AED 21,000. Engine replacement AED 26,500 relates to the January failure, not to the flood.

whatHappened: The flood genuinely damaged the interior and electrics of a car that was already off the road with a failed engine. He has added the January engine failure to the flood claim.
damage: Flood damage AED 21,000. Pre-existing engine failure AED 26,500.
thirdParties: The garage, which had the car in its care
missing: The garage's own insurance details
Whether the garage took reasonable steps to protect cars before the forecast rain
inconsistencies: He claims the flood damaged the engine; the job card shows the engine seized in January and was already dismantled
indicators: Earlier mechanical failure included in a weather claim
innocent: He may believe that once the car flooded, everything wrong with it should be paid
questions: Ask him whether he told the insurer about the January engine failure
Ask the garage whether its insurer covers customers' vehicles
steps: Pay the flood damage to the interior and electrics under comprehensive
Exclude the engine, explaining the job card evidence
Consider whether the garage's liability insurer should contribute, as the car was in its care
assessment: Mixed: a genuine flood loss with an older, unrelated engine failure added. Paying the flood part and excluding the engine is fair; a fraud referral is not needed unless he insists after seeing the job card.
action: Settle the flood damage and decline the engine with the evidence.
outcomes: Flood damage paid; engine excluded; he accepts
He insists on the engine; claim referred for review

title: Blamed in the police report, cleared by the dashcam
type: Lane change collision with a disputed police finding
story: Policyholder's Kia K5 and a Nissan Altima collided on Sheikh Zayed Road in Dubai. The police report, prepared at the scene from the two drivers' accounts, named her as at fault for a sudden lane change. Her dashcam shows the Altima moving into her lane.
statement: I was in lane three the whole time. The Altima came from lane four into me. The officer was in a hurry and the other driver spoke Arabic with him, I couldn't explain well. I didn't think to show the dashcam at the scene. I want the report changed so this isn't my fault.

accounts.text: 08:42:10 Kia in lane 3, steady. 08:42:14 Altima's left indicator flashes briefly as it moves from lane 4 into lane 3. 08:42:15 contact with the Kia's right front. The Kia does not leave lane 3 at any point.
Two-vehicle collision. Driver of the Kia K5 found responsible for changing lanes without due care. Driver of the Altima not at fault.

whatHappened: The dashcam shows the Altima changed lanes into her. The police finding was based on the two accounts at the scene, without the footage.
damage: Kia: right front wing and bumper, AED 9,800. Altima: left rear door.
thirdParties: Driver of the Altima and his insurer
missing: The outcome of an objection to the police finding
inconsistencies: The police report says she changed lanes; the dashcam shows she stayed in her lane
innocent: Language barriers and haste at the scene commonly lead to wrong findings
questions: Ask whether she still has the full original video file
steps: Help her object to the police finding within the allowed period, submitting the dashcam footage
Pay her repair under comprehensive while the objection is considered
Recover from the Altima's insurer if the finding is reversed
assessment: A genuine dispute that the footage should resolve. Insurers rely on the police finding, so the right step is to have the finding corrected rather than argue with the other insurer.
action: Support the objection, pay under comprehensive, and recover if the finding changes.
outcomes: Finding reversed; cost recovered and her no-claims record restored
Objection rejected; claim remains at fault

title: A camel on the road outside Al Ain
type: Collision with a straying camel at night
story: Policyholder's Toyota Fortuner hit a camel that walked onto a desert road outside Al Ain at about 22:15. The camel came through the windscreen. He suffered cuts and a broken collarbone. The police traced the camel's owner through its identification tag.
statement: There was no light out there and the camel was dark. I saw its legs in the headlights only at the last second. It hit the windscreen and the roof. I couldn't move my shoulder. The police said the owner's fence was broken.

accounts.text: Collision between a vehicle and a straying camel on an unlit desert road. Camel deceased. Owner identified by the animal's tag; enclosure fence found damaged 2 km away. Owner responsible for allowing the animal to stray. Driver injured and taken to hospital.
Bonnet, windscreen, roof panel, A-pillars and front bumper. Structural damage to the roof. Estimate AED 61,000. Vehicle value about AED 95,000.

whatHappened: A camel strayed through a broken fence onto the unlit road and he saw it only at the last second.
damage: Fortuner: front, windscreen and roof, AED 61,000. Driver: broken collarbone and cuts.
missing: Medical reports for his injury claim, if he pursues the owner
innocent: Straying camels on unlit roads at night are a known risk, and the broken fence explains how this one got out
questions: Ask whether he has personal accident cover on his policy for the injury
steps: Pay the repair under comprehensive
Recover from the camel's owner, who the police found responsible
Check his personal accident cover for the injury
assessment: Genuine. Owners of camels that stray onto roads can be held responsible, which gives the insurer a recovery route.
action: Pay the repair and pursue the camel's owner.
outcomes: Paid; partial recovery from the camel's owner

title: A blowout at 48°C on seven-year-old tyres
type: Rollover after a tyre failure on old tyres
story: Policyholder's Mitsubishi Pajero rolled over on Emirates Road near Sharjah at about 14:30 in 48°C heat after its right rear tyre burst.
