The tyre date codes show all four tyres were made seven years earlier. UAE rules treat tyres as expired five years after manufacture, and the policy requires the vehicle to be kept roadworthy.
statement: The tyres had good tread, I checked. I didn't know tyres have an expiry date. The car was driving fine and then bang, it pulled to the right and rolled. My son had a cut on his head but we're OK. I drove maybe 110, the limit is 120.

accounts.text: Single vehicle rollover following a rear tyre burst. Tyres found to be past their validity based on date codes. Driver and one passenger with minor injuries. Speed within the limit according to the driver.

Right rear tyre tread separation, typical of age-related deterioration in high heat. Tread depth adequate on all tyres. Date codes: all four tyres seven years old. Vehicle a total loss, value AED 54,000.

whatHappened: An aged tyre separated in extreme heat and the SUV rolled. The tread looked fine, which is why he did not realise the danger.
damage: Pajero total loss, AED 54,000. Minor injuries.
missing: Whether the vehicle passed its last annual inspection with these tyres
innocent: Most drivers judge tyres by tread, not age
The car may have passed its annual inspection with these tyres
questions: Ask when and where the car was last inspected for registration renewal
steps: Check whether the roadworthiness condition clearly covers tyre age
Consider whether the car passed its last inspection with the same tyres, which would weaken a decline
Decide, and explain the reasons in writing
assessment: Genuine negligence. The tyre age contributed directly to the loss, which supports relying on the roadworthiness condition, but if the car passed a recent inspection with the same tyres, a decline may be seen as unfair. A careful, documented decision is needed.
action: Decide on the roadworthiness condition after checking the inspection history; consider a partial settlement if the position is unclear.
outcomes: Declined under the roadworthiness condition
Car passed inspection three months earlier; claim paid in full

title: A new resident, driving on his home licence
type: Collision by a resident without a UAE driving licence
story: Policyholder, who received UAE residency four months ago, ran a red light in Abu Dhabi and hit a Hyundai Accent. When he bought the policy he answered that he held a valid licence to drive in the UAE. He was driving on his Indian licence and had not obtained a UAE licence.
statement: I thought my Indian licence was fine, I used it when I visited before. Somebody at work said I have to change it but I was waiting for my driving test date. The light turned red as I was going through. The other driver's back is hurting.

accounts.text: Driver of Vehicle 1 (Toyota Yaris) crossed on a red signal and struck Vehicle 2 (Hyundai Accent). Driver of Vehicle 1 is a resident without a UAE licence, driving on a foreign licence. Responsibility: driver of Vehicle 1. Driver of Vehicle 2 complains of back pain.

whatHappened: He ran a red light and caused the collision while driving on a licence that was no longer valid for a resident.
damage: Accent: right side, about AED 14,000; driver with back pain. Yaris: front end, AED 11,000.
missing: Medical reports for the Accent driver
inconsistencies: The proposal says he held a valid licence to drive in the UAE; as a resident he did not
indicators: Driving without a valid licence, contrary to the proposal answer
innocent: Many new residents do not know that visitor licence rules stop applying once they are resident
questions: Ask when his residency was issued and whether he had booked a driving test
steps: Decline his own damage, as the policy excludes driving without a valid licence
Pay the Accent driver's damage and injury claim, as the law protects third parties, then seek recovery from him
Advise him not to drive until he holds a UAE licence
assessment: Genuine accident with a serious licensing breach. Third parties must still be compensated, but the insurer can decline his own damage and has a right of recovery against him.
action: Decline own damage, settle the third-party claims, and pursue recovery.
outcomes: Third-party claims settled; recovery agreed in instalments
Policy cancelled for misrepresentation

title: A Sharjah scrape and a door that was already marked
type: Genuine side collision with earlier damage included
story: Policyholder claimed for damage along the left side of her Honda Civic after another car brushed it in a mall car park in Sharjah. The police report records "minor contact to the left rear door". Her renewal inspection photos from two months earlier already show a long scrape on the left front door. She first said the accident happened on the road, then in the car park.
statement: First: A car hit my left side on Al Wahda Street. Later: Sorry, it was in the mall car park, I mixed it up because I was going to Al Wahda Street. All the damage on the left side is from this. The doors were perfect before.

accounts.text: Minor collision in a mall car park. Vehicle 2 reversing made contact with the left rear door of Vehicle 1 (Honda Civic). Responsibility: driver of Vehicle 2. Damage noted: left rear door.

accounts.who: Renewal inspection photos, two months before
accounts.text: Six photos taken at renewal. Left front door: long horizontal scrape through the paint from the handle to the wing. Left rear door: no damage visible. Photos dated and geotagged at the inspection centre.

whatHappened: A reversing car genuinely damaged the left rear door in the car park. The left front door scrape was there before, and her account of the location was confused.
damage: Accident damage: left rear door, AED 3,200. Pre-existing: left front door scrape, AED 2,600.
thirdParties: Driver of the reversing car and his insurer
evidence: Police report describing the rear door only
missing: Mall CCTV of the car park collision
inconsistencies: She says the doors were perfect before; the renewal photos show the front door scrape two months earlier
She first gave a road as the location, then the car park
indicators: Pre-existing damage included in the claim
Changed account of the location
innocent: The location mix-up has a plausible explanation
She may have forgotten an old scrape on a door she does not often look at
questions: Show her the renewal photos and ask about the front door scrape
steps: Pay or recover the left rear door, which the police report supports
Exclude the front door with the renewal photos
Record the corrected location; no referral if she accepts the explanation
assessment: Mixed: a real collision with older damage added and a confused first account. The police report and the renewal photos give a clear basis to pay one door and not the other.
action: Settle the rear door and exclude the front door.
outcomes: Rear door paid by the reversing driver's insurer; front door excluded
She insists on both doors; claim reviewed by the fraud team

title: A Patrol on the dunes near Al Faqa, and no off-road extension
type: Rollover while dune driving on a policy that excludes off-road use
story: Policyholder rolled his Nissan Patrol onto its roof while driving over dunes near Al Faqa on a weekend trip with friends. Nobody was hurt. A friend's 4x4 pulled the car back onto its wheels and a recovery truck took it to Dubai. His comprehensive policy excludes use off paved roads unless the optional off-road extension is bought, and it was not bought.
statement: Everyone goes to the dunes at the weekend, the car is built for it. I went over a crest a bit fast and the sand gave way. I thought comprehensive meant everything. The salesman never mentioned off-road. The roof is crushed and the pillars are bent.

accounts.text: Single vehicle overturned in a desert area off the paved road near Al Faqa. No injuries. No third party involved. Driver licensed.

Exclusion: loss or damage while the vehicle is being driven off paved roads, including desert and dune driving, unless the off-road extension is shown in the schedule. Schedule: off-road extension not purchased.

whatHappened: A genuine rollover during dune driving, which the policy clearly excludes without the extension he did not buy.
damage: Patrol: roof crushed, A and B pillars bent, windscreen and side glass broken; likely a total loss.
missing: Sales records showing whether the off-road extension was offered
innocent: Many buyers assume comprehensive cover includes dune driving
questions: Ask for the sales call recording or quote to see whether the extension was offered
steps: Decline the own-damage claim under the off-road exclusion, explaining the wording and the extension in plain language
Check the sales records: if the extension was never offered or explained, handle it as a complaint about the sale
Offer to add the extension at renewal
assessment: Genuine accident, not covered. The exclusion is clear and the extension was not bought.
action: Decline with a clear explanation and review how the policy was sold.
outcomes: Declined; he accepts after the wording is explained
Complaint about the sale upheld; goodwill contribution offered

title: Found scraped in the Marina car park, reported four days later
type: Damage by an unknown party, reported to police days after it was found
story: Policyholder says he found a long scrape and dent on his car's rear quarter when he returned to it in a residential car park in Dubai Marina. He obtained a police report for damage by an unknown party four days later, because he was travelling for work. The garage needs the police report to repair the car. The building's CCTV is kept for only three days and has been overwritten.
statement: I came back late, saw the scrape in the morning and had to fly to Riyadh the same day. I did the police report as soon as I landed back. It's a residents' car park, someone must have scraped it parking. There's yellow paint in the scratch.

accounts.text: Report of damage to a parked vehicle by an unknown party, registered four days after the stated date of discovery. Location: residential building car park, Dubai Marina. No witnesses identified.
CCTV retention is 72 hours. Footage for the date given has been overwritten. Car park access logs show the policyholder's tag entering the night before and leaving the following morning.

whatHappened: Probably genuine car park damage by an unknown driver, but the four-day gap means the CCTV is gone and the timing cannot be confirmed.
damage: Lexus IS: rear quarter scrape and dent with yellow paint transfer; estimate AED 4,800.
missing: CCTV of the incident
Whether any resident in the building drives a yellow car
indicators: Damage reported to police four days after discovery
innocent: Work travel explains the delay, and the access log supports his movements
questions: Ask building management whether any yellow vehicle is registered to the car park
Ask for his flight booking to confirm the travel
steps: Accept the police report as meeting the requirement for repair, and note the reason for the delay
Check the damage height and the yellow paint against the car park, for example yellow-painted pillars or barriers
If consistent, pay the claim as unknown-party damage under the comprehensive cover, applying any excess the policy sets for unknown third parties
Explain that reporting promptly preserves CCTV in future
assessment: Insufficient evidence rather than suspicion. The travel and the access log support his account; the damage pattern can be checked against the car park.
action: Inspect the paint transfer against the car park and pay as unknown-party damage if consistent.
outcomes: Yellow paint matches a column guard near his bay; claim paid
Paid after his flight booking confirms the trip

title: Agency repair until three years old, and the car is three years and two months
type: Dispute over agency repair entitlement based on vehicle age
story: Policyholder's Lexus ES was rear-ended at a signal in Abu Dhabi; the other driver was found at fault but she has claimed under her own comprehensive policy for speed. The claims team approved repair at a non-agency garage because the car is now three years and two months old and agency repair is "for vehicles up to three years". Her renewal schedule, issued two months before the accident, lists "Agency repair: Yes" for the policy year without any age condition.
statement: I renewed two months ago and the schedule says agency repair. Nobody told me it would stop halfway through the year. The car has always been serviced at the agency. I want it repaired there with genuine parts, that's what I paid for.

accounts.text: Period of insurance: 12 months from renewal. Repair condition: Agency repair: Yes. No age limit stated in the schedule.
Vehicle first registered 3 years 2 months before the accident. Underwriting guideline: agency repair up to 3 years. Approved non-agency repair.

whatHappened: A genuine claim where the internal guideline conflicts with the schedule the customer was given, which grants agency repair for the whole year.
damage: Lexus ES: rear bumper, boot lid and parking sensors; agency estimate AED 9,600, non-agency estimate AED 6,900.
thirdParties: The at-fault driver and their insurer
evidence: Police report finding the other driver at fault
missing: Any wording elsewhere in the policy that limits agency repair by age
inconsistencies: The schedule grants agency repair without an age limit; the internal guideline sets one
innocent: Underwriting guidelines are not always reflected in the documents issued to customers
questions: Check the full policy wording for any age condition on agency repair
steps: Honour agency repair for this policy period: the schedule issued to her grants it without an age condition, and an internal guideline cannot override her contract
Recover the cost from the at-fault driver’s insurer under the police report
Fix the renewal documents so that any age limit is stated clearly at renewal
assessment: Genuine claim and a fair complaint. The schedule she was given decides the entitlement.
action: Authorise the agency repair and recover from the at-fault driver's insurer.
outcomes: Agency repair authorised; full recovery from the other insurer
Renewal schedules updated to show age limits

title: A tourist in a rental car, a police report, and an insurer that will not pay
type: Recovery from a rental car’s insurer after a tourist contests fault
story: Policyholder's car was hit at a roundabout in Abu Dhabi by a rental car driven by a visiting tourist. The police report found the tourist at fault for entering without giving way. The insurer paid her repairs of AED 14,500 under her comprehensive cover and claimed the amount from the rental car's insurer. That insurer has refused, saying the tourist emailed after leaving the country to say she was not at fault.
statement: The police came, looked at both cars and the position, and gave her the fault. She signed the report too. I don't understand how an email from abroad can change that.

accounts.text: Collision at a roundabout. Vehicle 2 (rental, driven by a visitor) entered without giving way to vehicle 1 already on the roundabout. Fault: vehicle 2. Both drivers signed.
Our insured's driver disputes liability by email and has left the UAE. We are unable to accept the claim at this time.

whatHappened: A collision caused by the tourist, recorded in a signed police report. Her later email does not change the report.
damage: Policyholder's Accord: front-right wing and bumper, AED 14,500, repaired.
thirdParties: The rental company and its insurer
missing: Any formal objection to the police report filed by the tourist
inconsistencies: The tourist signed the report but now disputes fault by email
innocent: Visitors sometimes sign reports they do not fully understand
questions: Ask the rental insurer whether any formal objection to the police report was lodged
steps: Press the recovery on the police report, which assigned fault and was signed by both drivers
Ask the rental insurer to show any formal objection; an informal email is not one
Escalate through the UAE’s insurance dispute channels if the refusal continues
Recover her excess as part of the claim and keep her informed
assessment: Disputed only by the other side's informal objection. The signed police report supports full recovery.
action: Pursue the rental car's insurer on the police report and escalate if it keeps refusing.
outcomes: Rental insurer pays after escalation
Recovered through the dispute process with costs

title: Wild boar on a country road in Brandenburg
type: Game animal collision under partial cover
story: Policyholder's Volkswagen Golf hit a wild boar on a country road near Eberswalde, Brandenburg, at about 21:30. He called the police, who contacted the local hunting tenant. The hunting tenant issued a game collision certificate. The policy includes Teilkasko (partial cover).
statement: It came out of the field on the right with two smaller ones behind it. I braked hard and hit the big one. I stayed in the car with the hazard lights on and called 110. The hunter came and took the animal away and gave me a certificate.

accounts.who: Game collision certificate from the hunting tenant
accounts.text: Collision between a passenger car and a wild boar (adult, about 80 kg) confirmed at the stated location and time. Animal recovered dead from the verge. Hair and blood traces on the vehicle's front bumper.
Front bumper, grille, radiator, left headlamp and bonnet. Parking sensor bracket broken. Estimate €4,380 including VAT.

whatHappened: A wild boar crossed from the field with its young and he could not avoid it; the hunting tenant recovered the animal and confirmed it.
damage: Front end, €4,380.
missing: The police case number, to file with the certificate
innocent: A boar crossing with its young near fields at night is typical, and the hunting tenant's certificate confirms it
questions: Ask for the police case number to attach to the file
steps: Pay under Teilkasko less the Teilkasko excess
Confirm that a Teilkasko claim does not affect his no-claims class
assessment: Genuine. Collisions with game animals such as wild boar are covered under Teilkasko, and the certificate from the hunting tenant is the standard proof. A Teilkasko claim does not reduce the no-claims class.
action: Pay the repair under Teilkasko.
outcomes: Paid €4,380 less the €150 Teilkasko excess

title: A lane change on the A3, and the dashcam question
type: Motorway lane change collision with dashcam evidence
story: Policyholder's Audi A4 and a BMW 5 Series collided on the A3 near Frankfurt when the BMW moved into the middle lane. Each driver blames the other. The policyholder has dashcam footage. The BMW driver's lawyer says the footage cannot be used because of data protection law and claims full damages.
statement: I was in the middle lane at about 130. The BMW was in the left lane, came up fast and then cut into my lane right in front of me. I braked but caught his rear. My dashcam was recording. His lawyer says the video is illegal, but I only had it running for safety.

accounts.text: Continuous recording. 14:21:05 BMW passes in the left lane. 14:21:07 BMW moves into the middle lane about 15 metres ahead of the Audi without indicating. 14:21:08 Audi brakes. 14:21:09 contact between the Audi's right front and the BMW's left rear.

Our client was established in the middle lane when your policyholder approached at excessive speed and failed to keep her distance. The dashcam recording was made in breach of data protection law and is not admissible. We claim €11,600 for repairs, assessor fees and loss of use.

whatHappened: The BMW cut into the middle lane close in front of the Audi without indicating. The Audi had little chance to avoid it.
damage: Audi: right front, €5,900. BMW: left rear, claimed €11,600 including assessor fees and loss of use.
thirdParties: Driver of the BMW, his insurer and his lawyer
missing: A reconstruction expert's view on the gap and speeds
inconsistencies: The BMW driver says he was established in the middle lane; the dashcam shows him moving into it two seconds before the impact
innocent: At motorway speeds, both drivers may honestly misjudge the gap
questions: Ask the policyholder whether her dashcam records continuously or only on impact
steps: Reject the BMW's claim based on the footage; Germany's Federal Court of Justice has accepted dashcam recordings as evidence in accident disputes despite data protection concerns
Expect the other side to argue a share of liability from the operating risk of her own car
Pursue her own damage against the BMW insurer
assessment: A genuine dispute in which the footage strongly favours the policyholder. Even so, German courts often attribute a share to each car's operating risk unless the collision was truly unavoidable, so a settlement of around 75 to 80% in her favour is realistic.
action: Defend using the footage and negotiate a liability split heavily in her favour.
outcomes: Settled 80:20 in her favour
Court finds the collision unavoidable for her; BMW driver fully liable

title: Lightning in the storm, and a car that no longer starts
type: Electronics damage after a nearby lightning strike
story: During a thunderstorm in Bavaria, lightning struck a tree about three metres from policyholder's BMW X1 parked at a hiking car park. The car would not start afterwards and several control units failed. There are scorch marks on the tree but none on the car.
statement: We were sheltering in the hut when there was a flash and a bang at the same moment. When we got back to the car, the dashboard was dead and the alarm was beeping. The tree next to it has a black stripe down the trunk. The car wasn't hit directly, I think.

accounts.text: Lightning strike recorded within 50 metres of the stated coordinates at 15:42. Peak current 38 kA.

Multiple control units without communication: body control module, gateway, infotainment and the 48-volt system controller. Damage pattern consistent with an overvoltage event. No physical damage to the bodywork. Estimate €7,850.

whatHappened: A lightning strike next to the car induced an overvoltage that damaged its electronics.
damage: Electronics, €7,850.
missing: The exact Teilkasko wording on lightning: direct strike only, or also overvoltage from a nearby strike
innocent: Electronics failing without any visible burn marks is consistent with a strike a few metres away
questions: Check the policy conditions for lightning and overvoltage cover
steps: Confirm the wording; many modern Teilkasko policies include overvoltage damage from lightning
Pay if covered, or explain the limit if only direct strikes are covered
assessment: Genuine. Whether it is paid depends on the policy wording: older wordings cover only direct strikes, while many newer ones include overvoltage damage.
action: Decide on the wording and explain the outcome.
outcomes: Covered under the overvoltage extension; paid less the excess
Older wording covers direct strikes only; claim declined with an explanation

title: The same old Mercedes at the same kind of junction
type: Provoked collisions by an organised group
story: The insurer's policyholder, a delivery driver, turned right at a junction in Berlin-Neukölln and collided with an older Mercedes E-Class that was overtaking on the right. The Mercedes driver claims €9,800 on a notional basis (repair cost from an assessor's report, without repairing the car), plus loss of use and assessor fees. The insurers' shared database shows the Mercedes and its driver in four similar claims in two years.
statement: Claimant, through his lawyer: Our client was driving straight on when your policyholder turned right across his path without looking. Our client's vehicle was assessed by an independent expert. We claim the net repair cost of €9,800 on a notional basis, assessor fees of €1,150 and loss of use.

accounts.text: I was indicating right and checked my mirror. The Mercedes came up fast in the cycle lane on my right as I turned. It felt like he was waiting for me. He jumped out and had a phone number for a lawyer ready.

The Mercedes (registered in the same name throughout) has been involved in four claims in two years, three at right-turn junctions, each settled on a notional basis without proof of repair. The same independent assessor and the same law firm acted in all four. The damage photos in this claim show the same area of the car as earlier claims, with no sign of repair in between.

whatHappened: Very probably a provoked collision: the Mercedes driver deliberately put his car in the path of a turning van to create a claim, and the same damage has been claimed repeatedly without being repaired.
damage: Claimed €9,800 notional repair cost plus fees and loss of use. Policyholder's van: minor scratch.
thirdParties: The assessor and law firm involved in all four claims
evidence: Claims history from the shared database
Policyholder's account of the overtaking in the cycle lane
missing: Footage from the delivery van's camera, if fitted
An independent reconstruction of the Mercedes' path and speed
inconsistencies: The claimant says he was driving straight on; the policyholder says he came up fast in the cycle lane
The same area of damage appears in earlier claims without repair
indicators: Repeat claims with the same vehicle, assessor and lawyer
Notional settlements with no proof of repair
Damage already paid for in earlier claims
Overtaking on the right at a junction
innocent: A driver can be unlucky more than once
Notional settlement is lawful in Germany; it only becomes a problem when the same damage is claimed again
questions: Ask the claimant for proof of repair after each earlier claim
Ask the claimant why he was overtaking on the right
steps: Reject the claim and demand proof that earlier damage was repaired
Commission an independent assessment of the Mercedes' damage history
Refer the pattern to the police and coordinate with the insurers of the earlier claims
assessment: Strong evidence of an organised scheme. The repeated unrepaired damage alone defeats much of the claim, and the pattern of junction collisions with the same assessor and lawyer points to deliberate provocation.
action: Reject the claim, demand repair evidence and refer the pattern to the police.
outcomes: Claim abandoned
Criminal investigation into the group; earlier insurers recover payments

title: A car park scrape, and he drove away
type: Leaving the scene after a parking collision
story: Policyholder scraped a parked Tesla Model 3 while parking at a supermarket in Hamburg and drove off without waiting or leaving his details. A witness noted his number plate and the police traced him. Two days later he reported the damage to his insurer. He is claiming the Tesla's damage under his liability cover and his own car under Vollkasko.
statement: I didn't think it was much, just a touch. I was late for my mother's appointment. I meant to come back. When the police called I told them the truth straight away. I know I should have waited.

accounts.text: Investigation opened for unauthorised leaving of the scene of an accident. Witness observed the vehicle touching the parked Tesla and leaving without stopping. Damage to the Tesla's rear door and wheel arch. Driver identified via the registration and admitted the collision.
Repair of the rear door and wheel arch, recalibration of a side camera: €3,950. Assessor fees €480. Loss of use for four days.

whatHappened: He caused a minor scrape and drove away, which is a criminal offence in Germany and a breach of his obligations under the policy.
damage: Tesla: €3,950 plus fees and loss of use. Policyholder's Opel Corsa: front bumper corner, €850.
evidence: Police notice with the witness account
missing: The outcome of the criminal proceedings, which does not change the insurance decision
innocent: Drivers sometimes panic or underestimate a scrape
questions: Ask whether he has a lawyer for the criminal proceedings
steps: Pay the Tesla owner's claim under the liability cover, as the injured party is protected
Take recourse against the policyholder for breaching his post-accident obligations, within the legal cap, usually €2,500
Decline or reduce his Vollkasko claim for the breach, depending on intent and on whether it affected the insurer's position
assessment: Genuine collision, serious misconduct afterwards. The third party must be paid, and leaving the scene allows the insurer limited recourse against him and grounds to refuse his own damage claim.
action: Pay the third party, take recourse within the cap and decide the Vollkasko claim on the breach.
outcomes: Tesla claim paid; €2,500 recourse taken; Vollkasko declined
Criminal proceedings end with a fine and points

title: Damaged by the workshop apprentice
type: Damage while the car was in a workshop's care
story: Policyholder left her Mercedes C-Class at a workshop in Stuttgart for a service. While moving it in the yard, an apprentice reversed it into a pillar, damaging the rear bumper and tailgate. The workshop owner admitted it and suggested she claim under her Vollkasko "to make it simpler".
statement: The workshop called me and said there had been a small accident in the yard. Then they said I should claim on my insurance. But it's their fault, so why should I lose my no-claims class?

accounts.text: We regret that our apprentice damaged your vehicle while moving it. The repair can be carried out by us. We suggest settling through your comprehensive insurance, as our business insurance takes longer.

whatHappened: An apprentice reversed the car into a pillar while moving it in the workshop yard, as the workshop itself admits.
damage: Rear bumper, tailgate and parking sensors, €3,200.
thirdParties: The workshop and its business liability insurer
missing: The workshop's business liability insurer details
innocent: The workshop may genuinely think the comprehensive route is quicker
questions: Ask the workshop for its business liability insurer and policy number
steps: Advise her that the workshop is liable and its business liability insurer should pay
If she uses her Vollkasko for speed, recover the cost and restore her no-claims class
assessment: Genuine. The workshop is liable; she should not lose her no-claims class for its mistake.
action: Direct the claim to the workshop's insurer, or pay and recover in full.
outcomes: Workshop's insurer pays; no effect on her no-claims class

title: An e-scooter, a pedestrian and last year's insurance plate
type: Injury caused by an uninsured e-scooter
story: On 3 March a former customer rode his private e-scooter into a pedestrian on a pavement in Cologne, and she broke her wrist. His e-scooter liability insurance with the insurer ran from 1 March of the previous year to the end of February and was not renewed. He was still displaying last year's insurance plate. The pedestrian's lawyer has claimed against the insurer.
statement: I didn't know the insurance stopped at the end of February. I thought it was one year from when I bought it. I'm really sorry about the lady. I was on the pavement because the road was busy, which I know isn't allowed.

accounts.text: E-scooter liability insurance, insurance plate for the year March to February. Cover ended at the end of February. No renewal. Reminder letter sent in January to the customer's address.

Our client was struck from behind by an e-scooter on the pavement and suffered a fractured right wrist. We claim compensation for pain and suffering, loss of earnings and household help from the insurer named on the insurance plate.

whatHappened: He rode on the pavement and hit a pedestrian three days after his insurance had expired. Without valid cover, the insurer named on the old plate is not liable.
damage: Pedestrian: fractured wrist, about six weeks of incapacity. E-scooter undamaged.
missing: Proof that the reminder letter was delivered, which supports the decline but is not essential
innocent: Many owners do not realise that e-scooter insurance runs from March to the end of February
questions: Ask the rider whether he has personal liability insurance, which normally excludes motor vehicles such as e-scooters
steps: Decline the claim against the insurer, because the cover had expired
Tell the pedestrian's lawyer to claim from the rider personally and from the German guarantee fund for victims of uninsured vehicles
Inform the rider that riding without insurance is a criminal offence and that he is personally liable
assessment: Genuine accident without valid insurance. The injured pedestrian is still protected through the guarantee fund, which can then pursue the rider. The insurer's role is to decline clearly and point the victim to the right route quickly.
action: Decline, and redirect the victim to the guarantee fund and the rider.
outcomes: Guarantee fund compensates the pedestrian and recovers from the rider
Rider prosecuted for riding without insurance

title: Paid on the expert’s report, without the repair, and with VAT
type: Notional settlement on an expert report where VAT is claimed but not incurred
story: Our policyholder reversed into Ms Krüger's parked car in a supermarket car park in Hanover. Liability is accepted. She has claimed on the basis of her expert's report without having the car repaired: €6,300 net repair costs at brand-workshop rates, plus €1,197 VAT, the expert's fee and a flat sum for expenses. Her car is six years old and has been serviced at independent garages.
statement: I'll decide later whether to repair it or sell it. The expert's report says €7,497 including VAT, so that's what I'm claiming. Why would I get less than the report says?

accounts.text: Damage to the rear bumper, tailgate and rear panel. Repair costs at brand-workshop rates: €6,300 net, €1,197 VAT, €7,497 gross. Vehicle age 6 years. Service history: independent garages.
I was reversing out of the space and didn't see her car behind me. I accepted it on the spot and gave her my details.

whatHappened: A clear liability claim settled on a notional basis. VAT is not payable unless it is actually incurred, and brand-workshop rates may be replaced by a cheaper equivalent workshop for a car of this age and service history.
damage: Her VW Passat: rear bumper, tailgate and rear panel.
missing: Quotes from an equivalent independent workshop nearby
innocent: Claimants often expect the gross figure in an expert report to be paid in full
questions: Confirm whether she has had the car repaired or replaced
steps: Pay the net repair costs: under section 249(2) of the Civil Code, VAT is only payable if it is actually incurred
Consider referring her to an equivalent independent workshop’s rates, since the car is over three years old and not serviced at brand workshops, giving her a concrete, reachable alternative
Pay the expert’s fee and the usual flat sum for expenses
Tell her VAT will be paid if she later repairs and shows the invoice
assessment: Genuine claim, overstated by the VAT. A notional settlement pays net costs; VAT follows only if incurred.
action: Pay net repair costs, the expert's fee and the expense sum, and explain the VAT rule.
outcomes: Net costs paid; VAT paid later on a repair invoice
Settled at independent workshop rates after a concrete referral

title: €612 cut from the workshop invoice, and the 2024 rulings on who bears it
type: Liability insurer reduces a repair invoice as excessive
story: Our policyholder rear-ended Mr Brandt in Stuttgart. He had his car repaired at a workshop of his choice and sent the invoice of €5,940. The claims team paid €5,328, cutting €612 for a "workstation change" charge, extra cleaning and a paint mixing surcharge that its estimating system marks as unnecessary. Mr Brandt has not paid the workshop the balance and the workshop is pressing him.
statement: I took the car to a proper workshop and paid what I could. I can't check whether a workstation change was needed, I'm not a mechanic. Your insurer caused this, why am I stuck between you and the workshop?

accounts.text: Repair per expert report: €5,328. Additional items: workstation change €227, vehicle cleaning and disinfection €148, paint mixing surcharge €237. Total €5,940.
Paid €5,328. Deducted €612 as not necessary according to the estimating system. No contact with the workshop.

whatHappened: A genuine repair where the insurer cut items the claimant could not reasonably judge. Under the Federal Court of Justice rulings of January 2024, that workshop risk falls on the liable insurer.
damage: His Audi A3: rear bumper, boot lid and rear panel, repaired.
missing: Whether he has assigned his claim to the workshop
innocent: Estimating systems flag common surcharges whether or not they were justified on a particular job
questions: Ask whether he has paid the balance and whether he has assigned his claim to the workshop
steps: Pay the €612: following the Federal Court of Justice rulings of 16 January 2024, the claimant who had the repair done can claim the full invoice even if some items were unnecessary; if he has not paid the workshop, payment goes to the workshop
In return, ask him to assign any claims he has against the workshop for overcharging, and pursue the workshop directly if the items were unjustified
Note that if the workshop itself claims under an assignment from him, it cannot rely on the workshop risk rule
Update the deduction practice for repaired-vehicle claims
assessment: Genuine, and the deduction is against current case law. The insurer pays and takes over the dispute with the workshop.
action: Pay the balance to the workshop against an assignment of his claims, and pursue the workshop if warranted.
outcomes: Balance paid; workshop justifies two of the three items
Practice changed for repaired-vehicle invoices

title: Fourteen days of loss of use, and a second car in the garage
type: Loss of use compensation claimed while another household car was used
story: Our policyholder hit Mr Wagner's car at a junction in Leipzig; liability is accepted. He did not hire a car during the repair and claims loss of use compensation for 14 days at the table rate for his car's class. The expert estimated 5 working days for the repair. He started the repair nine days after the accident, after a holiday. His wife's Golf was available at home, and he says he used it to get to work.
statement: I couldn't use my own car for two weeks, so I'm owed for two weeks. Yes, I borrowed my wife's Golf for work, but that's her car, not mine. And the holiday was booked months ago, I couldn't take the car in before.

accounts.text: Repair duration: 5 working days. Vehicle drivable and safe to use until repair, with a damaged front wing and headlamp alignment to be checked.
Vehicle delivered for repair 9 days after the accident. Repair completed in 5 working days.

whatHappened: A genuine claim for loss of use, overstated: the car was drivable before the repair, the necessary repair period was 5 working days, and a second household car was available and used.
damage: His Skoda Octavia: front wing, bumper and headlamp. Drivable.
evidence: His statement about his wife's car
missing: Whether his wife needed her car during those days
inconsistencies: He claims 14 days; the car was drivable before the repair and the repair took 5 working days
indicators: Loss of use claimed for days when the car was drivable and another car was used
innocent: Many claimants believe loss of use runs from the accident until the car comes back
questions: Ask whether his wife went without her car during those days
steps: Limit loss of use to the necessary repair period, here about 5 working days, because the car was drivable before
Consider the household second car: if it was genuinely available to him without hardship to others, loss of use may not be due at all; if his wife went without, a payment for the repair days is fair
Explain the calculation clearly and pay the undisputed repair costs
assessment: Genuine claim, exaggerated in duration. At most the repair days are payable, and the second car may remove the loss entirely.
action: Pay the repair costs and, depending on the second car's availability, loss of use for the repair days only.
outcomes: Loss of use paid for 7 calendar days
Loss of use declined because the second car was freely available

title: Twenty-six reports by the same expert, all generous
type: Series of inflated expert reports on liability claims
story: A claimant in Duisburg says our policyholder scraped his rear bumper while parking. His expert's report prices a new bumper, a new rear panel section, blend painting of both rear doors and €900 of diminished value for a nine-year-old car with 180,000 km. The claimant's photos show a scrape on the bumper corner only. The same expert, lawyer and workshop appear in 26 claims against the insurer in nine months, all with similar line items.
statement: (Lawyer for the claimant) The report is by a certified independent expert and must be paid in full, together with the expert's fee and our fees. Your policyholder admitted fault.

accounts.text: Photos: a 15 cm scrape on the rear bumper corner, no visible deformation of the rear panel. Report: bumper replacement, rear panel section, blend painting of both rear doors, diminished value €900. Total €4,980 net.

26 liability claims in 9 months with the same expert, lawyer and workshop. In 21 of them, blend painting of adjacent panels and diminished value were claimed regardless of vehicle age or mileage. Average report value 2.4 times the insurer's own estimates for similar photos.

whatHappened: A minor genuine scrape, valued by an expert whose reports consistently inflate repairs and add diminished value where little or none can exist.
damage: BMW 3 Series: scrape to the rear bumper corner.
missing: A physical inspection by an independent expert instructed by the insurer
inconsistencies: The report replaces a rear panel the photos show undamaged
Diminished value claimed on a nine-year-old car with 180,000 km
indicators: Same expert, lawyer and workshop across 26 claims
Repairs priced well above the visible damage
Diminished value claimed regardless of age and mileage
innocent: Hidden damage behind a bumper corner is possible, which an inspection would reveal
questions: Ask to inspect the car before it is repaired
steps: Accept liability for the scrape, but not the report: instruct an independent expert to inspect the car
Pay the reasonable repair costs on the inspection; resist diminished value on a car of this age and mileage unless clearly shown
Review the 26 claims together with the counter-fraud team and consider a complaint to the expert’s certifying body
Do not allege fraud in correspondence before the review is complete
assessment: Potential fraud by inflation across a series of claims. The scrape is real; the report's scope is not supported by the photos.
action: Inspect independently, pay the reasonable cost, and review the expert's claims as a group.
outcomes: Settled at €1,150 after inspection
Expert’s certification withdrawn after the group review

title: Priority to the right, and a tick added after signing
type: Junction collision with a joint report altered on one copy
story: Policyholder's Renault Clio was hit on the left side at an unmarked junction in a village near Toulouse by a Peugeot 308 coming from her left. At an unmarked junction in France, traffic from the right has priority, so she had priority. Both drivers signed a joint accident report at the scene. The other driver's copy, sent by his insurer, has an extra tick and a changed sketch.
statement: I came from his right, so it was my priority, there are no signs at that junction. We filled in the constat together on his bonnet and both signed it. On my copy, nothing is ticked for me except "was going straight on". Now his insurer says I "did not respect a priority sign". That box was never ticked when I signed.

accounts.who: Policyholder's copy of the joint report
accounts.text: Vehicle A (Clio): box 12 "was going straight on" ticked. Vehicle B (308): box 12 ticked. Sketch: A arriving from the right of B at an unmarked junction. Observations: none. Both signatures present.

accounts.who: Other driver's copy, as sent by his insurer
accounts.text: Vehicle A (Clio): box 12 ticked and box 17 "did not observe a priority sign or a red light" ticked in a different pen. Sketch: a "give way" triangle drawn on A's road. Observations field: "A did not stop". Both signatures present.

whatHappened: She had priority from the right at an unmarked junction. After signing, the other driver added a tick, a give-way sign to the sketch and an observation to his copy to shift the blame.
damage: Clio: left doors and pillar, €3,700. Peugeot: front bumper.
thirdParties: Driver of the Peugeot 308 and his insurer
evidence: Both copies of the joint report
Photos of the junction showing no signs
missing: The original top sheet, to compare inks and pressure marks
Street-level imagery confirming no give-way sign
inconsistencies: The two copies of the same signed report differ: one tick, the sketch and the observations appear on only one copy
innocent: Drivers sometimes add notes afterwards believing they are clarifying, not altering
questions: Ask the other insurer for the original top sheet
Ask the other driver why his copy differs from hers
steps: Send both copies to the other insurer and point out the differences
Rely on the unaltered copy and photos showing an unmarked junction
Apply the inter-insurer case grid on the agreed facts: priority to the right puts the fault on the other driver
assessment: A dispute created by an altered document. Changes made after signing, on one copy only, carry no weight, and the photos show no priority sign. The other driver is at fault.
action: Contest the altered copy and settle on the original facts, recovering from the other insurer.
outcomes: Other insurer accepts full responsibility
Case goes to inter-insurer arbitration; decided in her favour

title: Rockfall on an Alpine road in the rain
type: Damage from falling rocks on a mountain road
story: Stones fell from a slope onto policyholder's Dacia Duster on a departmental road in the Maurienne valley, Savoie, during heavy rain. A rock the size of a football dented the roof and broke the windscreen. A "falling rocks" warning sign stands 500 metres before the spot.
statement: It was raining hard and I heard a noise like gravel, then a big bang on the roof and the windscreen cracked. I stopped further on, where it was safe, and took photos of the stones on the road. A road maintenance truck came by an hour later to clear them.

accounts.text: Rockfall reported on the departmental road at the stated location on the date, following heavy rainfall. Debris cleared at 16:20. Section signed for falling rocks. Protection netting is installed on part of the slope; the fall occurred beyond the netted section.

whatHappened: Heavy rain loosened stones beyond the netted part of the slope and they fell onto the car, as the road service recorded.
damage: Roof dented, windscreen broken, €2,950.
thirdParties: The department, as the road authority
evidence: Photos of the stones and the car
missing: Whether his policy includes comprehensive cover or only glass cover
innocent: Rockfall during heavy rain on a section signed for falling rocks is common
questions: Ask whether his policy includes comprehensive cover or only glass cover
steps: Pay the windscreen under glass cover and the roof under comprehensive, if held
Consider a claim against the road authority only if the slope protection was clearly inadequate; the warning sign makes this unlikely to succeed
assessment: Genuine. The warning sign makes a claim against the road authority weak, so the customer's own comprehensive and glass cover are the practical route.
action: Pay under the policy.
outcomes: Paid under comprehensive and glass cover less the excesses

title: Flooded before the natural disaster decree
type: Flood damage awaiting a natural catastrophe decree
story: Policyholder's Citroën C3 was flooded to the dashboard in her street in the Pas-de-Calais after a river overflowed. She reported it the next day. Her comprehensive policy covers natural catastrophes, but under French law that cover applies only once a government decree recognises the event as a natural catastrophe for her commune.
statement: The water came up in the night, half the street is flooded. The car is full of mud. I need a car for work. Why can't you pay now? My neighbour says we have to wait for some decree.

accounts.text: Water line at dashboard height, mud in the cabin and engine bay. Electrical systems failed. Repair exceeds the vehicle's value. Value at the time of the loss €7,400. Total loss.
The commune has applied for recognition of a natural catastrophe for the flooding. The interministerial commission will consider the application; any decree will be published in the Official Journal.

whatHappened: The river burst its banks overnight and flooded the street, filling the car with water and mud to the dashboard.
damage: Total loss, value €7,400.
missing: The published decree recognising the natural catastrophe
innocent: Waiting for the decree is part of the French system; reporting early was correct, not premature
questions: Ask whether her policy also includes a "climatic events" or comprehensive guarantee that could pay before the decree
steps: Open the claim and keep the expert report on file
Once the decree is published, settle within the legal time limit, applying the statutory natural catastrophe excess
If the decree is refused, consider whether her comprehensive cover pays on its own terms
assessment: Genuine. The natural catastrophe system means payment must wait for the decree. The best service is to prepare everything now, explain the timing and pay quickly once it is published.
action: Prepare the settlement and pay promptly after the decree.
outcomes: Decree published six weeks later; paid €7,400 less the statutory excess
Decree refused; paid under comprehensive cover with its own excess

title: Burglars took the keys, then the car
type: Car stolen with keys taken in a burglary
story: Burglars forced a ground-floor window of policyholder's house near Lyon at night, took the keys from a bowl in the hall and drove away his Peugeot 3008. He filed a police complaint in the morning. His policy covers theft, but requires evidence of a break-in when the car is taken with its own keys.
statement: We were asleep upstairs. In the morning the window in the kitchen was open with marks on the frame, my wife's bag was gone and the keys and the car too. The police came and took fingerprints from the window. I'm very scared now, they were in the house while the children slept.

accounts.text: Complaint registered for burglary and vehicle theft. Kitchen window forced with a tool; marks on the frame photographed. Items stolen: handbag, two phones, vehicle keys and the Peugeot 3008. Vehicle entered in the stolen vehicles file.

whatHappened: Burglars forced the kitchen window, took the keys from the hall and drove the car away while the family slept upstairs.
damage: Peugeot 3008 not recovered, value about €24,500. Household items, claimed under the home insurance.
evidence: Police complaint and report with the forced window
missing: Recovery of the vehicle within the waiting period
innocent: Taking the keys in a burglary is a known way of stealing modern cars that cannot be started without them
questions: Ask him to hand over the second key
Ask whether there is any finance on the car
steps: Accept the burglary evidence as proof of a break-in, which satisfies the theft-with-keys condition
Wait the contractual period, usually 30 days, for possible recovery
Settle at the expert value if the car is not found
Point him to his home insurer for the household items and the window
assessment: Genuine. The forced window and the police report are the break-in evidence the policy requires. The customer has been through a frightening event and should be kept informed throughout the waiting period.
action: Settle after the waiting period if the car is not recovered.
outcomes: Car not recovered; paid €24,500 less the excess
Car found damaged after two weeks; repaired under the theft cover

title: A car that forced him off the road, and nobody saw it
type: Single-vehicle crash blamed on an unidentified driver
story: Policyholder reported that an unidentified car cut in front of him on the Lyon ring road at about 23:45 and forced him into the guardrail, then drove off. He filed a police complaint for a hit-and-run. If he alone were responsible, his no-claims coefficient would worsen; if an unidentified driver caused it, it would not. His car's connected data has been requested.
statement: A dark car came from the right lane very fast and cut in front of me. I swerved left to avoid it and hit the barrier. It didn't touch me. It kept going. I didn't get the number. I filed the complaint the next day.

accounts.who: Vehicle's connected-car data, provided with consent
accounts.text: 23:44:20 speed 118 km/h in a 70 km/h zone. No sudden steering input before the impact. Brake applied 0.4 seconds before the impact. Phone connected by Bluetooth with a messaging app active between 23:43 and 23:44. Impact with the left barrier at 23:44:31.
Damage along the left front side consistent with a glancing impact with the barrier at speed. No sign of contact with another vehicle. No evasive swerve marks noted by the police at the scene.

whatHappened: Probably he was driving much too fast while using his phone and drifted into the barrier. The fleeing car may have been invented to avoid the malus.
damage: Left front wing, wheel, suspension and door, €6,800. Guardrail damage.
thirdParties: The road operator, for the guardrail
missing: Ring road camera footage of other vehicles at the time
Witnesses
inconsistencies: He describes a sudden swerve to avoid a car; the data shows no sudden steering before the impact
He gives no speed; the data shows 118 km/h in a 70 zone with a messaging app active
indicators: Unverifiable third vehicle that changes the responsibility outcome
Data contradicting the evasive manoeuvre
innocent: A real car may have cut in without contact, and evasive steering may be small and hard to see in the data
questions: Ask him about his speed and phone use at the time
Ask the road operator for camera footage
steps: Request the ring road camera footage
Put the data to him in an interview
Treat the claim as responsible if there is no evidence of another vehicle, with the normal effect on his coefficient
Refer to the fraud team only if he maintains the account against the evidence
assessment: Potential fraud through a convenient phantom vehicle. The data points to speeding and distraction, but footage could still show a real car, so the claim should be handled as responsible pending that check rather than as fraud.
action: Handle as a responsible claim unless footage shows another vehicle; refer only if the false account is maintained.
outcomes: No other vehicle on the footage; paid as responsible with a malus
He admits the phone use; claim paid as responsible

title: A probationary driver enters the roundabout too early
type: Roundabout collision by a young driver with injury to the other driver
story: Policyholder's son Lucas, 19, a declared young driver on a probationary licence, entered a roundabout in Nantes in the rain without giving way and hit a Renault Mégane already on it. The Mégane's driver has neck pain and was off work for ten days.
statement: I thought I had time. The other car was coming round quite fast and the road was wet. I braked but slid into his door. The other driver was nice about it but said his neck hurt. My dad is going to kill me because of the premium.

accounts.text: Vehicle A (Peugeot 208, Lucas Martin): box "was entering a roundabout" ticked. Vehicle B (Mégane): box "was driving on a roundabout" ticked. Sketch shows A entering and striking B's right side. Observations by B: neck pain.
Cervical sprain after a road accident. Total temporary incapacity for work: 10 days. Physiotherapy prescribed.

whatHappened: A young driver misjudged the speed of a car already on the roundabout and slid into its side on the wet road.
damage: Mégane: right side doors, €4,100. Other driver: cervical sprain, 10 days off work. 208: front, €1,900.
missing: Final medical assessment of the other driver
innocent: A young driver misjudging speed on a wet roundabout is a common, honest error
questions: Ask the other driver about his treatment and any further time off work
steps: Accept responsibility under the inter-insurer agreement on the joint report
Compensate the other driver's injury under the Badinter law, through a medical assessment and an offer within the legal time limits
Pay the 208's damage if the policy includes own-damage cover
Apply the malus to the policy at renewal
assessment: Genuine negligence by a young driver. The other driver's injury must be compensated promptly under the Badinter law, which sets time limits for the insurer's offer.
action: Accept responsibility, compensate the injury and apply the malus.
outcomes: Injury settled after a medical assessment; malus applied
Policy premium rises at renewal; family adds a driver training course

title: Burnt on New Year's Eve in Strasbourg
type: Vehicle set on fire by unknown people
story: Policyholder's 2009 Renault Clio was set on fire by unknown people on New Year's Eve in a Strasbourg suburb, along with three other cars in the street. She has third-party cover with the fire and theft option. An expert valued the car at €1,800 before the fire. She expected more.
statement: Every year you hear about cars burning on New Year's Eve, and this year it was mine. I paid €6,000 for it four years ago and I spent money on new tyres and a clutch last year. €1,800 won't buy me another car.

accounts.text: Four vehicles set on fire in the same street between 00:30 and 01:15 on 1 January. Arson by unknown persons. No suspects identified.
Vehicle completely burnt. Value before the loss, based on the market for comparable vehicles, age and mileage: €1,800. Recent tyres and clutch noted, adding no significant market value.

whatHappened: Her car was one of four set alight in the street on New Year's Eve by people who have not been identified.
damage: Total loss, expert value €1,800.
missing: Evidence of comparable cars selling for more, if she disputes the value
innocent: A low valuation for an old car is normal and does not make the claim doubtful
questions: Ask whether she has evidence of comparable cars selling for more, to discuss the valuation
steps: Pay the expert value less any excess under the fire option
Explain that the policy pays the market value at the time of the loss, not the purchase price or recent repairs
Offer a counter-expertise if she disputes the value
assessment: Genuine. The frustration is about the valuation. A clear explanation and the option of a second expert opinion are the right responses.
action: Pay the expert value and explain how it was set.
outcomes: Paid €1,800; customer accepts
Counter-expertise raises the value to €2,100

title: A cyclist hurt in Lyon, and eight months to make an offer
type: Injured cyclist awaiting the compulsory compensation offer
story: Our policyholder turned across a cyclist, Ms Fontaine, in Lyon on 10 January. She suffered a fractured tibia and a broken wrist and has had two operations. Her doctors say her condition is not yet consolidated. It is now 25 August and no compensation offer has been sent to her. The file note says the handler was waiting for consolidation before making any offer.
statement: I've been off work since January. I've had two operations and physiotherapy three times a week. Nobody from the insurance has made me any offer, not even something provisional. My lawyer says there are rules about this.

accounts.text: Fracture of the left tibia with internal fixation, fracture of the right wrist. Second operation in May. Not consolidated; consolidation expected in 6 to 9 months.
Liability accepted. Awaiting consolidation before making an offer. Interim payment of €3,000 made in March.

whatHappened: A cyclist injured by our policyholder, with liability accepted. The insurer has wrongly waited for consolidation and is close to the legal deadline for an offer.
damage: Fractured tibia and wrist, two operations, off work for over seven months. Bicycle destroyed.
missing: A medical assessment for a provisional offer
Her loss of earnings documents
innocent: Waiting for consolidation is a common misunderstanding; the law requires a provisional offer meanwhile
questions: Ask her lawyer for her earnings documents
steps: Make a provisional offer now: the Code des assurances requires an offer to an injured victim within 8 months of the accident, which falls on 10 September, provisional if the condition is not consolidated
Base it on a medical assessment and her documented losses so far, with further interim payments if needed
Diary the final offer: it must follow within 5 months of the insurer learning of consolidation
Note the sanction: a late or manifestly insufficient offer attracts interest at double the legal rate
assessment: Genuine and serious, liability accepted. The insurer must make a provisional offer before 10 September rather than wait for consolidation.
action: Arrange a medical assessment and make a reasoned provisional offer before the 8-month deadline.
outcomes: Provisional offer made on 5 September; final offer after consolidation
Deadline missed; double interest applied by the court

title: Hit by an uninsured driver, with third-party cover only
type: Collision with an identified uninsured driver; compensation through the guarantee fund
story: Policyholder's car was hit at a junction in Marseille by a driver who ran a stop sign. The police identified the other driver and found he had no insurance. Policyholder has third-party-only cover, so his own policy does not pay for his car. He asked his insurer who will pay for the €3,800 of damage.
statement: The police said he had no insurance at all and they seized his car. I only have third-party cover because my car is old. Surely I'm not the one who has to pay when he broke the law?

accounts.text: Vehicle B failed to stop at a stop sign and struck vehicle A. Driver of vehicle B identified; no valid insurance; vehicle impounded. Driver of vehicle A not at fault.
Third-party liability (responsabilité civile) only. Legal protection option included.

whatHappened: A not-at-fault collision with an identified, uninsured driver. His own third-party policy does not cover his car; the national guarantee fund compensates victims of uninsured drivers.
damage: His Clio: front-left wing, bumper and headlamp, €3,800.
missing: The guarantee fund claim form
innocent: Owners of older cars often choose third-party cover without realising it leaves them exposed to uninsured drivers
questions: Confirm whether he has started a claim with the guarantee fund
steps: Explain that his third-party policy does not pay for his own car
Guide him to claim from the guarantee fund for victims of uninsured drivers (FGAO), within its time limits and subject to its own conditions and any deductible
Use his legal protection option to help him with the guarantee fund claim and any action against the driver
Record that he was not at fault so his bonus is not affected
assessment: Genuine and not at fault. The remedy is the guarantee fund, with help from his legal protection cover.
action: Explain the position, help him claim from the FGAO, and protect his bonus.
outcomes: Paid by the guarantee fund less its deductible
Legal protection recovers the deductible from the driver

title: Declared twelve days late because of a funeral abroad
type: Claim declared after the contractual period, with no prejudice to the insurer
story: Policyholder had a low-speed collision in a Toulouse car park and completed a joint accident report (constat amiable) with the other driver at the scene. She flew to Algeria the next day for a family funeral and declared the claim to her insurer twelve days after the accident. The claims clerk has proposed refusing the claim for late declaration.
statement: My uncle died and I left the next morning. I had the constat in my bag the whole time. I declared it the day after I got back. Nothing has changed, the other driver signed everything, and my car hasn't been repaired.

accounts.text: Signed by both drivers at the scene. Vehicle B reversing from a space into vehicle A which was passing behind. Both drivers' insurers and details complete.
Declaration received 12 days after the accident; contract requires 5 working days. Propose refusal for late declaration (déchéance).

whatHappened: A genuine car park collision with a complete joint report. The late declaration had a good reason and caused the insurer no harm.
damage: Her Peugeot 208: rear door and wheel arch, €1,900.
thirdParties: The other driver and their insurer
missing: Confirmation from the other insurer that it has the same constat
innocent: A bereavement abroad is an obvious reason for delay
questions: Confirm the car is still unrepaired for the assessor
steps: Do not refuse: under the Code des assurances, a late declaration can only lead to loss of cover if the insurer proves the delay caused it prejudice, and there is none here
Process the claim under the joint report and the inter-insurer agreements
Correct the clerk’s proposal and remind the team of the prejudice requirement
assessment: Genuine and payable. The delay is explained and harmless; refusing would be unlawful.
action: Accept the declaration and handle the claim on the constat.
outcomes: Claim handled normally; other insurer bears the cost under the constat
Team briefed on late declarations

title: Half at fault, charged the full malus
type: Complaint about the bonus-malus applied after shared liability
story: Policyholder and another driver both changed lanes into each other on a ring road in Nantes in the rain. The insurers settled liability 50/50. At renewal, his bonus-malus coefficient went up by 25%, the increase for a fully responsible claim. He complained in writing six weeks ago and has had only an automatic acknowledgment. He has asked how to go to the insurance mediator.
statement: Your own letter says liability was shared fifty-fifty. My friend who works in insurance says half liability means half the increase. I've written once and heard nothing. I want this corrected and I want to know how to complain properly.

accounts.text: Following the inter-insurer agreement, liability for this claim is shared: 50% your responsibility.
Bonus-malus coefficient: previous 0.68, new 0.85 (increase of 25% for a responsible claim).

whatHappened: A shared-liability collision rated as if he were fully responsible. The rules give half the increase for partial responsibility.
damage: His Mégane: front-right wing and door, repaired.
thirdParties: The other driver and their insurer
missing: The insurer’s substantive reply to the complaint
inconsistencies: Liability was settled at 50%; the malus applied was the full 25%
innocent: Rating systems sometimes apply a full malus by default when liability is entered as "responsible"
questions: Check how the liability split was entered in the rating system
steps: Correct the coefficient: for a partly responsible claim the increase is 12.5%, not 25%, giving 0.76 after rounding down to two decimals
Refund the premium overcharged and send a substantive written reply
Explain his rights: the insurer should answer complaints within two months, and he can refer the matter to La Médiation de l’Assurance if he remains unhappy
Check for other policyholders affected by the same rating error
assessment: Disputed on its face but clear on the rules: shared liability carries half the malus. The complaint should be upheld.
action: Correct the coefficient, refund the difference and reply substantively with his mediation rights.
outcomes: Coefficient corrected and premium refunded
Rating error found on other shared-liability claims and fixed

title: Hijacked in the driveway, found stripped in Soweto
type: Hijacking with tracker recovery
story: Policyholder was hijacked at gunpoint in her driveway in Randburg, Johannesburg, at about 19:40 as she waited for the gate to open. Two men took her Toyota Fortuner, her phone and her handbag. The tracking company found the vehicle the next morning in Soweto, stripped of its wheels, seats, airbags and infotainment unit.
statement: They came from behind the car when the gate was opening. One put a gun to the window and said get out. I left the keys and ran into the house. My daughter was inside. I called the tracking company from the landline and the police. I can't stop shaking.

accounts.text: Case of hijacking (robbery with aggravating circumstances) registered. Vehicle recovered by the tracking company the following day at an informal yard in Soweto. Vehicle stripped. No arrests.

Activation at 19:52 after the owner's call. Signal located at 03:10 in Soweto after the device was briefly jammed. Recovery with SAPS at 07:30. Wheels, front seats, airbags, steering wheel and infotainment removed.

whatHappened: She was hijacked at gunpoint at her gate, and the vehicle was stripped for parts overnight before the tracker located it.
damage: Fortuner stripped; repair estimate R245,000 against a retail value of R480,000. Phone and handbag stolen.
missing: The final assessment of whether repair or a total loss settlement is cheaper
innocent: The gap before the tracker found the car is explained by the thieves jamming the signal
questions: Ask whether she would like trauma counselling, which many policies include after a hijacking
Ask whether her phone and bag are covered under her household policy
steps: Repair the vehicle or settle as a total loss, whichever the assessment supports
Offer the trauma counselling benefit
Point her to her household policy for the phone and handbag
assessment: Genuine and traumatic. The claim is straightforward; the care with which it is handled matters as much as the payment.
action: Settle the vehicle claim promptly and offer trauma support.
outcomes: Repaired at an approved panel beater
Trauma counselling sessions taken up

title: Load-shedding, a dark intersection and two drivers who both stopped first
type: Intersection collision with traffic lights out
story: During load-shedding, the traffic lights were out at an intersection in Pretoria, so it was treated as a four-way stop. Policyholder's VW Polo and a Hyundai i20 collided in the middle. Each driver says they stopped first and the other went out of turn. There were no witnesses and no cameras, because the power was off.
statement: I stopped, looked, and went because I was first. The i20 came from the right and drove straight into my side. She says she was first, but she wasn't. There was nobody else around. Even the shops' cameras were off with the power.

accounts.text: I stopped at the line and the Polo was still approaching. I went, and he didn't stop properly, he rolled through and hit me. I've been driving this way to work for six years.

whatHappened: It cannot be established who arrived first. Both accounts are plausible and there is no independent evidence.
damage: Polo: driver's side doors, R28,000. i20: front, R19,000.
thirdParties: Ms Lerato Mokoena and her insurer
evidence: Photos of the cars and the impact points
missing: Any witness
Camera footage, unavailable because of the power cut
Accident reconstruction from the impact angles
inconsistencies: Each driver says they stopped first and the other went out of turn
innocent: At a dark four-way stop, two careful drivers can honestly each believe they were first
questions: Ask both drivers exactly where each car was when they first saw the other
Ask whether either car has a dashcam
steps: Look for any footage from cars or buildings with backup power
Compare the impact points with each version
If nothing else emerges, agree with the other insurer that each pays its own client's damage or a 50:50 split
assessment: Insufficient evidence to decide fault. Neither account is more credible than the other, so the fair outcome without new evidence is a shared result.
action: Pay the policyholder's own damage and agree a shared outcome with the other insurer.
outcomes: Each insurer pays its own client; excesses apply
Dashcam from a passing taxi found; liability decided on the footage

title: Rear-ended by an uninsured minibus taxi
type: Collision with an uninsured public transport vehicle
story: Policyholder's Toyota Corolla Cross was hit from behind by a minibus taxi at traffic lights on Klipfontein Road, Cape Town. The taxi owner has no insurance. The policyholder has a stiff neck and back pain. She asks who will pay for the car and for her medical costs.
statement: I was stopped at the red robot and the taxi just came into the back of me. The driver said sorry but he had no insurance. He gave me the owner's name and number. My neck has been sore since.

accounts.text: Rear-end collision at traffic lights. Minibus taxi struck the stationary Toyota. Taxi driver admitted fault. Taxi owner identified. No insurance for the taxi.

whatHappened: The minibus taxi failed to stop and hit her stationary car from behind at the red light; its driver admitted it at the scene.
damage: Corolla Cross rear end, R36,000. Neck and back strain.
thirdParties: Owner and driver of the minibus taxi
evidence: SAPS accident report with the admission
missing: Her medical records for an injury claim
innocent: Many minibus taxis are uninsured, and the driver's admission removes any doubt about fault
questions: Ask whether she has medical aid, which will usually pay her treatment first
steps: Pay her car repair under comprehensive cover less the excess
Pursue the taxi owner for the repair cost and her excess
Explain that her injury claim lies with the Road Accident Fund, not with her car insurer
assessment: Genuine. Her comprehensive cover pays the car, recovery from an uninsured taxi owner may be slow, and the Road Accident Fund handles her injury.
action: Repair under comprehensive, pursue recovery, and guide her to the Road Accident Fund.
outcomes: Repaired; partial recovery from the taxi owner in instalments
Road Accident Fund claim lodged for her injuries

title: Smash-and-grab at a red robot
type: Window smashed and laptop stolen at traffic lights
story: Policyholder was stopped at a red traffic light on a Johannesburg off-ramp when a man smashed the passenger window with a spark plug piece and took his laptop bag from the seat. The window and the laptop are both claimed under the car policy.
statement: It was over in two seconds, the glass exploded all over me. He grabbed the bag and ran down the embankment. My work laptop was in there. I opened a case at the police station.

accounts.text: Smash-and-grab theft from a vehicle at an off-ramp traffic light. Passenger window broken; laptop bag stolen. No injuries. No suspect apprehended.

whatHappened: An opportunist broke the window with a piece of spark plug porcelain and took the laptop bag in seconds at the traffic light.
damage: Passenger window, R3,400. Laptop and bag, about R21,000.
missing: Whether the laptop belongs to his employer
innocent: Smash-and-grabs at off-ramps are common in Johannesburg and match his account
questions: Ask whether the laptop is his or his employer's
Ask whether he has portable possessions cover on a household policy
steps: Pay the window under glass cover
Explain that the laptop is not covered by the car policy; it may be covered under his household portable possessions cover or his employer's insurance
Suggest smash-and-grab window film, which some insurers recommend
assessment: Genuine. The car policy pays for the glass; the laptop belongs under other cover. Pointing him to the right policy is the useful step.
action: Pay the glass and redirect the laptop claim.
outcomes: Window replaced; laptop paid by his employer's insurer

title: A case number that belongs to another crime
type: Theft claim with a false police case number
story: Policyholder claimed R38,000 for the theft of the canopy and tools from his Ford Ranger bakkie, saying it was broken into outside a client's site in Gqeberha. He gave a SAPS case number. When the insurer verified it, the station said the number belongs to a burglary at a different address recorded months earlier.
statement: I opened the case at the station the next morning, the lady at the desk gave me the number on a piece of paper. Maybe she wrote it wrong. The canopy was cut off and all my tools were inside. I need them back to work.

accounts.text: The case number provided relates to a residential burglary registered five months earlier at a different address. No case registered by the policyholder on or around the stated date at this station.
Replacement canopy R19,500 and a list of power tools R18,500. The quotation is dated one day before the claimed theft.

whatHappened: Unclear. A clerical error is possible, but no case was registered at all, and the replacement quote pre-dates the claimed theft.
damage: Claimed canopy and tools, R38,000.
evidence: Supplier quotation dated before the theft
missing: A genuine case registration
Photos of the cut canopy mounts
The client's confirmation that he was on site
inconsistencies: He says he opened a case; the station has no record of it, and the number belongs to another crime
The replacement quotation is dated before the claimed theft
indicators: False or borrowed case number
Quotation obtained before the loss
innocent: A clerk can write a number wrongly
He may have priced a canopy earlier for another reason
questions: Ask him to go back to the station and obtain written confirmation of his case
Ask why the quotation is dated the day before
steps: Give him the chance to produce a valid case registration
Check the canopy mounts and the client site visit
Decline and refer if no case exists
assessment: Potential fraud with two strong warning signs. He should be given a fair chance to correct a clerical error, but if no case was ever opened, the claim cannot stand.
action: Ask for a valid case registration; decline and refer if none is produced.
outcomes: Produces a valid case number from another station; claim paid
Cannot produce a case; claim declined and referred

title: Overtaking on a blind rise, with an expired licence card
type: Head-on collision while overtaking, and a licence card issue
story: Policyholder overtook a truck across a solid barrier line on a blind rise on the N2 near George and collided head-on with an oncoming Kia Picanto. The Picanto's driver has a broken leg. The policyholder's driving licence card had expired four months earlier, although he holds a valid licence category.
statement: The truck was slow and I thought I could see far enough. I was wrong. I'll take the blame. My licence card expired, I've been waiting for an appointment to renew it, the system is a mess. I've been driving for 30 years.

accounts.text: Head-on collision. Ford Ranger overtaking across a barrier line on a rise struck the oncoming Kia Picanto. Driver of the Ranger in possession of an expired driving licence card; licence record valid on the national system. Picanto driver hospitalised with a fractured femur.
We will not pay for loss, damage or liability if the vehicle is driven by a person who does not hold a valid driving licence for that class of vehicle.
