whatHappened: A dangerous overtaking manoeuvre caused the crash. The expired card is a separate administrative issue; his licence itself is valid on the national record.
damage: Ranger: front end, R165,000. Picanto: total loss, about R120,000. Picanto driver: fractured femur.
missing: The Picanto driver's insurer details
Proof of his renewal appointment
innocent: Licence card renewal backlogs are well known, and his licence was otherwise valid
questions: Ask for proof of his renewal booking
steps: Decide whether an expired card means he did not hold a valid licence; the Ombudsman for Short-term Insurance has looked at whether such technicalities caused the loss
Pay the Picanto's damage under his third-party liability cover if the licence point is not relied on
Explain that the Picanto driver's injury claim lies against the Road Accident Fund
assessment: Clear negligence in the driving, and a weak ground to refuse cover in the licence card. Relying on the expired card when the licence itself is valid and the card played no part in the crash is likely to be seen as unfair.
action: Treat the licence issue as immaterial, pay the third party and his own damage under the policy, and record the claim as at fault.
outcomes: Claims paid; premium increased at renewal
Insurer relies on the expired card; ombud rules it must pay

title: Found on bricks in Durban, with all four mags gone
type: Theft of wheels overnight
story: Policyholder found her VW Polo GTI on bricks outside her townhouse complex in Durban North, with all four alloy wheels and tyres stolen. The car's brake discs and sills were damaged where it was jacked up. She had locking wheel nuts fitted, which were broken off.
statement: I came out at six to go to gym and the car was sitting on bricks. They broke the locking nuts with something. The security guard says he didn't see anything. I opened a case at Durban North.

accounts.text: Theft of four mag wheels with tyres from a vehicle parked on the street outside a complex. Vehicle found on bricks. Locking nuts forcibly removed. No suspects.
Four 18-inch alloy wheels and tyres R42,000, brake disc replacement front R6,200, sill repair R3,800, new locking nuts R900. Total R52,900.

whatHappened: Thieves jacked the car up overnight, forced off the locking nuts and took all four wheels, damaging the discs and sills.
damage: Wheels, tyres, brake discs, sills and locking nuts, R52,900.
evidence: Photos of the car on bricks and the broken nuts
missing: Where the car is usually parked, for future risk advice
innocent: Forced locking nuts show the thieves came equipped, which fits a professional wheel theft
questions: Ask whether she can park inside the complex in future
steps: Pay under comprehensive less the excess
Note the broken locking nuts, which show she met any security requirement
assessment: Genuine. Wheel theft is common, and the broken locking nuts show she took reasonable precautions.
action: Pay the claim.
outcomes: Paid R52,900 less the excess

title: Torched outside his shop during the unrest
type: Vehicle burnt during public unrest; special risks cover applies
story: Policyholder's bakkie was set alight by a crowd during violent unrest in Pietermaritzburg while it was parked outside his hardware shop. A claims handler has drafted a rejection under the comprehensive section's exclusion for riot, strike and civil commotion. The policy schedule shows a SASRIA premium charged every month for special risks cover on the vehicle.
statement: The crowd came down the street throwing things and setting cars alight, I locked myself in the shop. By the time it was safe the bakkie was burnt to the frame. The police came the next day and gave me a case number. I pay for SASRIA every month, it's on my statement.

accounts.text: Public violence and malicious damage to property during unrest in the area. Several vehicles and shops set alight. Complainant's vehicle burnt while parked. Case registered.
Comprehensive motor. Exclusion: riot, strike, civil commotion and public disorder. SASRIA special risks cover: included, premium charged monthly.

whatHappened: The vehicle was destroyed in public unrest. That is excluded from the comprehensive section but is exactly what the SASRIA cover on his schedule is for.
damage: Toyota Hilux burnt out, total loss; retail value about R310,000.
missing: Any news or police reports confirming unrest in that street on that date, if SASRIA asks
innocent: Handlers who see the riot exclusion may not check the SASRIA section of the schedule
questions: Confirm the date and street against the reports of unrest
steps: Do not reject: the riot exclusion removes the loss from the comprehensive section, but the SASRIA cover on his schedule responds to riot and public disorder
Submit the claim under the SASRIA cover with the SAPS case number and evidence of the unrest, within the required time limits
Explain the process to him and keep him informed
Correct the draft rejection
assessment: Genuine and covered under SASRIA. The draft rejection looks only at the comprehensive exclusion.
action: Process the claim under the SASRIA cover and withdraw the rejection.
outcomes: Paid under SASRIA as a total loss
Handler guidance updated to check special risks cover

title: A pothole reported five weeks earlier on the municipal app
type: Pothole damage with a possible recovery from the municipality
story: Policyholder hit a deep, water-filled pothole on a municipal road in Pretoria at night, damaging two rims, two tyres and the front suspension. The claim is R18,400. A resident's report about the same pothole was logged on the municipality's service app five weeks before, with a reference number and a photo. The insurer is paying the claim and is considering recovery from the municipality.
statement: It was raining and the hole was full of water, it looked like a puddle. The bang was huge and two tyres went flat. A neighbour showed me that people had reported that exact pothole weeks ago and nothing was done.

accounts.text: Service request logged five weeks before the incident: "large pothole, danger to vehicles", with a photo and location matching the incident. Status: open, not attended.
Two alloy rims, two tyres, front left lower control arm and wheel alignment. R18,400.

whatHappened: A genuine pothole impact on a defect the municipality had been told about and left unrepaired.
damage: Two rims, two tyres, front suspension arm; R18,400.
evidence: Photos of the pothole at night
missing: Measurements of the pothole
Whether warning signs were placed
innocent: A water-filled pothole at night looks like a puddle, so hitting it is not careless driving
questions: Ask her for daylight photos and measurements of the pothole
steps: Pay her claim under the comprehensive cover, less her excess
Send the municipality written notice of the claim within six months, as the law on legal proceedings against organs of state requires, or the recovery may be lost
Use the service request to show the municipality knew of the danger and did nothing for five weeks
Include her excess in the recovery
assessment: Genuine, with a good recovery case because the defect had been reported. The six-month notice is the key deadline.
action: Pay the claim and serve notice on the municipality in time, using the prior report as evidence.
outcomes: Municipality settles after notice and the service request evidence
Recovery lost because notice was sent after six months

title: Hijacked at nine, but the tracker was cut at twenty to
type: Reported hijacking contradicted by tracking data
story: Policyholder reported that his Toyota Hilux was hijacked at gunpoint at 21:00 at a traffic light in Midrand. He opened a SAPS case at 23:30. The tracking company's data shows the vehicle drove to an address in Soshanguve at 20:15, stopped there, and the tracking unit raised a tamper alert at 20:40 before going offline. The Soshanguve address is registered to his brother-in-law.
statement: Two men with a gun came to my window at the robot and told me to get out. They drove off with the bakkie. I was so shocked I sat on the pavement for an hour before I went to the police. I don't know anything about Soshanguve, maybe the tracker is wrong.

accounts.text: 19:55 departed the policyholder's home. 20:15 arrived at an address in Soshanguve; ignition off. 20:40 tamper alert: unit power disconnected. No further signal. No movement recorded towards Midrand.
Complainant reports a hijacking at about 21:00 at an intersection in Midrand. Case opened at 23:30. No witnesses recorded. Intersection camera footage requested.

whatHappened: The bakkie was driven to his brother-in-law's address and the tracker was disconnected there before the time of the reported hijacking.
damage: Toyota Hilux reported hijacked; value about R480,000.
missing: Intersection camera footage in Midrand
His phone location data for the evening
inconsistencies: He says the bakkie was taken in Midrand at 21:00; the tracker shows it at a Soshanguve address with the unit disconnected at 20:40
indicators: Tracker disconnected at a relative’s address before the reported hijacking
Two-and-a-half hour delay before the police report
He denies knowing the address
innocent: Tracking units can misreport after tampering, but the tamper alert itself came before the reported time
questions: Ask him to account for the vehicle’s journey to Soshanguve
Ask the brother-in-law whether the bakkie was at his house
steps: Interview him with the tracking data, in line with the policy’s claims conditions
Get the Midrand intersection footage through SAPS
Do not settle while the tracking data is unexplained
If the data stands, reject the claim and report the false statement to SAPS
assessment: Potential fraud with strong data: the vehicle and tracker were at a relative's address before the reported hijacking.
action: Investigate with the tracking evidence and footage before any decision.
outcomes: Bakkie found at a scrapyard linked to the brother-in-law; claim rejected
Claim withdrawn after the interview

title: Rejected for no tracker, a condition nobody mentioned on the phone
type: Theft claim rejected for a tracking device condition not disclosed at sale
story: Policyholder's Toyota Fortuner was stolen from a shopping centre parking lot in Johannesburg. The claim was rejected because the policy requires an approved tracking device for vehicles of that model and value, and none was fitted. He bought the policy by phone. The call recording shows the sales agent did not mention the tracking condition. The policy documents emailed afterwards include it in the schedule's endorsements.
statement: The agent asked about my car, my address and whether I park in a garage. Nothing about a tracker. I would have fitted one, it's a few hundred rand a month. Now I've lost a car I'm still paying for. I'm going to the ombud.

accounts.text: Eighteen-minute call. Questions on vehicle, overnight parking, driver history. No mention of a tracking device requirement. Agent says: "You're fully comprehensive, you're covered for theft and hijacking."
Theft and hijacking cover for this vehicle is conditional on an approved tracking device being fitted and active. Documents emailed the day after the sale.

whatHappened: A genuine theft. The tracking condition is in the documents but was not disclosed in the sale, and the agent described the cover as complete.
damage: Toyota Fortuner stolen; value about R560,000; finance outstanding.
missing: Whether he read the emailed documents
Whether a tracker would likely have led to recovery
inconsistencies: The agent said he was covered for theft; the documents make theft cover conditional on a tracker
innocent: Customers buying by phone rely on what the agent says
questions: Ask whether he received and read the emailed schedule
steps: Review the rejection under the treating customers fairly principles and the Policyholder Protection Rules: a material condition that was not disclosed at sale, with the agent stating full theft cover, is unlikely to be upheld by the ombud
Consider paying the claim, or at least a fair settlement, rather than relying on the endorsement
Respond to his complaint in writing with reasons and explain his right to approach the ombud
Fix the sales script so material conditions are disclosed on the call
assessment: Disputed, but the sales failure weighs heavily against the insurer. Relying on an undisclosed condition is likely to be found unfair.
action: Reconsider the rejection, likely pay, and fix the sales disclosure.
outcomes: Claim paid after internal review; sales script changed
Ombud recommends payment in full

title: A motorcyclist who braked for no reason, and looked back first
type: Induced rear-end collision by a motorcyclist
story: Policyholder's Toyota Corolla Altis hit the back of a motorcycle on the Pan-Island Expressway when the rider braked sharply in free-flowing traffic. The rider and his pillion have claimed for injuries and medical leave through a law firm. The policyholder's front and rear dashcams recorded the event.
statement: The bike was in front of me in lane two, then he looked over his shoulder at me twice and suddenly braked hard. There was nothing in front of him. I hit his rear wheel at low speed. They both fell over very slowly, like they were sitting down.

accounts.text: 10:14:02 motorcycle in lane 2, traffic ahead clear for over 100 metres. 10:14:05 rider turns his head towards the car. 10:14:07 rider turns his head again. 10:14:08 motorcycle brakes sharply without any traffic or obstacle ahead. 10:14:09 low-speed contact. Rider and pillion lower themselves to the road.

Our clients were travelling normally when your insured failed to keep a safe distance and collided violently with the rear of the motorcycle. Both suffered injuries and have been given 21 days of medical leave each. We claim medical expenses, loss of earnings and damages.

whatHappened: The rider deliberately braked without reason after checking the car was close behind, to cause a collision and claim for injuries.
damage: Corolla: front bumper scratched. Motorcycle: rear mudguard. Injury claims for two people with 21 days of medical leave each.
missing: The riders' medical records
Any links to other similar claims
inconsistencies: The lawyers describe a violent collision caused by the insured; the footage shows the rider braking for no reason after looking back twice
indicators: Sudden braking in clear traffic after looking back at the car
Exaggerated fall
Long medical leave after a very low-speed contact
innocent: None that explains looking back twice and braking with a clear road ahead
questions: Ask the rider why he braked
steps: Deny liability and disclose the footage to the lawyers
Report the case to the police as a suspected staged accident
Check the riders and the law firm against other claims for similar patterns
assessment: Confirmed fraud on the footage. Staged motorcycle accidents are a known problem in Singapore and the authorities prosecute them; the dashcam leaves little room for doubt.
action: Deny, disclose the footage and report to the police.
outcomes: Claims withdrawn; riders charged with cheating
Policyholder's no-claim discount protected

title: A small scrape in the rain, reported a week late
type: Accident not reported within the required time
story: Policyholder's Honda Vezel scraped a Mazda 3 while changing lanes in heavy rain in Tampines. They exchanged details and she decided not to claim because the damage looked small. Seven days later the insurer received a third-party claim for S$4,200 from the Mazda owner. She had not reported the accident, as the policy and the Motor Claims Framework require within 24 hours.
statement: It was a small scratch on his door and on my bumper. I thought we would settle it ourselves, I even offered him cash. Then he went to his workshop and now it's S$4,200. I didn't know I had to report even if I don't claim.

accounts.who: Third-party claim from the Mazda owner's insurer
accounts.text: Our insured's vehicle was damaged when your insured changed lanes into it. Repairs carried out at an authorised workshop: right rear door, quarter panel and blending of adjacent panels, S$4,200. Photos and the report attached.

whatHappened: A genuine minor lane change scrape. She did not know she had to report it within 24 hours even without making her own claim.
damage: Mazda: S$4,200 as repaired. Vezel: bumper scuff.
thirdParties: Owner of the Mazda 3 and his insurer
missing: Independent assessment of the Mazda repair, which was done before the insurer could inspect
innocent: Many drivers think reporting is needed only when they want to claim
questions: Ask for her photos of the Mazda at the scene, to compare with the repaired damage
steps: Accept liability for the lane change
Check the S$4,200 repair against the scene photos, as the insurer could not inspect
Explain the reporting rule and any penalty the policy applies for late reporting
assessment: Genuine, with a reporting breach. Late reporting allowed the repair to be done without inspection, so the cost should be checked, but the breach does not change who was at fault.
action: Settle the third-party claim at a verified amount and explain the reporting rule.
outcomes: Settled at S$3,600 after review; her no-claim discount reduced at renewal
Policy applies a late-reporting penalty

title: Riding across the crossing instead of pushing
type: Collision with a personal mobility device user at a crossing
story: Policyholder turned left at a junction in Jurong West and hit a man riding a power-assisted bicycle across the pedestrian crossing at speed while the green man was showing. The rider broke his wrist. Riders are required to dismount and push across pedestrian crossings.
statement: I was turning left slowly and checked for pedestrians. There was nobody walking. Then he shot out from behind the bus stop on the bicycle, riding fast across the crossing. I braked but touched his back wheel. I didn't see him until he was in front of me.

accounts.text: Green man showing. Power-assisted bicycle approaches along the footpath at an estimated 20 km/h and continues onto the crossing without slowing or dismounting. Car turning left at walking speed. Contact at the second white stripe.
I was crossing on the green man. The car turned without giving way to me. My wrist is broken and I cannot work as a delivery rider for eight weeks.

whatHappened: The car turned into the crossing when it should have given way to anyone crossing, and the rider rode onto the crossing at speed when he should have dismounted. Both share the blame.
damage: Rider: fractured wrist, eight weeks off work. Bicycle rear wheel damaged. Car: minor scratch.
thirdParties: The rider of the power-assisted bicycle
missing: The rider's earnings records
inconsistencies: The rider says he was crossing normally; the camera shows him riding onto the crossing at about 20 km/h
innocent: Many riders do not dismount at crossings; the driver may have looked for walkers, not riders
questions: Ask the rider whether his bicycle is registered and whether he had his own insurance
steps: Accept partial liability: turning drivers must give way to people on the crossing
Argue contributory negligence for riding across at speed instead of dismounting
Negotiate a settlement with a reduction for his share
assessment: A genuine accident with shared fault. The driver should have given way, but the rider's speed and failure to dismount contributed. A negotiated split, perhaps 60:40 in the rider's favour, is realistic.
action: Negotiate an apportioned settlement.
outcomes: Settled at 60% of the assessed damages
Court finds 50:50 contributory negligence

title: A private-hire passenger hurt when another car ran the red
type: Passenger injury in a private-hire car with correct cover
story: Policyholder, a private-hire driver with the correct private-hire insurance, was hit on the passenger side at a junction on Bukit Timah Road by a car that ran a red light in heavy rain. His passenger, a 34-year-old woman, fractured two ribs. The red light camera recorded the other car.
statement: My light was green and I was going straight. The other car came from the left through the red, very fast for the rain. My passenger was in the back on the left side, she was crying in pain. I called the ambulance and the police.

accounts.text: Red light violation recorded at 21:42 by the vehicle that struck the private-hire car. Signal red for 2.1 seconds when the violating vehicle crossed the stop line.

accounts.who: Hospital discharge summary for the passenger
accounts.text: Fractures of the left 7th and 8th ribs. Admitted for two days for pain control. Medical leave for four weeks.

whatHappened: The other driver crossed the stop line 2.1 seconds into the red, as the camera recorded, and hit the passenger side of the private-hire car.
damage: Private-hire car: left side doors, S$9,800, and loss of income while it is repaired. Passenger: two fractured ribs.
thirdParties: Driver of the car that ran the red light and his insurer
missing: The other driver's insurer's acceptance of liability
innocent: A private-hire driver claiming lost income is normal, and he held the right cover for the work
questions: Ask the passenger whether she wants to claim directly from the other driver's insurer
steps: Pursue the other driver's insurer for the car repair and the driver's loss of income
Direct the passenger's injury claim to the other driver's insurer, which is liable
Confirm the policyholder's no-claim discount is protected as he was not at fault
assessment: Genuine and clear. The camera record establishes fault, the policyholder had the right cover for private-hire work, and the passenger should be compensated by the at-fault insurer.
action: Recover from the at-fault insurer and protect the policyholder's no-claim discount.
outcomes: Other insurer pays the repair, the driver's loss of income and the passenger's injury claim

title: A flowerpot from the 14th floor onto the windscreen
type: Damage from an object thrown or fallen from a high-rise flat
story: A ceramic flowerpot fell from a high floor of an HDB block in Ang Mo Kio onto policyholder's Mazda CX-5 parked at the open car park below, smashing the windscreen and denting the bonnet. The police are investigating it as killer litter. The flat it came from has not yet been identified.
statement: There was a huge crash and when I looked out of my window, my car had soil and broken pot all over it. Thank goodness nobody was walking there. Neighbours said it came from the 14th floor or higher. I called the police.

accounts.text: Report of an object falling from height onto a vehicle at the open car park. Investigation into high-rise littering opened. Surveillance cameras requested from the town council.
Windscreen replacement with camera recalibration S$1,450. Bonnet dent repair and respray S$980. Total S$2,430.

whatHappened: A flowerpot fell or was thrown from a high floor of the block and landed on the parked car.
damage: Windscreen and bonnet, S$2,430.
thirdParties: The unidentified occupant of the flat
evidence: Photos with soil and pot fragments
missing: Identity of the flat, if the town council cameras find it
innocent: Objects falling from high-rise flats are a known problem in Singapore, and the soil and pot fragments match
questions: Ask whether her policy has a windscreen benefit that does not affect her no-claim discount
steps: Pay the windscreen under the windscreen benefit and the bonnet under own damage
Recover from the occupant if the police identify the flat
assessment: Genuine. The windscreen benefit often has no effect on the no-claim discount; the bonnet may, unless the occupant is identified and the cost recovered.
action: Pay and pursue recovery if the flat is identified.
outcomes: Paid; flat identified and the occupant pays for the bonnet after prosecution

title: "I was driving", said the owner, but he was asleep in the back
type: Owner claims to be the driver to keep cover
story: Policyholder reported that he hit a lamp post near Sentosa Gateway at 03:20 while driving his BMW 320i home from a party. His policy excludes drivers under 25 who are not named on it. A car park gantry camera, 10 minutes before the crash, shows a young man driving and the policyholder in the back seat.
statement: I was driving, it was my fault, I was tired. My friend Daryl was in the car with me. Nobody else drove.

accounts.text: 03:09:44 exit gantry. Driver: young man with short dyed hair, wearing a white shirt. Rear seat: a man matching the policyholder, apparently asleep against the window. The car's plate is clearly visible.
Arrived 03:41. Two men at the scene. The younger man with dyed hair said "I was going too fast round the bend". The older man then said he had been driving.

whatHappened: Very probably his friend, under 25 and not named on the policy, was driving, and the policyholder took the blame to keep the claim within cover.
damage: BMW front end and airbags, S$18,600. Lamp post, claimed by the Land Transport Authority.
thirdParties: The Land Transport Authority, owner of the lamp post
evidence: Tow operator's note of the friend's comment
missing: The friend's own statement
Phone location data
Any traffic camera between the car park and the crash
inconsistencies: He says he was driving; the gantry camera 10 minutes earlier shows his friend driving and him asleep in the back
The tow operator heard the friend say he was going too fast
indicators: Driver identity changed to fit the policy terms
Excluded young driver at the wheel
innocent: They might have swapped seats in the 10 minutes between the car park and the crash, though there is no reason to think so
questions: Ask the friend, separately, who was driving at the time of the crash
Ask the policyholder why the gantry camera shows him in the back
steps: Interview both men separately
Decline the own-damage claim if the friend was driving, as an excluded driver
Pay the lamp post under the third-party cover as required by law, and recover from the policyholder
Refer for the false statement
assessment: Strong evidence that the owner is covering for an excluded young driver. A seat swap is possible but unlikely; the friend's own words at the scene point the same way. A false statement about the driver is a serious misrepresentation.
action: Interview both, decline own damage and recover the third-party outlay if the evidence holds.
outcomes: Friend admits driving; own damage declined and policy cancelled
Both maintain the account; case referred to the police for a false statement

title: A side-swipe in Johor Bahru, and two versions at the merge
type: Collision in Malaysia on a Singapore policy, with a disputed lane merge
story: Policyholder drove his Singapore-registered car to Johor Bahru for the weekend. Where two lanes merge after a traffic light, his car and a Malaysian car side-swiped each other. Both drivers made police reports in Johor within 24 hours, each blaming the other. The Malaysian driver has claimed against the policyholder's Singapore insurer for repairs and three weeks of car rental. The policyholder reported the accident to his insurer the next morning.
statement: My lane was the one that continued, his lane ended with arrows to merge. He tried to squeeze in at the last moment and hit my front door. I made the police report at the station near the checkpoint before driving back. I have a front dashcam.

accounts.text: Complainant states the Singapore car moved left into his lane while merging and hit his car. Complainant's car damaged on the right side.

Front camera: the policyholder's lane continues; arrows painted in the left lane indicate it ends. The Malaysian car comes alongside from the ending lane and moves right; contact at the policyholder's front-left door. The policyholder's car stays within its lane markings.

whatHappened: The Malaysian driver merged from an ending lane into the policyholder's continuing lane. The dashcam supports the policyholder.
damage: Policyholder's Mazda 3: front-left door and wing. Malaysian car: right-side doors.
thirdParties: The Malaysian driver and his insurer
missing: The Malaysian car's own insurer and any dashcam
Rental invoices
inconsistencies: Each driver says the other moved into their lane
innocent: Unfamiliar road markings across the border cause genuine misunderstandings
questions: Ask the Malaysian driver’s side for any footage and the rental invoices
steps: Confirm the policy’s geographical area covers West Malaysia, and that both reports were made in time
Deny the third-party claim on the dashcam evidence, or negotiate a split if the other side produces contrary footage
Handle the policyholder’s own damage under his cover and pursue the Malaysian driver’s insurer for recovery
Use a Malaysian adjuster for the third-party side if needed
assessment: Disputed, but the dashcam and the lane markings favour the policyholder. The Malaysian driver merged from the ending lane.
action: Defend the third-party claim on the footage and recover the policyholder's losses.
outcomes: Malaysian insurer accepts liability after viewing the footage
Settled 70/30 in the policyholder’s favour

title: Rear-ended by his friend, with a dent from three months ago
type: Friends’ collision used to claim for old damage
story: Policyholder Daniel Koh reported that he rear-ended his friend Jason Lim's car at low speed in a Jurong car park. Both reported the accident under the Motor Claims Framework and Mr Lim has claimed S$6,900 against Mr Koh's policy. The damage includes a rust-pitted dent in the bumper and a tail lamp with dirt inside its crack. The workshop is run by Mr Koh's cousin. A photo on Mr Lim's social media from three months earlier shows the same dent.
statement: (Daniel Koh, our policyholder) I was slow, maybe 10 km/h, and I tapped Jason's car when he stopped suddenly. We're friends so we went to my cousin's workshop, he gives good prices. I told him to claim from my insurance since it was my fault.

accounts.text: Fresh contact marks on the bumper corner consistent with a low-speed tap. Separate dent with rust pitting in the paint, older than the incident. Tail lamp crack contains dirt and moisture. Estimated fresh damage S$1,300.
Photo posted by Mr Lim three months before the incident, showing his car at a car meet. The dent on the rear bumper is visible in the same position.

whatHappened: A real low-speed tap between friends, used to put older damage on the policyholder's insurance.
damage: Fresh contact marks on the bumper corner. Older dent and cracked tail lamp included in the S$6,900 claim.
missing: Car park CCTV
The workshop's photos before repair
inconsistencies: The claim includes a dent visible in a photo taken three months before the incident
indicators: Claim between friends repaired at a relative’s workshop
Old damage included in the estimate
Claim far above the fresh damage
innocent: Friends often use a familiar workshop, and the workshop may have quoted everything it saw
questions: Ask Mr Lim to explain the dent in the earlier photo
Ask the car park for CCTV
steps: Offer to pay the fresh damage only, about S$1,300, and decline the older items with the photo as the reason
Put the photo to both men in interviews
Refer to the fraud team if they persist with the full amount
Note the link between the policyholder and the workshop
assessment: Potential fraud: a genuine minor tap with older damage added, arranged between friends and a related workshop.
action: Pay only the fresh damage and investigate if the full claim is pressed.
outcomes: Claim reduced to S$1,300 and accepted
Referred after the claimant insists on the full amount

title: "I was driving," until the workshop camera showed her son
type: Wrong driver given to avoid the young and inexperienced driver excesses
story: Policyholder reported that she hit a bollard while parking at a condominium in Tampines. Her policy has a S$600 excess, plus additional excesses of S$2,500 each for a young driver and an inexperienced driver. The car's own camera and the condominium's CCTV show her 22-year-old son, who passed his test a year ago, driving. When shown the footage she admitted it and apologized.
statement: I panicked. My son is careful, he just misjudged the bollard. I knew there was a big excess for young drivers and I thought it was a small accident, it wouldn't matter who drove. I'm sorry, I should have told the truth.

accounts.text: A young man drives the car into the bay and strikes the bollard. He gets out from the driver's seat. The policyholder arrives ten minutes later.

Excess: S$600. Additional excess S$2,500 where the driver is under 27, and S$2,500 where the driver has held a licence for less than 2 years. Named drivers: policyholder only. Unnamed drivers permitted with the additional excesses.

whatHappened: A genuine bollard strike by her son. She named herself as the driver to avoid S$5,000 of additional excesses, then admitted it.
damage: Toyota Corolla Altis: front bumper and grille, S$2,900.
missing: The son's own account of the incident
inconsistencies: Her report named herself; the footage shows her son driving
indicators: False statement about the driver to reduce the excess
innocent: A parent protecting a child in a moment of panic, corrected before payment
questions: Confirm the son’s licence date
steps: Apply the correct excesses for the actual driver: S$600 plus both additional excesses; with damage of S$2,900, the excesses exceed the loss, so nothing is payable
Record the false statement and treat it seriously: a deliberate misstatement in a claim can justify refusing the claim and may affect future cover
Warn her in writing, as the statement was corrected before any payment
Offer to add her son as a named driver at the correct premium
assessment: Suspicious conduct on a genuine incident: a deliberate but corrected misstatement. Applying the correct excesses resolves the claim.
action: Apply the correct excesses, record and warn about the false statement, and update the named drivers.
outcomes: No payment due after excesses; warning issued
Insurer declines to renew after a second misstatement

title: A delivery rider’s S$85,000 claim and the online assessment tool
type: Injury claim valued above the court’s online assessment range
story: Our policyholder turned right across a delivery rider at a junction in Tampines. The rider fractured his wrist. His lawyers claim S$85,000, including six months of lost earnings. The court's online assessment tool, using past cases, suggests a range for the wrist injury well below that and a liability split favouring the rider. The delivery platform's records show he resumed deliveries three weeks after the accident.
statement: (Through his lawyers) Our client could not work for six months and still has pain gripping the handlebars. He supports his parents. The insurer's driver turned without looking.

accounts.text: Liability: right-turning car mainly at fault; rider may bear a small share for speed. Quantum for a wrist fracture with good recovery: a range far below the amount claimed. Loss of earnings to be proved by records.
Account inactive for 21 days after the accident date. Deliveries resumed thereafter at about 80% of previous weekly volume, returning to normal within two months.

whatHappened: A genuine injury mainly caused by our policyholder. The claimed earnings loss is overstated: he returned to work after three weeks.
damage: Fractured wrist treated with a cast; physiotherapy. Motorcycle repaired.
missing: A specialist report on any lasting grip weakness
inconsistencies: Six months of lost earnings claimed; platform records show work resumed after three weeks
indicators: Earnings claim contradicted by platform records
innocent: He may have worked in pain at reduced volume, which is a real loss for a shorter period
questions: Ask for his earnings before and after the accident from the platform
steps: Accept that liability rests mainly on the policyholder
Value the injury using the online assessment range and the medical evidence
Pay lost earnings for the three weeks off and the reduced volume afterwards, on the platform records
Make a reasoned offer and use the tool’s range in negotiation or mediation
assessment: Genuine injury, overstated claim. The assessment tool and the platform records set a fair range well below the demand.
action: Offer within the tool's range with proven earnings losses.
outcomes: Settled at S$31,000
Resolved at court-assisted mediation within the tool’s range

title: Whiplash in Cork, and a fitness contest three weeks later
type: Genuine rear-end collision with an exaggerated injury
story: The insurer's policyholder admitted rear-ending a Ford Focus at traffic lights in Cork in the rain. The Focus driver claimed for a soft-tissue neck and back injury through the Injuries Resolution Board, describing six months of severe pain that stopped him working out or lifting his child. His public social media shows him competing in a fitness competition three weeks after the accident.
statement: Claimant, in his application: Since the accident I have had constant pain in my neck and lower back. I could not return to the gym, I struggle to lift my two-year-old, and I have had to give up five-a-side football. I have attended physiotherapy weekly.

accounts.text: I was slowing for the lights and my foot slipped on the wet pedal. I hit his car at maybe 10 or 15 km/h. He got out, stretched his neck and said "I'll be grand". His car had a dented bumper.

Public posts by the claimant 3 weeks after the accident: video of him performing deadlifts at a local fitness competition with the caption "new PB 180kg". Further posts at 6 and 10 weeks show heavy training and a five-a-side match.

whatHappened: A genuine low-speed rear-end collision that may have caused some short-term stiffness. The claimed severity and duration are contradicted by his own posts.
damage: Focus rear bumper, €1,250. Injury claim presented as six months of severe soft-tissue injury.
missing: The claimant's GP records
An independent medical examination
inconsistencies: He says he could not return to the gym or play football; his posts show heavy lifting at three weeks and football at ten weeks
indicators: Injury severity contradicted by public social media
Account of daily limitations inconsistent with his activities
innocent: Some people train through pain, and posts do not show how he felt afterwards
A short-term injury may still be real
questions: Ask the claimant to explain the training videos in the light of his description
Ask his physiotherapist about his progress at three and ten weeks
steps: Pay the property damage
Value any genuine injury under the Personal Injuries Guidelines for a minor soft-tissue injury that resolved within weeks
If the claim is pursued in court as presented, ask the court to dismiss it under section 26 of the Civil Liability and Courts Act 2004 for knowingly false or misleading evidence
assessment: A genuine accident and probably a minor genuine injury, but the claim as presented is exaggerated. Irish law allows a court to dismiss an injury claim entirely where the claimant knowingly gives false or misleading evidence, which gives the insurer a strong position.
action: Offer a modest amount for a short-term injury; defend and seek dismissal if he maintains the exaggerated claim.
outcomes: Accepts a small settlement for a minor injury
Court dismisses the claim under section 26

title: A slip onto a parked car after the Auckland rain
type: Landslip damage to a parked car
story: After days of heavy rain in Auckland, a bank behind policyholder's property in Titirangi collapsed and pushed mud and a tree onto her Toyota Corolla parked in the driveway. The house was also affected. She asks whether the government's natural hazards insurer covers the car as well as the house.
statement: We heard a roar in the night and in the morning half the bank was on the driveway with the car buried to the windows. The council has red-stickered the back of the section. I've lodged a claim for the house, but they told me the car isn't part of it.

accounts.text: Vehicle partially buried in mud and debris. Roof and bonnet dented by the tree, windscreen broken, mud inside through the broken windows. Repair estimate exceeds the market value of $9,800. Total loss.

whatHappened: Days of rain saturated the bank behind the house until it collapsed, burying the car in mud and a fallen tree.
damage: Corolla total loss, market value $9,800.
missing: Confirmation of any finance on the car
innocent: Slips after days of heavy rain are common in Auckland's hillside suburbs, and the council notice confirms this one
questions: Ask whether there is finance on the car
steps: Settle the car as a total loss under her comprehensive motor policy
Explain that the Natural Hazards Commission covers homes and some land, not vehicles, and that injuries would be covered by ACC
assessment: Genuine. Her motor policy is the right cover for the car; the government scheme covers the house and land.
action: Settle the total loss promptly.
outcomes: Paid $9,800 less the excess

title: Crushed in a multistorey car park in an earthquake
type: Earthquake damage under a special rider
story: A strong earthquake partly collapsed the mechanical multistorey car park where policyholder's Toyota Aqua was stored in Kanazawa, Ishikawa Prefecture. The car was crushed. Standard Japanese car insurance excludes earthquake damage, but her policy includes an earthquake, eruption and tsunami rider that pays a fixed amount for a total loss.
statement: The car park shook very badly and the frame of the tower collapsed onto the cars on the lower levels. Nobody was hurt because it was night. My car is flat on top. I am glad I added the earthquake rider when my agent suggested it.

accounts.text: Structural collapse of the lower levels of the mechanical parking tower during the earthquake. Fourteen vehicles affected. Vehicles to be removed by a specialist contractor once the structure is made safe.

whatHappened: The earthquake collapsed the lower levels of the mechanical parking tower onto the cars stored there, including hers.
damage: Car crushed, total loss.
evidence: Policy schedule showing the earthquake rider
missing: The contractor's date for removing the car from the collapsed tower
innocent: Mechanical parking towers are vulnerable in strong earthquakes, and fourteen cars were damaged in the same collapse
questions: Ask whether she needs help with transport in the meantime
steps: Pay the fixed total loss amount under the earthquake rider
Explain that the rider pays a set amount, which may be less than the full market value
assessment: Genuine. Without the rider, the standard policy would not pay. The rider's fixed payment should be made quickly, with a clear explanation of how it differs from a market value settlement.
action: Pay the fixed rider amount.
outcomes: Paid the fixed total loss amount of ¥500,000 under the rider

title: Robbed at gunpoint at a São Paulo junction
type: Armed robbery of a vehicle
story: Two men on a motorcycle robbed policyholder at gunpoint at a junction in Zona Sul, São Paulo, at about 20:15, taking her Hyundai HB20 and her phone. She filed a police report (boletim de ocorrência). The car has not been recovered after 30 days. Her policy pays according to the reference value table for the model.
statement: I stopped at the red light and they pulled up beside me. One pointed a gun at the window and told me to get out and leave the phone. I did everything they said. I went to the police station that night with my husband.

accounts.text: Robbery of a vehicle with a firearm. Victim removed from the vehicle, which was taken along with a mobile phone. Vehicle included in the stolen vehicles database. Not recovered.

whatHappened: Two men on a motorcycle robbed her at gunpoint at the lights and drove off in the car, which has not been found.
damage: Vehicle not recovered. Value under the reference table about R$68,000. Phone stolen.
missing: The vehicle transfer documents signed over to the insurer
innocent: Armed robberies at traffic lights are sadly common in São Paulo, and her account matches the police report
questions: Ask whether there is any finance on the car
Ask whether she needs support after the trauma
steps: Pay the agreed percentage of the reference table value after the waiting period
Collect the keys and transfer documents
Note that the phone is not covered by the car policy
assessment: Genuine. A violent robbery, with straightforward cover based on the reference table value once the vehicle is not recovered within the waiting period.
action: Settle at the reference table value.
outcomes: Paid 100% of the reference table value

title: A third-party certificate that the database has never seen
type: Collision with a driver holding a fake insurance certificate
story: Policyholder's Toyota Camry was hit on the side by a Honda Accord at a junction in Ikeja, Lagos. The Accord driver showed a third-party insurance certificate. A check on the Nigerian Insurance Industry Database shows no such policy; the certificate number does not exist and the named insurer has no record of it.
statement: The Accord came out of the side road and hit my door. The driver was apologetic and showed me his insurance paper, so I thought his insurer would pay. Now you tell me the paper is fake.

accounts.text: Certificate number not found. Vehicle registration has no active policy recorded. The insurer named on the certificate confirms it did not issue the document.

I bought the insurance from a man near the vehicle licensing office for ₦5,000. He said it is the same as the one from the company. I didn't know it was fake. I don't have money to pay for your customer's car.

whatHappened: The other driver caused the collision and was uninsured, having bought a fake certificate from a roadside vendor.
damage: Camry: driver's side doors, ₦1,850,000.
thirdParties: Mr Babatunde Adeyemi, driver of the Accord
The vendor who sold the fake certificate
missing: Police report of the collision
Details of the vendor
inconsistencies: The certificate shown at the scene does not exist in the database or with the named insurer
indicators: Fake third-party certificate bought from a roadside vendor
innocent: The Accord driver may genuinely not have known the certificate was fake
questions: Ask the Accord driver to describe the vendor and where he operates
steps: Pay the Camry repair under the policyholder's comprehensive cover
Pursue the Accord driver personally for recovery, possibly by instalments
Report the fake certificate to the police and the insurance regulator
assessment: The policyholder is covered by his own comprehensive policy. The fraud was committed by the vendor of the fake certificate; recovery from the uninsured driver will be difficult, but reporting the vendor protects others.
action: Pay the claim, seek recovery and report the fake certificate.
outcomes: Repaired under comprehensive; partial recovery from the driver
Vendor arrested in an enforcement operation

title: A boda boda, a matatu and a crowd that saw everything differently
type: Collision between a public service vehicle and a motorcycle taxi
story: An insured 14-seater matatu and a motorcycle taxi (boda boda) collided at a roundabout on Thika Road in Nairobi in the rain. The rider and his passenger were injured. A crowd gathered and blamed the matatu. The police abstract has not yet been issued. The rider's lawyer has written demanding compensation.
statement: Driver, Peter Mwangi: I was going round the roundabout slowly in the rain. The boda came from my left without stopping, carrying a passenger with no helmet, and hit the side of the matatu. The crowd attacked my vehicle and wanted to beat me. I drove to the police station for safety.

accounts.text: Our client was lawfully riding when the matatu, driven at high speed and without due care, knocked him down. He and his passenger suffered fractures. We demand compensation and the insurer's confirmation of cover within 14 days.

Report of an accident between a matatu and a motorcycle at the roundabout. Matatu driver reported to the station after a crowd gathered. Motorcycle rider and passenger taken to hospital. Investigation ongoing; abstract to be issued.

whatHappened: It is not clear who caused the collision. The driver and the rider give opposite accounts, the crowd was hostile, and there is no independent evidence yet.
damage: Rider: fractured leg. Passenger: fractured arm. Matatu: side panel and windows broken by the crowd.
thirdParties: The boda boda rider and his passenger
missing: The police abstract
Independent witnesses
CCTV from businesses near the roundabout
Passengers' statements from the matatu
inconsistencies: The driver says the boda entered without stopping; the lawyer says the matatu knocked the rider down at high speed
innocent: Crowds at accidents often blame the larger vehicle, and the driver fleeing to the police station was for his safety
questions: Ask the matatu passengers for their accounts
Ask the rider's lawyer for the medical records
steps: Collect statements from the matatu passengers, who are independent of both drivers
Obtain the police abstract and any CCTV
Reserve for the injury claims and decide liability once the evidence is gathered
Assess the crowd damage to the matatu under the own-damage cover if held
assessment: Insufficient evidence to decide liability. The matatu passengers are the best source of an independent account. Until then, the insurer should reserve and investigate rather than accept or deny.
action: Investigate before deciding; respond to the lawyer that the claim is under investigation.
outcomes: Passengers support the driver; liability apportioned against the rider
Liability shared; injury claims settled at a reduced amount

title: A flash flood in Shah Alam, and no special perils cover
type: Flood damage without the special perils extension
story: Policyholder's Perodua Myvi was submerged to the windows in a flash flood in Shah Alam, Selangor. His comprehensive policy does not include the special perils extension, which covers flood, storm and landslide. He bought the policy online and says he did not see the option.
statement: The water came up so fast, in one hour the whole taman was flooded. The car is full of water and mud. I have comprehensive insurance, I thought that means everything is covered. Now they say flood is not included?

accounts.text: Comprehensive private car policy. Extensions purchased: windscreen. Extension not purchased: special perils (flood, storm, landslide, earthquake). Online purchase journey shows the special perils option displayed with an extra premium of 0.5% of the sum insured.
Vehicle submerged to window level. Engine, electrical systems and interior damaged by flood water. Repair estimate RM 18,500.

whatHappened: A flash flood filled the neighbourhood within an hour and submerged the car to its windows. His policy does not include flood cover.
damage: Flood damage, RM 18,500.
missing: A record of how prominently the special perils option was shown at purchase
innocent: Many customers believe "comprehensive" includes floods
questions: Check how clearly the special perils option was shown at purchase
steps: Decline the claim because the special perils extension was not purchased
Explain clearly what comprehensive cover includes and excludes
Offer the extension at renewal and explain his right to complain if he believes the option was not shown fairly
assessment: Genuine loss but not covered: flood is excluded from standard comprehensive motor cover in Malaysia unless the special perils extension is bought. The decline must be clear and kind, and the sales journey should be checked for fairness.
action: Decline with a clear explanation and offer the extension for the future.
outcomes: Declined; customer adds special perils at renewal
Complaint to the financial ombudsman; decline upheld as the option was clearly shown

title: The cyclist ran the red, and the motorist still pays half
type: Car and cyclist collision under the Dutch vulnerable road user rule
story: Policyholder was driving through a green light in Utrecht when a 34-year-old cyclist rode through a red light in front of him. He braked but hit the cyclist, who broke her collarbone. Under article 185 of the Dutch Road Traffic Act, the motorist's insurer must pay at least 50% of an adult cyclist's damage unless the collision was due to force majeure.
statement: My light was green and I was doing about 40. She came from the right, looking at her phone, straight through her red. I braked hard but couldn't stop. I feel terrible, but I don't understand why my insurance has to pay when she ran the red.

accounts.text: I was waiting at the crossing on foot. The cyclist didn't stop at the red light and was looking down at her phone. The car had green and braked straight away.
Fracture of the right clavicle, treated conservatively. Off work for six weeks. Bicycle frame bent.

whatHappened: The cyclist rode through a red light while looking at her phone and the driver, on green, could not stop in time.
damage: Cyclist: fractured collarbone, six weeks off work, bicycle damaged. Car: bonnet and windscreen.
missing: The cyclist's loss of earnings figures
innocent: The cyclist's phone use explains the red light, and the driver's frustration at paying is understandable
questions: Ask the cyclist for her loss of earnings and costs
steps: Accept liability for 50% of the cyclist's damage under article 185: running a red light does not amount to force majeure for the driver
Pay the policyholder's own car damage only if he has comprehensive cover
Explain the rule to the policyholder: it protects cyclists and pedestrians even when they are at fault
assessment: Genuine. Dutch law protects vulnerable road users: even when an adult cyclist is mainly at fault, the motorist's insurer pays at least half unless the driver can show force majeure, which is very hard to prove.
action: Pay 50% of the cyclist's damage and explain the rule to the policyholder.
outcomes: Paid 50% of the cyclist's damage

title: A friendly accident report, and a black box that says the car was parked
type: Collision report signed by friends contradicted by telematics
story: Policyholder and the driver of a Fiat Panda signed a joint accident report saying the policyholder rear-ended the Panda in Naples at 18:30. The Panda's owner claims €4,800 under direct compensation. The policyholder's car has a black box installed for a premium discount, which shows it parked with the engine off from 17:10 to 21:40 that day.
statement: Yes, I hit him from behind, it was my fault. We signed the form together. He is a friend of a friend. I just want it closed.

accounts.text: Engine off and vehicle stationary at the policyholder's home address from 17:10 to 21:40. No acceleration events recorded during that period. Last trip before: 16:35 to 17:10, no impact events. Next trip at 21:40, no impact events.
Rear bumper and tailgate damage with dust and oxidation in the creases. No paint transfer matching the policyholder's car colour. Damage does not appear recent.

whatHappened: Very probably no collision took place. The joint report was signed to obtain payment for older damage on the Panda.
damage: Claimed €4,800 for the Panda's rear. Policyholder's car undamaged.
thirdParties: Owner of the Fiat Panda, a friend of a friend
evidence: Black box data showing the car parked
missing: Statements from both drivers taken separately
Phone location data
inconsistencies: The joint report places the policyholder's car in a collision at 18:30; the black box shows it parked with the engine off
The Panda damage is old and has no paint transfer
indicators: Joint report signed by acquaintances with an eager admission of fault
Telematics contradicting the collision
Old damage presented as new
innocent: A black box can fail, though it recorded the trips before and after normally
questions: Ask the policyholder whether he was driving another car that day
Ask the Panda owner how he knows the policyholder
steps: Reject the direct compensation claim with the telematics evidence
Report the suspected fraud to the anti-fraud archive and consider a criminal complaint
Review the policyholder's policy for cancellation
assessment: Potential fraud with strong evidence: the black box shows the policyholder's car parked at the time of the alleged collision, and the Panda damage is old. Italy's anti-fraud framework expects insurers to act on such evidence.
action: Reject the claim and report it.
outcomes: Claim withdrawn
Both drivers reported for insurance fraud

title: Swept away in the DANA floods, on a third-party-only policy
type: Flood total loss covered by the extraordinary risks scheme
story: Policyholder's Seat Ibiza was swept along a street and piled against other cars during catastrophic DANA flooding near Valencia. Her policy covers only compulsory third-party liability. She assumed nothing would be paid. In Spain, extraordinary risks such as floods are covered by the Consorcio de Compensación de Seguros for insured vehicles.
statement: The water came down the street like a river and took all the cars. Mine ended up on top of a van two streets away. I only have basic insurance, so I thought there was nothing to do. A neighbour told me about the Consorcio.

accounts.text: Area declared affected by the flooding. Damaged vehicles to be removed by municipal services to designated sites. Owners to keep proof of ownership and insurance.

accounts.who: Expert assessment for the Consorcio claim
accounts.text: Vehicle swept by flood water, mud throughout, structural damage from impact with other vehicles. Total loss. Market value at the time of the flood about €6,900.

whatHappened: Flood water swept the car two streets along and left it on top of a van, destroying it.
damage: Total loss, about €6,900.
evidence: Proof of a valid motor insurance policy
missing: Ownership documents, if they were lost in the flood
innocent: Believing a third-party-only policy pays nothing for flood damage is a common and understandable mistake
questions: Ask whether she needs help with the Consorcio application
steps: Help her claim from the Consorcio de Compensación de Seguros, which covers extraordinary risks for insured vehicles, including those with only third-party cover
Provide proof of the policy and support the expert assessment
assessment: Genuine. Although her own policy covers only third-party liability, the Consorcio pays for flood damage to insured vehicles, so the best service is to help her claim.
action: Guide her through the Consorcio claim.
outcomes: Consorcio pays the vehicle value

title: Assessed at €12,000 by the Injuries Resolution Board, and a handler who wants to reject it
type: Decision on a statutory injury assessment within the guidelines
story: Our policyholder rear-ended Ms Byrne's car in Galway. She suffered a neck injury and a wrist sprain. The Injuries Resolution Board assessed her claim at €12,000 under the Personal Injuries Guidelines, supported by a medical report. The handler wants to reject the assessment because "whiplash is overpaid". If the insurer rejects it, the Board will issue an authorisation and she can sue.
statement: (Through her solicitor) Our client has accepted the assessment. She has had physiotherapy for five months and still has symptoms in her wrist. If your client rejects it we will issue proceedings.

accounts.text: Neck soft-tissue injury, substantial recovery within six months. Wrist sprain with persisting symptoms at five months, prognosis for recovery within twelve months. No pre-existing problems.
General damages assessed under the Personal Injuries Guidelines for the dominant wrist injury with an uplift for the neck injury, plus special damages. Total €12,000. Claimant has accepted.

whatHappened: A genuine injury fairly assessed under the Guidelines. Rejecting it would mean litigation with higher costs and little prospect of a lower award.
damage: Neck soft-tissue injury and wrist sprain. Car damage settled separately.
missing: Any medical evidence the handler relies on for a lower figure
innocent: Handlers sometimes judge awards by pre-Guidelines experience
questions: Ask the handler what in the medical evidence supports a lower figure
steps: Check the assessment against the Guidelines brackets for the dominant injury and the medical prognosis
Accept within the time allowed if, as it appears, the assessment is within the Guidelines
Explain to the business that rejection leads to an authorisation, court proceedings and legal costs that will likely exceed any saving
Reject only with specific medical or factual grounds, recorded on file
assessment: Genuine and fairly assessed. Accepting the assessment is the sensible and fair outcome.
action: Accept the €12,000 assessment within the time allowed.
outcomes: Assessment accepted and paid
Rejected, then settled in court at €13,500 plus costs

title: Rear-ended in Christchurch, and she wants him to pay for her neck
type: Injury claim against the at-fault driver where ACC covers personal injury
story: Policyholder was rear-ended at lights in Christchurch. She has a neck injury and two weeks off work. She has asked her insurer to claim compensation for her injury and lost wages from the other driver, along with the repairs to her car. The other driver admitted fault and is insured.
statement: He was on his phone, he admitted it. My neck still hurts and I lost two weeks' pay. In Australia my cousin got money from the other driver's insurance for her injuries. Why can't I?

accounts.text: I looked down at my phone and went into the back of her car. My fault completely. My insurer's details are attached.
Neck sprain. Two weeks off work. ACC claim lodged by the GP on the day of the consultation.

whatHappened: A genuine not-at-fault collision. Her injury is covered by ACC, which bars suing for personal injury compensation; her car damage is claimed from the other driver's insurer.
damage: Her Corolla: rear bumper and boot, NZ$3,200. Neck sprain, two weeks off work.
thirdParties: The other driver and his insurer
evidence: GP note with the ACC claim
missing: ACC’s decision on weekly compensation
innocent: Rules in Australia are different, which is a common source of confusion
questions: Ask whether ACC has confirmed her weekly compensation
steps: Explain that ACC covers her injury, treatment and lost earnings on a no-fault basis, and that New Zealand law bars suing for compensation for a personal injury covered by ACC
Claim her car repairs and excess from the other driver’s insurer, or pay under her own policy and recover
Help her follow up the ACC weekly compensation
assessment: Genuine and not at fault. The injury goes through ACC; the property damage goes against the other driver's insurer.
action: Explain ACC, and recover her vehicle damage from the at-fault driver's insurer.
outcomes: ACC pays weekly compensation; car repaired and recovered
She accepts the explanation after a call

title: A pedestrian in Osaka, and the compulsory cover’s ¥1.2 million ceiling
type: Serious pedestrian injury exceeding the compulsory insurance limit
story: Our policyholder struck a 70-year-old pedestrian, Mr Sato, at a crossing in Osaka in the rain. He suffered a fractured hip and has been in hospital for six weeks. Medical costs so far are ¥3.4 million. The policyholder has both the compulsory automobile liability insurance and our voluntary insurance. The family has asked who will pay the hospital and whether they need a lawyer.
statement: (Mr Sato's daughter) My father was on the crossing with the green light. The hospital is asking us for payment. He may need care at home after this. We don't know which insurance pays what.

accounts.text: Pedestrian struck on a crossing while the pedestrian signal was green. Driver states rain on the windscreen reduced visibility. Driver at fault.
Hip fracture, surgery and six weeks of inpatient care. Costs to date ¥3,400,000. Rehabilitation expected for several months.

whatHappened: A serious pedestrian injury caused by our policyholder. The costs already exceed the compulsory insurance limit for injury, so the voluntary insurance must cover the rest.
damage: Fractured hip, surgery, long rehabilitation.
missing: A prognosis for long-term care needs
innocent: Rain on the windscreen at a crossing explains, but does not excuse, the driver not seeing him
questions: Ask the family about his care needs after discharge
steps: Offer one-stop handling: the voluntary insurer deals with the family and the hospital for the whole claim and recovers the compulsory portion from the compulsory insurer
Pay the hospital directly so the family is not asked for payment
Explain that the compulsory cover pays injury losses up to ¥1.2 million and the voluntary insurance pays above that
Assess consolation money and future care fairly, and tell the family they may consult a lawyer
assessment: Genuine and serious; the policyholder is at fault. The voluntary insurance carries most of the cost above the compulsory limit.
action: Take on one-stop handling, pay the hospital directly, and plan for care costs.
outcomes: Settled after rehabilitation including home care costs
Family instructs a lawyer; settled at court standards

title: A friendly report signed by both drivers, and no offer after six weeks
type: Direct compensation claim handled outside the statutory offer period
story: Policyholder was not at fault in a junction collision in Milan and claimed under the direct compensation system, which means her own insurer handles the claim. She submitted a joint accident report (CAI) signed by both drivers on 2 March, with photos and a repair estimate. On 15 April she had received no offer and no reasons. She has complained to the insurer and says she will go to the regulator.
statement: The other driver signed that it was his fault. I sent everything the same day. I've had no offer, no refusal, nothing. I've read that there are deadlines. My car has been parked for six weeks.

accounts.text: Signed by both drivers on 2 March. Vehicle B failed to give way at a junction and struck vehicle A. Vehicle B driver accepts responsibility.
Claim received with the signed CAI, photos and estimate on 2 March. Inspection done 10 March. No offer or reasoned refusal issued. Complaint received 15 April.

whatHappened: A straightforward not-at-fault claim with a CAI signed by both drivers, left without an offer past the statutory period.
damage: Her Fiat 500: front-right wing and bumper, estimate €2,300.
thirdParties: The other driver and his insurer
missing: Any reason recorded for the delay
innocent: Inspection backlogs after holidays can delay offers, but do not extend the legal period
questions: Check whether other direct compensation claims are overdue
steps: Make the offer now: under article 148 of the Code, the insurer must make a reasoned offer or refusal within 30 days where the CAI is signed by both drivers (60 days otherwise, 90 for injuries)
Pay interest for the delay and answer her complaint within the regulator’s time limit
Tell her she can complain to IVASS if she is not satisfied
Fix the cause of the delay
assessment: Genuine and overdue. The 30-day period for a jointly signed report has long passed.
action: Make the offer with interest, answer the complaint, and explain the IVASS route.
outcomes: Offer accepted within a week of the complaint
IVASS complaint leads to a sanction for repeated delays

title: A fourteen-year-old Ibiza worth €1,800 and a repair bill of €4,200
type: Third-party claim where repair costs far exceed the car’s market value
story: Our policyholder hit the side of Ms Ruiz's 14-year-old Seat Ibiza in Valencia. Liability is accepted. The repair estimate is €4,200. The car's market value (valor venal) is about €1,800. She insists on repair, saying the car is in excellent condition, has low mileage and she cannot find a replacement for that money. The handler has offered €1,800.
statement: I've looked after that car for fourteen years and it has 90,000 km. For €1,800 I'd get a wreck. I use it every day to take my mother to the hospital. It was his fault, why should I lose my car?

accounts.text: Market value of a comparable Seat Ibiza of this age: about €1,800. Vehicle in above-average condition, 90,000 km, full service history.
Two doors, B-pillar repair and paint: €4,200.

whatHappened: A genuine claim where repair costs more than twice the market value. Spanish practice usually pays market value plus an uplift for the owner's loss when repair is disproportionate, but the gap and the car's condition are argued.
damage: Seat Ibiza: two doors and B-pillar.
missing: Quotes for comparable cars in similar condition
innocent: Owners of well-kept older cars face real replacement difficulty
questions: Ask her for listings of comparable cars in similar condition
steps: Do not stop at the bare market value: offer the market value plus an uplift for the owner’s loss (valor de afección), as Spanish practice commonly allows where repair is disproportionate
Consider whether the repair is truly disproportionate given the car’s condition and her daily need; courts may allow repair where the cost is not excessive in context
Make a reasoned offer explaining the basis, and keep the option of paying for repair if the difference is modest
assessment: Genuine, with a real dispute about measure. €1,800 alone undercompensates her; a reasoned uplift or a negotiated repair is fairer.
action: Offer market value plus an afección uplift with reasons, and consider repair if the gap narrows.
outcomes: Settled at €2,700 including the uplift
Agreed to pay for repair after she finds no comparable car

title: Rear-ended on the Federal Highway, and his no-claim discount on the line
type: Own-damage knock-for-knock claim where the other insurer disputes liability
story: Policyholder was rear-ended in heavy rain on the Federal Highway in Kuala Lumpur. To get his car repaired quickly he claimed under his own policy through the knock-for-knock arrangement, which protects his no-claim discount when he is not at fault. The other driver's insurer now disputes liability, saying the policyholder braked suddenly for no reason. The policyholder's dashcam shows a motorcycle cutting in front of him.
statement: A motorcycle cut across in front of me in the rain and I had to brake. The car behind was too close. I made the police report the same evening. I chose the knock-for-knock claim so I wouldn't lose my 55% discount.

accounts.text: Motorcycle cuts across from the left lane without signalling about 15 metres ahead. Policyholder brakes firmly; the car stops. About 1.5 seconds later the rear impact occurs.
Our insured states your insured braked suddenly and without reason. We do not accept liability under the knock-for-knock arrangement.

whatHappened: A rear-end collision after the policyholder braked for a motorcyclist. A following driver should keep a safe distance, so liability rests mainly with the other driver.
damage: His Honda City: rear bumper, boot and tail lamps, RM 5,600.
thirdParties: The other driver and his insurer
missing: The other driver's police report
inconsistencies: The other driver says he braked for no reason; the dashcam shows a motorcycle cutting in
innocent: From behind, a driver may not see why the car in front braked
questions: Ask for the other driver's police report
steps: Repair the car under the knock-for-knock claim and keep his no-claim discount protected while liability is resolved
Send the dashcam footage to the other insurer: braking for a hazard does not shift fault from a driver who failed to keep a safe distance
Pursue recovery under the knock-for-knock arrangement and escalate through the industry dispute process if refused
assessment: Disputed only on a weak point. The footage shows a real hazard, and the following driver was too close.
action: Protect his discount, share the footage, and recover from the other insurer.
outcomes: Other insurer accepts after viewing the footage; discount protected
Resolved through the industry dispute process in his favour
